Marketing of Fruit.
Mr. HEALY: I beg to move:
That in the opinion of this House
the Marketing of Fruit Act should be
amended so as to allow the free flow
of Northern Ireland apples to Great
Britain as was the case prior to the
Act.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the hon. Member goes on I would like to point out
that any exhibits he brings into the
House will become the perquisites of the
Speaker.
Mr. HEALY: The Motion that I introduce in this House is not, unfortunately, a new one. I almost wish it were.
It is a grievance having no relation to
They
politics, and therefore rather unique in
this House. The persons concerned are
the potential supporters of the Government in that historic part of Northern
Ireland known as the Diamond.
ought not to need any introduction to
this House, the Prime Minister of which
is said to delight in a picture of the
Battle of the Boyne. The inhabitants
there are largely the descendants of the
men who established the Orange Order
about the year 1786. The fact that I am
voicing their grievance is due to the
reluctance of hon. Members on the
opposite side to put the Government in a
difficulty, or, as it is said, to embarrass
the Government. I hope that in the near
future hon. Members will do what their
conscience dictates rather than what the
Whip directs. Certainly there was not
much evidence of that yesterday on the
discussion on the Magistrates' Bill.
I
do not know of any people who talk so
much about civil and religious liberty and
who have less personal liberty than the
back benchers.
The apple growers of Armagh are not
coming before you in the guise of
beggars. They are simply asking you to
leave them alone, to keep your hands off
the industry that their forefathers and
themselves have established and for which
they created a market without any Government assistance or aid. They secured
their markets before the Government
existed and they have held them through
good seasons and bad seasons until the
Department of Agriculture came along
and by all these foolish restrictions closed
them down. When this matter was before this House in December, 1931, I
read several letters from wholesale agents
in Great Britain to the effect that they
were perfectly content with the quality of
the fruit consigned from Northern Ireland, and that neither they nor their
customers desired a change. The packing
and marketing were excellent and they
did not see why there should be any of
these irksome restrictions imposed by the
Government of Northern Ireland. Hon.
Members who are interested can read the
correspondence given in Hansard of '15th
December, 1931, from fruit buyers who
tell the Government frankly what they
want. They ask the Government to leave
the growers alone and let them supply
the markets they created themselves. An
Edinburgh firm put the whole matter in
a nutshell. They said:
Marketing of Fruit
Marketing of Fruit
13 DECEMBER 1934
The apples are graded and packed
as we want them, and we find the
growers only too ready to adopt any
suggestion that the salesmen think it
advisable to make. We feel the Act is
not in the interests of the fruit trade,
and particularly the growers.
That is from one of the largest firms on
the other side dealing in this commodity.
In the circumstances, what excuse can
there be for introducing restrictive legislation for which neither the buyers, the
growers, nor the consumers asked?
There are three categories or grades of
fruit mentioned in the Fruit Marketing
Act, "extra fancy," "fancy," and a
third class described as "C." In the
"extra fancy" class the fruit can bear no
blemish at all. It must be, in the words
of the regulation, "entirely free from
blemish." In the No. 2 grade, the
"fancy" class, the blemish must not exceed the size of a threepenny piece, while
in the third or "C" class the total skin
blemish must not exceed the size of a sixpence.
My contention is that it is not possible
for Northern Ireland to produce fruit,
particularly apples, as perfect as that.
Ninety-five per cent. of the growers
petitioned against this Bill in 1931, and
yet not a single member of the Ulster
Fruit Growers' Association, who spoke
for the 95 per cent., is represented on
the Advisory Committee. The other 5
per cent. of the fruit growers are represented on the Advisory Committee by
certain people nominated by the officials.
I may say that the Advisory Committee
is found to be a very convenient body
at times for the Department as they
adopt every suggestion put before them.
The whole fruit area of Northern Ireland is approximately 7,300 acres. The
Armagh growers account for 5,300 acres
of that area. The 1,454 growers who
signed the second petition against the Act
represented no fewer than 3,670 persons.
When the inspectors went to attend meetings in County Armagh three years
ago the police had to be called in
to render protection and to save them
from the fury of these peaceful,
law-abiding people. The police, as
matter of fact, have still to attend when
the inspectors are charged with the duty
of examining strawberries. They toss
them out upon the banks and sometimes
a
upon the roads. There is no necessity for
inspection of that type. All that it is
necessary to do is to remove one, two, or
three strawberries in the centre of the
basket to see whether topping is practised
or not.
""
The Prime Minister, whom I see
present, will recall a meeting that he
addressed in Newry shortly before the
introduction of the Marketing of Fruit
Act. It is not possible to reason with
a prophet; all one can do is to follow
the advice of a famous statesman to
"wait and see." The Prime Minister
prophesied, as Members of the Government have done on various other
occasions, a very rosy future for the
people for whom this Act was designed.
The small man who had two or three
barrels of apples would be in the same
position as the big man, because there
would be additional buyers. Relying
upon the accuracy of the Prime Minister's forecast, the Portadown Urban
Council, with a great deal more optimism
than I should have thought was justified,
opened a second market. They thought
the ordinary Saturday market would not
suffice. With what result?
It was no time until the extra market
had to be closed, for not only were there
not more buyers than before, but the
heavy restrictions imposed actually
drove away the few English buyers who
had been coming into the area, so that
instead of being in a better position they
were actually in a worse position in consequence of the fruit marketing legislation. It has indeed happened in Portadown that after apples have been
examined and passed for the home market
there was no demand, and they had to be
taken outside the town and dumped behind a ditch. All the time these restrictions have been drying up the export
trade the imports have been absolutely
free, and what can only be described as
windfalls from the Colonies and America
are flowing into Northern Ireland week
by week. They are subsidised by grants
of at least 1d per lb. Freights are lower
from Canada to Belfast than from
Armagh, Portadown, or Annaghmore to
the London market.

Let us see how this Act works.
November, 1931, just after the Act had
gone on the Statute Book, exports from
Northern Ireland were only 300 tons. In
the corresponding month for 1930 they

were 2,419 tons. That is what the Apple
Act did for the growers of Northern
Ireland. In 1931 the Government,
following a debate in this House, found
it necessary to give certain concessions.
I said that the third grade apples could
not have a greater blemish than what
would amount to the size of a sixpence.
The Government found it necessary in
1931 to allow apples with a greater
blemish to be exported. This concession
was not entirely without its drawbacks,
because the apples that had formerly
gone out of this country labelled as No. 1
or No. 2 grade, which found such a ready
market in Great Britain, had now to be
labelled as "imperfect."
Hon. Members can realise what their
feelings and thoughts would be if they
saw articles for human consumption
labelled "imperfect." At all events, it
would not give them a very high opinion
of their food value. Whilst the best
fruit, therefore, that Northern Ireland
could produce, which had hitherto sold
as first and second grade in the English
market, was going out with this blighting
description of "imperfect," the Government were actually permitting little
apples of two inches in diameter
out labelled "choice."
go
Outside
comic opera we could not find a parallel
for a situation of that kind, the best
apples Northern Ireland can produce
going out marked "imperfect" and the
others marked "choice."
to
I do not know how it can be explained,
but those are the facts. Unfortunately,
what would seem a comedy to the average
man becomes a tragedy for the farmers.
Their fruits are rotting in the orchards,
while the British buyers are willing and
desirous of purchasing. Between the
buyer and the seller the Government intervened and said, "You must not buy,
you must not sell." But even the slight
concession of allowing first and second
grade fruit to be marketed as "imperfect" has now been withdrawn, which
makes matters infinitely worse than they
were. There is no "imperfect" grade
now, so that the largest apples go out
under the designation of third grade or
culls. The best apples, such as I have in
my hand at the moment-
Mr. ELLIOTT: Pass them over here.

Mr. HEALY- -are not allowed to
leave Northern Ireland. Why? Because you observe here-
Mr. ELLIOTT: Pass them over here.
Mr. HEALY: I am quite sure they
would be acceptable over there, but they
are all right where they are at the
moment. The total blemish on this
apple is just larger than a sixpence, and
therefore it cannot leave Northern Ireland except it goes as a cull, and it must
be exported along with a little apple two
inches in diameter. No wonder hon.
Members look in surprise, but that is the
regulation of the Ministry. That is what
your officials have done. That is the
plight they have landed you into.
Then there is such a thing as a percentage of error. If there is more than
a 5 per cent. margin of error, though
some of the marks may be caused by the
brushing of leaves when the apples are
young, the whole consignment is condemned. In Canada and the United
States, which have had a longer experience of grading and exporting apples
than you have, 15 per cent. is allowed,
three times the percentage here. I do
not know what justification the Minister
of Agriculture is going to offer for that.
I think it would take a great deal of
explaining away.
I want now to give you a few figures
concerning this matter. From October,
1932, to April, 1933, the exports to Great
Britain from Belfast were 6,162 tons.
That was when the slight concession of
an "imperfect" grade was in operation.
In the same period in 1933-1934, when the
concession was withdrawn, instead of the
exports amounting to 6,162 tons they
amounted only to 2,137 tons. And remember that in 1932 there was, in
addition, the export to the Irish Free
State, which is entirely closed now.
give again the figures for the nine months
ending September, 1933. During that
period there were 3,806 tons, and for the
nine months ending this year the apple
industry has collapsed to such an extent
that there were only 908 tons exported.
If we go back to 1921, before this House
was set up or before this Government
came into existence, we find that the exports from Belfast only in that year were
4,215 tons of apples. In addition, there
were large consignments from Greenore,

Let me give the House another figure
with regard to licences. The number of
people who took out licences to export
apples in 1932 was 53; for 1933 the
number had gone down to 28; and in
1934 I believe there is a still further fall.
Is it any wonder, therefore, that the
farmers are in desperation and asking for
the repeal of the Act or, at all events, its
immediate amendment. Is it any wonder
that the inspectors, who know the feeling
of the country far better than the officials
of the Ministry, refuse to go to a meeting
in any apple growing district unless they
are provided with police protection?
I said that the Ministry for a short
period gave certain concessions. When
the Advisory Committee pressed for concessions there was a meeting held on the
6th September, 1933. Seeing no prospect
except that of allowing the apples to rot
in the orchards, the Government gave
way and allowed them to export these
apples, as I have explained, as imperfects
as well as the two-inch ones. But on the
4th October the Department of Agriculture were actually issuing instructions as
if no concessions at all had been given.
In the meantime the members of the
Advisory Committee had been exporting
themselves, and the first intimation that
the growers in Armagh had that the
apples were being allowed to go out was
when they received some communication
from the London dealers. In other words
the Department were allowing certain
favoured people to send out apples while
the majority of the growers were not
aware of the concession at all. This
instruction to me has a very unpleasant
odour. The Department evidently got
into a bit of a panic, because it was then
announced that a permit to export might
The home market here is very limited
and very restricted. It may be said that
Belfast offers a very good market and that
a certain industry established, or subsidised by the Northern Government
offers an outlet for the farmers. At this
moment I believe the price for a good
quality apple in a certain canning
industry in Northern Ireland is 1s. 6d.
per barrel. Imagine a man gathering
good fruit, grading, barrelling, and bringing it to the canning factory, and then
receiving the sum of 1s. 6d. for each
barrel of apples.
It may be said that conditions in the
English markets are not very good at the
moment. The Minister may argue that,
but I would point out to him that the
scare story of apples rotting in the
English orchards only refers to apples
used for cider making. The cider making
people have found a substitute for that
apple, and you do not find any apples
corresponding to what are firsts and
seconds in Northern Ireland rotting in
the orchards of England. The prices for
those apples in the English market are
still of a satisfactory character, if they
could get there.
The Government are attempting the
impossible in endeavouring to produce
apples entirely free from blemish, and the
sooner they realise that the better. In
this they are not walking step by step
with the English Ministry of Agriculture.
There is a milder climate in England, and
the storms that trouble apple growers in
this country at certain times of the year
are not quite so bad there. And there is
no compulsory grading in England. I
believe the idea of the Ministry when they
introduced this Act as a Bill was that in
a short time England would introduce
compulsory grading. But the English
people do not like compulsion. They will
not have compulsion either in relation to
apples or any other Department of the
Ministry of Agriculture. All that
happens in the case of these apples is that
in the early spring the leaves sway about
and mark the apples. It does not detract
in the least from their food value, and
the English people, who have been buying
these for the last fifty years, know that

as of any importance whatever.

The Minister must realise that even he
himself, with his considerable experience,
cannot produce perfect apples. Recently
an exhibition was held in Belfast at which
the Minister was one of the exhibitors.
I believe there were two lots of apples
exhibited there from the Minister's own
garden, "Worcester Permains," and
Peasgood Nonsuch," and I am sure
they were the very best he could produce.
They were described to me by a very
large grower and a very keen authority
as being spangled with black scab
like the firmament on a starry night.
The plate of "Peasgood Nonsuch
had at least one apple with a
blemish the size of a shilling. Neither of
those collections, I am told, would pass
for even C grade if tested by the standards
of his own officials. How, therefore,
would the Minister make his living, if he
had to, by sending those apples out of this
country as the people who live in Armagh
have to do?
""
The British people would not stand for
one hour the restrictions that are being
heaped upon the growers of Northern Ireland. The last step taken by
by the
inspectors suggests to me that one of the
officials from the museum of antiquities
must have strolled into the Department
and forgotten to return. The well-known
bushel measure, which you observe here,
the bushel measure which is well known
all over Great Britain and in this country,
is going to be replaced by what? By a
creel. The creel is a very old Irish
institution, but it is used for a very
different object. The peculiarity about it
is that the Ministry specify that the new
creel is to be 24 inches in depth, 14 at
the top, and 10 at the bottom. You can
imagine the difficulty of handling a conveyance of that kind and also the amount
of space that will be wasted where these
things are piled one on top of the
other in a railway waggon or a motor
lorry. You will see the serious difficulty
that is going to arise. And are the
people going to have to scrap all their
stocks of these baskets that they have been
accumulating over a long period?
I now come to the question of the
Advisory Committee. I say that the
Advisory Committee is entirely unrepresentative of the growers. The Fruit
Growers' Defence Association embraces
95 per cent. of the real growers and
shippers, and they are left without a
single representative on
the Advisory
Committee while the other five per cent.
get all the places. Some time ago the
Advisory Committee objected to the
stringent conditions under which E.F.,
which are the initials for the extra fancy
or No. 1 grade apple, was exported. The
condition was that it
"must be entirely free from blemish."
There was a long discussion at the
Advisory Committee, and in the end Dr.
Gordon agreed that the Ministry would
revise this restriction. When the condition was revised the word "entirely" was
omitted, and it then read:
"must be free from blemish.”
And when the Advisory Committee went
home thinking they had got some concession they found they were in exactly the
same position. It simply meant that Dr.
Gordon pulled the wool over their eyes,
and I think that indicates the mentality
of the Advisory Committee. I suggest
that the Minister should be prepared to
rise above petty vanities and the hurt
feelings of officials and carry out the duty
which at this moment stares them in the
face. The people who know the needs of
the industry are the only ones whose
advice is worth anything or should be
accepted. I hope he will go into the
matter again and see if he will take one
or two nominees from the Association.
Instead of the Ministry's inspectors
going about the country and interfering
in something for which they have no
practical experience, teaching people who
have spent 25 years, and some of them
a longer period in the industry, what
they should do-instead of doing that I
suggest a far more profitable way of
utilising them would be testing the sprays
supplied to growers all over the country,

Britain during the years 1929 to 1931

Marketing of Fruit
13 DECEMBER 1934
possible to include the present year's
shipments, because the present shipping
year is not yet finished. The contention
that the Government's action has reduced
the export of apples is quite wrong. It is
obviously wrong. It is very unfortunate
that during the present season shipments
to Great Britain show a considerable
decrease, but this is entirely through
natural causes and not through any cause
of the working of the Act. It is sad that
in this country-unfortunately it is perfectly true that hundreds of tons of
apples are lying rotting under the trees.
The same condition exists in England.
What the producers of apples are suffering from in this country is an abundance
of apples and not from an Act which is
calculated to benefit them.
During October, 1933, over 70,000
tons of apples were imported into Great
Britain from foreign countries, but
during October, 1934, only 33,000 tons
were imported. Correspondingly, shipments from Northern Ireland to Great
Britain during October, 1930, were about
900 tons, while in October, 1934, they
were only about 400 tons. The hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Healy) will notice that
the ratio as between Northern Ireland
and other exporters is about equal. I
admit that the prices which our apples
have been able to receive on the British
market this season have been very small,
but they have been well up to the
average realised by any other apples on
the British market. Opponents of the
Act assert that owing to Government
interference they have been unable to
sell apples on the English market. I now
propose to give a series of simple figures,
which I think will finally establish my
case.
In 1933, which was a year of average
prices, out of 618 consignments two were
rejected by the inspectors, that is to say
.3 per cent. In 1934, out of 545 consignments three were rejected, that is .5
per cent. It is difficult to find here any
justification for the accusation that the
inspectors have acted harshly under the
Act or that the Act is unfair to any great
extent to the trade. In 1933 there were
881 tons of graded apples passed through
the fruit examination station. In 1934
there were 767 tons. That is to say, that
in spite of this alleged interference committed under the Act the trade in graded
apples is only 13 per cent. less than it
was in the previous year.
Mr. HEALY: Do not the figures apply
only to Nos. 1 and 2 grades?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Gentleman
might ask one of his colleagues to make
this point for him when the Minister
has finished.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The hon.
Gentleman, I think, challenged a statement of an hon. Member for one of the
Armagh constituencies. The figure of
50 per cent. does apply to the two higher
grades. The point I wish to make is
that grading at the very most affected
the trade by 13 per cent. I should like
to refute the claim that ungraded apples
would have found their way into the
British market-into a paradise. In
1933 some 362 tons of ungraded apples
passed through the examination station,
and in 1934 only 20 tons passed through
it. There was no demand for ungraded
apples. Therefore, Government interference, which the hon. Gentleman objects
to, is interference to the extent of 13
per cent. I do not admit that Government interference has done it. The real
reason for the bad year and lack of shipments is the over-abundance of apples on
the other side. In any case, there is a
definite figure. Perhaps I took up the
hon. Gentleman wrongly, but I know that
a certain number of people say we should
carry out the laissez faire policy and
have no supervision over any apples sent

The PRIME MINISTER- -by not
indicating assent to the proposition just
put forward, I would, after consulting
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Agriculture, like to say that everybody
in the House is desirous of a success being
made of every undertaking for the good
of the people of Ulster. I am quite sure
that hon. Members opposite are
anxious as I am that prosperity should
follow this great industry of apple growing, just as they are anxious to see other
branches of agriculture and our shipbuilding prospering to the fullest possible
extent. The Acts of Parliament that
have been introduced, chiefly by my right
hon. Friend behind me, for the purpose
of helping the primary industry of Ulster,
that is agriculture, have all aimed at
holding our own in the great British
market.
I believe I am right in saying that if
it had not been for the Act passed in connection with apple growing there would
have been no sale in England for our
apples. That is my deliberate opinion,
because, as each year passes, the competition for really first-class graded
apples, potatoes, and other commodities
is so much intensified that if Ulster does
not keep in step in that direction, or
slightly ahead, we would be put out of
the market. We have no other place to
turn, because the consumption in Ulster
itself cannot meet the production that
might result if more went in for apple
cultivation.
We are most anxious that peace and
harmony should prevail in all these
industrial areas. Unfortunately, any endeavours that my right hon. Friend's predecessor made when we met the leaders
and agitators against the Act were quite
futile. The circulars they have distributed, the publications they have sent to
the Press, and their communications with
myself were all directed against doing
anything to help. There was nothing
helpful in the suggestions made. Their
proposal was to scrap everything: to
scrap even the Government, and scrap
so-and-so. That does not lead anywhere.
I will go so far as to say that my right
hon. Friend and I are as patient
individuals as you will find in Ulster, and
now, when it is getting near the Christmas season, when there should be a spirit
of peace and goodwill to all men, if these
gentlemen will come along and meet my
right hon. Friend and me at any time,
we will be only too delighted to go into
the matter most meticulously and try to
get them to meet us as far as possible in
any arrangement that might be made to
help the industry in which we are all just
as interested as they are.
Before I sit down I would like to make
a remark, but only a remark, because the
subject is inapplicable at the present time,
with regard to the fishing on Lough
Neagh. I look upon the fishing on Lough
Neagh and the apple industry as being
two gold mines if all concerned would
only come together and make up their
minds to make them a success. Then
they might be almost two primary
industries instead of being secondary
industries as they are at the present time.
I throw out the suggestion to hon. Members opposite, who, I know, are as
interested in the industry as are any of
us on this side. I would like to say also

this business whatever. I know nothing
about the politics of the fishermen or the

The late Mr. Hugh T. Barrie, whom
the Prime Minister knew well, was vicepresident of the Department of Agriculture when they applied the Potato Act.
After a month's experience they found it
was unworkable and that it retarded
trade. They practically lost the British
market. Mr. Hugh T. Barrie, as a

heard the views of both sides, he unreservedly withdrew the Act and allowed
free trade again.

merchants, and others freely to export

the highest price possible in the British
market.

likely to set up this committee than to
bring in legislation. I would not by any
means feel inclined to retard or restrict
the Government if I thought they were
sincere, but from my experience in this
House I realise that the only time the
Government take into consideration
public opinion is a few short months before election time, but from one election
to another, with the exception of those
few months, the Government goes its own
way.
I think they will be compelled to take
heed to the voices which will be raised
in this House in favour of this Motion.
They may put it off from to-day until
to-morrow, but at no far distant date
they will have to take up this question
and provide a solution to the present
difficulty in industry and out of industry. As I previously stated for one
end of the question, I put the solution
to the Government through the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education. Here is a solution to the

other end, pensions at 60 at an increased

he

give the same answer.
Mr. GORDON: Then you agree?

Adjournment.
SEARCH OF LICENSED PREMISES
AT CLOGHER.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Wilson Hungerford).
Mr. ELLIOTT rose.
Mr. SPEAKER: Before the hon.
Member for South Tyrone speaks, the hon.
Member for Pottinger wishes to ask
about the business.
Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to ask the
Acting Prime Minister what business he
intends to take next week.
Mr. ANDREWS: This debate will be
resumed.
Mr. ELLIOTT: In accordance with
notice which I gave earlier in this day's
proceedings, I wish to bring before the
House an incident which took place in
my constituency in South Tyrone some
time ago and which I think requires
some redress. The aggrieved person in
this case is Michael Connolly, a resident
in the town of Clogher. He is a Roman
Catholic and also a spirit merchant. I
cannot do better in putting his case before
the Government and this House than to
read a copy of a letter which he himself
sent to the County Inspector of Police of
that county. The letter says:
Sir.
I am the owner of licensed premises
in the town of Clogher, and on
Saturday last, 13th inst., about 12 midnight, when retiring to bed I heard a
knock at my front door. On inquiring through an upstairs window who
was there, I was told, "Police on
duty." I came down at once and
admitted Head-Constable Cowan. He
pushed the door of the bar, which was
locked, and I asked if he wanted to see
in, and he said "Yes."
He searched the bar, a snug at the
rear, scullery and examined the yard
with a flashlight. He then returned
through the bar, examined the kitchen,
pantry, cupboard under the stairs and
front sitting-room.
He then inquired if there was anyone upstairs, and I replied, "Only my
wife and family." Apparently he was
not satisfied with my assurance and
proceeded upstairs, entering, without
knocking, the bedroom of my motherin law, a woman over 70 years of age
in very
delicate health. He then
searched the wardrobe on the landing,
then the upstairs sitting-room, and
the children's bedroom at back. He
then returned to the landing and
entered my wife's bedroom while she
was feeding her seven-months'-old
baby. He then came downstairs and
said, "Everything appears to be
regular," and departed without any
apology for what I consider an
warrantable and officious intrusion on
the privacy of my wife and family.
un-
I desire to make it clear that I do
not object in any way to the police
authorities carrying out their sometimes unpleasant duties, but I think
there was no justification for his
search of my bedroom when my
children were asleep, or could Head-
Constable Cowan have had any suspicion of any breach of the licensing
laws being committed. Had he used
ordinary intelligence he would have
seen by my half-dressed condition-I
was wearing shirt, pants and slippers.
without socks-that there could be no
one on the premises.
Even a publican should have some
rights to privacy in his own home, and
I protest very strongly against the
conduct of the Head-Constable on this
occasion.
Unless I receive an assurance that
similar conduct, without reasonable
justification, will not be repeated, I
shall with much reluctance, be compelled to have the matter raised in
Parliament.
I am,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Michael Connolly.
One would have thought when this
aggrieved publican from Clogher wrote
such a letter to the County Inspector of
Police in Omagh, the County Inspector
would have at least come to Clogher,
called upon this aggrieved person, and
made some inquiries from him. The
reply which he sent reads:
Sir,
I have to acknowledge receipt of
your letter of 18th inst. conveying a
complaint as to the action of Head-
Constable Cowan during a search of
your licensed premises on the night of
13th inst. I have made inquiry into
the circumstances but am unable to
discover that the Head-Constable acted
L
Search of Licensed Premises 644
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
improperly or exceeded his duty. I
regret that you should have been in
any way inconvenienced.
I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
R. K. Spears,
County Inspector.
One would be quite interested to know
from whom the County Inspector made
his inquiry. I have no doubt he made
it from the Head-Constable who carried
out this unwarranted raid, and he could
not expect that the Head-Constable who
carried out the raid would admit for a
moment that he did anything out of
order. He never went to Mr. Connolly.
He never went to Mr. Connolly's house,
and never asked Mr. Connolly, or his
wife, or mother-in-law, or any member
of the household to contradict or endorse
any statement made in that letter.. He
made no inquiries at all, unless onesided inquiries from the Head-Constable
who carried out the raid.
Mr. Connolly is a citizen of the town
of Clogher. He is an ex-member of the
Royal Irish Constabulary. He knows
well what the duties of the Constabulary
are, and he has stated very clearly in
his letter to the County Inspector that
he does not object to reasonable inspection
at any time, day or night, by the police
authorities of his licensed premises. If
it is going out from this House and from
this Government that any publican-and
I think everyone in this House well
knows that I do not hold any brief for
publicans, but I represent every one of
my constituents in South Tyrone irrespective of religion and irrespective of
profession and I intend to do my duty
by every constituent in that area
fairly as I possibly can.
as
Here is a man of good character. He
owns this public-house in Clogher and
at the hour of midnight, when his wife
and mother-in-law and family of eight
are all in bed and he himself is retiring
to rest for the night, the police come
and knock at his door for admission.
Connolly did not say, "You are not
going to get in." He immediately went
downstairs and opened the door and said,
"Do you want in." The Head-
Constable said, "Yes." He came in,
examined the bar, and everything was in
perfect order. He examined the downstairs apartments, and again everything
was in perfect order. He was still not
satisfied, and having a flashlight he
went into the yard and examined it
meticulously from one end to the other.
Still he thought, or must have thought,
that this publican had some person concealed on his premises, and he proceeded
upstairs.
The first room he went into was the
room where the publican's own motherin-law of seventy years of age was lying
in bed. He goes into her bedroom at
midnight to find if she has someone concealed on the premises. Then he goes to
the room where the little children are
asleep. Those of us in this House with
families of our own know what it means
for anyone to intrude at midnight in a
bedroom where little children are asleep,
but here we have a Head-Constable,
cloaked and clothed in all the authority
and uniform of the police entering this
room where little children are asleep at
midnight. He is not satisfied even with
that, but goes to the man's own bedroom, as if even the publican would have
some man concealed in his own bedroom
where his own wife is lying in bed with
a little child. He searches that bedroom and again finds no person concealed there.
I have always stood for fair play, and
I will stand for fair play for a publican.
I consider this man has been scandalously
treated; that the privacy of his apartments has been deliberately outraged by
this Head-Constable being either overzealous or carrying out his duty in a way
that is most reprehensible. I could not
help thinking that Head-Constable
Cowan has been impelled perhaps to
carry out this raid from some outside
official source.

APPEALS FROM PUBLIC

1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if applicants who appeal against decisions of the
Public Assistance Board will be allowed
to have a representative to state their
case before the Appeal Court.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Statutory Rules made by
the Unemployment Assistance Board permit a claimant appearing before
Appeals Tribunal to be accompanied by

the facts of his case.
PUBLIC ASSISTANCE APPEAL
COURTS.
an
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the
names, addresses, occupations, and qualifications of the members of the Belfast
Appeal Court established under the
Public Assistance Board to adjudicate on
questions of appeal; the names and qualifications of the chairmen of these courts;
and the fees paid for each sitting to the
chairmen and other members of the
court.
The following question also stood in the
name of Mr. Beattie :-3. To ask the
Minister of Labour whether he can state
the name and address of each member of
the Appeal Courts of the eight area districts outside of Belfast and the amount
of the fees paid for each sitting of the
court.
Mr. ANDREWS: With the hon. Member's permission, I propose to answer this
question and the next one together.
Including 25 chairmen, who act also
for courts of referees and pensions courts,
there are 507 persons serving on the Unemployment Assistance Tribunals. I do
not think the hon. Member will desire
that I should have a complete list printed
of their names, addresses, occupations,
and qualifications.
For the information of the hon. Member, however, I desire to state that the
workers' panel is composed of 343 members, of whom 304 have already, for a
considerable time, served also on the court
of referees' panel, and that the Assistance Board's panel numbers 139 persons.

and chairmen receive travelling expenses

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask

Unemployment Insurance Acts have been

under the Public Assistance Board, and

with the past practice of the right hon.
Gentleman's Department.
Mr. ANDREWS: I would like notice
of that question, because I really did not

Rent (Restrictions) Amendment Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. BYRNE: In proposing the Second
Reading of this Rent Restriction Bill
to-day, I would ask the House to leave
out political differences and political
opinions, and although this Measure is
coming from this side of the House I
hope they will give it fair and due consideration. I hope also when I have done
I shall have satisfied the House that such
a Bill is necessary.
From the war years until now the rents
of workers' houses have been increased by
from 30 to 40 per cent., while rents of
shops and business premises have also
been increased by unreasonable amounts.
The rents of new houses and shops and
business premises are likewise unreasonable and have secured for classes of
property owners unreasonably high
profits for their investments in both old
and new properties. The high profits
from property rents cannot be compared
with those secured in industry and they
must be brought down to the level of
returns from industry. That is the
object of this Rent Bill.
The Bill proposes pre-war rents for old
property and to equalise the rents for
new property with the old where equal
accommodation is provided. It proposes
to set up fair rents courts to adjust
rents on the basis of justice for all concerned. Every section of the Bill, if and
when law, seeks to obtain simple justice.
from landlords for their tenants. For
that reason Members of Parliament
should regard this Bill as worthy of their
earnest and active support on the occasion
of this its Second Reading. Any Amendments they wish to submit for consideration on the Committee stage will receive
sympathetic hearing and every endeavour
will be made by the promoters and supporters of the Bill to meet the view of
those who desire amendment of its provisions.
What effect would this Bill have in connection with revaluation? Appeals
against revaluation must be in, the Press
say, by 3rd June. If the Bill is law
before then its effects will be known to
those making such appeals and their
course of action in that connection would
be clear. If Parliament rejects this Bill
all rents will soar with a resulting flood
of indignation from Ulster's tenants
which this Parliament cannot withstand.
Nor will Parliament be able to free itself
from public contempt for having failed
to avail of the magnificent opportunity
which this Measure presents to safeguard
the interests of Ulster's tenants of every
class and also Ulster's industries, in so far
as these interests are affected by the
question of rents. If Parliament passes
this Second Reading they will make a
gesture of understanding of their duty to
those they represent, to the tenants who
live by our industries, and to the industrialists whose business, built up by a lifetime of hard work, the rejection of this
Bill will destroy. Let Parliament, therefore, beware that the eyes of every
Ulsterman is upon them, watching
breathlessly for the decision which means
their bread and butter. Let Parliament
show that they know that their first duty
is the good of Ulster's people.
Parliament show that they are loyal to
none but their own people and their own
people's industries, and let Parliament
show that they will vote for Ulster's
people and prosperity, and pass the
Second Reading of this Bill.
Let
This Measure, I think, is overdue. The
neighbouring Parliaments in England
and the Irish Free State have passed
Acts with regard to landlord and tenant.
In 1927 the Imperial Parliament passed
an
Act which granted power to the
county courts of England and Wales as
follows:-1, To award compensation to a
tenant for any improvement on his holding which adds to the letting value of the
holding; 2, if the lease is renewed the
court can fix the rent payable by the
tenant, irrespective of the value attributable to the improvement in respect of
which compensation would have been payable; 3, if the tenant proves that, by
reason of the carrying on of a business
for a period of not less than five years,
goodwill has become attached to the
premises whereby the premises could let
at a higher rent than they would in the
absence of such goodwill, he may be
awarded compensation for such goodwill;
4, the court may grant a new lease for a
term not exceeding 14 years where the
693 Rent Restrictions Bill-

12 MARCH 1935
Second Reading
tenant alleges that the amount of compensation which could be allotted to him
under the Act would not compensate him
for the loss of goodwill he would suffer
if he is compelled to remove to other
premises; 5, in certain well defined
circumstances the landlord may be given
possession of the premises, notwithstanding the proved claims of the tenant.
This Act became law on 22nd
December, 1927, or nearly eight years
ago, and during that period tenants in
Northern Ireland have been at the mercy
of their landlords, although English
tenants were protected. Many cases are
well known where terms for new leases
could only be described as harsh, and
also cases where the goodwill created by
the tenant has been used as a lever to
extort an increased rent. There has been
other legislation in this matter. In 1931
a Landlord and Tenant Act was passed
in the Irish Free State even more farreaching than the English Act. It provides that improvements were to be paid
for by the landlord. It enacts that on
the termination of his tenancy the tenant
shall, subject to certain reasonable restrictions, be entitled to a new tenancy on
terms to be agreed upon between him
and the landlord, or in default of such
agreement on terms to be fixed by the
court. Where the landlord requires the
premises for rebuilding or estate scheming
the tenant is entitled to compensation for
disturbance.
Notwthstanding the example shown by
the two neighbouring Governments, the
Government of Northern Ireland have
hedged and shirked. In 1931 they said
they had the Measure under consideration. In 1932 they put the Bill on the
list for that Session. At the same time a
deputation was received by the Parliamentary Secretary of the Home Ministry
to discuss the terms of the new Bill.
Nothing more was heard of the matter
and on a question being asked in the
House of Commons on several occasions
the questioner was referred to previous
answers which, as I have said, stated that
the Government had the Bill under
consideration.
I will now submit a few grievances
I have noted here with regard to landlords and tenants. The first I would like
to mention is that of Mr. David Bowen,
Grosvenor Road. He bought in 1917 the
residue of a lease granted in 1911 at a
On
rent of £70 for a term of 20 years.
expiry of the lease in 1931 the lessors
demanded a rent of £200, and finally
Mr. Bowen had to pay £150 rent. That
could not occur in England or the Free
State. Here is another example John
Murray, Peter's Hill, was the leaseholder
of the public house and the adjoining
house at a rent of £122 10s. On expiry of
the lease Murray offered £100 rent for
the public house alone. This offer was
declined by the landlord, and so he left.
James W. Gyle, Madrid Street, on the
expiration of his lease was offered a new
lease at terms which were equivalent to a
price of £7,000, so he gave up possession.
Afterwards a tenant was given the
premises at one third of what Mr. Gyle
was asked to pay. John Mooney, Upper
Library Street, paid £675 for the lease
in 1928. The lease expired in 1930 and
he offered a fair rent of £70 which was
refused. He left the premises. Mr.
McNiff, Divis Street, paid £815 for
possession in 1924. The property was in
Chancery and was acquired by a solicitor.
McNiff's rent was £50 when he bought,
but the new owner asked for £90 rent
and a fine of £100. I think that should
convince the House that there is great
need for legislation in the direction I have
mentioned.
There is one other thing I would like
to refer to; and that is those who live
in houses which became decontrolled in
the years 1925 and 1932. You are aware
that houses between £8 and £26 valuation became decontrolled in 1925 and that
continued until 1932 when this Government passed an Act bringing back those
houses under control. Now there are
thousands of tenants who are forced to
occupy houses which became decontrolled,
and the landlords when they got
possession of the houses could charge
whatever rent they wished, and they took
advantage of that. Those of us who were
on the Select Committee know very well
that up to 100 per cent. increased rents
were charged by the agents and landlords.
at that time.
I would like to give the Government an
example. Take three houses in one street.
A remains in his house the rent of which
is 10s. a week. B after 1925 gives up
possession of his house, and the landlord
could charge whatever he liked. The
incoming tenant paid up to £1 a week for
that 10s. house. C in 1932 left his house,
Rent Restrictions Bill-

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Byrne]
and after that the landlord or agent
could not raise the rent at all. Therefore, you see that these people are
suffering and they are paying to-day 100
per cent. more than they should pay.
The idea is that the Government if they
do not accept the Bill should set up what
is called a fair rent court. I know the
Members of the Government have said
that such and such a court would not be
right at all, that it would be a loss of
time and all that sort of thing. I think
there are Members here who will
remember when the land courts were set
up.
At those courts the tenants and
landlords would bring in representatives
and fair rents were fixed. I remember
'well that in one townland if a tenant
entered the court and got a reduction of
25 per cent., that governed the whole
locality. It settled the rent in regard to
every tenant. In 1932 the Government
passed a splendid Act which put an end
to the hire purchase system.
All we want to see is a rent court which
I will settle a fair and reasonable rent for
the houses. If a man lives in a house let
at 10s a week and his neighbour is in a
similar house at £1 a week, is that
justice? I say that the Government
should take this matter up and not allow
this state of affairs to continue. With
regard to the establishment of a rents
court, I may say I was a member of the
Select Committee that was set up. On
one occasion when Mr. McConnell was
giving evidence before that Select Committee I asked this question:-
"What is your opinion with regard
to the establishment of a fair rents
court?"
This is what Mr. McConnell said:-
:-
"I would be in favour of a fair rents
court. I was born and reared in the
country in County Antrim, and I am
very fond of my own county. I remember when I was a young lad in
1881 and 1883 the tenants were very
hard pushed, and under the Gladstone
administration a fair rents court was
set up. That was the salvation of the
farmers. They got a fair rent fixed by
having a valuer from each side, who
went into the question of the value of
the land and buildings and the amount
of money invested in the property. As
a result a just rent was fixed, and that
saved the farmers of that day."
A resolution was adopted by this
Select Committee in regard to houses
between £8 and £26, but before I read
that resolution I shall give some instances
of houses which became decontrolled and
of which the agent or landlord got
possession. 290 Springfield Road, rent

quarterly, raised to £11 5s and rates.
137 Alexander Park Avenue, £26 and
rates yearly, to £40 and rates. 27
Mountcollyer Avenue, £2 7s 9d to £3 15s
monthly. 148 North Queen Street, from
12s 6d to 30s weekly. 23 St. Aubyn's
Street, from 36s monthly to £2 10s 4d
monthly. 40 Glentane Street, from £26
and rates to £45 and rates yearly. 227
and 233 Newtownards Road, from £45
and rates to £70 and rates yearly. 26/28
Mileriver Street, from 7s 9d to
weekly. 29 Upton Street, from 8s 9d
weekly to 15s weekly. 53 Dromore
Street, Cregagh, from £21 yearly to £30
yearly. I have had hundreds of cases
before me since I took an interest in this
matter of high rents.

passed by this House.
But, after all, it makes a very great
difference in considering matters of this
kind whether these Departments actually
fall as a burden on the public purse or
whether they are to be self-supporting to
a very great extent.
In the case of the
Milk Marketing Act, which forms part of
the necessity for the extension here, it is
hoped that that will be a self-supporting
industry. We are hoping that if there
are to be any extra charges in connection
with milk there will also be extra benefits
derived by the public. We hope that
there will be improved health and
stamina amongst our people and that they
will have a better supply of milk than
they have had hitherto. Those are
benefits that will be good value for whatever extra money may be involved. After
all, surely we in the towns must have
some consideration for our country people
throughout the Six Counties. We have
seen that the competition amongst our
farmers has reduced the production of
milk to an absolutely unprofitable basis.
If that competition had gone on the
source of supply would probably have
been shut off to such an extent that the
milk would have been a good deal dearer
to the purchasers in the towns than it will
be under the new arrangement.
One question put to me was: "If you
wanted these premises in Ormeau
Avenue, why did you not go out and buy

Government, at the outset in 1921, had

on the spur of the moment and within
a short time, they would have paid
infinitely more than they have done

ago.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The reason
for having to come to the House for this
additional sum lies in the fact that before
the passing of the Local Government Act
in 1934 the local authorities were liable
for the expenses of prosecutors and witnesses in criminal cases at the Assizes
and Quarter Sessions, and these sums
were subsequently reimbursed by the Government. It was found that it is a very
much more convenient system by which
these sums are paid in the first instance
by the Government, instead of this
roundabout method by which the local
authority first paid the money and then
got reimbursed by the Government. The
total sum involved is £750, but there
have been appropriations-in-aid amounting to £200 and the sum is as stated. I
beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

Mr. BEATTIE: Yes. These are the

Minister of Labour is not living up to

the new law which operated for a few
weeks, a brother-in-law by marriage only
was expected to keep his wife's brother.
There was a liability thrown on a
stranger to keep a stranger and all
because he happened to be married to
the other fellow's sister, who had been
dead for six years. Representations
were made to London and they discovered it was only blood relations that
came within the regulations then operating. I want a restoration of the status
quo operating prior to the new regulations coming in, when a large percentage of the people were receiving grants.
Owing to the collapse of the regulations
all these people have been denied the
right to any assistance. We have got to

rights to these people. You may say
they are only a small percentage, but
this small percentage must be catered for
immediately. To-morrow, when the

old age pensions and insured pensions to
those persons who are claimants under the
Act. The Estimate is divided into two
parts. It will be observed that we want
£14,000 for pensions and £6,000 for

to estimate accurately and to determine
the number of pensioners who will continue to draw pensions during the whole

the interest hon. Members take in

they will be delighted to respond to my
invitation to grant the amount of money
that we require.

Loans Guarantee (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Question proposed: "That it is expedient to amend the Loans Guarantee
Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922 to 1933,
by extending to the thirty-first day of
March, nineteen hundred and thirtyseven, the
the period within which the
Ministry of Finance may give guarantees
under the Loans Guarantee Act (Northern Ireland), 1922.—(Governor's recommendation signified.-Mr. Barbour).
Mr. BARBOUR: This Money Resolution is, as usual, the forerunner of a Bill
which will be introduced in the course
of a few days and which will possibly
afford hon. Members a wider scope for
debate than the Money Resolution itself.
But the Committee will expect from me
in moving the extension of the Loans
Guarantee machinery for a further period
of two years from the 31st instant some
brief observations in relation to the Government's general policy underlying this
decision.
In the first instance, hon. Members will
have noted from the Parliamentary
Returns which have been furnished from
time to time that these facilities have
played their part in the recent restoration of shipbuilding activity in Belfast,
which has made such a welcome
appearance.
Hon. Members will be aware that legislation in the Imperial Parliament has
recently had the effect of re-introducing
into shipbuilding a form of State assistance analogous to the trade facilities of
the Imperial Act of 1922. This scheme.
is usually referred to as the "Scrap and
Build Scheme," and can be taken
advantage of by shipowners requiring new
tramp and cargo liner tonnage of particular types. This particular legislation
was not applied to Northern Ireland by
the British Act by reason of the
existence in Northern Ireland of the
Loans Guarantee machinery, and it is,
accordingly, necessary that this Government should continue the operation of the
Loans Guarantee Acts.
On this particular question of policy,
therefore, I would say that the Government is satisfied that the conditions with
regard to unemployment and the dependence to a very large extent of our
Province upon this great staple industry
of shipbuilding, with which the Act is
necessarily in the main concerned, justify
the continuance of these facilities.
There is one particular phase of our
recent Loans Guarantee activities to
which some reference ought, perhaps, to
be made. I refer to the guarantees which
have been given in a few cases in respect
of loans raised for the construction of
subsidy houses. As hon. Members are
aware, the Housing Act of 1933 provides
for a certain standard of State assistance
in this connection, and at the time that
Act was passed it was certainly not intended that the facilities of the Loans
Guarantee Acts should be superimposed
upon it.
The Government is satisfied
that it is wrong in principle to do so,
and since coming to this conclusion has
informed applicants that guarantees
under the Loans Guarantee Acts in
respect of loans to be expended in the
erection of subsidy houses cannot qualify
for the dual form of assistance. I beg
to move.

the White Star Line and other companies

to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Com-

operation of this Loans Guarantee Act.
It is an absurdity for any hon. Member
to make any such suggestion. He knows
or he ought to know that orders for sixty
ships have been brought to Belfast that
would not have been brought here had it
not been for the Loans Guarantee Act.
As shown by the paper we have before
us at the present time, Blue Star Line
ships are actually being built in Belfast
at the present moment. The hon. and
learned Member should remember that
the Belfast shipbuilders have a very difficult task in securing orders for Belfast
in competition with firms on the other
side of the Channel, because in Northern
Ireland we have no materials from which
to manufacture ships. Everything we
require has to be brought over here, but
with the assistance of the Loans Guarantee Act the Government has actually
succeeded in securing orders for sixty
ships for Belfast. The shipyard workers
themselves have on many occasions made
public their sense of gratitude to the
Government for the benefits of the Loans
Guarantee Act.
I wonder if the hon. and learned Member for Central has been sleeping while
all these ships have been built in Belfast.
Loans Guarantee (Money)—
13 MARCH 1935
Committee
Does he not remember the many orders
for ships that were secured as a result of
this Act. He is alarmed now because of
the precarious state that shipbuilding all
over the world is in, but Members of both
the Socialist and Nationalist Party are
continually putting down Motions condemning the Government for not taking
any steps to provide work for the people,
and then they get up in this House and
condemn the Government for bringing
in a Loans Guarantee Act which provides
employment for the people. I am bound
to say that I agree with the Member for
South Derry (Mrs. Parker) when she
says the Opposition must oppose anything the Government introduce, whether
they are in favour of it or not.
At any
rate, on behalf of the shipyard workers
I say that we are grateful to the Government for what they have done in
connection with the Loans Guarantee
Act.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I am glad, Mr.
Deputy-Chairman, that you ruled I
should not speak before the Member for
Duncairn (Mr. Grant), because I
welcome the opportunity of removing a
few of the misleading statements you
have ruled he was in order in making.
I hope you will rule that I am equally in
order in replying to him. In the first
place I want to tell him that it is not the
duty of an intelligent person to oppose
everything the Government introduces,
even when they agree with it, but it
seems to be the policy and the duty of the
back benchers and lackey members on the
Government benches to vote against
everything which emanates from the
Opposition benches when it happens to be
a constructive proposal which they give
their approval to, but nevertheless
vote against, in the Division lobby.
Furthermore, it is not true to suggest by
innuendo that because a man happens to
be of the Socialist faith he must, ipso
facto, care less for the welfare of his
fellow-men than the man who is a Tory
just because his father was a Tory, and
not because of any intellectual conviction,
like the Member for Duncairn. A man
can have deep Socialist convictions and a
deep regard for his fellow-men, and
a Socialist is, naturally, going to look
upon the Loans Guarantee Act from the
point of view of what the ultimate effect
of it is going to be in the interests of
those in the area he represents, having
regard to all the circumstances.
There is one side of the Loans Guarantee Act about which the full story has
never been written, and that is what the
final economic consequences of the Act
will be. The man who would say at the
present moment that he knows all about
it is simply talking in the realm of
problematical things. I am glad the
Member for Duncairn has removed the
scales from all our eyes, because there
was some ambiguity in the minds of all
reasonable persons as to what had been
accomplished in Belfast as a direct
result of the Loans Guarantee Act and
nothing else. The Member for Duncairn
said that sixty ships had been built as a
result of that Act, but prior to the last
election for this Parliament when he
was engaged in one of those fervent 1690
stunts, the same gentleman informed us
that those sixty ships had been built in
Belfast not because of the operation of
the Loans Guarantee Act, or anything
the Government had done, but because
of the efforts of the strong, horny-handed
sons of toil in Belfast who were able
to give a greater physical and mental contribution to the building of ships than
were their shipbuilding brethren in any
other part of Gt. Britain. Of course,
he was giving them a pat on the back
that night for a particular reason.
These are all extraneous matters.
(Hon. Members: Hear, Hear.) They
are extraneous matters that were first
introduced by the Member for Duncairn,.
the evil influence of which might spread
if they were not contradicted. Anatole
France, a famous writer whose works I
am very fond of, once said that when
you start a foul story or concoction on its
travels you can never catch up with it,
and I have found that proved time and
time again in the House of Commons.
There are one or two aspects of the
Loans Guarantee Act off the beaten
track that I want to refer to. The total
amount we are involved in at the moment
is £11,759,000. In other words, through
the instrumentality of this Parliament,
and directly through the action of the
Minister of Finance, we have pledged the
credit of the community in the hope that
by so doing we can absorb some of our
unemployed into employment. When I
said earlier that the ultimate result of
that policy could not be determined at
the moment, I meant you would have to
wait and see how the thing finally worked

out and what final responsibility would
rest upon this section of the population
before you could actually say whether it

The Member for Duncairn, like a few
other Members I am looking at at the
present time, regardless of sex, is a great
defender of the rights of private property
and the efficiency of private property,
and yet this paper we hold in our hands
is an indication of the fact that private
property has been so unskilled in its
manipulations that it required the special
machinery of social credit, the credit of
the people of Northern Ireland, to bolster
up the efforts of people who are supposed
to be so efficient that they could run the
universe.
The future productive capacity of our
people is pledged to the extent of nearly
£12,000,000 in order to bolster up that
very indifferent organisation. In everything we deal with in this House, whether
it be shipbuilding, housing, textiles, con.
struction of roads or streets, or any
branch of agriculture, we find that these
people who claim the right to hold
unchallenged supremacy in the walks of
life and industry have to come to this
House and in one form or another have
their efforts bolstered up by the social
credit of the community. While they
deny that in practice such a thing is
possible, they come and claim the
assistance of the State in order to make
their work possible.

Financial Provisions-
Committee
13 MARCH 1935
a
The first part of the Resolution relates
to the use of the Capital Fund handed
over to this Government by the Imperial
Government ten years ago in order to
make up to Northern Ireland the
deficiencies that existed in public buildings here compared to those in the Irish
Free State. The use to which the Fund
was to be put is governed by an Act of
this Parliament, and the greater part
has now been expended on prison reconstruction, agricultural institutions,
training college for teachers, and the like.
A small part of the Fund is as yet not
earmarked, and it is now proposed to
widen the purposes to which it may be
applied so that it may be made available
for meeting the cost of additional
reformatory accommodation at Malone
Training School, and also for meeting the
cost of such extra accommodation for the
Civil Service as may be found necessary
owing to the creation of new activities by
legislation of this House.
Passing to the second part of the
Resolution before you, I would remind
you of the scheme of Government
guaranteed loans to farmers through the
banks for the purchase of livestock, seeds
and fertilisers, set up by the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Acts, 1929 and
1930. In order that these loans might be
available to the borrowers at not exceeding 3 per cent., the Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Act, 1933, further
provided for the payment of a Government subsidy of portion of the interest.
on these loans, with the result that of the
4 per cent. interest charged by the banks
the Exchequer has been paying 1 per
cent as a subsidy. It has been decided to
issue new short-dated loans of this type
direct to the farmers from the Government Loans Fund at 3 per cent. interest
and to take on to the Fund outstanding
loans, thus eliminating the banks from
the scheme and saving the Exchequer the
1 per cent. subsidy. The whole matter
is one of machinery and the conditions
relating to the loans will not be altered
in any way.
The third item relates to the salary of
the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
In common with other civil servants, it is
proposed that his basic salary shall be
consolidated with the bonus now payable
thereon and that the new scale of salary
shall be charged in its entirety on the
Consolidated Fund. Hitherto only the
basic salary was charged on the Consolidated Fund, the bonus being met from
the Vote.
Mr. BEATTIE: Capital Fund.
Mr. BARBOUR: No, Consolidated
Fund. It is an annual charge. The
concluding portion of the Resolution
relates to the maintenance of the Ulster
Division War Memorial at Thiepval. It
will be recollected that in the year 1928
the House appropriated a capital sum
towards its future maintenance, and this
Fund has been administered by a local
committee. That committee has now
recommended that the maintenance of
the memorial should be undertaken in
future by the Imperial War Graves Commission, and it is now proposed that the
Capital Fund be handed over to them.
If the income of the Fund is insufficient
to meet the cost of maintaining the
memorial, it is proposed to supplement it
by a further annual sum not exceeding
£120 in any one year, and additional
annual provision within this limit is
accordingly made as a Consolidated Fund
charge. I feel confident that hon. Members will entirely agree with this modest
further provision for this object. I beg
to move.

Mr. SPEAKER: Right hon. and hon.
Members will observe that Questions 15
and 18 would anticipate the debate which
is to take place this afternoon, and therefore these two questions would be out

POSITION OF JUNIOR ASSISTANT
MISTRESSES.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the number of junior assistant mistresses in the
service of the Ministry; whether it is
proposed to retain the services of these
teachers in the event of the schools in
which they are employed being amalgamated or superseded by provided schools;
and whether he can state if the service
of these teachers are dispensed with what
compensation is it proposed to award.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The number
of junior assistant mistresses employed in
public elementary schools in Northern
Ireland on 31st December last was 583.
When schools are amalgamated or
superseded every effort is made to ensure
that no undue hardship is caused to
members of existing staffs, including
junior assistant mistresses. The statutory regulations for the staffing of public
elementary schools give the Ministry
power to prescribe the terms and limitation of recognition of such teachers as
may be redundant to normal requirements in the new school or in the school
in which amalgamation takes place. In
cases where teachers are not absorbed
into the permanent staff a reasonable
period is given to them to obtain other
posts unless they have been notified at
the time of their appointment and as a
condition of employment that they will
have no claim to consideration in the
new or amalgamated school.
The Ministry has no power to award
compensation to teachers on loss of employment.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Parliamentary Secretary whether the
policy now adopted is different to the
assurance he gave in 1925 in the House
of Commons that the redundant teachers'
interests, financial and otherwise, would
be safeguarded in the amalgamation or
superseding of schools, and whether that
declaration remains up to date.
Mr. ROBB: I am not aware of any
change of policy.

829 Unemployment Assistance Bill-

14 MARCH 1935
Second Reading
Adjournment of the House.
Resolved: "That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until Tuesday
next."-(Captain Dixon).
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): The object of
the Bill now before the House is to
restore the cuts that have been made in
transitional payments and to continue to
pay applicants any increase over these
payments determined by the Board. This
means that in any case where the Board's
determination is greater than the determination under the Public Assistance
Committee the applicant will be paid the
higher figure, and the regulations do not
operate where there would have been a
reduction.
The Act of 1934 provides that the
needs of an applicant for public assistance shall be determined by the Board
and his needs assessed in accordance with
regulations made by the Board and
accepted by the Minister. The Board in
Northern Ireland has recommended that
the regulations governing payment of
allowances shall be similar to those
adopted for the purpose of the scheme
in Great Britain. The Minister agreed
with this recommendation, which accordingly has been laid before the House.
The House is fully aware of the developments both here and across the water
which have led to the introduction of
the present Bill.
The institution of the public assistance
scheme was not in any way intended as
an economy at the expense of the unemployed. Accurate estimation of
claims was impossible. It was fully expected that the application of the basis
of assessment provided by the regulations
would result in a large increase in total
expenditure on allowances to persons who
come within the scope of the scheme after
the first appointed day. Our experience
has been that at least 70 per cent. of the
cases which came before the Board under
the regulations resulted either in increases above that given by the Public
Assistance Committee or in no change.
In spite of all our precautions and our
anxiety to make the scheme a success and
acceptable, individual cases have come
to light in which it would appear that
the regulations were operating rather
harshly-in particular, those portions of
the regulations which deal with the
earnings of other members of an applicant's household, and with the downward adjustment in the allowance
where a family occupied a low-rented
house, and where, if the family were
of a large number, there was a further
cut in respect of each member of the
household in excess of five.
The Board has a wide discretion in
the application of the regulations and all
these sources of grievance would have
been ultimately removed as greater experience was gained. Exceptional needs.
and exceptional circumstances would
have been appropriately examined. The
application of an equal code of rules to
people who had been treated differently
by local areas was bound to have different
consequences for individuals in increasing the benefits of some whilst decreasing
the benefits of others.
The cumulative effect was that the
anticipated easing of the circumstances of
the unemployed was not completely
realised. Finding that the regulations
were not working according to our anticipation the Minister decided to call a
halt and where allowances had been reduced to have them restored-except
where reductions were brought about by
changed circumstanes-and where allowances had been increased by the Board
to pay these higher allowances.
It is intended to carry out a complete
review of the existing regulations and
this interim arrangement is adopted.
solely for that purpose. The present Bill
follows the lines of the Bill before the
Imperial House of Commons which was
passed during the month of February.
Clause 1 of the Bill provides that applicants for public assistance shall be
assessed at the old transitional payment
rate, subject to change of circumstances,
or, in accordance with the regulations
of the Board, the governing factor
being to pay on the more favourable
basis of assessment. In cases where an
applicant had no previous transitional
831 Unemployment Assistance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Gordon]
payments prior to the 7th January, or
where his circumstances had changed,
the Board's officers are required to estimate as accurately as possible the amount
necessary to meet his needs.
The Act of 1934 provides that there
shall be no appeal to the tribunal
against the determination of the regulations except by leave of the chairman
of the tribunal, and directs that the
chairman's leave shall not be granted
unless it appears to him to be doubtful
whether the applicant's need has been
determined and assessed in accordance

other special circumstances affecting the
case.
The Temporary Provisions Bill, as
originally introduced into the Imperial
House of Commons, did not alter this
position. But on the Committee stage it
was urged that in order that the
claimant might be fully satisfied that
justice was being done to him he should
have an absolute right of appeal to the
tribunal without the chairman's leave,
in regard to the assessment of the amount
of his supplementary allowance.
Government accepted this contention,
and I am glad to say we have embodied
this provision in the Bill now before the
House.

The question
whether an
applicant is entitled to a supplementary
allowance depends upon two factors:-
Firstly, what is the assessment under the

amount at which the Public Assistance
Committee would have fixed his assessment for transitional payments.
It will be seen from the examples I

Major MCCORMICK: I raise now the
matter of revaluation because of the
answer or want of answer which I received
from the Minister of Finance on the question of deferring the Valuation Act for
five years. I understand it would require
legislation to put that into effect, therefore I will not pursue that further but
will deal with the large issue which is
involved. The Revaluation Act is
having very far-reaching effects upon
industry and upon the residential buildings of our Province.
The Act is very drastic. When it was
going through this House it was pointed
out that it would be a very serious matter
for our people. I was not against the
principle of revaluation then, and I am
not against it now, and when the Bill
was going through I asked, owing to the
depressed state of trade and industry in
general, that it should be deferred for at
least five years. The Minister would not
listen to me. I hope that now, after
mature consideration and in view of the
outcry against the Measure, he will give
the suggestion some little consideration.
As I say, I am not against the
principle of revaluation. I agree that
in a prosperous community, in a
country that is improving, in a city
that is extending its boundaries
values will change, but I also agree that
a change in values does not necessarily
mean that they will rise in order to carry
out the literal meaning of revaluation.
It has been said, time and again, that
there has been no revaluation since the
Griffith Act of 1863, but whilst there has
been no revaluation since that time I
think I am right in saying there has not
been a single year in which there has not
been a revision of valuation.
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. The
hon. and gallant Member for St. Anne's
is speaking out of order. He can only
discuss the administration of the Act
which has been passed. He cannot give
reasons for or against that Act having
been passed. I think I explained that
to the hon. and gallant Gentleman when
he spoke to me at the Chair.

cussions of this Act, which is of a very

am not against Englishmen at all. They

They were responsible for valuing the

rest assured that his friends who sell

SCHOOLS.
8. Mrs. PARKER asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether steps will be taken
on lines approved by the Minister of
Home Affairs, to make the teaching of
road safety a compulsory item in all
elementary school curricula.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The demands upon
the time available for
primary education are already so great
that it is not considered suitable to make
the teaching of road safety a compulsory
part of the elementary school curriculum.
To do SO would mean that proportionately less time could be devoted to
necessary school subjects.
The Ministry has, however, been so
strongly impressed by the importance of
the matter to which the hon. Member
refers that in its most recent circular to
school managers and teachers upon the
subject, issued only last week, it has gone
so far as to urge teachers to arrange that
at intervals of not less than a month the
children shall be assembled and given
special instruction, illustrated by means
of the blackboard or otherwise, upon the
dangers of motor traffic.
In order that for the future teachers
may be properly equipped to give such
instruction, my right hon. Friend, the
Minister for Home Affairs, has also expressed his willingness to arrange for the
holding of classes or demonstations by
specially qualified members of the
R.U.C. The Ministry has impressed
upon teachers the desirability of attending any such classes, and the Stranmillis
Training College Committee has approved.
of the holding of classes at the college for

SYSTEM OF REVALUATION.
10. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Finance whether, in adopting
the English scales of allowances for the
purpose of the Northern Ireland revaluation, due regard was had to the fact that
in

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
19 MARCH 1935
Mr. POLLOCK: The Statute of 1852
merely requires the Commissioner of
Valuation to estimate the rent at which
premises might be expected to let on a
yearly tenancy. The question whether
those premises are freehold or leasehold
does not arise, as a prospective yearly
tenant would not concern himself with
the landlord's liability for ground rent.
The net annual value of two similar
properties will be the same although one
may be held in fee simple and the other
on lease subject to a ground rent. No
deduction, therefore, falls to be made in
the latter type of case.

of this 12 are in receipt of pensions payable by the Imperial Government exceeding £150 per annum. The figure of

Fund, the Road Fund, the Milk Fund,

Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
