[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Provision of supplementary allowances).
Question proposed: "That the Clause
stand part of the Bill."
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to say
a few words on this Clause. The
question I was concerned with was the
amount of money recoverable by the
applicant, who was unfortunate to be reduced between the 7th January and the
last day of the reduction. I think that
is a very important thing. This is a
Measure to legalise that position so that
you can restore the cut taken away from
the applicant. I am making my statement on broad lines. It is well-known
by those who are in touch with this
matter that upwards of 60 per cent. of
the applicants were reduced. I may be
wrong, but that is the general opinion.
I do not belong to the infallibility
department, and I am speaking from
knowledge gained from those I have come,
in personal contact with.
I would say
from that knowledge that 60 per cent. of
them were reduced. When the decision
to restore the cut was given I advised all
those persons in touch with me to apply,
and I presumed that they would be paid
back. Some of them were reduced 2s 6d,
2s, 1s 6d, and other small sums. Nevertheless those small sums amount to something to the individual. I must credit
the Department with the fact that as far
as possible they made retrospective payments, but I am given to understand
that there is an outstanding number of
persons who have not got the retrospective payments to which they were
entitled.
I do not make this statement by way
of a grumble or grouse. I do so in the
hope that the Ministry will immediately
restore all the cuts from the first day of
their operation. If the applicant is then
dissatisfied and feels he is entitled to
903 Unemployment Assistance Bill-- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee
[Mr. Beattie]
further restoration, I think it is the duty
of the Ministry to have a staff to advise
applicants how to make inquiry for a
restoration of the amounts. I think the
staff is entitled to do that work. It is
not part of my work, although I have
done the work since the start. I feel
that a little more consideration should be
given by a particular section of the staff
in the way of advising and instructing
applicants how much they are entitled to
receive and whether they have received
the total amounts they are entitled to
get. I want to leave that with the
Ministry. I hope that my remarks are
not taken as a criticism of the administration.
I want to draw the Minister's attention to another point. I had the brown
form of determination, and the claim I
referred to on the Second Reading of the
Bill was to the effect that the man was
getting 10s less than he was previous to
his son getting employment. I am glad
to say that that case has been increased
by 50 per cent. Although that increase
has been given it sets out on the determination form "This determination
does not include the following members
of your family-William, Samuel and
John." It happened in this case that
Samuel's income was the determining
factor in the father's claim of 26s 6d,
which was reduced to 6s 6d. I want the
Minister to explain why, at the bottom
of that form, the names are set out of

seeing that Samuel's income was the

think there is something wrong with this
brown form which you use when setting
out the determination allowance. Not
only that, but I find that form is misleading so far as the parent is concerned.
This morning I had several of these
forms presented to me. Maggie, Jane,
Arthur and Jim are set out in regard to
income. They are the determining factor
of the assessment. The claimants told
me that if the income received by the
children was not taken into account they
were entitled to receive 24s. I had to
explain to these people that the income of
those children was taken into consideration, although the form states it is not
taken into consideration. The Minister
should get a copy of this brown form and
see the last paragraph which, I think, is
misleading. I believe that fact has been
recognised in Great Britain and that that
paragraph is to be reconstructed. I want
the Minister here to pay special attention
to that paragraph so that we may not
have as many queries in future as we have
had in the past.
May I also say that this Clause contains the sting of the whole Bill? There
is a principle contained in it with which I
cannot agree. Clause 1 really is the
whole Measure as it stands. This is only
a short Bill and Clause 1 contains the
principle of the whole Measure.
Mr. ANDREWS:
are you referring to?
Which Sub-clause
Mr. BEATTIE: Amongst others Subclauses (2) and (5). The principle in the
Clause in my opinion is the destruction of
family life. I cannot be a party to that.
At last Friday's sitting of the appeal
court I instructed all my claimants what
to tell the court and the court heard them
very sympathetically. This is going to
lead to grave anomalies. To illustrate, I
may be living next door to an applicant
under this Clause. He has two sons and
two daughters who are working for small
wages and the total amount received from
the four is sufficient to reduce the father's

Here is what I feel is going to happen.
I can transfer my
child to the house next
door and the head of the house will get
24s. That can be followed by civil court
proceedings, but in the name of heaven
how are you going to follow up all the
cases? My boy may be going to live
with his uncle, or a boy from that home
may come to live with me. Do you think
the children of the present day because
they are bringing in 10s. a week are going
to stand their father being cut to the
extent of 15s.? That is what the principle of the Clause is leading to.

Mr. POLLOCK : My right hon.
Friend (Mr. Barbour) in moving the
Money Resolution preliminary to this Bill
a few days ago explained in some detail
the four points which are now covered in
the four Clauses of this Bill. The first
Clause deals with the extension of the use
of Capital Fund No. 2 so as to enable a
small residue to be used for capital construction work generally; in particular, I
should mention a new wing at Malone
Training School.
In case the House should desire some
further information I may explain that
the £400,000, of which this fund
originally consisted, owing to judicious
investment, to the natural increase of
Financial Provisions Bill-
19 MARCH 1935
Second Reading
was
market values, and appreciation of investments became approximately £500,000.
Out of this new total of £500,000 the
House will remember that a sum of
transferred to the
£100,000
Exchequer a year ago by Act of Parliament to help to balance the Budget. Of
the remaining £400,000, expenditure on
public buildings to date amounts to about
£360,000, with a further £20,000 earmarked. There is, therefore, about
£20,000 unallocated as yet, plus some
accrued interest, and this the Bill proposes
to earmark for general capital purposes.
One such purpose is in sight, namely, a
new wing at Malone Training School for
reformatory boys so as to leave more room
for the Borstal inmates.
As I say, if the House is concerned to
learn particulars of how that money was
expended it would, perhaps, be appropriate that I should give that information. On the Training College there was
spent a sum of £187,000; on prisons and
prison extensions, £37,850; on Borstal
institutions, £12,000; on the criminal
lunatic asylum, £5,400; on Queen's
University Faculty of Agriculture,
£34,000; on agricultural institutions,
£46,000; on the Royal Ulster Constabulary Depot, at present being constructed, £35,000. It will thus be found
that there is a surplus remaining of about
£20,000 of that original fund of £400,000.
The second Clause involves the taking
over by the Government Loans Fund from
the banks, the loans to farmers for live
stock, seeds, fertilisers, and so forth, and
the issue of new loans. These were very
small amounts and the distribution of
them was conducted generally through the
banks. The bank loans at present outstanding amount to about £35,000, and,
as I have said, the Government propose to
repay that and to conduct for the future
the distribution of these loans to the
farmers directly from the Department.
In the third Clause there is provision
made for the salary of the Comptroller
and Auditor-General being put upon the
Consolidated Fund as a consolidated sum.
This is necessary owing to the consolidation of salaries and the cost-of-living
bonus, and involves no actual expenditure.
I come now to the last Clause in the
Measure, which relates to the transfer to
the Imperial War Graves Commission of
the fund set apart for the maintenance of
the Thiepval Memorial and the provision
of a contingent additional amount of
annual income for the upkeep of the
Memorial. From the recent examination
made by the members of the committee
appointed to care for the upkeep of the
memorial it was found that the surroundings had got into a very unkempt condition not at all creditable to the Province,
and certainly forming a very remarkable
contrast to the appearance and condition
of other monuments in the near neighbourhood. Having regard to the difficulty
of controlling the work there because it
is in rather a remote position-it has been
found that the present is a suitable opportunity for securing the services of that
great body the Imperial War Graves Commission in order that our monument,
which in itself is a very dignified and
beautiful structure, should be maintained
in a proper and creditable condition and
worthy of the men who fought and died in
that district.
The House should remember that the
Imperial War Graves Commission is a perpetual organisation, intended to continue
in effect for all time to take care of all
the British monuments in France and,
indeed, I think elsewhere. They are fully
equipped with engineers, architects, and
all the necessary material for caring for
the great number of monuments that are
to be found in France or other countries.
The committee came to the conclusion
that it was very desirable that their
services should be retained in order that
the Thiepval Memorial of Ulster should
be properly attended to. Such other
memorials as, for example, that of Newfoundland-a very small country of only
450,000 people-present a very creditable
appearance compared with the condition
of our memorial, and, therefore, I think
that, having regard to all the circumstances, the House will approve of the
expenditure of this £120 so that the
services of the Imperial War Graves Commission may be availed of for the preservation of this monument. I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Herring Industry Act, 1935.
Mr. BARBOUR: I beg to move:
"That an humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland as follows:
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects the Commons of
Northern Ireland in Parliament
assembled, do by this humble Address
pray that it may please His Majesty to
make provision by Order in Council
under sub-section (1) of section fifteen
of the Herring Industry Act, 1935,
that the said Act shall extend to
Northern Ireland so far as it relates to
matters within the powers of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland."
The Herring Industry Act, which this
Resolution proposes should be applied in
its full extent to Northern Ireland is one
which, in the words of the Secretary of
State for Scotland, who introduced the
Bill in the House of Commons at Westminster, is "to enable the herring
industry with financial assistance to re
929 Herring Industry Act

19 MARCH 1935
Herring Industry Act
organise itself." As hon. Members are
aware, the herring fishing industry of
the United Kingdom has been passing
through very difficult times, largely
owing to the contraction of the export
market for cured herring, which has been
the mainstay of the industry in the past.
Before the war the Continental markets,
principally in Russia and
Russia and Germany,
absorbed over 70 per cent. of the total
herrings caught by United Kingdom.
boats but, with the altered conditions
resulting from trade
and
barriers
currency restriction, the export of cured
herring has fallen by two-thirds, while
the home market, in comparison with
1913, has fallen by one-third.
This decline in the demand has reduced
the industry to such straits that the
Imperial Government asked the Sea-Fish
Commission, set up under the Sea-
Fishing Industry Act of 1933, to report
specially on the herring industry as a
matter of urgency. The Commission
visited the principal herring ports of
Great Britain, and two representatives
also visited Northern Ireland. In
August last the Commission presented a
Report which recommended a reorganisation of the industry and the setting up
of a Herring Board for the United
Kingdom, clothed with powers to carry
out a reorganisation in all branches of
the industry from the catching of the fish.
to the marketing of cured herring. The
Herring Industry Act, however, does not
go quite so far as to impose on the
industry the scheme outlined by the
Commission, but it provides for the setting up of a Board whose first duty is to
prepare, in consultation with all the
interests concerned, a scheme for the reorganisation, regulation and development of the industry..
The powers which may be conferred on
the Board by the scheme are such as,
subject to the approval of the appropriate Ministers and to confirmation by
the Imperial Parliament, the Board itself
considers to be necessary in order to
attain the object in view. Amongst
those powers are, first, reorganisation by
the process of eliminating redundant
boats; secondly, regulation of the operations of fishermen, salesmen, curers, processers, and exporters, by means of a
licensing system and by the fixing of
prices, and lastly, development, by promoting sales, extending existing and
opening new markets, and by research.
work. The scheme may also provide for
the delegation of functions of the Board
to local committees, and it is probable
that, as recommended by the Commission, an area committee will be set up
to operate the scheme in its application
to Northern Ireland.
not
more
During the first three years of its life
the Board will receive a grant from the
Imperial Exchequer not exceeding
than
£125,000, of which
£75,000 may be applied to administrative expenses and the balance to research
and the promotion of sales. Over and
above these sums the Board will have at
its disposal a maximum amount of
£600,000, which it is empowered to use
to the extent of £200,000 in the making
of loans in connection with operations
involving the outlay of working capital,
and to the extent of £400,000 in the
making of loans for the construction, reconditioning and equipment of herring
fishing boats.
It is anticipated that the scheme will
be ready for submission to the Imperial
Ministers at the end of this month.
Three weeks must elapse to allow for
the presentation and consideration of
objections, but the Ministers hope that
it will be possible to submit an agreed
scheme for the final approval of Parliament by the end of April.
Now as regards the application of the
Act to Northern Ireland, there arises the
constitutional question involved in the
fact that practically all of the powers
which the Board can be expected to
wield, with the sole exception of those
relating to export, are powers which, in
their exercise here, this Parliament, and
not the Parliament at Westminster,
would normally be called upon to confer.
Consequently, in so far as those powers
are concerned, that is to say, those relating to the transferred service of fisheries,
the Imperial Act will not apply to
Northern Ireland unless and until the
Resolution now before this House receives the approval of both Chambers,
and until His Majesty's assent to its
application in respect of those transferred
matters is signified in the form of an
Imperial Order in Council.
Hon. Members will naturally ask
whether, in submitting this Resolution for
the acceptance of this House, the Govern-
Herring Industry Act
Herring Industry Act
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
ment has satisfied itself that it is acting
in the best interests of the Northern Ireland herring industry. The answer which
I make to that question is that we have
kept in the closest possible touch with the
Imperial Departments concerned since the
Sea-fish Commission issued its report on
the herring industry, that we have
been apprised to the full of every turn in
the negotiations and conversations that
have taken place between those Departments and the various interests in Great
Britain, and that we have kept our own
local interests in turn fully informed of
every development, in order that they
would be in a position to advise us
whether Northern Ireland should or
should not be included in the scheme.
The advice which we have thus obtained
finds expression in the Resolution before
the House to-day.
In asking the House to approve this
Resolution the Government is acting in
what it believes to be the best interests of
the Northern Ireland herring industry.
It is apparent that we are now at the
point where a great national effort is
going to be made to rehabilitate an
industry that has suffered, perhaps more
than any other, from the disruption which
followed the War, and in our view it is
essential that Northern Ireland should be
brought within the field which that effort
is intended to benefit. I beg to move.

Supposing I were the Minister of Agriculture and I want to be quite frank
and say that I have no ambitions that

Italians, and other foreign people to come
into Northern Ireland and establish
creameries to the detriment of the Ulster
creameries? The right hon. Gentleman

is a rebel to his country in so far as his

because, like myself, I do not believe he
reads literature very much. Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that practically
every creamery throughout Northern Ireland and a large percentage of the
farming community are opposed to the
policy adopted by the right hon. Gentleman? I believe the right hon. Gentleman
has brought a hornets' nest about his
head. I would appeal to the right hon.
Gentleman to justify his action.

Perhaps I should go further-because

One other question which was raised, I
think, by three hon. Members, two of them
while I was out of the Committee, was the
question of flax. That has been exercising our attention for a matter of two
months, and, although I can show the
hon. Gentleman the difficulties that exist,
I cannot for the moment give him a
satisfactory solution. The difficulty of
the flax problem is entirely different from
that of any other scheme. The greater
part of the raw material that is required
in the linen industry comes from abroad.
Therefore, if you have any scheme for
the assistance of the growing of flax in
this country, and if you fix a minimum
price, the result will be that the
foreigner, when he produces his flax, may
produce that flax at a lower price than
you have fixed as your minimum in this
country. The linen merchants are compelled, because theirs is an exporting
trade, to go to the cheapest market for
their raw material. The natural consequence of that is that the farmer in this
country here will blame the Government,
or rather my Ministry, and will say
"You have fixed a minimum price, but
it is no use because nobody is buying our
goods." The same thing would apply if
the ten per cent. duty had been retained
on flax, as was at first intended. The
result of that would have been that you
would simply have prevented a certain
amount of raw material from coming in.
You would have put up the cost of raw
material and thrown back on to the competitors some of the flax that you were
keeping back by the ten per cent. tariff,
so making their raw material cheaper than
yours. The difficulty is that the bulk of
the raw material comes in and the bulk
of the finished article goes out, so that
no financial scheme that I can see could
possibly work on any of the present
marketing principles.
The only line along which I can hope
to assist the flax growers is by the work
which the Ministry has been carrying out
for many years in regard to the production of high grade fibre seed. At the
present moment the amount of seed available will sow roughly 10,000 acres, and
we anticipate that there will be 25,000
acres grown this year. The best inducement to a large crop, with all its
advantages to the farmer, is the price
prevailing at present, but to make any
artificial price for an article of which we
have never grown more than one-fifth of
our requirements, and the great bulk of
which comes from abroad, is to my mind
practically impossible.

Oral Answers to Questions.
REBUILDING OF GOVERNMENT
HOUSE.
1. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state if any
steps have been taken towards the rebuilding of Government House, Hillsborough.
not
re-
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Although, as hon. Members
will quite understand, it was
practicable to proceed with
building of Government House until our
claim for insurance had been definitely
settled, my Department has been giving
much time and labour to the preparations
of the reconstruction scheme whilst the
negotiations were being carried on with
the insurance companies.
I am glad to add that agreement has
now been reached in regard to our claim,
so that the work of rebuilding can now
proceed with all possible expedition.
REVALUATION ANOMALIES.
2. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that the recent revaluation has created
anomalies, and, if so, whether he is prepared to introduce an Anomalies Bill to
correct these anomalies.
Mr. POLLOCK: I assume that what
the hon. and gallant Member is referring
to is the fact that the general all-round
increase in valuations disturbs various
Acts of Parliament where valuations are
taken as forming the basis of certain
statutory charges, licence duties, reliefs
or qualifications. I
in due
propose,
course, to submit to this House a Bill
in order to bring those Acts into conformity with the new valuations in such
a way that the mere alteration of values
will not militate adversely against the
persons affected.
I should prefer to call such a Bill a
Consequential Provisions Bill rather than
an Anomalies Bill.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Arising out of that
answer, can the right hon. Gentleman
state whether the Bill is likely to be
brought forward in the present session?
Mr. POLLOCK: I hope so. The
session will last into July.
COMMENCING HOUR IN SCHOOLS.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state if he will
consider the advisability of recommending education authorities to change the
commencing hour in all schools to 10 a.m.
from the 1st October to the 31st March.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The Ministry
does not consider that present hours of
opening of schools are too early and, in
these circumstances, I am not prepared to
make a recommendation of the nature
suggested.

DOWN REGIONAL COMMITEE
INQUIRY.
4. Major McCORMICK asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether it is a fact that the
recent inquiry into the conduct of the
Architect and Director of Education of
the Down Regional Committee has cost
the ratepayers over £8,000; and whether
he will consider the abolition of the Local
Government Auditor and staff in order
to avoid wastage of this sort.
Mr. ROBB: The answer to both parts
of the question is in the negative.
Lieut.Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of that answer, is it not a fact that the
education authority for County Down
were perfectly justified in clearing up
these gross irregularities in open court,
and, therefore, was not the actual cost
of that inquiry, £3,320, fully justified in
clearing up anything in the administration of County Down?
Major MCCORMICK: Would the Parliamentary Secretary state that if that
committee had acted twelve months before
they did this cost to the public would
not have been incurred?
Dr. WILSON: In view of the present
unsatisfactory state of the finances of the
City of Belfast, would the hon. and
gallant Member not be better advised to
look after the finances of the city and
leave the county alone?
Major MCCORMICK: Supplementary
to that I would say
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps the hon. and
gallant Member would wait. Mr.
Beattie.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
the Chairman of the Down Regional Committee is the new chairman who has been
responsible for clearing up any mess that
has taken place? (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
5. Major McCORMICK asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether, in view of the findings of the recent inquiry into abuses
under the County Down Regional Committee he will consider the advisability
of the dismissal of the Chairman and
Committee.
Mr. ROBB: The answer is in the
negative.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is it not a
fact that the Members of the Down
Regional Committee and those members of
that committee who are Members of this
House are perfectly capable of dealing
with these matters without interference
by the hon, and gallant Member for St.
Anne's?
Major MCCORMICK: Would the Parliamentary Secretary say that they have
dealt properly with the affairs of that
committee?
THE KING'S SILVER JUBILEE.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is prepared
to declare the 6th May, 1935, as a holiday for all officials and employees of the
Police Courts in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This matter will
receive my sympathetic consideration,
but I am doubtful whether there is any
statutory authority which would enable
me to carry out the suggestion of the
hon. Member.
REPORTED ATTACK ON
NATIONALIST BAND.
7. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether a party of
Nationalist bandsmen were waylaid on
Sunday in Church Lane, Belfast, by a
mob from the Custom House Steps;
whether inoffensive persons, including
young girls, were savagely beaten;
whether the bandsmen's musical instruments were destroyed; and whether any
of the assailants have been brought to
justice.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The facts of
the regrettable incident to which the hon.
Member refers are briefly as follows:-
On Sunday evening last the Devlin
Memorial Band, accompanied by a number of girls and youths, while marching
from its bandroom in York Street to the
market area unfortunately departed from
the approved route, and the arrange-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
21 MARCH 1935
ments made by the police authorities were
thereby, to a certain extent, rendered unavailing.
The band while marching through
Church Lane-which was not contemplated in the approved route-was
followed by some of the crowd coming
from the Custom House. The crowd indulged in a certain amount of shouting
and the members of the band discarded
their instruments and ran towards the
markets. The crowd did not follow, but
in the confusion some of the band
instruments were damaged. The members of the band returned in a few
minutes and picked up the instruments.
A constable who saw the band turning
into Church Lane accompanied it and
additional police arrived immediately
afterwards on the scene. The police did
not witness any assaults and in the
general confusion it was impossible to
identify any of the crowd.
Although I am glad to say that the
disturbance, such as it was, was not of
the serious character suggested by the
hon. Member, I am much concerned that
such an incident should have taken place,
and it is a question for consideration
whether, in the interests of peace and
good order, I may not find it necessary
to prohibit bands from marching through
the streets on Sundays, except with the
express permission of the authorities and
over a definitely prescribed route.
TOWN PLANNING.
8. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the impending extension of the
boundary of the City of Belfast and other
urban areas, he will consider amending
the Towns Planning Act in order that
the amenities of the countryside shall be
preserved and improved.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware of any circumstances to suggest
that the Planning and Housing Act
(Northern Ireland), 1931, would require
amendment in order that the developments which the hon. and gallant Member apprehends could be met. The Act,
as he is no doubt aware, applies to rural
as well as to urban local authorities and
affords them wide powers for the preservation of amenities and of the beauty of
the countryside. Further, it includes
provision enabling two or more local
authorities to combine for the purpose of
planning schemes.
Major McCORMICK: Would the
Minister say whether the Act has the
force of law or not?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Of course it
has. I am amazed at my hon. Friend
suggesting that it has not.
KNOCK VILLAGE FATALITY.
9. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the Belfast Coroner's finding as
to the absence of control over a man-hole
at Knock village, whereby a child's life
was lost, he will cause an inquiry to be
held with a view to compensation being
granted to the widowed mother.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I regret I
have no powers in the direction indicated
by the hon. and gallant Member, but it
is satisfactory to observe from the reports
of the inquest that some practical
sympathy has been offered by the contractors for the works at which the
accident took place.
POLICE ADMINISTRATION IN
COUNTY TYRONE.
10. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
date on which the present county
inspector of police for County Tyrone
took up duty there; the number of
official police inquiries held in the county.
since that date; the number of districtinspectors, head-constables, sergeants and
constables involved in these inquiries,
and the total number of official police
inquiries held in County Tyrone during
the five years immediately preceding the
present county inspector's appointment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The present
county inspector of Tyrone took over
charge of the county on the 1st April,
1931.
The number of official police inquiries.
held in the county since that date, a
period of four years, was eleven, involving one head-constable, six sergeants, and
six constables.

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
•
[Sir Dawson Bates]
The number of official police inquiries.
held during the five years immediately
preceding the 1st April, 1931, was sixteen, involving two sergeants and sixteen
constables.
During the period from 1st April,
1931, to date, there were, in addition to
the courts of inquiry, 51 instances in
which disciplinary charges were preferred
against members of the Force, and were
admitted; while during the five years
prior to 1st April, 1931, there were 85
cases of this nature.
Captain DIXON: May I ask if this
county inspector was not the most
popular and most efficient county
inspector for all purposes when in
East Belfast?
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
11. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
efficiency in the police force in County
Tyrone is judged by the number of
prosecutions a member of the Force can
institute; whether, owing to the attitude
adopted by the present county inspector
on this matter, many members of the
Force, being unable to rise to their
standard of prosecutions, are being unduly harassed on that account; and
whether he is prepared to issue instructions condemning such a standard and so
put an end to petty prosecutions which
are being instituted by members of the
Force in order to try to keep in the
good graces of the county inspector.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer
to the first part of the hon. Member's
question is in the negative, and the
matters referred to in the latter part do
not, therefore, arise.
While I cannot but regret that the
hon. Member should have attempted, by
the entirely unwarranted suggestions
underlying his question to vilify a most
zealous and efficient officer, I welcome
the opportunity of testifying to the high
esteem in which this officer is held by his
authorities. This opinion has, I may
say, been endorsed by Lord Justice
Andrews, His Majesty's Going Judge of
Assize, at Omagh on Tuesday last, when
he congratulated the members of the
Royal Ulster Constaulary in the County
of Tyrone, from the county inspector
down, on the very high percentage of
detection of crime in that county.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I consider the reply to
my question unsatisfactory, and I propose raising this matter on the Motion
for the Adjournment.
MARKET TOLLS.
12. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce
legislation at an early date, embodying
the recommendations outlined in the
Market and Tolls Commission report.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government has the matter under consideration,
and has in view the introduction of legislation on the basis of the Market and
Tolls Commission's report.
THE BLIND PERSONS ACT.
13. Mr. MIDGLEY (for Mr. Henderson) asked the Minister of Labour
whether he is prepared to revise the provisions of the Blind Persons Act so that
all those diagnosed as not able to follow
any industrial occupation by reason of
loss of vision will be eligible for a
pension.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The conditions here for the
receipt of blind pensions are exactly the
same as in the rest of the United Kingdom, and for reasons of which the hon.
Member is aware, I regret that I cannot
undertake to make the departure suggested.
SPAHLINGER VACCINE.
14. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is now in a
position to make a statement upon the
results of the use of the Spahlinger
vaccine for tuberculosis in cattle.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I hope that the
report on the experiment in question will
be in the hands of the printers within the
next few days, and I do not, therefore,
wish to anticipate the report by making
a statement at this stage.

Vote on Account
FALL IN MILK CONSUMPTION.
15. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the reason why the consumption of
milk for domestic or household purposes
has fallen during the past three months.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: My Department has in recent months made enquiries
from time to time in regard to the
quantity of milk sold for human consumption. The reports received as a
result of these enquiries have been conflicting, and the Ministry accordingly is.
not satisfied that there has been any
diminution in the quantity of milk sold
for actual human consumption. The
hon. and gallant Member will realise that
no reliable figures for liquid milk consumption were available prior to the
scheme coming into operation.
I should like to inform the hon. and
gallant Member that in my view the consumption of milk will increase. At
present, as in Great Britain, it is
lamentably low, and I shall not be satisfied until we have doubled the consumption of liquid milk in Ulster to the great
benefit of the community as a whole.
Major MCCORMICK: Will the right
hon. Gentleman take the statement from
me that large numbers-
Mr. SPEAKER : I will not.
(Laughter.) The hon. and gallant Member must not make a statement when it
should be a supplementary question.
Major MCCORMICK: Does the right.
hon. Gentleman agree with me that a
large number of my constituents do not
take grade A milk owing to the price of
it, and that they will not accept grade
B, and largely depend on tinned milk?
Mr. MIDGLEY: Is the Minister
aware that the medical superintendent
officer of health of Belfast has already
reported to the Public Health Committee
that there is a diminution in the consumption of liquid milk, and that at the
present moment he is preparing a report
based on the observations of the health
visitors?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: If it is a
fact that the hon. and gallant Member is
unable to drink milk will the Ministry
provide him with a comforter?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think that is
a matter for the Ministry of Commerce.

CLAUSE 4 (The Thiepval War
Memorial Fund).
Question proposed: "That the Clause
stand part of the Bill."
SHILLINGTON:
On the
Major
Second Reading of this Bill I raised a
question in regard to this Clause, and I
do not know whether the Minister has
had time to think over the matter. The
Advisory Committee in connection with
the Thiepval War Memorial are most
anxious that the War Graves Commission should take entire charge of this
memorial. They feel it is the only way
in which it will be properly looked after,
but I think I am right in saying that
the committee never contemplated that
this would necessitate the transfer of this
capital sum to the War Graves Commission. They consider that it still
should be held by the Ministry of
Finance and the income paid over to the
War Graves Commission. The original
idea of the Advisory Committee was that
the memorial should be handed over to
the War Graves Commission, but if that
is found to be difficult in carrying out,
without transferring the capital sum, I
do not know what the attitude of the
committee would be. As a member of
the Advisory Committee I do not support the Clause and must enter my
protest. It was never considered in this
form by the committee.
Mr. POLLOCK: I must honestly confess that when my hon. and gallant
Friend mentioned this matter first I did
not consider it of such consequence as to
disagree with him, but on a close analysis
of the whole situation I am bound to say
that I think the course suggested by this
Clause to be carried out would confer
greater and more permanent benefits to
the upkeep of our memorial than to leave
it in the hands of a body that is only
temporary in its work. Ministries go,
Governments go, and committees go, and
I think it will be agreed on all hands that
the effect of the disturbance of all these
bodies in the future might possibly lead
to the money which we now contemplate
leaving in the hands of the War Graves
Commission being devoted to purposes
other than that originally intended. This
committee which was appointed in order
to take care of the monument has not
considered, as my hon. and gallant
Friend has said, the question of the
transfer of the Memorial Fund. Hon.
Members, I am sure, will admit the
strength of the argument I am using,
that is to say, the possibility in the
future that this fund, which was
Financial Provisions Bill-
Third Reading
21 MARCH 1935
intended to perpetuate for all time a
memorial to our soldiers who fell in
battle, if left with the Ministry of
Finance or a committee might be disturbed and might be devoted to objects
other than that contemplated.
Let me say that the overseas Dominions
-I do not pretend I know all their
arrangements have adopted this course
for the great convenience that will accrue
from the arrangement. There will be
absolute security a hundred years hence
that the money will be in the hands of
an existing body whose duty it will be to
take care of the money when all of us
will have disappeared. I submit that the
hon, and gallant Member should not press
this and that on close examination of the
facts I have mentioned he will come to
the conclusion that for the ultimate
safety of the Fund it would be much
better in the hands of a permanent body
that will exist for all time to take care
of the monument of which we are all so
proud.
I do not like to run across the idea
of one who has given great service to the
work connected with the monument and
its preservation. My hon. and gallant
friend has done that, and I pay that
tribute to him in connection with the
matter. If he would examine the
question from the point of view I have
now submitted I have hopes that he will
perhaps agree that the Government are
acting in the interests of everybody. This
does not affect the powers of the Committee, as anything they want done can
be done within the limits of the funds
at their disposal. If they desired to improve the surroundings or make any improvement whatever, I know for a fact
the War Graves Commission would be
prepared to accept any suggestion of any
kind from the committee. It is on these
grounds I submit my arguments, and I
hope attention may be directed to them.
Major SHILLINGTON: While I am
not prepared to deal with what the
Minister has said, I may say I only make
my protest to keep faith with the fellow
members of the Committee, of which I
am a member and of which the Minister
of Finance is also a member. I am
confident they never contemplated that
their recommendation would mean going
as far as the Government evidently seem
to think they should go in this matter.
From the argument of the Minister of
Finance I think that if the Government
want to be perfectly right they should.
provide a further capital sum, the income
from which would produce this sum they
contemplate paying year by year towards
the upkeep of this memorial. I must
confess the Minister has not satisfied me
with the arguments he has produced, but
he
have
may
satisfied other hon.
Members.
Mr. BEATTIE: I think the best
memorial the Ministry could spend money
on would be some memorial to the living.
The CHAIRMAN: That, as the hon.
Member knows, is totally outside the
scope of this Clause.

in the House during the earlier stages of

raised the question of loans to farmers,
and the Minister then said there was provision for loans to farmers in some other
Acts. I find there are loans to owners

Landed Property Act, and there are loans
for the improvement of agricultural holdings under the Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Act.
Mr. POLLOCK: May I intervene for

Friend. He is apparently addressing a

Financial Provisions Bill-
Third Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. POLLOCK: I thought the Third
Reading had been passed.
Mr. SPEAKER: No. Perhaps the
hon. Member would repeat his statement.
We are on the Third Reading of the
Exchequer and Financial Provisions Bill.
Mr. O'NEILL: I am speaking in connection with loans to farmers for improvements to their buildings. I would suggest
that a provision should be included in this
Bill for the granting of loans to farmers
for the improvement of their holdings.
The other Acts under which loans for
buildings are granted are not so advantageous. Loans for seed, stock, manures,
and such like things are now given at 3
per cent., but the figure under the
Landed Property Act, I understand, is 4
per cent. or even 5 per cent. I think it
unreasonable that a farmer who can
borrow from one Department of the
Government at 3 per cent. would have to
pay 4 per cent, or 5 per cent. to another
Department. I suggest that the Minister
under the Bill now before the House
should have power to advance money to
farmers at the same rate of interest as
they pay for loans for seeds and manures.
It is because of the difficulty of securing
loans under previous Acts that I would
like the Minister of Finance to adopt my
suggestion. There is no reason that I
know of why a farmer should have to go
to the expense of proving title and
various other things in connection with a
loan for the improvement of his holding.
I remember raising this matter a few
years ago. A farmer at Ballynahinch
wanted a loan in order to improve his
farm buildings and he said it would cost
almost £20 to get a loan of £50. The
Minister himself admitted it would cost
more than £6. I do not see why a
farmer should have to go to the expense
of £6, apart from interest, to acquire a
loan. I suggest the Minister should
under the present Bill procure authority
to advance money to farmers, whether for
stock, manures, seeds, or improvements to
farm buildings and that the rate of
interest should be only 3 per cent.
Mr. POLLOCK: In reply to my hon.
Friend, as a matter of fact farmers can
have loans for improvements to their
properties at the rate of 3 per cent. provided they do not extend over a period of
five years.
To grant loans on such terms
is, I think, a very generous act on the
part of the Government toward the
farmers. If it is a long-dated loan the
rate will be 4 per cent. It does not
require any further legislation, I submit,
to enable farmers, if they are in any great
difficulty, to get the necessary accommodation under the Measures already in
existence. It was because of this it was
felt it was not necessary that there should
be anything additional in this Bill.
Three per cent. for a period of five years
is very generous on the part of the
Government.
Mr. BEATTIE: What does the city
owner get?
Mr. O'NEILL: Can a farmer have it
for five years for the improvement of his
holding?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes. What I have
said is that if the loan does not extend
beyond a period of five years the rate
charged to the farmer will be only 3 per
cent., but if it is a long-dated loan,
twenty years, for example-
Mr. BYRNE: I would say that five
years is a very short time because not
every farmer can avail himself of it. For
instance, if a man wanted to erect a
building or put up an extensive hayshed
five years would be a very short time in
which to raise the money. I suggest that
if the time was extended to ten years it
would be of great advantage to the
farmer.
Mr. SPEAKER: I suggest this question should be raised really in its proper
place, that is on the Estimates. We are
at present actually outside the Bill. I
allowed the hon. Member for Mourne to
make his point, but we are really out of
order.

Act, 1935, that the said Act shall extend

made the following amendment: Before
the word "Commons" insert the words

House that this is purely a formal matter.

Oral Answers to Questions.
GUARDIANS' DEDUCTIONS FROM
OLD AGE PENSIONS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether his attention
has been directed to a resolution passed
by the Belfast Board of Guardians at
their meeting held on

Tuesday, 19th
March, 1935, "That the Board should.
not accede to the request of the applicants on behalf of old age pensioners for
the recovery of all deductions from
pensions during their stay in the Institute"; whether this deduction of money
by the Guardians has been declared
illegal in the High Court, and, if so,
whether he will insist that all claimants
for a refund must be paid in full.
The following Question also stood upon
the Order Paper :-
2. Mr. BEATTIE: To ask the Minister of Home Affairs whether he is prepared to issue a summons against the
Belfast Board of Guardians for illegally
receiving sums of money from old age
pensioners.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): With the hon.
Member's permission, I will answer this
question and question No. 2, standing in
his name, together.
I have seen the resolution to which
the hon. Member refers, and I am not
aware of any High Court decision bearing on the matter. I can see no grounds
for questioning the legality of the
Guardians' action in the past, or of their
proposals as to the future, in regard to
old age pensioners in the workhouse.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the unsatisfactory answer to these questions, I have
already handed in Notice of Motion
which will deal with the two questions
concerned.
HILLSBOROUGH WATER SUPPLY.
3. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if his
conversations with the Ministry of
Finance have led to the provision of a
suitable water supply for the village of
Hillsborough.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The proposal
for obtaining a supply of water for the
town of Hillsborough from the lake in the
grounds of Government House is still
under consideration; but I am informed
by my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, that he expects to be in a
position to come to a decision on the
matter very shortly.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
26 MARCH 1935
CERTIFICATES OF STANDARD
EXPENDITURE.
4. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs when he proposes to issue the certificates of standard
expenditure and standard grant for the
five years commencing 1st April, 1935.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As my hon.
and gallant Friend suggests, the certificates now in force expire on the 31st of
this month and new certificates, fixing
standard grant and standard expenditure
for the ensuing five years, would in
normal circumstances be issued about this
period.
But owing to the new valuations coming
into force on the 1st April, 1936, if certificates were issued now they would
require complete revision after that date,
and the Government has accordingly
decided to extend the original certificates
for a further year. Legislation covering
the matter will be introduced at an early
date, and in the meanwhile draft certificates for a quinquennium commencing
1st April, 1936, will be forwarded to
local authorities for their observations
during the course of the next week or so.
WIDTH OF FIRST-CLASS ROADS.
5. Mr. MIDGLEY (for Mr. Henderson) asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state if any steps are
being taken in agricultural areas under
town planning to have all first-class roads
made seventy to one hundred feet wide
in order to take the increased volume of
motor traffic in the future.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No such
steps are being taken. The cost of any
general scheme such as the hon. Member
suggests would be prohibitive, but apart
from the question of cost it is clear that
such a drastic programme of road widening is neither necessary nor desirable.
The hon. Member is, no doubt, aware
that local authorities, with the assistance
afforded from the Road Fund, have been
widening and improving their roads.
where such works are desirable in the
public interest, and this policy will be
continued.
Dr. WILSON: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman whether he is aware that
the policy of the County Down surveyor
at the present time is to narrow down
the main road from Banbridge to Hillsborough, and if that policy is consistent
with safety first?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware of the policy of the County Down
surveyor, but if my hon. Friend will
place facts before me I will see what can
be done.
CIVIL SERVANTS' CONSOLIDATED
PAY.
6. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
if the new consolidated rates of pay for
civil servants are subject to the "cuts"
imposed in 1930, and whether the "cut"
has been restored in full or in part.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock) I presume that the hon. and
gallant Member has in mind the economy
cuts made in the salaries of Members of
the Government, Members of Parliament, teachers, and so forth, in April,
1931.
It will be remembered that when those
cuts were made, the Government considered that the automatic operation of
the Civil Service bonus arrangement had
already insured an adequate reduction of
Civil Service salaries consequent on the
fall in the cost of living and Civil Service salaries were not, therefore, subjected to an economy cut; a further reduction in the salaries of civil servants
did, however, take place in September,
1931, when bonus became related to a
cost-of-living figure of 50 instead of 55.
I do not, therefore, regard the
arrangement now made for the consolidation of basic pay and bonus as being in
any sense a restoration of an economy
cut; but, having regard to the method
adopted in the Imperial Civil Service, I
have decided to withhold half of the
comparatively trifling increases due
under the revised arrangements until
such time as the consolidation takes full
effect in Great Britain.
VALUATION APPEALS.
7. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether, if a person
wishes to appeal against his valuation,
the Commissioner will, on application,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major McCormick]
supply him with the gross figure at which
the valuer assessed the property concerned and the process of calculation by
which the final valuation figure was
arrived at.
Mr. POLLOCK: This matter is within
the statutory discretion of the Commissioner, but the hon. and gallant Member
may rest assured that every facility will
be given to intending appellants for the
prosecution of their appeals.
FUTURE OF STORMONT CASTLE.
8. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
if it is a fact that the Government have
already given instructions for the
preparation of plans for a new residence
for the Prime Minister, and whether
these plans are already completed or in
course of preparation.
Mr. POLLOCK: Various alternatives
for accommodating additional staff have
been under consideration, including a
tentative proposal to utilise Stormont
Castle for this purpose.
As no conclusion
has yet been reached in this matter, no
final instructions of the nature referred
to have been given.
RESIDENCES ON HILLSBOROUGH
RESEARCH FARM.
9. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
number of residences provided on the
Hillsborough Research Farm, the rateable value of these residences and by
whom the rates are paid.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked to reply to this question.
There are in all sixteen houses or
residences under the control of the
Trustees of the Agricultural Research
Institute. Fourteen of these are provided by the Trustees for the accommodation of the farm staff and their use constitutes part of the wages of the staff
concerned. As the Trust is a charity no
rates are payable in respect of these
houses.
The remaining two houses are let, the
Trustees paying the rates which in each
case are included in the rent. The
current valuation is in each case £24 and
the new valuation will in each case be
£36.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Would the
hon. Gentleman explain how an institute
of the nature of Hillsborough Research.
Station becomes a charity?
Mr. GORDON : That is a legal
question to which I cannot give an
answer.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask if the same
conditions apply to the residences on the
Ministry's estate at Loughrey?

Mr. BEATTIE: As this is a day of
roving on all matters pertaining to
administration, I think I have a licence
which will cover the points I want to
place before the House. I will first deal
with the Ministry of Home Affairs in so
far as the payment of the police and control of local government bodies are concerned. I would like the Parliamentary
Secretary to pay the attention to my remarks which I believe they deserve. We
have a very large number on the police
pay roll in Northern Ireland, and we
expect to get from them a return equal
to the amount we spend. We are at all
times anxious to protect the police against
being used for any purpose other than
what they were really intended to cover.
The police, however, were on last
Friday used in the Donegall Road area
for the purpose of covering up the bailiff
system in Northern Ireland. It is well
known to every Member of the House
that there has been for some time in
operation in that area a rent strike
against those property owners who have
increased rents which the tenants had no
possibility of meeting. Owing to the circumstances, the tenants had no option
but to take the line of least resistance and
refuse to pay the exorbitant rents
demanded.
Under your jurisdiction the landlords
took action for decrees of ejectment. The
law gives them the right to have the protection of the police in so far as keeping
peace and order in the city is concerned.
I have in my possession information showing that the police were used inside the
dwellings to assist the bailiffs in clearing
out the furniture. I am not saying this
is truthful, but I am asking you to make
a statement about it. The police in
uniform and plain clothes went into these
homes along with the bailiffs. I claim
that the bailiff has no right to protection
once he is inside the house. He goes inside
at his own risk. The only duty the policeman is asked to perform is to keep the
peace and prevent injury or loss of life.
(Hon. Members: Oh.) It is quite true.
A policeman cannot go inside the dwelling to assist the bailiff in removing
furniture from that home. He will stand
by and keep the peace and see that no
harm comes to anyone who is putting the
decree into operation. I want to bring
this communication before the House :-
To Mr. J. Beattie, M.P.
At
As you are probably aware of the
rent struggle which is taking place in
the city at the moment the above
organisation would like to draw your
attention to an incident which happened on last Friday, 22nd inst.
about two o'clock in the afternoon a
body of police, estimated at between 40
and 70, descended on the residents of
Rockland Street, Donegall Road, accompanied by five bailiffs and a number of
plain clothes men. They thereupon
forced their way into the houses and
terrorised the women. The bailiff
brandished-
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Brandy?
Mr. BEATTIE: No, we do not represent the brandy trade like the hon. and
gallant Member. The least he says about
brandy the better. This matter is too
important and too serious to be talking
about brandy. We have not the wherewithal to pay for brandy. The writing
in this letter is not too clear, but I make
it out to be that some important weapon
was brandished,
and he also held up a blue document,
which turned out to be a distress
warrant. The tenants had only been
on strike five days, and in view of the
tenants having paid two weeks in
respect of the houses and had not eaten
up one week's rent until the strike had
been in progress, the legality of the
whole thing is very doubtful. As a
matter of fact, some of the police who
took part in the raid said it was illegal.
Therefore, we would be greatly obliged
if you would ask a question on this
matter in the House.
That is presented by peaceful residents
in that street, who before taking their
homes had to pay two weeks rent, and
the rent strike was only on five days when
decrees were granted to the owners, and
the bailiffs, five in number, with a
regiment of police terrorised the residents.
Having drawn the Minister's attention to
this matter I am sure he will explain why

[Mr. Beattie]
the bailiffs insisted on the police going
into the homes of these people and giving

We
The next thing I want to bring before.
the Minister is the administration of local
government services. We have spent
huge sums on local government.
have made grants in respect of poor law
and exceptional distress. We have also
had elections taking place so that boards
of guardians would be composed of public
representatives elected by the people. We
have spent money in that direction for a
number of years now. I have found that
one board under your jurisdiction has
not lived up to the expectations of the
general public, or this House in particular, inasmuch as the standard of
decency in public life should be clean
and unsoiled, without any corruption.
We have seen references in the Press to
their low down mean action during the
last few weeks. I have in my possession
documentary evidence showing that
money given to the Belfast Board of
Guardians has not been put to the use
for which it was set out. I say it is the
Minister's duty as local government chief
to see that every board under his jurisdiction works in harmony with the law
laid down.
I am going to tell you now of what
we have come through during the last
three months, and give examples of
illegality that have been presented to us
by High Court judges and others. The
practice is still continuing at the present
moment in the Belfast Board of
Guardians of taking from old age pensioners and others money that they should
not be deprived of. The whole thing is
so farcical that I am going to present to
the House a document that should not be
recognised by anyone. This is a document you get patients of the guardians
to sign declaring that they will make
small contributions for their maintenance
in the institution. This form is 539 B.
It was drawn up when pensions were
granted so as to remove any difficulty
that relatives or friends of pensioners
might have when they were going to claim
pensions on their behalf, but it never
applied to old age pensions or as we would
call them the 65 and 70 pensions, because
it is set out at the top of the document,
"This form does not apply to old age
pensioners."
That form has been used for a number
of years by the agent of the Belfast Board
of Guardians, and he drew under it a
total sum of £3,000 odd in the last
seventeen months. He was the recognised
agent and approved of by the Ministry of
Home Affairs. On two occasions the
local government auditor-I will not
mention his name-drew the attention of
the guardians to the illegality of the
deduction. In fact two local government
auditors did that-one in 1932 and one
in 1933. Nevertheless you have turned
a Nelson eye on the position and taken no
action. The point is that a sum of
£3,455, or an average of £203 monthly,
has been taken from pensioners in the
past seventeen months.
Mr. SPEAKER: I should have interrupted the hon. Member before. He will
remember he has already discussed this
question on the Vote on Account.
Mr. BEATTIE: Not this question.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
now speaking about the Belfast Board of
Guardians. Is that not right?
Mr. BEATTIE: There are three or
four aspects of the Belfast Board of

Mr. SPEAKER: I understand that.
As a matter of fact, the hon. Member is

Mr. BEATTIE: I do not want to go

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): Perhaps the
hon. Member will tell us what they are
now.
Mr. BEATTIE: I will, from your own
auditors' minute which you have in Home

Union, but they had no power to interfere. That was bound to come to your

his observation that the Home Office took

Mr. BEATTIE: Yes, the amounts are
still being deducted. There has been a

you had taken a note of the local government auditors' remarks in the minute,
that list, which up to date totals £3,455,

Minister of Labour credit. He took
note, because he sent a man up to see that

I want to tell the Minister of Labour
that his conditions are not being fulfilled.
The minute here proves that his conditions have been put out of consideration altogether. The mark or signature
is not received from the patient. I do
not think that was the intention of the
right hon. Gentleman. The mark or
signature should have been received from
the patient, but to-day, I understand,
the books never go back to the ward for

I do not want. to go any further with
this at the moment, because I have put a
Motion down. I will have to extend it
to cover not only pension rights but also
the purchase and feeding of pigs, the contract for the boilers at present being
installed in the maternity home of the
Belfast Union, the contracts for food and
clothing, and that for lighting.
I am not accusing the Home Secretary
or the Parliamentary Secretary personally. As far as I can see they have
done everything they possibly could
except suppress the Board of Guardians
and appoint Commissioners as they did in
the case of Donaghadee and Armagh.
They were not as cruel in Donaghadee
and Armagh as the Belfast Board of
Guardians have been. When hardships
of the kind mentioned are being inflicted
upon the very oldest members of our community, it is the duty of the Home Minister to dismiss the Guardians.
In my
opinion they are a disgrace. I hope he
will do that if any more injustices are
perpetrated. I will leave the fuller
presentation of my case until my Motion
comes before the House. I believe I have
got in my point about pensions sufficiently, perhaps, to secure the sympathy of
the Parliamentary Secretary and his
chief so that they may get this thing
stopped once for all.
Before I leave that point I make a
charge if the Minister of Home Affairs
is prepared to accept it. The practice for
which one man got six months in jail is

master. He is being compelled by the
Guardians to continue that illegal
practice, and if he does not continue it
the Guardians will have him dismissed.
You need not turn up your face. This is
a statement you can inquire into and find
out about. The present master is being
compelled to carry on in the same illegal

six months. There is the documentary
evidence of it. The Parliamentary
Secretary cannot shake his head at a
matter so serious as this. I know the
Guardians. I am only now coming forward with stuff I, myself, spoke about
when I was a member of that Board, and
you allowed the police to put me out on
two or three occasions. You allowed the
police to evict me from the Board of
Guardians when I was there trying to

honour to the public boards of our area.
Mr. HANNA: The hon. Member will
not suggest that that was an improper use
to put the police to.
Consolidated Fund Bill—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. BEATTIE: It was an improper
use of the police, because I was trying to
clean up the Board. If you do not agree
with a cleaning-up process I would like to
hear your reply. I am not accusing the
police, because I am aware of the fact
that every member of that Board is a
satellite of yours or of your party. As
long as I am a Member of this House I
will proceed as I am doing now until I
see every piece of corruption cleaned from
the Belfast Board of Guardians. This is
only the beginning of a big cleaning-up
process which I hope will not stop at the
Belfast Board of Guardians. We have
other boards requiring strict attention.
But in view of the grave hardships
inflicted upon the old people here I
demand the restoration of that £3,455.
I want now to draw the attention of the
Minister of Labour to the administration
of the Acts under which he operates.
I am not going to be unduly critical of
the administration in view of the newness
of the legislation. One thing I do feel is
that he has inflicted a cruel hardship
upon a loyal band of civil servants employed under him for many years, by
sending them away from their wives and
families to lodgings in outlying districts.
I am not so sure that the allowances
granted, if any, are sufficient to cover the
requirements of these people who are compelled by the working of this new law to
go into various districts and take over
control. I have heard
one or two
grumble about it. I ask the Minister to
look into the expenses that a civil servant
requires over and above his usual allowance to maintain decency and get comfortable lodgings to which he is entitled
in the country districts where he is assisting in carrying out the new laws.
I want also to draw the attention of
the Minister of Labour to the Blind
Persons Act. The Minister took over
this service from the Minister of Home
Affairs, and we thought by the amalgamation we would get a cheaper service.
Perhaps some thought we were going to
get a more sympathetic service. I want
to say that the percentage of pensioners,
when the administration was carried out
by Home Affairs, has gone down considerably. Hundreds of persons who
were then granted pensions and were very
sympathetically considered, are now
denied the right to pensions altogether.
That is not the way to economise in order
to show a reduction in the estimate for
the Department for the following year.
I do not say the Minister of Labour is
less sympathetic than the Minister of
Home Affairs, but I do not know why
this is done. It should not be done.
When one Department authorised and
confirmed the qualifications of certain
people for pensions those pensions should
be allowed to remain. I should like to
see some relaxation granted, especially in
regard to conditions governing the Blind
Persons Act. The conditions now have
reached the extreme point as regards
qualifications. That point was never
reached before. I hope the claimants for
old age pensions will have every consideration given them.
Then we have the administration of
the Unemployment Insurance Acts. I
feel that, as the Minister of Labour is
spending huge sums of money, he should
make a real united effort with this House
and with every local authority in
Northern Ireland with the object of finding out how we stand industrially. Will
we be able in the future to maintain an
industrial army of 300,000 people? If we
are not, then we have to make provisions
in accordance with our responsibilities.
Mr. GORDON: Did you say 300,000?
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes. I would say an
industrial army of 300,000. I do not
mean to suggest that the remainder of
the million and a quarter people are
hangers-on or drones. I am not suggesting any such thing, but I do not think
we have any millionaires or multimillionaires in Northern Ireland. Most
people in Northern Ireland contribute in
some way, either by hand or brain, to the
prosperity of the Province as a whole.
Perhaps the hon. Gentleman will understand it more clearly this way: We have
a standing army at the moment of 70,000
unemployed people. Is it possible to
absorb those people into industry in
Northern Ireland at present? In my

Since then we have voted, including

The only additional revenue which is

we
will receive from the Imperial

a

Exchequer £100,000 more than we

able to even up our accounts.
I repeat
that we have voted £480,000 more than
our revenue as estimated by the Minister
of Finance, but I have no doubt that

balance in hand. I do not profess to see

increased amount from the British
Exchequer under the heading of income
tax receipts and customs and excise.
What does this all point to? Let me
say that our Reserve Fund, from which
we have taken £300,000 in the last two
years, has now a balance of only £130,000
remaining in it. These factors point to
this-we have either to look for new
sources of revenue or to reduce our expenditure. Let me deal with the expenditure. As far as I can gather, and I
referred to the Ulster Year Book to try
to bring the figures up to date, over 75
per cent. of our expenditure is governed
by known factors. Those factors are the
social services, which we, as part of the
United Kingdom, have undertaken to
maintain on an even scale. So long as
that policy is maintained-and if it is
not maintained the Government will be
immediately challenged by the majority
of the electors the only field in which
we can exercise economy is that of
administration. I have given the percentage of our expenditure in relation to
social services.
As regards revenue, 79 per cent. of our
revenue is a Reserved Service, and is expanded or contracted by the policy of the
Imperial Government. The remaining
21 per cent. of our revenue, over which
this Parliament has control, and some
of which is already subject to taxation on
a higher rate than the corresponding
scale in Great Britain, is not capable of
further expansion. Until revaluation
comes in our only sources of extra revenue
are the education levy and the unemploy
ment levy. Here I may say I understand that this is not the proper time to
discuss revaluation, as a debate on that
subject is coming on at half-past four,
but in connection with this revaluation,
whereby in future we hope to make our
expenditure and revenue balance, there
is a widespread feeling throughout the
Six Counties, of which the Government
that
must be fully aware,
we have
reached, if we have not passed, the taxable capacity of this Province.
It is a well-known axiom that when
taxation becomes excessive there is an
immediate reaction on trade and employment. I have said that the only possible
source of economy open to us, 80
long as we maintain our policy of
equal social services and any change
in that policy would be immediately
challenged in the House-is in administration. You would naturally rule
me out of order if I attempted to discuss that subject now, instead of on the

come
when they
forward.
What I am trying to point out is this.
The financial expedients by which we
have balanced our revenue and expenditure in the past have reached the limit
beyond which we no longer carry
them out. Our expenditure, which is
now governed by the policy of equal social
services, can be no further increased without straining the taxable capacity of the
Province beyond the point which it can
bear. What do these two factors point
to? In my opinion these two factors
point to the conclusion that sooner or
later our financial relations with Great
Britain will have to be examined, both
by the Imperial Government and our own
Government, in the light of these two
governing factors which I have tried to
indicate to-day.

The Revaluation of Northern Ireland.
MOTION TO POSTPONE THE ACT.
Major McCORMICK: I beg to move:
That, in the opinion of this House,
the operation of the Revaluation Act of
1931 should be postponed for five years
so far as rating and taxation effects are
concerned.
In addressing myself to the Motion
standing in my name I should like Members to understand that I am deeply
appreciative of the difficulties that face
the Government on this revaluation subject. Because of its grave importance to
all our people-whether they be property
owners or simple tenants of houses or
shops-I say this revaluation is and will
be felt by every person in the community.
Therefore, whilst recognising that it now
has the force of law, I ask in this Motion
that it should be postponed in its operation regarding taxation and rating for
five years. Legislation, of course, would
be required to effect this, but that should
not be an insuperable obstacle. I do not
propose to do much more than deal
with the reasons that, in my opinion
and that of others, call for postponing the operation of this
this Act.
I might recall the Griffiths Valuation of 1863. This Act was on a different
basis of values entirely from the present
Valuation Act, which I will call the
Robson Valuation of 1931. I will leave
it to others or to history to say which is
or was the more popular Act. After all,
history might record Griffiths as the
greater sinner of his time, but certainly
his sins disappeared when St. Robson
came on the scene.
The fact of the increased values, and
of the unpreparedness of the community
to meet them, is one of
chief reasons
my
for the postponement of the Act's operation. The term revaluation literally
means to revise or revalue a certain
article or property; it may be greater or
lesser. That is all very well in theory, but
the fact remains that in practice it means
increased values in 99 cases out of 100.
It means not only increasing them, but
doubling them and trebling them. I
would earnestly appeal to the Government for a postponement, on the
ground of confusion in the public mind,

Restriction Act, and on the ground that
values have been founded upon abnormal
conditions of rental-where the standard
that is set does not bear any relation that
is uniform and can only add to the discontent at the unfairness of this revaluation. It is safe to say that the appeals
will take some years to be heard, that at
least two judges of appeal will require to
be appointed to deal with them; therefore, it is a reasonable thing to say that
postponement would bring about a settlement and anomalies would be set right.
Whilst the argument holds good that
the times of depression in trade and

Mr. POLLOCK: The discussion has
ranged over so many features of this complicated problem that it would be very
difficult for me to take up the different
satements that have been made and deal

May I say by way of preface that the
Government cannot accept the Motion of

passing a Measure three years ago by

With that preface may I take up some
of the features of his claim. In the first
place, he spoke of the relative poverty of
Ulster. Now, I should like to remind
hon. Members that Ulster is materially
richer to-day than when this Government
took over power. All the indications of
that which can be investigated go to prove
the truth of the statement which I have
made. Therefore, to say because of
poverty we are not entitled to value the
hereditaments in the Province and put
them on a basis of equality is absurd.
The hon. and gallant Member spoke of
the terrible burden of taxation. Let me
remind the House that Ulster is not taxed
anything like as heavily as she was when
we took over power. In the year 1920-21
income-tax alone was 6/- in the £, and
now it is down to 4/-. That, as hon.
Members know, is a most remarkable
reduction, and a reduction which this
Government properly appreciates were it
not for the fact that it certainly renders
our financial arrangements a little more
difficult than they ought to be. A few
nights ago in addressing my constituents
I had occasion to go into that matter with
a little more particularity and I asked, or
rather suggested, that if they would
examine all the indices which can be
examined in connection with that problem
they would find that the trade, industry
and business of Ulster was in a more
favourable position to-day than it ever
has been in its history. This is proved by
the returns of the Belfast Harbour Board
in regard to the exportation and importation of goods. You cannot get any better
barometer of our position than that which
I have submitted.
I am now dealing simply with a few
general matters which have no direct
relation to valuation, but, at any rate, what
I have said tends to show that the change
which the hon. and gallant Member suggests has very little foundation in the
facts as they exist. I had prepared a considered statement to remove a great many
of the misconceptions and misapprehensions in regard to this whole matter. Let
me remind the House that when the
Belfast Corporation in 1906 called for a
valuation of the Province there was much
discussion by the inhabitants of Belfast,
and the fuss, turmoil and trouble which
ensued in connection with it were as great
as, if not greater than, anything we are
experiencing at the present time. I have no
doubt that when the people have twelve
months' experience of this matter, which
we are now discussing, the whole atmosphere will be so calm that people will
wonder what all this fuss and turmoil was
about.
As to the technical features of the whole
problem, it would be difficult for me to
take them up in detail, but I will deal with
the matter basing my remarks upon the
general statement which I had prepared
in order that if it is published in extenso
in the newspapers the people of Belfast
and the Province will understand the
exact nature of the application of this
matter to valuation. The first matter I
would touch upon is that of its relation
to income-tax, which has been rather
engrossing the Members who took part in
the debate. The advocates of one side or
the other are depending upon the effect
on the rates, but there are a great many
owners of property in this Province who
are subject to income-tax. The matter
is governed by the Income Tax Act of
1918. That Act provides that tax under
schedule A, that is, on property, is to be
ascertained according to the valuation in
force for the purposes of poor rate. That
is to say, that this valuation of ours effects
a dual purpose, and is to be accepted
by the inland revenue authorities as well
as by the rating authorities. It might,
therefore, be thought that if this Government postponed the effect of revaluation
for a further five years income-taxpayers
would escape from paying the proper
amount of income-tax due. That is a matter
to which, perhaps, my hon. and learned
Friend (Mr. Black) will pay some atten-
But there is a provision in the
same Act which says that if the Commissioners of Inland Revenue are satisfied that
the valuations in force are not correct they
tion.

Now I turn from income-tax matters,

Of course if I had time I could have
shown that, so far as income-tax is concerned, the anomalies were of such an
extraordinary character that it is really
remarkable that the British Government
allowed the matter to remain untouched
for so long. It is because of those

forced upon us. When I submitted the
Act in this House in 1931 I gave
