anomalies of such an extraordinary
character that the House was absolutely
convinced of the necessity for revaluation
as far as income-tax was concerned. I
need not go into those now, but when the
question is raised again I think it will
be necessary to do so in order that the
Government may show that the British
Government, at any rate, can show an
absolute vindication of its demand that a
revaluation should be made.
With regard to the individual ratepayer, there is no injustice except where
anomalies may exist. I would like to remind the House that in the valuation of
350,000 hereditaments it is not conceivable that every single one should be
absolutely correct, or that nobody could
find a loophole in them. There must
necessarily be some such cases, but those
can be dealt with on appeal. Injustice
exists now by reason of the fact that the
houses of a substantial number of per
sons, for one reason or another, have
never come up for annual revision, while
newer houses or houses in areas where the
rate collectors have been more efficient
in listing houses for revision, for example
in Belfast, have been paying rates on
valuations which were unfairly high compared to the valuations of their neighbours. As the hon. Member for Dock
(Mr. Midgley) very eloquently pointed
out, that
where great anomalies
existed, that some people were paying
on very high valuations and others on
very low valuations.
is
The consequence is that the former
class of householder has been paying
much less in rates than his due
proportion, and his neighbour for years
past has had to make up the difference.
This state of things obviously could not
be allowed to continue.
Looking at the situation broadly, unless local authorities embark on new expenditure no ratepayer who was fairly
assessed in the past will have to pay a
penny more in rates. If, however, a
ratepayer's valuation has been increased
in excess of the general percentage increase in the district he undoubtedly will
have to pay something more, but, while
he will lose, others whose valuations have
not been increased up to the full average
of the district will obtain a certain
relief-a relief to which they are entitled.
But the variation as between one and
another ought not to be very great.
Before leaving the individual, perhaps
I should refer to a few special cases where
buildings which have not been valued in the
past, or which were valued but appeared
in the exempt list, have now been valued
and have not been exempted. Since the
first Irish valuation was made and certain
premises became exempt there has been
created a whole body of case law in Great
Britain and in Ireland dealing with
exemptions, and if past practice has been
altered by the Commissioner in any case
hon. Members may be assured that he
has acted strictly on legal advice. I am
aware that some of these cases are diffi

ult, but the machinery of appeal to the

Turning now to the effect on local
authorities, revaluation should be welcomed by them in principle, on the
ground that they do not wish to favour
one ratepayer at the expense of another,
and now that all valuations have been
brought to their proper level local authorities can rest satisfied that in levying
their rates they are not doing any injustice as between one ratepayer and
another. We must all assume that the
mere fact of there being an increased
valuation of the area is not going to
lead local authorities into extravagant
or additional expenditure. Ratepayers
themselves must see to this.
am
The main fear of local authorities is
the effect of revaluation on derating
grants, more particularly in rural areas,
and this is where a great deal of complication will necessarily arise. It is because of this complication that I an
treating this subject from a considered.
and prepared statement rather than an
impromptu or extemporaneous reply, as
I desire to explain the relationship
between the local authorities and the
Government in respect to this derating
problem consequent on revaluation.
Hon. Members will understand that this
has been brought about by the fact that
agricultural land and farm buildings have
not been revalued. Assume that before
derating came into operation the valuation of agricultural land and farm buildings in a rural area compared with that
of other buildings was as five is to one.
This is just an example I am submitting.
This ratio may now be altered to, say,
4 for agricultural land and farm buildings and 1 to all other buildings. The
effect of this will be that in striking a
rate for, say, the sum of £120, while in
the past £100 of this was raised off land
and £20 off buildings, in future the
amounts would be £90 off land and £30
off buildings. As it is the Government
which now pays the rates on the land, it
follows that where in the past it gave,
in the example quoted, a sum of £100 to
a local authority it will in future only
give £90, and in consequence the
deficiency in derating grant must be
borne by the remaining
remaining ratepayers.
Local authorities appear to overlook that
the reason for their being hit in this
way is because when derating came into
operation buildings generally were undervalued and they were paying a smaller
proportion than they should of the whole
county rate. The farmers were being
unduly burdened in consequence, and
now as the Government has taken on the
place of the farmer it is the Government
which gets the relief.
I realise, however, that the increased
burden which would be thrown on local
authorities because of this change is
appreciable, and therefore I have made
it clear in replying to a question some
days ago that the Government intends
to observe faithfully the provisions of
Section 24 of the Valuation Act of 1932,
and consult with the local authorities
before finally determining whether this is
a burden proper to be borne by them. I
am sorry that I canot follow this subject
any further as my time is up, and I now
beg to move "That the Question be now
put."

Loans Guarantee Bill
27 MARCH 1935
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 27th March, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
SPEED LIMIT FOR MOTORS IN
BUILT-UP AREAS.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he has considered the advisability of introducing a
reasonable speed limit for motor vehicles
in built-up areas in Northern Ireland on
similar lines to the thirty miles per hour
limit in England; whether in England
this new regulation has resulted in any
congestion on thronged roads, or the
slowing down of traffic at the boundaries
of cities or towns; and whether there is
any noticeable diminution in the practice
of fast-moving vehicles speeding and overtaking others.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This is a matter
that I have had under consideration from
time to time. It is obviously much too
early to form any conclusion as to the
efficacy or otherwise of the speed limit in
built-up areas which has been put in
force in Great Britain, but I am watching the experiment carefully.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
right hon. Gentleman is high speed not
the cause of a very large number of road
accidents in Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. If I had
formed that opinion I would put the speed
limit into force in Northern Ireland
straight away.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In moving the Second Reading
of the Loans Guarantee Bill I feel that
this is the appropriate occasion on which
I am permitted to rehearse the full story
of the operations of that Act since its
beginning, also its present position and
future outlook. I would remind the
House that shortly after our Government
and Parliament were established, the
British Government, with a view to encouraging expenditure on new works of
capital value, adopted the policy of
guaranteeing loans made to those persons
who were prepared to embark on capital
expenditure of that kind. The Act
which was passed to carry out this policy
was known as the Trade Facilities Act.
With a view to providing employment in
Northern Ireland, our Government
decided to follow the British policy, and
passed a similar Act known locally as the
Loans Guarantee Act.
•

Following the British practice,
appointed a small Advisory Committee of
businessmen, whose duty it was and is to
analyse the applications of those who
wished to take advantage of the Act, and
to express their views, after a careful
examination of the financial standing of
the applicant company, as to the nature
and value of the security offered.
personnel of this Committee has, through
death or resignations, changed from time
to time, and at present consists of a wellknown chairman of a very large business
enterprise in Belfast, a leading city
accountant, and a retired banker. I feel
that no more representative or efficient
body could have been found to advise our
Government in regard to these matters.
At this point I would like to pay a
tribute to the self-sacrificing and patriotic
labours of these gentlemen, and the
valuable services they have rendered to
this Province without expecting fee or
reward.
The Loans Guarantee Act, although
available for capital expenditure in the
form of new works of any kind, was
necessarily mainly taken advantage of in
this community by shipowners in connection with their
their shipbuilding programmes, and it is, therefore, to this

shown by the Parliamentary returns,
which have been furnished to the House

£16,000,000 have been given by our

Act.

hon. Gentleman's recollection
of my
words is at fault. I do not think I ever

Now, let me remind the House that
the Loans Guarantee Act is intended first
and last to provide employment for
Ulster labour. Successive Parliaments
in this Province over a period of twelve
years have endorsed and approved its
value; and it must be remembered that
these twelve years have been marked by
conditions of commercial uncertainty and
depression unprecedented in modern
history.
The operations of the Act began at the
early period between 1922 and 1926,
when we succeeded in securing valuable
Royal Mail contracts for the yards on the
basis of the joint assistance of the
Imperial Government. The Imperial
Government covered with its guarantee
employment created in Britain by the
manufacture of raw material, and the
Northern Parliament covered the local
employment in the building of the ships
and the manufacture of the machinery.

Is it any wonder that I and my
colleagues whole-heartedly co-operated
with the British Government in the reorganisation of this great shipping edifice
which occupies such a pre-eminent
position in our mercantile marine? This
reorganisation, so far as the two Governments' financial interests are concerned,
amounts to this: the fleets of the old
companies, including those built under
guarantees, were handed over in three
groups; the first group was handed over
to a new company operating on the South
American route, the second to a new
company operating on the West African
route, the third to a new merger company
operating in the North Atlantic, in
exchange for shares. We are, therefore,
dependent on the earnings of these fleets
to meet the dividends on those shares held
by us, but the ships in which we were
interested, owing to their new construction, had such high values in relation to
the rest of the fleets that we have a very
satisfactory position in relation to earnings. The mortgages on the ships have
been, in brief, exchanged for more liquid
assets, namely, shares, and these shares
are held by us in companies untrammelled
by previous complications or any prior
changes.
To-day, therefore, I am glad to say
that the tonnage produced by these loans.
is of such a splendid modern type, and
the management of the companies which
now operate it is so efficient and successful, that we may reasonably hope for a
favourable ultimate outcome.
I now briefly touch on the third group
of ships which operated on the North

is likewise transformed into shares, and
indeed we have under the scheme a very

British Government.

It is true that the foregoing reorganisations had only been successfully effected

It may be that some excuse may be
found for the exaggerations in regard to
the character of our guarantees, because
of the complexity of the Royal Mail
organisation and the inevitable confusion

called the parent companies of so many

deficiencies concern in the main the
unfortunate shareholders of these concerns, and may I say definitely that our
securities are quite independent of the
parent Royal Mail Steam Packet Company and the parent Elder Dempster
Company, which have gone into liquidation after a somewhat notorious ending.
Neither has the liquidation of the White
Star Line, which has been recently
reported, any reaction whatever on our
guaranteed position. These liquidations
were merely the cutting away of dead
wood which never had any direct interest
to Northern Ireland. To summarise the
position, it is that, on the transfer of
our ships to the new companies, our
interests from that moment lay with the
trading results of the new companies.
To these results we must look for funds
to recoup us in respect of the payments
we have made-I hope only temporarily
-and it will be of interest to the House
to know that, arising out of the close
touch with the Boards of these concerns,
at the heads of which are such eminent
shipowners as Lord Essendon and Sir
Richard Holt, I am glad to be able to
report that the time is not very far distant when substantial receipts will be
forthcoming from this source; in fact, I
have reason to believe that we may
shortly hear of a positive result in rela
tion to 1934. Be this as it may, these two
companies are setting aside large reserves,
thus increasing the value of our security,
and at the same time placing themselves
in a position to build the new tonnage
which would be of such interest to us in
Belfast. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I need not remind hon. Members that in

means the throwing out of employment of

they can I use the expression ?—rust
through disuse what is the effect if, as

ment, all our great shipyards or many

unless he wished it and unless he thinks

period 1922-1926 when ships were built
for the four companies in arrear with
their interest. It was in that period that
the results of the collapse of the Royal
Mail group began to take effect. It might
not happen in one hundred years that
anything like the collapse of the Royal
Mail group would take place, because it
was so phenomenal in British industry
that really no description that I can give
would give full colour to what took place
in regard to it. I do not mean to the
Royal Mail Company itself; I refer to
the reactions upon the other companies in
which we are interested, because all the
companies of a very large group were
affected by the Royal Mail collapse.
The hon. and learned Member for
Central and the hon. Member for Mourne
are mistaken in supposing that we have
any touch at all with the Royal Mail
Steampacket Company proper. The companies now working in connection with
those that were affected by the Royal Mail
collapse are large, prosperous companies
making considerable sums of money and
putting large sums to reserve. Those
sums are intended for the purpose of
building new ships which are required,
notwithstanding the fact that some
Members have stated that additional shipping is not required. There are so many
redundant ships of a particular class that
there must necessarily be large shipbuilding increases in the very near future.
I say, taking that broad view, and

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
What I wanted particularly to impress
upon this House is, that such a thing as
took place in those four years to which
I have referred is not likely to take place
again, and that the twenty companies we
have been interested in from that period
forward have lived up to their obligations.
There is no difficulty about their living
up to their obligations, as they are paying the interest upon their money and
also the extinction money.
The position is not at all serious, except
in so far as we were caught in the reactions of the Royal Mail collapse in the
years 1922-1926. We are working out of
it now by reason of the fact that the
magnificent tonnage we have providedthe finest tonnage on the ocean-is the
greatest asset to these companies. These
ships have helped to leaven, if I may say
so, the tonnage of the older type in
existence, and which must gradually be
eliminated from the ocean before really
prosperous conditions can obtain for the
shipping of Britain. That is why the
President of the Board of Trade has
undertaken what is called the scrap-andbuild policy, that is to say, he desires
that there should be new tonnage in place
of useless, obsolete ships, so that the
British mercantile marine may be provided with the most modern and
economical shipping which can compete
with anything the foreigners can produce.
That is the general position in regard
to shipping, and therefore for the future
I have not the slightest fear that any
engagements we may enter into in respect
of the operations of the Loans Guarantee
Act will be of such a character that the
Government will
run anything but a
minimum risk. I do not, in fact, think
from this time forward there can be the
slightest possible risk run by the Government in anything they may undertake
in connection with the Loans Guarantee
Act.
So far as the hon. Member for Mourne's
remarks are concerned, we need not discuss them, because he was rather confused
and did not seem to understand what
exactly the position is. I have only to
repeat that in passing the Second Reading
of this Measure the Government will not
regret that they have again continued
this policy for two years. After that
the Government and Parliament can
settle for themselves what will be done,
but in the meantime I think it is a wise
proceeding.

28 MARCH 1935
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 28th March, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
DUNDONALD SEWERAGE
SCHEME.
1. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state if in the Dundonald sewerage
scheme it is proposed to allow the
sewage to flow into the Knock River,
and what will eventually become of this
sewage before it reaches its outlet in
the Lough.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is not proposed
to allow the sewage from this scheme to
flow into the Knock River. By arrangement with the Belfast Corporation the
Dundonald sewage will be discharged
into the sewers of the Corporation.
MILK FOR ICE-CREAM.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Henderson) asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether any representations have been
made to him by the members of the
Northern Ireland Ice-Cream Temperance
Association to have the price of milk
reduced to the same price as that which
prevails in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): The answer

Oral Answers to Questions.
AMALGAMATION OF MARKETING
BOARDS.
1. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether, in the interest
of economy, he will consider the amalgamation of the different agricultural
marketing boards into one small council
consisting of not more than five representative members.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Basil Brooke): I think the
hon. Member is under a misapprehension
as to the number of marketing boards.
established. Only two agricultural
marketing boards have been set up,
namely, the Pigs Marketing Board and
the Bacon Marketing Board.
an
Parliament last session passed
Agricultural Marketing (Pig Industry)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1934, for the
specific purpose of co-ordinating the work
of these two boards and this has now
been done.
THE PIGS AND BACON BOARDS.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Agriculture whether his attention
has been called to the report issued on
the 25th ultimo by the Bacon Marketing
Board, complaining of the hostile propaganda by the Pigs Board and stating that
foreign and Empire bacon is on sale at
very cheap prices, while the cost of homeproduced bacon has very substantially
increased and its consumption materially
diminished owing to fictitiously high
prices; and whether he proposes to take
steps for the protection of producers and
consumers of the home product in view
of these disquieting statements.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have seen in
the Press the report issued by the Bacon
Marketing Board to which the hon. and
learned Member refers. I am unaware
of any hostile propaganda to the Bacon
Marketing Board on the part of the Pigs
Board.
I am unable to follow the arguments of
the hon. and learned Member in the
latter portion of his question. As, however, he appears to be under some misapprehension as to the correct facts, I
may be permitted to state concisely the
present position.
During the first four months of 1935
it is anticipated that the supply of
foreign bacon imported into the United
Kingdom under the quota arrangements
will be at the rate of 5,921,000 cwts. per
annum, as compared with 11,650,920
cwts. in 1932. The output of bacon in
the United Kingdom this year is esti
mated at 2,842,000 cwts. as compared
with 1,750,000 cwts. in 1932. The expansion of the pig industry in the United
Kingdom is thus apparent. The expan
sion in Northern Ireland has been even
greater and the output of bacon pigs in
1935 is estimated at 542,000 as compared with 300,000 in 1932, and our output is still steadily increasing. I feel
that the House will agree with me that
a very large measure of protection to the
home producer has been afforded by these
measures. The consumption of bacon
produced from Northern Ireland pigs has
increased by over 80 per cent. and the
consumption of United Kingdom produced bacon by 68 per cent., and the
suggestion that the consumption of the
home product has materially diminished
is grotesque. There is, further, no
vestige of truth in the suggestion that
home bacon is sold at fictitiously high
prices. The home product is sold on the
United Kingdom market in open competition with foreign and Empire bacon,
which the hon. and learned Member complains is sold at very cheap prices. I
fail to appreciate how the price of the
home product can, therefore, be fictitiously high. I may add that the
prices paid by curers for pigs are determined by means of a formula related to
the current price of bacon which was
agreed upon between the Pigs and Bacon
Marketing Boards. Here, again, no
question of a "fictitious" price arises
for, under the formula, pig prices are
related to bacon prices which, in turn,
are governed by the free play of conditions on the United Kingdom market.

ACTIVITIES OF THE
WARBLE FLY.
3. Mr. STEWART asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether it is the intention
of his Department to introduce to the
farmers of Northern Ireland "Polvo" in
order to restrict the activities of the
warble fly.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Action on the
lines suggested by the hon. Member has
been taken by my Ministry for several
years.
During the past six years demonstrations have been carried out by my
Ministry in conjunction with the County
Committees of Agriculture with a view
to encouraging the dressing of cattle with.
"Polvo" wash to destroy warbles. These
demonstrations have been uniformly
successful and will be continued.
Exhibits showing the damage done to
hides by the warble fly have been staged
in the Ministry's educational exhibit at
the Royal Ulster Agricultural Society's
Show at Balmoral during the past six
years, and it is also proposed to continue
these. The exhibits have been valuable
in drawing attention to the treatment
advocated.
Further, advantage was taken of the
facilities offered by the British Broadcasting Corporation to broadcast messages to farmers at the appropriate
season, advising them to treat all cattle
for the destruction of warbles. A leaflet
giving the results obtained in Northern
Ireland from dressings of "Polvo" was
published by my Ministry in 1931 and it
has been in wide and constant circulation to the farming community ever
since. I am sending a copy of the
leaflet to the hon. Member for his information.
I think it is generally realised
amongst the agricultural community that
efforts are likely to be made in the near
future to stamp out warble fly in the
United Kingdom and thus prevent the
great annual loss to our cattle industry
occasioned by this pest. I am at present
considering what further steps can be
taken in Northern Ireland in this
matter.
Mr.
CHRISTIE: Would it. be
advisable to place these exhibits in local
shows as well as in the Belfast show,
showing the ravages of the warble fly?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: If it has not
already been done, I will consider that.

CLAUSE 1 (Judge of court of quarter

Question proposed: "That the Clause

Ι
Mr. CRAWFORD: I wish to say a
word on this Clause 1. It looks an
innocent and harmless Clause on the surface of it. It mentions that the county
court judge is to be the sole judge at
quarter sessions. Every person has confidence in the county court judges.
have had the honour and pleasure of sitting with them, and have found them to
be exceedingly courteous and able men.
Anything that I say now is not to be
taken as a reflection on them in the
slightest degree. They have discharged
their duties satisfactorily. I would like
to ask what does this apparently harmless
Clause mean? It deprives county
justices of the privilege and honour that
they now enjoy of acting as colleagues in
the criminal portion of the quarter
sessions business. Borough magistrates
have not had the privilege of acting at
general or quarter sessions for some years
past, but the county justices have had
this right for a great many years, indeed
for centuries. This Clause proposes to
deprive these justices of the honour of
sitting at quarter sessions.
I would like to draw the attention of
the Committee to this fact, that away
back as far as 1375-6, in the 14th
century, in the days of Edward III,
magistrates were appointed to try at
quarter sessions all felonies and trespasses whatsoever committed within the
county. Under his grandson, Richard
II, not only were they expected to attend
quarter sessions, but were actually paid
4s per day for attending to their duty.
Four shillings does not seem very much
now, but it was a big sum in those days.
Even if they were asked to do it for only
fourpence or for nothing, I say this is a
thing that should not be easily done away
with. In 1590 a new form of Commission was agreed upon. This combined the particulars of a number of
statutes and the central facts of it with
some variations are in use to this day.
Now this Government says the magistrates are not qualified to act. I do
think that is a reflection on the education
and civilisation that we are proud to
boast has taken place. Surely the people
unfortunate enough to be magistrates
have shared in the advance of that education and civilisation? This honour and
privilege that they have enjoyed should
not now be taken from them.
In my experience--and I have a
lengthened experience-magistrates have

court of summary jurisdiction.
were many occasions

which magistrates sat when it was not clear whether
they were sitting as a court of summary
jurisdiction or not. The framework of
this Clause is that a resident magistrate
can sit either in or out of petty sessions,
and that when a resident magistrate is
sitting the fact that he is sitting constitutes a court of summary jurisdiction.
The necessity for that-as some hon.
Members opposite who are well acquainted
with the law will know-is that in a
great many of the Acts which confer
jurisdiction upon a court of summary
jurisdiction the words "summary jurisdiction" are used, and they are used in
different senses. Now when you look at
any of these Acts and take it in conjunction with Clause 2 of this Bill, it will be
quite plain whether the court is a court
of summary jurisdiction or not. It is a
court of summary jurisdiction if it is presided over by a resident magistrate,
whether he is sitting in petty sessions or
out of petty sessions.
With regard to the remaining duties
which are left to ordinary justices of the
peace by this Bill, such as taking depositions and doing other things which the
Committee will see are set out in the next
Clause, the ordinary justices will sit not
in petty sessions but out of petty sessions
and, therefore, they will not constitute
a court of summary jurisdiction. But
they will be entitled to take depositions.
As most hon. Members are aware, when
a magistrate takes depositions he does not
adjudicate upon the matter that is then
before him. He merely reduces to writing, in the form of depositions, the
evidence of all the witnesses; those
depositions have to come before the
Attorney-General
to see whether a
prosecution is to be directed; and if a
prosecution is directed then the case goes
before a jury, who find the facts, presided over either by a county court judge
or a judge of the High Court. Members
of the Committee will realise that the
taking of depositions is a matter that
very often can be satisfactorily done by
an ordinary justice. It will be a convenience that in certain cases an ordinary
justice should be allowed to take depositions. When you look at the framework
of the Bill, and once the general
principle of the Bill is conceded, I submit that this is a necessary part of the
Bill and that the real matter of principle
is one which arises not upon this Clause
at all but upon the succeeding Clause 3.

Veterinary Surgery Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move the
Second Reading of this Bill. The Bill
seeks to check the recurring losses to
farmers and stock owners and to prevent
torture to animals caused by the misguided activities of venturesome amateurs
who rashly undertake the treatment of
serious cases of illness or injury to
animals, cases in which trained skill is
indispensable. Unnecessary losses and
at times indescribable and horrible
suffering are caused to dumb creatures by
these activities in cases where qualified
veterinary practitioners by proper prescriptions and proper treatment could
have averted losses and rescued the
animals. I do submit to the House that
at the present time, as the law stands,
there ought to be some limitation on
activities of this kind. It is hardly
right that unqualified and untrained
persons should be free to practice what I
would call their prentice hands in difficult
and hazardous cases-cases where the
work should be undertaken by qualified
and trained men who have fitted themselves for the task by intensive study of
years as a matter of fact five years—
and by the ability to pass examinations
of a high standard and to have reached
certain degree of professional competence.
a
The Royal College of Veterinary
Surgeons conducts all the qualifying
examinations for veterinary surgeons in
Great Britain, in the Irish Free State,
and in Northern Ireland.
The profession has one course of examination
and one course of training. It has one
standard of learning, a high standard,
throughout these Islands. The college I
refer to is the supreme training authority
for all students in the three territories.
As matters now stand, any jack-of-alltrades with no qualifications whatever is
free to undertake veterinary surgery and
veterinary medicine even in aggravated
cases, without any restriction whatever
in Northern Ireland. Their names need
not appear on the register of the College
of Veterinary Surgeons and need not
appear on any register at all. It is perfectly true that they cannot use the title
veterinary surgeon or use the affix V.S.
It is perfectly true they cannot sue in
courts for any work done as a veterinary
practitioner, but there are some who
flourish notwithstanding and who, I
submit to the House, flourish on confusion and illusion.
For ordinary practical purposes there
are many, especially in the poorer ranks,
Veterinary Surgery Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
who cannot tell the difference between
trained and untrained men. I should
like to read to the House a letter I
received from a distinguished veterinary
surgeon in one of the Northern Ireland
towns. He says:
"In this town, in the main street
with myself, there is a man practising
who was chauffeur to my predecessor.
He is now running a car round the
country attending cases, and keeps an
open surgery. I wrote several times
to the secretary of the Royal College
of Veterinary Surgeons, but got a
reply that nothing could be done as
the law stood. I think it is rather
hard on a man who has gone through
college and studied to pass all the
examinations and then to find that the
law allows a man whose experience is
as chauffeur to a veterinary surgeon,
to start to practise on his own, and
as you know many people will come to
him if he attends to a case for a few
shillings less. These things lower the
status of the veterinary surgeon and
do not encourage men to become
veterinary surgeons. I have a son of
my own I would like to see qualified,
but I would be chary in advising him
as matters stand now. Every other
profession seems to have some measure
of protection, but veterinary surgeons
have absolutely none."
There is nothing in this Bill that
directly or indirectly seeks to interfere
with home remedies and ordinary home
cures by persons in Northern Ireland
keeping animals for profit or otherwise.
There is nothing in the Bill which can
possibly be construed as restricting in the
least way the enterprise and activities of
farmers or their servants or stock owners
in performing ordinary operations or
administering ordinary cures incidental
to the care and management of animals.
No restriction of that kind is intended.
I do submit that farmers require a professional man in the cure of their animals
in serious disorders, serious injuries, or
serious illnesses of any kind, and they
should be facilitated in distinguishing
between the qualified practitioners on the
one hand and their crude imitators on
the other.
In all cases of grave operations the
practice of skilless men, sometimes called
horse doctors, sometimes called horse
surgeons, sometimes called cow leeches and
sometimes called cow doctors, whatever
title may be used, dabbling in cases of
serious complaints, is not a practice to be
encouraged in the public interest. It
means loss to the farmers and it means
torture to dumb animals. It is lowering
and prejudicial to the status of an
honourable and public-spirited profession. As I said before, it is not all
the unqualified men who pretend to interfere in cases of this sort. It is what
might be called the swankers and
adventurers. I do say that the ordinary
unqualified man draws the line before
venturing to interfere.
If the House thinks it wise to adopt
this Measure its presence on the Statute
Book will be deterrent to these venturesome spirits. There can be no denying
the fact that it is harmful for the
unqualified tyro to practise and diagnose
cases of a serious nature. There is
anthrax, swine fever, and foot-andmouth disease. In cases of that kind a
correct diagnosis is indispensable. The
contagion may spread with lightning
rapidity. The tyro, in his blindness,
may embark on a futile and mistaken
regimen, and then what happens?
calls in the qualified man and calls him
when it is too late. The peculiarity of
some of these men is that they will not
prescribe any of their raw cures for their
own ailing animals. They are astute
enough in their own interests to summon
in a qualified man. And yet they do
not hesitate to run risks at the expense
of their own neighbours.

In the British House of Commons there

Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the
answer is perfectly simple. The justice
of the peace who is taking depositions
does not in any way determine the result
of the case. Under his supervision
depositions are taken down. They are
forwarded in due course to my right hon.
Friend, the Attorney-General, who in
his turn decides whether there is a prima
facie case to be sent either to quarter
sessions or to the assizes. Then, again,
it comes before a grand jury, who in
their turn also decide, or it is decided
by petty jurors.

I recently read of a case which was
tried before a resident magistrate in
County Tyrone, where a motorist was
charged with being drunk in charge of

in the witness box that the police doctor
who examined the motorist would not
certify that he was drunk. Yet, if the
case was properly reported, the resident
magistrate, in fining the defendant, said
he could not get behind the police
evidence. This in spite of the fact that
the policeman had admitted the police
doctor would not say the man was drunk.
That very decision damns this whole Bill,
because the Government, through the
Minister of Home Affairs, holds that a
trained lawyer is the proper person to
try these cases, and yet in a case where
a trained doctor is in a position to say
whether a man was drunk or sober the
Crown will not produce him. If that is
in keeping with the spirit of British.
justice I do not know what British justice
is. Here is an actual case where a
resident magistrate accepted the police
evidence that a motorist was drunk,
although the policeman himself in the
box admitted that the police doctor certified the man was not drunk.

This is a re-casting of the Clause as it
originally appeared in the Bill. This,
again, was done at the representation of
the Incorporated Law Society and some
other persons who were interested in this
particular matter. It will be noticed
that the main difference is in regard to
the power of the court to adjourn these
applications for possession of premises.
As the Clause originally stood, it would
have been open to the resident magistrate to adjourn the cases generally without giving any reason, and it was pointed
out that that might operate as a hardship, because, in the event of a great
number of cases, instead of endeavouring to get through the cases the resident
magistrates might adjourn them without
giving any reasons. Under this redrafted Clause
the court may stay or suspend the
execution of the warrant for such
period or periods as it thinks fit, subject to such conditions, if any, in
regard to payment of arrears of rent,
rent or mesne profits, and otherwise
as the court thinks fit,
making it possible for the court to make
conditions when adjourning the case.
Then the second portion of the redrafted Clause enacts that the warrant
issued under this section shall remain in
force for three months, and for such
further period as the court may from
time to time direct. It was pointed out
that there might be cases, owing to a
person being away, or some other
fatality, in which the warrant for possession of the premises might run out
before it was possible to have it properly
executed. Accordingly the Ministry,
having looked into the matter, have prepared this redrafted Clause, which, I
think, will commend itself to the Committee.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

the sums

would be a great hardship on an individual who was not responsible for his
cattle breaking out on to the road that

reason I have put down this Amendment.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: I beg
to move,
"That the Clause be read a
Second time." This is a matter of some
little difficulty. The Government did not
intend that the new jurisdiction given to
petty sessions courts in ejectments should
be exclusive, that is to say, they did not
intend-and I think the Committee
would not think it proper-that all the
ejectment jurisdiction should be driven.
into the petty sessions courts. For one
thing it would overload the courts and
the business would not be as well done as
it ought to be done. But there is a rule
in the county court with reference to
costs. A county court judge has discretion in cases which might have been
brought at petty sessions to refuse costs
to the successful plaintiff because he
might have gone into the inferior court.
The Government wanted to make it
plain that that should not be so and that

HOME FOR MENTALLY DEFECTIVE
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In general, the maximum total
charge for a certified copy of an entry of
birth whether obtained at the Union
Workhouse, Belfast, or elsewhere in
Northern Ireland, is 3s. 7d., made up of
1s. search fee, 2s. 6d. for the certificate,
and 1d. Stamp Duty. These charges
were fixed as long ago as 1863 upon the
basis of the services rendered. Since
that time, numerous Statutory Provisions
have come into force under which certificates are provided at reduced fees when
In some
required for special purposes.
such cases, the total charge is 1s. per
certificate, but more generally 6d. only
is charged.
The bulk of the certificates issued are
provided at the cheap rates. The fees
paid represent the remuneration of the
issuing officers, and in the circumstances
no further reductions are contemplated.

HENDERSON
asked
the
1. Mr.
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Education whether he can state the

afflicted children will be opened.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): It is anticipated that the Haypark School will be
brought into operation before the end of
this year; it is at present impossible to
give an exact date. I can, however,
assure the hon. Member that the work of
adapting the premises which have been
acquired for the purpose of the school is
now well advanced. I may add that the
medical officer of the Ministry of Home
Affairs has also made good progress in
the
selection of mentally defective
children likely to benefit by the type of
instruction to be provided.

A STAG HUNT.
the
his
3. Mr. HENDERSON asked
Minister of Home Affairs whether
attention had been drawn to the cruelty
that took place recently when a stag
hunted by the County Down Stag Hounds
had to swim across Belfast Lough; and
whether he will introduce a Bill to
prevent cruelty of this kind being
practised.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): In the absence
of my right hon. Friend I have been
asked to reply:
I have no information in regard to the
incident referred to by the hon. Member
beyond what I have seen in the public
Press. I may say, however, that I have
been informed by those acquainted with
the habits of stags that it is not unusual
for these animals in their wild state
voluntarily to swim great distances, and
I am not therefore prepared to accept the
hon. Member's suggestion that any
cruelty was caused.

Unemployment (Extension of Enactments) Order (Northern Ireland),
1934.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Order in Council made under
section fifty-six of the Unemployment
Act (Northern Ireland), 1934, for extending and modifying the said Act so
as to make provisions thereof correspond
with the provisions of the Unemployment
Act, 1934, passed by the Parliament
of the United Kingdom be hereby
approved."
Mr. ANDREWS: Hon. Members will
recollect that the Northern Ireland
Unemployment Act of last year was
passed through both Houses of Parliament before the corresponding Act had
passed through all its stages in the
Imperial Parliament. Section 56 was
therefore inserted in our Northern Ireland Act whereby the Governor, by Order
in Council, might extend or modify our
Act in the event of any amendment being
made in the British Measure after our
Act was passed. The reason for this
course being adopted was that our House
would not, it was recognised, at that
time be in Session.
Certain minor Amendments, mostly of
a drafting nature, were in fact subsequently made by the Imperial Parliament,
and these Amendments were applied to
the Northern Ireland Act by Order in
Council, as provided for. Approval of
the House is now sought, as otherwise the
Order would cease to have effect after a
period of twelve months.
The Amendments made by our Order
are, as I have said, of a minor description, the only ones of any moment being
contained in paragraphs 8 and 12:-
Sub-section 3 of Section 27 of the A
Unemployment Order

the section

we

That is the reason why I want to know-
Mr. SPEAKER: I may point out to

Unemployment Order
Business of the House
4 APRIL 1935
Mr. GORDON: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: No one outside an
asylum would suggest that the Amendments should be rejected, but I feel that
some of the Amendments could be
improved. One improvement I could
suggest would be the lightening of the
qualifications of the individual.
Mr. ANDREWS: That would not be
step by step.
Mr. BEATTIE: I have a right to suggest what an Amendment should do from
the point of view of the Northern Ireland
worker. I have repeatedly said that the
opportunity for qualifying under the
statutory conditions and maintaining the
conditions of insurance is smaller in
Northern Ireland than in Great Britain.
That is due to the limited opportunity
the insured worker here has of getting
qualification. As you have transgressed
as regards the step-by-step policy, I feel
I am justified in asking you to reduce the
qualification of insurability in Northern
Ireland to at least 15 per cent. below
that of England.
Mr. ANDREWS: What about Wales?
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not concerned
with Wales. There is no water border
between Wales and England. In England, Scotland and Wales the people can
go from north to south, but Northern
Ireland's area is confined to the Six
Counties. The majority of the insured
population have only a limited scope
inside the Six Counties to seek insurable
employment. I feel that the 15 per cent.
is a moderate figure. If I got that percentage of qualification I would say I
had got something which will assist and
relieve the great hardships imposed on
insured persons regarding disqualification. I will be told that cannot be
granted and that it would interfere with
the parity arrangement. I hope I have
made the House conversant with the
interference in that parity arrangement.
Why put in a residence Clause which
does not apply to Great Britain? I feel
that the Amendments could have been
improved if we had been consulted as to
what is suitable to our area.
I am not going to say that the conditions in Northern Ireland are the same
as in Great Britain. What may be good
for Britain may be bad for Northern
Ireland, and that has been proved
beyond the shadow of a doubt. As the
Amendments have to be accepted in toto
I am compelled to accept them. Nevertheless I think that one or two of them
could be reasonably objected to on the
ground that instead of following step by
step they are creating further injustices
upon a section of the community who
have too many injustices to bear at the
moment. Owing to the ruling of the
Chair I have to confine myself to the
narrow issue of accepting or rejecting
the Amendments. I accept the Amendments with the protest that any further
legislation regarding unemployment insurance should be done in the open
House and not by Order in Council.

Oral Answers to Questions.
COST OF DRAINAGE SCHEMES.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can
state the number of engineers, surveyors, draughtsmen, clerks, etc., both
permanent and temporary, employed on
the staff of Director of Works, exclusive
of staff engaged on the Bann Drainage
Scheme; the cost of this department
during the years 1933-34 and 1934-35,
inclusive of travelling and subsistence
expenses; what duties are performed by
this staff other than preparation and
supervision of drainage schemes; how
many drainage schemes have been undertaken by this department, and in how
many cases the estimated cost has been
exceeded and by what amount.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I would refer the hon. Member to the published Estimates for the
years in question, which set out in
detail the Ministry's engineering and
architectural staff, all of whom are under
the control of the Director of Works, the
costs of their salaries and of their
travelling and subsistence expenses. The
duties performed by this staff are also
fully set out in the Estimates for Public
Works and Buildings: many of the works
undertaken involve both architectural
and engineering problems. In addition
to works directly financed out of funds
provided by this House, the Director of
Works and his staff perform agency services for the Imperial Office of Works
and local authorities in Northern Ireland. The sums estimated to be
recovered in respect of these services
appear in the Appropriation-in-Aid subhead in the Estimates. Finally, the
Director of Works acts as inspector of
railways on behalf of the Ministry of
Commerce and undertakes the supervision of the reconstruction of harbours
in some cases where Government has
given financial
to local
authorities.
assistance
As regards drainage schemes, to which
the hon. Member specifically refers, in
recent years, at the request of county
councils, investigations have been made.
into some fifteen drainage proposals,
apart from the Bann, Lough Erne and
Quoile River, which are of direct Government interest. Of those investigated,
the councils concerned have only proceeded with two schemes, and the Ministry's engineers who have undertaken the
work on their behalf anticipate that the
cost will not exceed the estimates.
As regards the Bann, it is yet too
early to say whether the completed
scheme will be within the estimate; the
Quoile is costing more than was anticipated and the excess is likely to run
into £5,000.
RENT STRIKE IN BELFAST.
2. Mr. BYRNE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been called to a rent strike which has
been in operation for some time in Belfast, and, in view of the fact that the
Government refused to set up a Fair
Rents Court, what action the Minister
proposes to take to bring this dispute to
an end.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna): In the
absence of my right hon. Friend I have
been asked to answer this question.
My attention has been called to the
dispute to which the hon. Member
refers. The matter is one for the courts,
arising as it does from contracts between
private parties. I have, therefore, no
authority to intervene and it does not
seem that any action on my part is
called for or would be appropriate.
Mr. BYRNE: Is the hon. Gentleman
aware that there is a great deal of unrest all over the city, and if this thing
continues it will be unfair as regards the
high rents.

Mr. POLLOCK: I am not in a
position to make any comment on the
alleged sale of Messrs. Workman, Clark
and Co. to the National Shipbuilders'

CLASS V. No. 1.
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £48,886 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum which will come in course of payment during the year ending 31st March,
1936, to defray the salaries and
expenses of the Ministry of Education
(15 and 16 Geo. V, c. 3, Sec. 4 (N.I.)).
(Note.-£17,000 has been voted on
Account).
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Hon. Members will find this Estimate on page 106
of the Book of Estimates. It has been
found convenient in former years to present both these Votes together to the
Committee and I propose to follow the
same course on the present occasion.
Last
the Estimates voted for
year
Education came to a total of £1,977,688;
this year the amount required shows an
increase of about £25,000, and for the
first time, I believe, the sums asked from
Parliament exceed the two-million mark;
to be precise, the amount of the two
Votes is £2,002,761. To this sum must
be added
a sum of about £110,000
defrayed by the Education Committees
from the rates in order to get the exact
figure of the cost of education from
public funds. In regard to the amount
of the Vote, I should like to make two
or three brief observations.
I would call the Committee's attention in the first place to the fact
that the amount now spent on education
is only very slightly larger than the
moneys voted in Northern Ireland for
this purpose in any of the last ten years.
We can all readily think of many other
essential services whose cost to the State
has grown
seriously within the same
period, but notwithstanding the many
developments introduced in education
here since 1923, and especially the great
improvements in school buildings and
equipment, I think it is a matter of congratulation that we have been able to
keep down the cost. It is the ambition
of the Government and of the Ministry
to provide as good an education for our
children here as is available to people in
Great Britain, and though I do not at
all claim that that aim has yet been
accomplished, I would like to point out
that for every £3 spent on education
in Great Britain from public funds we
here in Northern Ireland are only spending £2.
That is a concrete fact that cannot be
controverted, and it should be kept
seriously in mind when people begin to
talk of extravagance in spending too
much money on schools. And while, as
I have mentioned, the annual cost of
education to the State is almost stationary
in Northern Ireland the estimates of the
English Board of Education show an
increase of over £3,000,000 as compared
with ten years ago, and are almost a
million higher this year than last.
cannot be said, therefore, that our expenditure is on a "step-by-step" basis
with Great Britain, though I am hopeful
that it will be recognised that our
facilities are not less suitable for our
population than those across the Channel.
It
Turning to Vote 1, salaries and
expenses of the Ministry, the amount
required, £65,886, is less than last year
by £452. The decrease is due partly to
savings on retirement of certain senior
officials and partly through transfers of
some of the older clerical officers to
another Ministry, their places being
taken by younger and less expensive
officers. Otherwise there is little change
to record. The part-time officer who
acted as bursar of Stranmillis Training
College has been promoted and his place.
has been filled by a full-time executive
officer; the cost falls on the Training
College funds.
The first item in Vote 2, for educational services, is the cost of the training
colleges for elementary teachers at
£22,590. This is an increase of £850,
due to the fact that the number of
students in training is 10 more than last
year. There are at present 119 men and
212 women in the colleges, of whom 18
are taking third and fourth year courses.
9 APRIL 1935
Estimates-
Ministry of Education

and a renewal fund is being built up out
of savings in running the college which
will enable these buildings to be replaced
by new ones in a few years' time. The
amount of this fund stands at present at
about £6,000.
The examinations for admission to the
colleges held last year showed more favourable results than in recent years; there
was a larger number of candidates, and
the number that passed successfully and
became qualified for achorlarships was
318 against 295 in 1933. In the latter
year the full number required to fill the
vacancies in Stranmillis was not forthcoming, so that the college was not up
to its full quota, but last year the more
favourable results enabled the deficiency
to be made up; hence the increase of 10
students as compared with a year ago.
It should not be forgotten that the
standard of education from entrants to
the colleges is now appreciably higher
than some years ago, inasmuch as since
1929 the examination has been assimilated to the secondary leaving certificate.
It is safe to say, therefore, that the
standard of the students' education is
higher now than previously, a condition
which I am sure the Committee will
appreciate. It is also noteworthy that
the number of university graduates
entering the colleges is steadily increasing, and there are at present 12 such in
training; the course in their case is of
one year's duration.
I may add that the Ministry's system
of pupil teacherships has proved very
successful in raising the quality of the
candidates for training; the competition
is very keen and very few of these young
persons fail to pass the junior certificate;
last year all but one of those who sat for
the King's Scholarship Examination were
successful. Pupil teachers are selected
by competitive examination from all
over the Province, and we are getting
some very brilliant boys and girls to form
the future staffs of our elementary
schools.
The demonstration school at Stranmillis was reopened to the pupils last
month, and its reorganisation will add
much to the efficiency of the training
in methods of teaching of the King's
scholars. The Ministry is providing a
residence for the principal of the college
in the grounds, with a view to the better
supervision of the establishment; the
cost will be met by an adjustment of the
principal's salary. In this connection
the Committee of Management has not
lost sight of the fact that some of the
hostels first erected at Stranmillis a dozen
years ago were of a short-lived character,
I now come to the main item of the
Ministry's expenditure for elementary
education, salaries and other emoluments
of public elementary school teachers,
which is responsible for £1,352,000, an
increase of £9,125 on last year. The
greater part of this increase is due to the
award of increments of salary in the
normal and super-normal scales. There
is a decrease of £700 under the head of
capitation grant, the Estimate being
based upon a lesser aggregate average
attendance, corresponding to the diminution in the birth rate which took place in
1922, as compared with 1921. Any
marked decrease in the attendance at
the schools will, of course, cause a
decrease in the number of teachers and
the cost of education generally, but it
is not possible at present to make any
accurate estimate of what such decrease
is likely to be.
In connection with the many very
large schools that are now being provided
in Belfast and other urban centres the
Ministry has for some time been seriously
considering the staffing arrangements.
These large schools are furnished with
rooms specially equipped for the teaching of domestic economy, science, drawing, handwork-all forms of practical
instruction now considered indispensable
in elementary schools for elder pupils.
The usual staffing in our elementary
schools, which is on a less liberal scale
than obtains in Great Britain, is contrived for classes of about 40 pupils in
average attendance, and such classes can
be handled successfully by skilful
teachers, but when it comes to the teaching of the practical subjects which I have
just mentioned, classes so large as this
cannot be properly instructed, and unless
we can arrange for taking the pupils in
smaller groups such subjects cannot be
efficiently dealt with.
A more liberal staffing in such ca
becomes indispensable in the interest
efficiency, and I am glad to be ab
tell the Committee that the Ministry
recently obtained the approval
Ministry of Finance for the
of additional teachers in 1

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
Where there are suitable rooms for
practical subjects; there will be provision
for an additional assistant in such a
school, provided there is an average

in the current financial year.

The number of pupils enrolled in the
senior standards of the elementary
schools continues to increase, and while
this must be regarded as a satisfactory
sign of progress, it tends to increase the
cost of education, as the more pupils in
the higher standards the larger are
the numbers attending classes
mathematics, a subject which is usually
taught out of ordinary school hours and
for which extra fees are paid to the
teachers, such instruction being in the
nature of over-time”
work. An
increase of £2,425 is set down in the
Estimates for extra fees, and in addition
to mathematics the increase is also caused
by more teaching of horticulture in rural
schools. This is a branch which has
grown very considerably in recent years,
and I think the Committee will agree
that it is one deserving of every encouragement. Teachers' courses in
horticulture are held every summer at
Stranmillis Training College, and are
fully attended by teachers of country
schools from all over the Province.
fact, the desirability of having more such
classes is evident in order to accommodate
the numbers applying for admission.
Hitherto the classes have been free, but
in future years it is proposed to charge
a moderate fee for attendance. The
utility of attendance by teachers at
refresher classes is becoming more and
more recognised, and such attendance is
an excellent means for teachers to keep
alive their freshness and interest in their
work.
In
Speaking generally, there has been
little change in the past year in the
steady record of progress which is now
customary in the work of our elementary
schools. Many new schools have been
built during the year by the education
authorities, and the voluntary school
managers have also shown some activity
in this respect. Transfers of schools to
the education authorities are still taking
place, though at a slower rate than
formerly. Thanks to the mild winter,
the schools have, on the whole, been freer
from epidemics than usual, and there is
no doubt that the comfort of the children
has been greatly increased in recent years
by the healthier conditions caused by the
great improvement effected in the school
buildings. This improvement is much
more marked in Belfast and the three
adjoining counties than in the western
parts of the Province. It is regrettable
that so many managers are still reluctant
to transfer their schools in the counties
of Londonderry, Tyrone and Fermanagh.
The amount required for secondary
education is £174,750, £3,200 more than
last year.
This increase is entirely due
to the continued upward trend of the
numbers of pupils attending preparatory
and secondary schools; this increase
necessarily leads to more teachers being
employed, involving an increase in the
charge for teachers' increments of salary
which are paid by the Ministry, and
increased numbers mean, of course, an
increase in the capitation grants. The
growth of attendance at secondary schools
is one of the most striking features of our
educational progress in the last few years;
since 1925 this increase has been exactly
50 per cent., and the cost to the Vote
has risen in an exactly similar proportion
from £116,000 in 1925-26 to £174,750 in
the present Estimates.
I have referred at the beginning of
these remarks to the fact that our education Estimates to-day are much the same
as ten years ago; it is interesting, therefore, to note the definite increase in
grants to secondary education by a sum
of £58,000 in the period mentioned.
Would it be incorrect to say that a large
number of the complaints of alleged extravagance in educational expenditure
come from members of the community
whose sons and daughters attend
secondary schools? And if so, is it quite
fair of them to complain, when it is the
education of their own children that produces the chief item of increased
expenditure?
The grants for technical instruction are
£2,300 more than last year. This is
entirely in the teachers' increment grant
and is due to an increase in students,
leading to an increase in the number of
teachers. These grants do not, of course,
comprise the whole, or even the greater
part, of the cost of technical instruction
in the Province; at £69,500 they represent rather more than one-third of the

Ministry of Education
and it will be only gradually that its full
usefulness will become apparent.
total cost. The remainder of the cost is
paid from the funds of the education
committees, to which the Government
contributes the grant-in-aid estimated
this year at £177,500, as well as the
derating grants.
It is gratifying to note the steadily
increasing interest taken in technical
education, and the increase in the number
of pupils of 13 years and over in the
junior technical schools is a sign that this
form of vocational instruction is being
appreciated more and more as time goes
on. Indeed the accommodation available,
particularly in Belfast, is not sufficient.
Last year there were over 1,200 applicants
for admission to the two full-time day
schools in the Municipal College of Technology, but only 700 could be admitted:
the Junior Technical School conducted by
the Christian Brothers in Belfast could
not admit more than 60 out of 400
applicants.
The amount of the Ministry's grant
under Section 76 of the Education Act,
1923—that is, the grant of a subsidy to
the education authorities amounting to
the yield of eightpence in the pound on
the old valuations before derating comes
to £177,500, which is £2,000 more than
last year.
The increase in the amount
has no special significance in regard to
the development of the activities of these
authorities and is due to an adjustment
of the payments accruing within the
financial period. There is always an
arrear left over from the previous year
which falls to be paid out of the following year's Vote.
It is expected that the Haypark
Special School for mentally deficient
children will be brought into operation
in the autumn, and a sum of £750 is provided in the Estimates for the salaries of
the teachers who will be employed
there. The accommodation is based on
an attendance of 40 day pupils and 80
boarders, and for some time past the
education authorities have been taking
steps through their medical officers to
inspect and select children suitable for
admission. Such children need to be
very carefully graded in order that full
benefit may be derived from the institution, and only children who are capable
of receiving some elementary form of
education can properly be received into
the school. The opening of the school is
a new experiment in our education system
A small item that appears for the first
time in these Estimates is a grant of
£150 towards expenses incurred by the
Northern Ireland Joint Committee on
Adult Education in holding courses of
lectures. Lectures and classes on educational subjects for adult workers have
been for many years a feature of educational activities in Great Britain, and
large sums are devoted to this purpose in
the Estimates of the Board of Education.
Through the enterprise of the University
and the Workers' Educational Association lectures for adults have been given
during the past winter in eight or nine
centres in Northern Ireland and have
received a gratifying measure of support.
I have not thought it necessary on this
occasion to make a long statement on this
Vote. Our educational system is now
advancing on lines that are familiar to us
all. All the reforms and facilities that
were implicit in the Northern Ireland
Education Act of 1923 have been brought
into existence to a greater or lesser extent
and with a varying degree of success
according as the local education committees function with more or less energy
and efficiency. As might be expected, the
results are more conspicuous in Belfast
and the large urban centres than in the
remoter parts of the Province, but I think
nobody will deny that what has been
accomplished in the last dozen years in
improving the schools is in excess of what
most of us expected only a few years ago.
Much more, no doubt, remains to be
done, but I am confident that with the
support of public opinion and relying on
the efforts of a very hard working and
efficient staff of teachers, to whom I desire
to pay a sincere tribute, there is no
reason why the education system of
Northern Ireland should not prove in
every way worthy of the population for
whom it ministers. I beg to move.

of the educational system adopted in

That system of inspection to my mind
is obsolete and not in keeping with our
present day system of education; in other
words, it is a misfit in our educational
system. I might be asked then what I
would place as a check upon a teacher who
might slack and might not give the service
the Ministry think he should give. I
would suggest to the Parliamentary
Secretary-and I make this suggestion off
my own bat without any authority behind
me-that education would be well served
by the abolition of the highly efficient
mark in the teaching profession. It also
would be well served by the abolition of
the super-normal scale of salary. I think
we would make a step forward if we were
to adopt the policy of trying to find a
scale of salaries for all teachers at a point
between the super-normal scale and the
low scale, and apply that, plus the increments, as the normal scale.
That might be a contentious matter, as
the Parliamentary Secretary knows, for
one-third of the teaching profession in
Northern Ireland, but nevertheless I
realise that two-thirds of the teachers
never attain to that position. Therefore,
although I am putting it forward to the
Parliamentary Secretary I know there
might be opposition from that one-third,
but we might allow those at present on
the super-normal scale to remain on it.
If this scheme for the abolition of the
present inspection system, which I have.
briefly outlined, were adopted I believe.
we would get the full fruits of our educational system. We would get the best
results from our teachers, and we could
justify all the expenditure proposed in

Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise to move the
Motion standing in my name.
I should
like, if it facilitates the business of the

to accept the principle of this Motion on

Education
detailed matter. In submitting this
Resolution this afternoon, "That in the
opinion of this House the Government
should immediately introduce a Bill to
amend the Shops Act," I am mainly concerned with stressing one point and with
trying to bring the conditions of the shop
assistants of Northern Ireland into conformity with the conditions that prevail
throughout Great Britain as the result of
the passing of the Amending Shops Act.
in December, 1934.
The history of shops' legislation, I
think it will be conceded by every Member of the House, is a history of long
suffering and long delayed reforms with
regard to the operatives in the various
shops. I am sure some Members of this
House, particularly on the Government
side, because they do not take much
interest in these things with one or two
honourable exceptions, will be surprised
to know that the mass of shop assistants
in Northern Ireland at the present time
are working under a Shops Act that is
almost 50 years' old-49 to be precise;
and fundamentally the conditions in
relation to juveniles at any rate, all those
under 18 years of age, have not been
interfered with legislatively for a period
of 49 years.
In Great Britain that
position has been departed from as a
result of the amending Act of 1934, and
so we have this position in Northern Ireland where the social amenities are
supposed to be on a par with the social
amenities in Great Britain, that the distributive workers are in a position of
decided inferiority as compared with
their confrères in Great Britain.
My Motion is to secure from the
Government an indication that they will
at the earliest possible moment bring
legislation in Northern Ireland into
harmony with legislation in Great
Britain. Under the 1934 Shops Act, as
amended by the Imperial Parliament,
juveniles-all those under 18 years of age
have had their hours considerably
reformed. Under the old Act of 1886
which is the Act still applicable to
juveniles in Northern Ireland employees
in shops throughout Great Britain were
subject to a working week of about 74
hours, inclusive of meal times. These
conditions prevailed for almost 50 years.
until the Imperial Parliament decided to
amend them. In Northern Ireland we
have not amended them yet.
juveniles are still subject to a working
week of 74 hours. In Great Britain
under the new Act as applicable from
December 1934 juveniles-I am speaking
from memory-are subject to a week of
52 hours which will prevail up to the year
1936 and thereafter the juveniles will be
subject to a 48 hours' week.

was interrupted yesterday I had got up
to speak on education from the point of

working classes, and I want to say at the

commend any activity on the part of the

this afternoon, as I submitted twelve

in regard to education it is insignificant
in some respects compared with what still
remains to be done. I said yesterday,
and I repeat now, that the educational
facilities in Northern Ireland fall far
short of what they ought to be, especially
in regard to higher education.
Now, I am not going to review the
events in the educational world before
the setting up of the education authority
in Northern Ireland, and I am not going
to take up the time of the House
by referring to the leeway-a very substantial leeway indeed-which had to be
made up by the education authority in
Belfast and Northern Ireland. I have
had the privilege of serving on the local
education authority for ten and a half
years almost now, and I know what has
been done by the education authority.
But there are points which I wish to
place before the Parliamentary Secretary
this afternoon in the hope that he will
give some indication to the public as to
what the policy of the Ministry is going
to be in regard to the points which I
will put forward. If I put the points
emphatically I hope the Parliamentary
Secretary will not think they are put
forward with any degree of bad temper
or with any degree of carping criticism
merely with regard to his Ministry. They
are put forward because I feel very
strongly upon them.
One of the first points which I wish to
emphasise is the lamentable lack of

provided by the Ministry of Education
and the local authorities so far as the
children of Northern Ireland are concerned. I repeat now, and I repeat this
in a challenging fashion, because I want

that Northern Ireland provides the worst
facilities in Europe for higher education.
I quoted statistics twelve months ago, I
will refer to them here and there to-day

both sections of the Press and politicians
in SƠ representing education conditions

make it appear that the best facilities
the country exist here in the
upward and onward march from
the elementary school to the university
Indeed this-I may almost use the word

collusion, between politicians and the

I submit that the condition of things

Even in those countries where I dislike
the form of Government from the point
of view of brutal dictatorship, education
facilities are better than they are in
Northern Ireland. Furthermore, the
system of secondary education as it does
exist is completely unsatisfactory in
regard to the majority of the people who
are able to embrace such opportunities
as do exist.
As a result of my ten years' experience
on the local education authority, I am

who

schools have saved us more than the cost

ten years, 1923-33, the number of pupils

by 21,000. If we had had to provide
schools and teachers for those 21,000 it
would have meant 650 new teachers; but
with the new schools it has been possible
to get those extra pupils provided for by
370 teachers, thus saving 280 teachers,
representing something like £70,000
annually for salaries.

deal of unemployment elsewhere, and the
percentage of unemployment amongst
teachers is very small compared with the
percentage in other branches of life, as
the hon. Member knows. I think those
new schools have justified themselves, and
that the money spent on them has been
well spent.

Mr. HENDERSON: The Government
ought to see that special facilities are given

Another matter which has given me
very grave concern, and which I have
studied night and day, is the problem of
providing for the education of afflicted
children. This Parliament has been in
existence now for a number of years,
and why was not a home for these
afflicted children built long ago. The
policy of this Government is to get rid
of them and let them go wherever they
like. Hundreds of these Ulster children
are scattered throughout Great Britain
and the Free State. The Ministry of
Education has allowed afflicted children
from Ulster to be sent to Dublin, where
their parents never see them from one
year's end to another. Is that a proper
policy to adopt? Do you not think it
would be in the interests of these poor
children if they were housed and
educated in a home in their own country
where their parents would have access
to them once or twice a week. The
Ministry neglects them like everything
else. For the past ten or eleven years
I have continually drawn the attention
of this House to this question of afflicted
children, but apparently all the speeches
I have delivered on the subject have
fallen on deaf ears. The Parliamentary
Secretary should have a better excuse
for the delay in providing a suitable
home than the one he gave in reply to
a question the other day. There is no
earthly reason why the Government
should not provide a proper home in
Northern Ireland for these afflicted
children. The reason they have not done
so is because they do not care what becomes of children who are at present
scattered all over Great Britain and the
Free State. They do not care whether
the parents of these children, who love
them, ever see them or not.
I should like to support those hon.
Members who have spoken against the
practice of home work. We think the
children of to-day are being punished by
the amount of home work that is forced
on them at the present time. It is only
a waste of time, and it is the greatest
punishment that could be inflicted on
the children. If you take the houses
that are at present being constructed in
Norhern Ireland, when the father and
mother get in, if they are at all fat,
there is no room for the children to do
home work. They are over-crowded, and
home work in such an environment is a
burden on the parents and a punishment
for the children. Why should school
children be asked to work longer hours
than a man employed in the shipyard?
We should give the children all the
education necessary in the schools during
the day, and it should be the policy of
the Ministry to see that after school
hours the children are provided with
playing fields and proper facilities for
engaging in gymnastic displays and other
forms of recreation to develop their
bodies, instead of punishing them by
giving them homework to do. They
come home from school about four
o'clock, and then they have to start to
do home work that occupies them until
six or seven o'clock. That is wrong, and
the sooner it is stopped the better.
Another matter I want to deal with concerns children in agricultural areas who
have to walk two or three miles to school.

draw upon the enhanced salaries of the
present day. Therefore, it would be
quite impossible to grant any such remission as the hon. Member suggests.
The amount that is being contributed

the construction of the whole educational
