Running all through everything that he
had to say was this fallacy, that the
schools were divided into Protestant
schools and Catholic schools. They are
not so divided. The division is between
provided or transferred schools-I will
call them provided schools and voluntary schools. There are about 1,700
schools altogether, and 1,150 of these
schools are voluntary schools. Of these
1,150, 700 are under Roman Catholic
management and 450 are under management other than Roman Catholic. The
distinction between schools, you see, is
not between Catholic and Protestant
schools, but it is between schools whose
managers have been willing to share with
the local education authority who provide
the rates, for their assistance the management of the schools, and on the other
hand those schools whose managers prefer
to retain in their own hands the entire
control of the schools.
Mr. BEATTIE: The entire control?
Mr. ROBB: I say entire control in
this sense.
Schools of both classes have
teachers in them, and those teachers must
teach up to the standard set by the
Ministry, but the teachers in both classes
of schools are paid direct by the Ministry.
But in so far as the functions of management, to use that word, are concerned,
the distinction in our schools is quite
simple. It is the distinction between
those managers who retain in their own
hands the full management of the school,
and those schools where the managers
have surrendered the management to the
education authority acting through the
local management committee. The
management of the school involves the

1 have said, 1,150 schools in which the

Address to His Majesty 1364
Address to His Majesty
HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 11th April, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Royal Assent.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the
Bar) reported to the House, that His
Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland,
in the name and on behalf of His
Majesty the King, had been pleased to
give his Assent to the following Bills
agreed upon by both Houses:
Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
Provisions),
Exchequer and Financial Provisions,
McWilliams' Divorce.
Order of Supply.
Resolved, "That notwithstanding anything contained in Standing Order No.
15, other Government business have precedence this day of the business of
Supply." (The Prime Minister).
Adjournment of the House.
Resolved, "That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until Tuesday
next." (Captain Dixon).
Royal Silver Jubilee.
Address to His Majesty.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move, "That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty as follows:-
Most Gracious Sovereign,
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to congratulate
Your Majesty on the auspicious attainment of the twenty-fifth year of Your
Majesty's eventful and beneficent
reign, and to assure Your Majesty that
this House profoundly shares the great
joy with which Your Majesty's subjects throughout the world celebrate
Your Silver Jubilee, joining with them
in praying earnestly for the continuance during many years of Your
Majesty's life, health and happiness."
In moving this Address I feel confident that it is the desire of Parliament,
as representing the people, to express its
devotion to our King Emperor, to pay a
spceial tribute to Their Majesties on
very auspicious occasion, and to tender
our humble duty and grateful thanks for
the high honour His Majesty conferred
upon the people of Ulster by addressing
in person both Houses of her legislature
at their inauguration; for permitting His
Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, in
His Majesty's name, to open the building we now occupy; for graciously conferring the title of Earl of Ulster upon
His Royal Highness the Duke of
Gloucester, and that of Baron Downpatrick on His Royal Highness the Duke
of Kent, and for the many occasions on
which Their Majesties have been
graciously pleased to evince personal
interest in our local affairs.
To all whom it may concern we would
have it known that this day and, please
God, for all time, we are in the
British Commonwealth of Nations.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We are
of it, and proud of it. We are in the
Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We are of it and proud of it. We are
in the United Kingdom of Great Britain
and Northern Ireland. We are of it,
and proud of it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
All because of our passionate devotion
and loyalty to The Throne, we echo from
this Assembly the sentiment which prevails throughout the Homeland and His
Majesty's wide flung Dominions-Long
live the King. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolved, "That this House do
approach His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland with the request that
he will be pleased to cause the said
Address to be presented to His Majesty."
(The Prime Minister).
1365 Summary Jurisdiction Bill-

11 APRIL 1935
Report Stage
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Summary Jurisdiction and Criminal
Justice Bill.
As amended considered.
CLAUSE 6 (Appointment of resident
magistrates).
(1) The Governor of Northern Ireland shall have power, having regard
to the recommendations of the Minister of Home Affairs and (so far as
relates to numbers) of the Minister of
Finance, from time to time to appoint
fit and proper persons, being at the
dates of their respective appointments
either barristers-at-law of not less than
six years' standing practising in
Northern Ireland or practising solicitors of the Supreme Court of Judicature in Northern Ireland of not less
than six years' standing, to be
resident magistrates.
(2) Every resident magistrate shall,
notwithstanding anything in any enactment hold his office during good
behaviour, but may be removed from
his office by the Governor of Northern
Ireland upon the address of both

I would like to say a word or two on
some of the Clauses. The first Clause to
my mind is a very serious one. With one
stroke of the pen and two or three words
of his lips the Minister of Home Affairs
uproots a tree of 600 years' planting. In
the history of our Northern Province
there have always been a few men, and
sometimes ladies, who were considered
worthy to take their part in considering

pass that there are no people worthy to
do the duties our forefathers did in days
that are gone.
I submit that is a great
reflection upon the education and civilisation of the present generation of people.
To sit with the county court judge was

would never reflect upon the chairman of

the land. I have absolute confidence in
them, one and all. I think that permission to sit with the chairman of

are not worthy to do it," although by

offence or not. I submit that loyal people

they are driven into by this Clause.

was going to say his nose-his face into

The man who goes into a bookmaker's

Oral Answers to Questions.
BELFAST UNION CLERKSHIP.
1. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
prepared to ensure that some person from
the present staff qualified by training in
poor law administration and having many
years of experience will be appointed
Clerk of the Belfast Union Workhouse.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am not prepared
to give any such assurance as is sought.
In any case, the appointment of the
Clerk of a Union rests, in the first place,
with the Board of Guardians concerned.
The Ministry's function is limited to
approving or disapproving the appointment, and if a suitable and properly
qualified person is appointed the Ministry would have no justification for withholding approval on the ground that he
was not a member of the Guardians'
present staff.
Dr. WILSON: Arising out of that
question, might I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether its object is to suggest that no countrymen need apply?

under the Allotments Act, 1932, for the
years 1933 and 1934.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will be
pleased to do so.

CONDITION OF HOUSES IN
MILL ROW, ARMAGH.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether an area known
as Mill Row, in the rural district of
Armagh, comprising 49 houses, and
owned by the Armagh Spinning Co., is
in a very bad condition; whether the
houses are unsanitary and require
general repair; whether, in winter time,
19 of the houses are flooded by an
adjacent river; whether he will state
who is responsible for the upkeep and
repair of the street, which is in a filthy
condition generally, especially during
inclement weather; and whether he is
prepared to enforce the Public Health
Acts so as to ensure elementary hygiene
and healthy homes for the people concerned.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have
received representations regarding the
area in question and my Ministry has
been in communication with the Armagh
Rural District Council respecting it.
As regards the houses, the Council
state that these have been under the
constant supervision of their officers and
are quite good. When the Callan River
rises to an abnormal level some are
liable to flooding, but the Council state
that they are unable to prevent this.
The condition of the roadway, I am
informed, is as described, but there is a
doubt as to who is responsible for its upkeep. The Ministry has advised the
Council to consult its solicitor on this
point and to serve notice on the person;
or persons, he considers liable to abate
this nuisance. The Council having
agreed to do this, no further action on
the part of my Ministry appears to be
necessary at present.
UNEMPLOYMENT ACT.
THE SECOND APPOINTED DAY.
5. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can indicate the
date of the second appointed day in connection with Part 2 of the Unemployment Act.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): It is intended that there
should be a uniform date for this purpose throughout the United Kingdom,
and due notice will be given when the
matter has been decided.
INSPECTION OF SPINNING
MILLS.
6. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether, in view of the conditions of excessive dampness prevailing
in spinning mills in which girls have to
stand all day, and also in view of the
unhealthy conditions prevailing in preparing rooms in which workers must
work continuously in clouds of dust, he
will take steps to ensure that adequate
inspection is carried out so as to enforce
the full provisions of the Factory and
Workshop Acts.
Mr. ANDREWS: My Department is
keenly alive to the importance of safeguarding the health of the workers in
spinning mills, factories and workshops,
and very regular inspection has taken
place during the past 14 years. Large
sums have been spent by firms concerned
on ventilating and heating plants with a
view to removing dust and excessive
dampness as far as is practically possible; in fact some firms have exceeded
the statutory requirements. If, however, the hon. Member knows of any
concern in which he considers that the
condition of affairs can be improved and
will let me have particulars, I shall have
the matter fully investigated.

7. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the amount of rates involved under the
Derating Act on city, urban or other
properties not necessarily agricultural.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked to reply to this question.
I am willing to give the hon. and
gallant Member the fullest possible information on any matter on which he is
in doubt and which comes within the
scope of my Department; but
but his
question, as framed, does not indicate
what figures he desires me to give him or
the particular aspect of rating or derating with which he is at the moment
concerned.
Major McCORMICK: Does the
Minister not realise with the amount of
discussion that is going on regarding
derating that it is a matter of public
interest to know how much to put down
to derating?

HOUSE OF COMMONS Public Works and Buildings 1416

is still uncompleted. In spite of the

Toome has effected considerable improvement both as regards intensity and duration of flooding. This fact is borne out
by the evidence of persons residing on

space of time with very little inundation

Lough Erne Drainage Board's application for a lowering of the statutory

the remainder of the two-year period the

The Quoile River Drainage Scheme requires a further Exchequer contribution

Appropriations-in-Aid in respect of equipment and staff appear in this Estimate

increase in the anticipated discharge of
flood waters without any appreciable
inundation of lands. In the case of the
Blackwater River the scheme is nearly

wages like those. How can you expect to
get employers to depart from sweating
principles when you persist in paying

of 29s per week is simply an absolute

that ought to be paid. In view of the

I should suggest that one of the acts of
justice or restitution the Government
should embark on immediately is the
question of looking into all these wages.
Now we go below that. Houses of
Parliament and Administrative Offices at
Stormont-2 electricians (67s 6d per
week), 2 fitter mechanics (65s per week,
one with an allowance of 5s per week for
supervisory duties), 1 pump, fan, etc.,

should be looked into. In my opinion all
wages below 50s a week should be looked
into from the point of view of at least
establishing a minimum of 50s, and all

with a view to establishing a minimum of
£3. I do not understand why hon.
Members opposite do not show more
enthusiasm in these matters. I know
some of them understand the wages question perfectly well, but some do not seem
to understand it as well as they should.
I never could understand the psychology of any Member of this House who
defended wages which were below the
standard required to maintain a wife and
children in decency-I do not say comfort
because you could not get comfort on
those wages-but at least in some measure
of decency. I would appeal to the right
hon. Gentleman to bring his great
influence to bear upon his colleagues to
have this matter considered so that an
early announcement may be made by the

not present this afternoon. I suppose he
is away considering how he is going to

I would suggest that each Member of the

We come now to Stormont estate.

I notice also what I might call the
hardy annual in this Estimate. Each year
I have challenged those responsible for
the setting up of the wages basis, or what
I might call the human value. If those
persons were compelled to live upon the
value they have set upon other human
beings they could not exist for twentyfour hours. The hon. Member for Dock
(Mr. Midgley) has referred to items
under what I might call the heading of
manual labour. Who set the value upon
manual labour in the Estimates we are
now asked to pass? Those at the head
of the house,, those who take to themselves anything from £1,500 to £1,700 a
year. They say, "We in our day and
generation are the wise heads. We know
the value of the labour of a boiler man,
a groundsman, an electrician, or a man
of the general labouring type." If it
was they who set out the value of a
boiler man at 45s a week they certainly
have very little respect for the value of
that individual's labour, because if I
asked the same individuals to go and fire
a boiler for fifteen minutes at a time
they would fail in the operation inside
three minutes and would have to be
carried out of the atmosphere in which
the boiler is situated.
Those gentlemen have valued labour of
which they have no experience. I say if
the working classes are going to have to
suffer from having the value of their
labour assessed by men whose own value
is away in the region of the hundreds,
then we are going to have something to
say about it in the future. I always
claimed that every man, when he is
properly valued, is entitled to give service for the money received, but when I
go further into these Estimates I hope to
touch upon the sore spot in connection
with these valuations and to show who
are responsible in this Committee for
placing such a low value on labour of
such a very important kind as that to
which I now refer.
I also want to refer to the groundsmen
on the Stormont estate. They have to
stand all classes of weather. They may
be at the front gate or half-way up the
Processional Avenue when a blizzard
takes place, and before they can reach the

32s a week sufficient to provide those men
with the decencies and the comforts that
they are entitled to? We are responsible
for looking after this estate, but we must
put the value of the keepers very low
when we say they are equal to only 32s
or 35s a week. They get only 32s when

ask for Hillsborough Castle. The head

Going back to the subject of the
Stormont estate. I wish to say that
money could be usefully spent in erecting

be serviceable not only to the groundsmen

showers do not give due notice of their

money to burn. Certainly this is proof

If that £1,400 was spent in the feeding of

I wish to say something on the subject

Flax Cultivation.
Major McCORMICK: I beg to move.
"That in the opinion of this House, flax
cultivation in Northern Ireland should be
encouraged by a guaranteed price to
farmers and control by the Ministry of
Agriculture in regard to improved
methods of culture."
I would like to say at the outset that I
bring a matter of such great importance.
before this House with a feeling of great
hope that the outcome of such discussion
may place before us the true position and
the difficulties that heretofore have been
most hurtful-I mean so far as hindering
the greater cultivation of what should be
a staple industry in the same sense as our
linen is, and in the past was more so,
the staple industry of our Province. The
two are bound inseparably, and if we
produce the one which is vital to our
commercial needs, why not produce the
other. Let me say that I do not take
up this subject of flax growing because of
the present prices and the "flutter"
amongst spinners over the Continental
flax market, which has tended to create a
panic where, indeed, no anxiety should
exist. But rather knowing that in the
past there has been a wide gulf fixed-a
want of sympathetic dealing between
farmer and spinner.
Mr. ANDREWS: No.
I will put it
Major McCORMICK:
mildly if you like. There is a want of
co-ordination between the farmer and
the spinner. I think that the Ministry
of Agriculture, with all its advantages,
should be available to help both parties,
and thus arrive at a basis of dealing which
must result in financial benefit to the
farmers, security of supply to our
spinners, and in helping the needs of
unemployed to a very great extent.
This Motion was postponed until to-day
for two reasons. The principal one was
that a conference was proceeding, the
Minister of Finance being the chief figure,
and whilst we do not always see eye to eye
with the right hon. Gentleman, I have to
admit we cannot do without him, and on
various matters it is necessary that the
financial side should be considered.
Appreciating the difficulties of the
finances of the Government at the present
time, yet having in my mind the
great help that has already been
extended to farmers through the
means of the Pig Marketing Board, the
Milk Board, etc., appreciating what has
been already done, I do not propose that
flax cultivation should receive a subsidy.
More, I feel it does not require it. The
growing of flax is a sound proposition.
It can stand on its own feet shall I say,
more so than pigs. Though pigs have legs,
it has been shown they are not able to
stand on them. Flax has no legs but it
can stand on its own feet. More than 60
years ago Ireland grew 300,000 acres of
flax, and Northern Ireland in 1918,

111,000 acres. Of course that was during
the war period of stress when things were
not normal, but climatic conditions have
not altered to the extent that it cannot
be done again. Yet to-day only some
23,000 acres are grown in Ulster-that is
the
for the year-and 95 per cent.
acreage
of flax used to-day comes from foreign
countries. But I do say that our small
farmers should be encouraged to go into
the flax industry by the advance of 25 per
cent. cost on their acreage in flax by a
loan through Government means: The
hard knocks in flax prices the farming
community have received from time to
time can only be smoothed over by some
inducement of this kind, and which I
have computed would be less than
£100,000. This £100,000 would be a loan
well secured on the flax acreage. It
would be the best loan ever advanced by
the Government, because it would be the
safest, and would ensure employment to
many thousands of our people. Besides
it would mean the circulation of a huge
amount of money in our agricultural
areas. For instance, if 100,000 acres of
flax were produced in Ulster we should
have 20,800 tons of scutched flax at 10s
a stone. Later on I will show that flax
can be produced at a profit at a less price.
I want to get the highest price I can.
Mr. ANDREWS: It depends upon the
yield.
Whatever the
Major McCORMICK:
yield, the price of flax should be the same.
I mean the price per stone. I am sorry
the right hon. Gentleman misunderstood
me. That 20,800 tons of scutched flax
at £80 would be £1,664,000. From that
we would have 10,000 tons of scutched
tow at £30, which would be £300,000.
We would also have 22,500 tons of seed
at a price of £32, which would bring in
£720,000, and the wages for work would
be £500,000. That would give employment for 5,000 men for twelve months at
£2 per week. I notice the sympathetic
attitude of the Minister of Labour, but I
want more than a sympathetic attitude.
I want his co-operation in such a fine
opportunity to find employment for our
people. I think, indeed, it is to the
advantage of his Ministry that we should
have fewer people unemployed. Everyone is agreed that the one
way of
stimulating the growth of flax is to make
it worth while to the growers, and one of
the fundamentals governing this is the
development of pedigree strains of flax to
give the highest yields of fibre. In this
respect one is bound to remark upon the
attempts to propagate improved strains of
seed. How difficult this is has been
observed by the difference in the price
charged by Lambeg to the wholesale seed
trade for pedigree seed, and the ultimate
price charged to the farmers. I think it
is up to £83 a ton. As more equal and
direct distribution is essential, as is also
a more reasonable price.
In this Motion it is laid down that a
guaranteed price to the farmer is necessary in order to get him not only to start
growing flax, but make it a continuous
crop from year to year, so that by this
means we can count on 70,000 to 100,000
acres in crop instead of the 23,000 acres
or thereabouts we now have in Ulster.
Whatever that guarantee is to be, I am
perfectly satisfied to leave the matter in
the hands of a Flax Board or some other
co-ordinating board, to decide, and this I
suggest should be composed of farmers
and spinners under the Ministry of Agriculture.

In conclusion, as I have said before,
the present method of handling flax in
Ireland does not lend itself to increased
acreage or uniformity of fibre. It
would take between 100,000 acres and
160,000 acres to meet our annual consumption, and in order to cope with this
Flax Cultivation

acreage and give uniformity of flax fibre,
the following scheme would require to be
adopted :-
(1) The farmer to get best quality seed
available and be responsible for the crop
until ready for pulling.
(2) An intermediate company or flax
board would require to buy the flax when
it is almost finished growing, or on foot.
Central
(3)
flax retteries would
require to be established in different
parts of the Province where flax growing
is taking place, and all flax to be brought
to these retteries after pulling.
(4) When flax is dried and stacked
before retting, the seed should be saved,
which at present is largely lost to everyone concerned.
(5) The great difficulty at present with
Irish flax growing is that so many small
lots grown in various parts and steeped
in various waters of different temperatures give very erratic results in fibre
spinning. Fibre under-retted and overretted, also the quality of the water, has
a very great effect for good or bad on
the fibre.
(6) Scutching of flax requires to be
greatly reformed from the present method
to the modern method employed by
Courtrai scutchers.
(7) If spinners required flax from
Russia or Courtrai to suit their requirements we could easily export our Irish
surplus flax to other countries, and thus
bring about a better balance of trade
which is to be desired. I beg to move.

heavily in giving a guaranteed price for

it would be most dangerous for the
Government to undertake this guarantee,
having regard to the fact that the
growth of flax is such a speculative affair.
In the oldest country, and perhaps one
of the newest countries where they grow
flax, in Egypt, you can, with a considerable amount of certainty, anticipate the
type of crop which you may possibly produce, in so far as you can rely upon the
climate and rely upon the water supply
so far as it is obtained from the flooding
of the land in which the flax is grown.
Therefore, for that reason, flax has been
grown in Egypt very successfully even at
the present time as it was some thousands
of years ago. But in Ireland, where you
are so largely dependent upon climate,
both as to temperature for raising the
heat of the water in which you ret the
flax and as to the temperature of the sun
for drying the flax after it is taken out
of the retting pool, it becomes a matter
of tremendous speculation as to whether
or not you will have first of all a good
crop, and secondly, a crop which gives a
good yield.
And may I, in passing, compliment
the Ministry and the Lambeg Research
Association upon the fact that they have
increased the yield per acre during the
past few years to the extent of something
over 25 per cent., which I think is a
great credit to the work which has been
done at the Lambeg Research station.
Nevertheless, in spite of that I do think
that it would be most dangerous for us
to embark upon this enterprise. However, there is no way in which you will
encourage the growth of flax in Northern
Ireland more than by giving a good price
for it and, if possible, a guaranteed
price. But let me say that there is no
trade in this part of the Province which
is better off than the spinning industry
itself.
Therefore, if a guaranteed price is to
be given, I suggest that it is the duty
and the privilege of the Flax Spinners'
Association and the Linen Manufacturers' Association to give this guaranteed price, because of the risk that would
ensue if the Government did so and also
because of the fact that the Member for
Antrim (Mr. Crawford), when advocating this proposition, suggested that no
additional officials should be appointed.
Now I would like to ask him how he is
going to superintend first, the growth of
the fibre; secondly, the very important

without appointing a large number of

Therefore, I would like to hear what the

I should like to say that I am very

the whole administration which would be

It should be remembered in the first
place that our flax growers have only
one market, and that is the North of
Ireland market, and even at the best
Northern Ireland only supplied one-fifth
to one-third of the requirements of the
trade. On the other hand, the finished
article-linen-is sold roughly in this

Kingdom and 60 per cent. exported.
That means that two-thirds of the raw
material comes from abroad. That is, at
the most, an optimistic estimate. Therefore, that two-thirds obviously commands
the price of the market. We have no
control of that two-thirds, nor have we
any control over the 60 per cent. of the
finished article which is sold in foreign
countries. I think it must be quite
obvious to the House that if you cannot
control the price of your raw material
and you cannot control the price of your
finished article, the problem is not
analogous to any of the marketing
schemes that have been set up.
The spinners are in the position that
they cannot pay more for Northern
Ireland flax. I will put it this way.
They are obliged to buy flax in the
cheapest market. If they go abroad to
foreign countries, Russia or Belgium,

It may be asked why should the
Government not take on this duty, which
has been put down by some people as a
form of insurance against the complete
destruction of our linen trade, owing to
the fact that they cannot get sufficient
raw material. I think I can show figures
from which the House will realise that,
although it sounds very easy to say, "The
Government should step in and do something," that doing something will
amount to a very large figure indeed. I
am sure the hon. and gallant Member
will recollect that a little time ago he
suggested to the Prime Minister that no
fresh legislation should be brought in
which would involve a large expenditure.
This would, in fact, involve a very large
expenditure. Let us assume for a
moment that 10s, which is about this
year's average, is a fair price to the
farmer, and that we are going to guarantee a 10s minimum price. The market
may fall to 7s, and there is no reason
why it should not. It fell to that figure
in 1931, and to 5s in 1930.
This
means that the Government,
under those circumstances would lose anything from 3s to 5s per stone if they were
paying the difference between the price
actually paid and the guaranteed minimum price. We will take it that the
offer of such a guaranteed price would
send up the acreage to at least 40,000
acres. That is an acreage rather below
the acreage suggested by certain gentlemen who are interested in this question
of flax production. The actual figure
suggested was 50,000. For the purpose
of calculation we will take 40,000. That
is also the figure for the pre-war period.
We also take an average yield of 40
stones to the acre, which is not an
excessive amount. Commercial strains
actually average 35, and the strains
developed by the Ministry average somewhere about 51. I think that is a fair
figure to take.
That would mean, in fact, in Northern
Ireland a production of 1,600,000 stones
of flax, which at 3s a stone would amount
to £240,000. That is only if prices
dropped from 10s to 7s. If prices
dropped to 5s a stone, as they did once,
and the Government had to make the
difference up from 5s to 10s, the sum
required from the Treasury would be
£400,000. I feel sure the House will
realise that in demanding this they are
really demanding a thing that is impossible and for which the finances of this
country certainly would not stand. The
solution which we see is that by increasing the supply of pure seeds which are
bringing up the average product return
per acre from 31 stones, which is its
present commercial return, to somewhere
about 51 stones, it would mean to the
farmer an increase of no less than £7 an
acre.
So far as this Ministry is concerned,
we have been working at these pure line
seeds for many years in conjunction with
Canada, and we are gradually getting
a considerable bulk of seed which will be
available for the farmers. But we are
faced with the difficulty that where you
get a bad price for flax in a previous
year the demand for flax seed invariably
drops. The result is that a Canadian
farmer, having got a bad price as a result
of bad prices for flax in the previous year
sows less flax seed, and you are, therefore, faced with an insufficient supply of
seed for the acreage you may require in
any year. That, I hope, we shall get
over in time, but it is an extremely difficult problem to solve.
This year we have in this country pure
line seed to sow 10,000 acres, and I think
that if we can produce a flax that will
increase the return from 31 stones to 51
stones, and if we can, by bulking, reduce
this good line seed to a price lower than
it is at present-in some cases the price
is 90s, and there is no reason why it
should not be between 50s and 40s-we
shall have done far more in helping the
farmer than by giving a guarantee,
which is impossible, or by giving a
subsidy, which would be of little avail
and would cost a great deal of money.

Wednesday, 17th April, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
EFFECT OF REVALUATION ON
PROPERTY TAX.
Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Finance how the property tax payable
by owner-occupiers of dwelling-houses
and owner-occupiers of shops and other
business hereditaments as part of income
tax will be affected by increased revaluations of their premises.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the hon. and
learned Member's question is that,
broadly speaking, the general effect of
increased valuations on owner-occupiers
of dwelling-houses is that they will be
liable to pay more income tax under
Schedule A of the Income Tax Act, 1918,
whilst the position of owner-occupiers of
shops and other business hereditaments
will, in general, remain unchanged, as
the
increase in assessments under
Schedule A resulting from increases in
valuation will in their case be offset by
correspondingly greater allowances in
respect of their Schedule A assessments
which will be given in computing their
assessments under Schedule D.

17 APRIL 1935
A year ago, when I introduced the
Estimates of my Ministry, we all felt, I
think, that we were emerging from the
trough of depression and that brighter
prospects were opening for our industries.
To-day as I look back over the year I feel
that, whilst our fullest anticipations may
not have been realised, the last twelve
months must be considered, nevertheless,
to have been a time of definite progress
and to mark a real step towards recovery.
It is in the sphere of international trade
that our anxieties continue. The growth
of tariffs, of quotas, of exchange
restrictions, of import licences, of
economic nationalism, has proceeded
without check, and has continued to
thwart and impede the natural course of
economic development, which demands.
mutual dependence in the mutual
interest. These obstacles to international trade, inspired, one might
imagine, by some malign influence, have
united with the lack of a stable international monetary standard to increase
the difficulties of export trade. The
statistics of world commerce collected by
the League of Nations do not yet suggest any substantial movement towards
recovery.
Turning, however, to matters nearer
home, it is cheering to observe that there
has been an undeniable improvement in
British industry and trade. The United
Kingdom at least has made its contribution towards checking the steep decline
in world trade which occurred in the
worst period of the slump during the
years 1929 and 1932. United Kingdom
imports rose in 1934 by almost 8.5 per
cent. in value, and exports by almost
7.3 per cent. above 1933 figures. Unemployment figures for the whole Kingdom showed a decrease during 1934 in the
number unemployed of 15.4 per cent. as
compared with the average for 1933, and
are the lowest since 1930, while the
average number actually in employment,
namely, 10,136,000, was the highest
since 1929 and the second highest since
the war.
In Northern Ireland, too, signs of
better times are not lacking. The estimated value of imports into Northern
Ireland rose in 1934 by almost 10 per
cent. and exports by almost 21 per cent.
above 1933 figures. The average number of unemployed in Northern Ireland
during 1934 decreased by 8.7 per cent.
from the average for 1933 and, like the
figure for the United Kingdom, is also
the lowest figure since 1930. The
activity in our shipyards in 1934 was
greater than in any year since 1930 and
we have every reason for confidence that
it will be well maintained in 1935.
As regards our own sea-borne trade,
while the official returns are not yet
available an indication of its progress
may be gathered from the recently published account of the trade of the port
of Belfast, which represents the main
gateway of Ulster's commerce. The
tonnage of vessels cleared at the port
totalled almost four million, the highest
total in the history of the port. The
tonnage of goods exported and imported
was the highest in the post-war years
and represented almost 3 million tons.
While mentioning these indices of progress, I would, however, add a note of
warning that there is to-day no ground
for complacency, that such satisfaction as
we may derive from the figures cited is
merely in relation to the world position
as a whole, and that we have still a long
and arduous journey to make before we
return to what we could regard as a
reasonable standard of prosperity.
Last year I commented on the improvement in the linen industry during 1933,
and I am glad to say that this improvement has been well maintained. Exports
of linen piece-goods increased slightly,
and the total value of linen goods
exported increased by about 4 per cent.
Although the increase is not large it can,
I think, be considered encouraging,
having regard to the many adverse
factors to which I have previously
referred. The slowness of demand in the
United States of America, our largest
market, accounts mainly for the relatively
small increase, whilst exchange restrictions and uncertainties arising out of
currency devaluation, have continued to
hamper business. However, the relative
prosperity of the home market, which now
absorbs roughly 45 per cent. of the production of the linen trade, and improved
conditions in the British countries overseas more than counterbalanced the
decline in foreign trade. I think I can
say quite justifiably, having due regard
to world conditions, that the past year
can be described as a relatively satisfactory year for our linen trade in
Northern Ireland.
Ministry of Commerce
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour.]
I am confirmed in this view by the
steady level at which it has been possible
to maintain employment during the year.
Few variations were experienced, and the
average percentage of unemployed
workers in the linen trade fell from 20
per cent. of the insured workers in 1933
to 17 per cent. in 1934.

I am glad to be able to inform the Committee that the work for which this grant

which

A situation, which we had to consider

Majesty's Government were convinced of

the Research Associations, provided that
industry was prepared in its turn. to
increase the funds for research work
obtained by private subscriptions.

With regard to our fisheries, I have
both good and bad news to report-bad
in the sense that fish have been scarce:
good in the sense that active measures
are being taken to set our fishing industry
on a remunerative basis.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about the
Portavogie herring fisheries?
Mr. BARBOUR: We are doing our
best for them, too. During 1934 the
Ministry of Commerce 1474
Estimates-
17 APRIL 1935
herring almost completely forsook Irish
waters, and a difficult situation was thereby created for our fishing industry; so
much SO that only by Government
financial assistance was it possible to prevent the boats being laid up and the
crews dispersed.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the Minister
say why the herring have disappeared
from our waters?
Mr. BEATTIE: Due to the undecided
ownership of the waters.
Mr. BARBOUR: The Committee, however, will remember that last
year I
reported the discovery of escallop beds as
a result of a survey undertaken by my
Ministry. These beds have been successfully exploited by our fishermen, 72 boats
being engaged in the intensive dredging
during 1934, and the rediscovery of the
escallop has to some extent counteracted
the absence of the herring.
The old maxim which attributes to
necessity the motherhood of invention is
well illustrated in the case of our Kilkeel
fishermen who, faced with the failure of
last summer's herring fishing, were
spurred on to new methods during the
winter. Whereas in previous years the
boats had been laid up on the beach, this
winter they were in constant use, as the
fishermen had turned their hands to
Danish seine netting. This initiative was
amply rewarded, for the fishermen met
with good catches the quality of which.
ensured them of good markets, and they
will be able to face the coming herring
season with as full an equipment as they
would have had with a normally good
summer fishing to help them.
During February of this year, it was
realised that, while Portavogie fishermen
engaged in whiting fishing were enjoying
good catches, their system of marketing
their catch was far from satisfactory. In
the majority of cases the fisherman did
not know until the Saturday the price he
would receive for the catch which he had
sold on the Monday. In other words, the
fishermen took all the risks not only of
the sea, but of the market too. Officers
of my Ministry, therefore, put before the
fishermen and buyers a scheme by which
the price would be fixed in writing before
the sale was completed, and I am happy
to report that the scheme was accepted.
The Ministry looks for its observance by
all parties concerned.
The sphere of activity of my Ministry
in fishery administration is increasing.
The Fisheries Act of 1934 entails considerable administrative duties, notably
in the reorganisation of the system of
electing boards of conservators. Of the
activities of the new Herring Board,
within whose jurisdiction Northern Ireland has been brought at the express
desire of the Northern Ireland Parliament, it is as yet too early to speak, but
I would remind the Committee that one
proposal for the aid of the English and
Scottish herring industry, a Fishery
Loans Scheme, has been for some time
administered by my Ministry to the
material advantage
of our fishing
industry. Any further proposal of a
practical nature will be welcomed wholeheartedly as a means of improving the
lot of those engaged in a noble and
ancient calling.
I now come to exhibitions. At the
British Industries Fair, which closed
recently, my Ministry had for the first
time the co-operation of the Pigs and
Bacon Marketing Boards in the organisation of the Northern Ireland exhibit. A
striking display of bacon and hams
resulted, and it is believed that very useful propaganda has been done. I am told,
in fact, that the inquiries at the stand.
indicated that the demand for bacon of
the rolled type is greater in the South of
England than had previously been surmised, and our exhibit has accordingly
been the means of indicating to curers in
Northern Ireland a possible new field for
development. The exhibit is, of course,
not confined to bacon but covers, as it has
always done, other food products as well,
and provision is made in the Estimate for
participation on the same lines in the
1936 fair.
I think most of the Members of the
Committee have now some knowledge of
the nature of the commercial services
which my Department provides with the
object of assisting Ulster exporters to
maintain their markets outside the
United Kingdom and, if possible, to
penetrate new fields. Information is
collected by the Ministry, and constantly
revised, upon such subjects as market
conditions, tariff changes, importers and
agents abroad. All this information is
kept at the disposal of exporters.

The Committee will, of course, be

it is intimately associated
associated with the

The
year which has passed since I last presented the Estimates for this service has
again been one of responsible progress.
The returns from the various statutory
supply undertakings for the calendar
year 1934 have recently been received,
and they show an increase in the total
sales of current from 873 million units to
117 million units, which is approximately
33 per cent. While this increase may
be to some extent accounted for by the
gratifying improvement in industry,
particularly in the shipyards of Belfast,
it is also due to the rapid progress which
is being made in the electrification of
rural and semi-rural areas by the
Electricity
Board and the Antrim
Electricity Supply Company, as well as
by the Belfast Corporation within the
city itself and in the rural districts
immediately adjoining, which form part
of the Corporation's area of supply.
The Electricity Board have now
virtually completed their main transmission system in the Counties of Down
and Armagh and have extended their
high tension lines westward as far as
Omagh, while work is at present proceeding with the continuation of the line from
Omagh to Londonderry, which will form
a link inter-connecting the generating
station of the Londonderry Corporation
with that of the Belfast Corporation. In
addition, the Board have proceeded
rapidly with the provision of supplies in
all the districts reached by their main
lines, and at the present time they are
supplying current in 61 towns and
villages which, prior to the setting up of
the Board, had not enjoyed the amenities of an electricity supply, as well as
in 34 other towns and villages where they
have acquired the local supply undertakings.
The most gratifying feature in this
development is the ready manner in which
the population are availing themselves of
the facilities offered. The tariffs have
been framed to this end, and of the
21,000 consumers connected with the
Board's mains, approximately one
three are using current for purposes other
than electric lighting, so that electricity
can now no longer be regarded as a
luxury of the town dweller, but is being
made available for improving the amenities of life in the rural districts. As an
indication of the development of the
Board's activities, I may mention that
the units purchased by the Board from
the Harbour Power Station for the
years 1932, 1933, and 1934 amounted to
2,680,000, 7,810,000 and
and 15,971,000
respectively, while the number of units
generated in stations owned by the Board
rose from 688,000 in 1932 to 1,405,000
in 1934.
As regards power for industry, here,
again, the response in the districts outside Belfast, if slower than that from the
domestic consumer, is not unsatisfactory. The provision of abundant
supplies of electricity for power purposes at attractive rates in the rural districts of Northern Ireland should
contribute towards the development of
industries in our rural areas, and the
arrest of the movement of the population towards the towns.
The results already obtained by the
Electricity Board and the Antrim

always expected that the consumers

I may remind hon. Members that the
Electricity Board has to stand on its own
feet. It is responsible for its own
finances. Of course, hon. Members will
realise that in its earlier stages it has the
great benefit of a Government guarantee,
but it will be the duty of the Board when
it gets its undertakings sufficiently
developed to raise the capital necessary
to replace the loans by which the undertaking has been financed up to the
present. That will have to be done on
its own showing, on its own obvious
solvency, and so the Board, being responsible for the working of the undertaking
and for showing a profit on the undertaking, must run the undertaking on
strictly commercial lines and study every
economy that it can.
Now, as regards the Portavogie meeting which was held to discuss the operations of the Herring Act, it seems to me
that the fishermen at Portavogie have
been under a certain amount of misapprehension. The Herring Act, as hon.
Members know, has only recently been
passed, and the gentleman who was to
have undertaken the position of chairman
of the Board, I understand, through bad
health, has not been able to take up his
duties, as had been hoped, and so a new
chairman has had to be appointed. I do
not think they are in the position yet of
really having formulated definite
scheme or a scheme they have sufficient
confidence in as to the likelihood of its
a
being accepted by the fishermen at large
to say just how the Herring Act is going
to work.
I daresay that other hon. Members of
the Committee like myself have seen a
Press report of the meeting of fishermen
which took place at Portavogie, and so I
think I am entitled to refer to it. At
this meeting the scheme for the reorganisation of the United Kingdom
herring industry, as presented by the
recently created Herring Industry Board,
was read and apparently considered in
some detail. The Press report contains
the text of a petition which it was decided
by the meeting to submit to our Prime
Minister, asking that Northern Ireland
should be excluded from the area of the
Herring Industry Board's jurisdiction.
The fishermen who attended the meeting appear to have been under a misapprehension in thinking that the question as to whether Northern Ireland
should or should not be included within
the Board's jurisdiction was still open for
discussion. A decision on that question
was taken some few weeks ago in this
House when, after all the Northern Ireland interests concerned had been consulted, this House passed a Resolution
requesting His Majesty to make the necessary Order in Council bringing Northern
Ireland within the Board's jurisdiction.
An Order in Council to that effect has
since been made, so that the Herring
Industry Act
to
actually applied
Northern Ireland at the time when the
meeting at Portavogie was discussing the
question whether or not it should apply
here.
Whilst, therefore, it was not open to
the fishermen at so late a date as the 6th
instant to discuss a matter that had been
decided both by this Parliament and the
Imperial authorities at Westminster, it
was, however, open to the fishermen to
discuss and offer suggestions in regard to
the details of the scheme which the
Herring Board has presented for the
approval of the Imperial Ministers concerned. The statements attributed to
certain speakers at the Portavogie meeting are, in my opinion, wholly mischievous in so far as they were intended
to represent the position which has been
created by the extension of the Herring
Industry Act to Northern Ireland.
In the petition itself it is stated that
the effect of the scheme may be to bring

Mr. BARBOUR: So far as the Lough
Swilly Railway is concerned, the policy
is that which has obtained now for some
years.
This Committee has always hoped
that this grant to the Londonderry and
Lough Swilly Railway might terminate.
We had hopes that we had arrived at a
stage when the grant might be discontinued, but, just as we were arriving at
that period we had the very unfortunate
railway strike, which gave that line, as
well as other railway companies, a setback and retarded recovery, if it were
so written that the railways should recover. Having in view the passing effect
of that strike, and also the fact that
both in the Irish Free State and in
Northern Ireland Road and Rail Transport
Bills have either been passed or are
shortly to be brought before Parliament,
it was thought that we were justified in
continuing our support to this railway
for a short period longer, in order to see
whether the new legislation would help
them to survive the period of very severe
trial through which all railways are passing at the present time. We have always
been influenced in our judgment of this
matter to a very great extent by the
importance to the city of Derry of the
traffic arising on the Lough Swilly Railway, both coming into the city of Derry
and passing through the port of Derry.
For that reason we have been very
anxious indeed to perserve this means of
transport if it is in any way possible.
I was very pleased indeed by the

With regard to the Ulster Industries
Development Association, to which the
hon. Member for Pottinger referred, this
was really started, not so much with the
hope of attracting new industries to
Northern Ireland, as to give help and
stimulus to such industries as already
existed in Northern Ireland. Hon.
Members will realise that when the
Government of Ireland Act was passed
and Ireland divided into two areas, the
Irish Free State and Northern Ireland,
the flow of business throughout Ireland
was interrupted very considerably indeed.
A number of our industries in Northern
Ireland were depending to a very considerable extent upon the connection
which they enjoyed throughout the Irish
Ministry of Commerce 1506
Estimates-

Free State. The establishment of the
customs boundary between Northern
Ireland and the Irish Free State cut off
a very large volume of trade which some
of our manufacturers in Northern Ireland
had developed and enjoyed. And so it
was the suggestion of our Prime Minister,
who wanted to try to help those industries which had suffered by loss of connection, that, by rousing in Northern
Ireland a sense of patriotism and by encouraging people to support the manufacturers of Northern Ireland, we might
increase the amount of labour given in
Northern Ireland, both by using more
Northern Ireland products and by giving
preference to Northern Ireland for
goods which hitherto we had bought
elsewhere. That really is what the
Ulster Industries Development Association has been working for, and we are
very much indebted to those gentlemen
who have associated themselves with this
movement. As a matter of fact, I have
had reports from manufacturers in
Northern Ireland stating that their
business has developed to a most encouraging degree, and that they consider
this Association has been very helpful
towards that end.

With regard to the hon. and gallant
Member for Clifton (Major Hall-Thompson) and the use of concrete poles, this
is one of the things for which the Ulster
Industries Development Association have
worked, namely, to encourage the use of
local manufactures. But there again I
have to repeat that the Ulster Electricity
Board is a commercial concern, and,
though the amount of money involved
may not appear to the hon. and gallant
Gentleman to be substantial, they have
to exercise their discretion as to the suitability of concrete poles as compared with
wooden poles and also have to be guided
by the question of cost. But I can assure
the hon. and gallant Gentleman that,
although little may appear to have
materialised since last he raised this
matter before the Committee, it is not
being overlooked by the members of the
Board, and I will be only too glad to
bring it to their attention again and
try to get them interested to see if they
can give a further trial to concrete poles.
With regard to the question of the
Clogher Valley Railway, if the hon.
Member for South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy) could make any suggestion to us

and Fermanagh we regard as duties we

I am very much interested in the
herring question. I never understood
why the herring disappeared from Northern Ireland waters. I do not know if
the Ministry of Commerce have ever instituted an inquiry into that subject. It is
a subject of very great importance. The
herring represented a very valuable asset
of trade in Northern Ireland. What is the
cause of the almost complete disappearance of the herring from Northern Ireland waters? If there is an explanation,
I have not heard it. The right hon.
Gentleman says the herrings have gone,
but we have got the scallops. We have
rediscovered the scallops. Has the scallop
taken the place of the herring? I do
not think anyone would suggest that the

I do not know that the scallop is finding

as a substitute for the herring, or whether

As regards the bag net, this is an old
story. The hon. Member must realise
the difficulty of the Ministry in these
fishery matters. Unfortunately, owing
to the limited supply of fish, and the
desirability at all times of preventing the
breeding stock being unduly depleted, the
efforts and study of the Ministry have
to be directed to restriction rather
than to the encouragement of the
most efficient method of catching fish.
Object lessons are only too frequent where
the supply of breeding stock has been
unduly depleted by the short-sighted
policy which it is only a human thing
for fishermen to adopt, and that is to
catch the greatest number of fish with
the prospect and belief, that if they do
not take them someone else will.
The result of the inquiry which was
promoted some time ago as to bag-net
fishing-I am putting it in my own words
-was that the only ground on which
they could justify the substitution of the
bag nets for draft nets would be on the
basis of three to one. As the hon. Member
for North Derry has said, I think there is
only one proprietor who owns three draft
nets, who would be in the position to substitute a bag net. I am sure this is a
step that might recommend itself very
well to the owners of draft nets, but we
are up against great difficulty in the
matter. As to what the hon. and learned
Member for Central said on the question
of imports and exports, so far as quantity
was concerned, the best indication I could
give of the volume of trade passing in and
out of Belfast was to give the tonnage
figures relating to the harbour of Belfast.
Naturally in a public place like this I
do not think it would be proper to give
an advertisement by publicity of the
successful firms in our area, but I am very

was more pleasure to contemplate the instance of success of firms than to look on
the other cases which, unfortunately,

of our own Province. The number of telephones in Northern Ireland has doubled
within the last eight or nine years, while

banks, which runs into many millions,

years.
I cannot at a moment's notice

I would have no difficulty in collecting

faith.
In my speech in opening this matter

I now come to a new heading under
Sub-head K2. In September last representatives of the Sligo, Leitrim and
Northern Counties Railway Company interviewed my colleague, the Minister of
Finance, and myself, and placed before
us the financial position of the company.
These representatives were supported by
delegates of the Belfast Harbour Commissioners and of the Londonderry Harbour
Commissioners. It was explained to us
that when the necessary provision for
renewal of lines and rolling stock had
been made the railway was being carried
on at a loss; that the holders of the A
and B debentures, having consented to
take only 1 per cent. interest on their
holdings for the years 1933 and 1934,
were unlikely to be prepared to renew this
arrangement for a further period without
some guarantee for the continued payment of this reduced rate of interest; and
that unless, over and above this, some
assistance was forthcoming the company
would be forced to close the line.
paying 1 per cent. debenture interest and
making the usual provision of £3,500 for
renewals, the total debit balance at the

the end of 1934 this debit balance had increased to £13,989.
After
I should perhaps remind the Committee that the Sligo, Leitrim and Northern Counties Railway connects Sligo
with Enniskillen, and is an important
link for traffic passing between the ports
of Belfast and Londonderry and the
counties of Sligo, Leitrim, Roscommon,
and Mayo. Cattle from a number of
fairs have regularly been consigned by
rail for transport via this railway and
the Great Northern Railway to the ports
of Belfast and Londonderry. If this
link were broken by the closing of the
Sligo and Leitrim Railway much traffic
might be permanently lost to the railways and ports of Northern Ireland.
I am satisfied that the loss of traffic has
arisen mainly from a factor outside the
control of the railway company, namely,
the economic dispute between the Imperial Government and the Irish Free
State Government, and that it is not in
any great measure due to the competition of road goods traffic, although there
has been a heavy loss of passenger traffic
in recent years. I am convinced also
that the closing of the railway is very
much to be deprecated from the standpoint of Northern Ireland, and that a
Government subsidy for a limited period
is justified in this case, and would promote the interests of commerce and
shipping in Northern Ireland.
Accordingly, after careful consideration of all the factors involved, the
Government have decided, subject to the
approval of the Committee, to make a
grant of £2,500 per annum for a period
of three years to the company as from
the 1st January last. The three-year
period is proposed as giving a reasonable
time for the question to be determined
whether the railway can continue to
operate or not.
The grant is made on the clear understanding that the A and B Debenture
holders will continue to accept during
the period
period of the grant interest
at the rate of 1 per cent. per annum ;
that it will not form a precedent for any
continuance of the grant after the end
of the three-year period, whatever may
be the financial position of the company;
and that if the railway returns during
the three-year period show any substantial improvement the Government
will consider themselves at liberty to
reduce the amount of the grant.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DUTIES ON NORTHERN IRELAND
IMPORTS.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Commerce whether it is a fact that
about £12,000,000 of the £45,000,000 of
goods imported into Northern Ireland
during 1934 represented goods from
foreign countries which have been
shipped direct to British ports where the
duties on such goods were collected;
whether any part of such duties went
into the Northern Ireland Exchequer, or
whether such duties went in their entirety into the British Exchequer.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In the absence of my right hon.
Friend I have been asked to reply.
I have no information as to the proportion of the goods imported into
Northern Ireland in 1934,
which represents goods from foreign countries shipped
direct to ports in Great Britain, but I
can assure the hon. and learned Member
that Northern Ireland has received her
proper share of the duties paid on such
goods through the medium of the
residuary share of reserved taxes.
The
duties collected on goods consigned to
Northern Ireland, whether shipped direct
into Northern Ireland or indirectly
through ports in Great Britain, are
attributed to Northern Ireland as part of
her share of the reserved revenues. On
the other hand, the duty collected in
Northern Ireland in respect of goods consigned to Great Britain from foreign
countries and shipped direct to Northern
Ireland ports is attributed to Great
Britain. The net result is to give to
Northern Ireland the revenue from such
dutiable goods consumed in the country.
ROAD TRANSPORT REGULATIONS.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
building operations are being retarded,
due to the road transport regulations;
whether it is a fact that lorries are being
stopped by the police in the mornings
when bringing bricks to the various building sites; whether the procedure is to
stop the lorry and escort it back to the
city, although other weighbridges are
nearer, and have the lorry weighed to see
if it exceeds the permissible weight;
whether it is a fact that there is a
scarcity of bricks in Belfast and the bricklayers depend on these lorries to bring
bricks for them to start work each morning; whether each time a lorry is stopped
a delay of over two hours occurs; whether
bricks vary considerably in weight owing
to rain; and what action he proposes to
take to remove this anomaly.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am not aware that
building operations are being retarded as
suggested. Since the appropriate section
of the 1934 Act came into operation on
1st October last only 33 vehicles carrying bricks were stopped and weighed in
Belfast. Of these 33, 25 were found to
be overloaded, the average overloading
being about half-a-ton. In one case a
lorry licensed to carry 3 tons was found
carrying 4 tons 7 cwts.
In every instance the vehicle was
weighed at the nearest available weighbridge. In most cases these were within
a mile-in no case beyond the statutory
limit of 2 miles and I am informed that
there was no undue delay in the process,
certainly nothing approaching 2 hours.

1 am
aware that there is a certain

COST OF A BIRTH CERTIFICATE.
4. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
grave dissatisfaction prevails as to the
result of the imposition of a charge of
3s 7d in respect of birth certificates required by children in scholarship and
technical examinations; whether many
children are debarred from entering the
examinations because of the inability of
their parents to raise this amount;
whether this results in preventing able
children from securing higher education
through the poverty of their parents; and
whether he will take steps to have this
unjust imposition removed with all convenient speed.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply
to this question.
Birth certificates are not required from
candidates for this Ministry's technical
school examinations, and in the case of
applicants for scholarships to secondary
schools the question of what evidence of
age shall be required is one for the various
education committees by which the
scholarships are awarded.
I am not aware to what extent, if at
all, children have been debarred from
entering for the examinations because of
the inability of their parents to raise the
amount necessary to pay for a birth
certificate, but I can see no reason why
birth certificates should be required from
any but the successful applicants.
I may add that, in the year 1930, the
Ministry drew the attention of the
education committee to this matter and,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
18 APRIL 1935
for their guidance, furnished a revised
model scholarship scheme framed so as,
if adopted, to remove this cause of complaint and allow committees to accept a
statement or other evidence of age without insisting upon a formal birth certificate, the latter only to be required if and
when a candidate had been successful in
obtaining a scholarship.
This suggestion of the Ministry's was
incorporated in their schemes by about
half of the committees, but a number of
the others-including Belfast-still require the production of a birth certificate
from all applicants, whether successful or
not.
The matter is one primarily for the
education committees themselves, but the
Ministry would be prepared to give its
immediate approval to a proposal by any
committee so to amend its scholarship
scheme as to require a formal birth certificate only from successful applicants.
