sum that will come in course of payment
during the year ending 31st March, 1936,
to defray the salaries and expenses of
the Ministry of Home Affairs (15 & 16
Geo. V, c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 & 17 Geo. V,
c. 31 (N.I.); 20 Geo. V, c. 21, s. 7
(N.I.), etc.).'-(Note-£14,000 has been
voted on Account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have no
doubt it will meet the wishes of the
Committee if I follow the general practice
in giving on this Vote a short account
of the general activities of the Ministry,
including the various services for which
the bulk of the money is provided in the
subsequent Votes. I may say, and it is
perhaps a matter for congratulation, that
the Estimates this year present no
startling features or novel items and are
of a purely normal character.
On the Vote for a net sum of £55,457
for the Ministry itself there is little to
be said. No change has taken place in
the numbers on the establishment, and
the net increase of £864 over last year
arises from causes which are common to
all the Ministries, namely, provision for
a full year for the partial restoration of
the cuts in salaries which was made as
from the 1st July last year and for the
normal increments on salaries.
Turning now to the functions of the
Ministry, the Committee are fully conversant with the number and variety of
subjects for which I am responsible. I
shall be forgiven if I confine my remarks
to those which appear to be of more
general public interest. If any hon.
Member is specially interested in any
subject on which I may fail to touch, and
he draws my attention to it on the appropriate Vote, I shall be happy to afford
such information as I can.
As the successful administration of all
services depends upon the efficient maintenance of law and order, I think it
would be appropriate for me to deal
generally with this question first. During the past year, I am glad to say that
the various judges of assize have found it
possible to make references of a satisfactory character to the peaceful conditions which they found prevailing
throughout the Province. This happy
state of affairs is, of course, mainly due
to the good sense and the law-abiding
character of our citizens, and also, as I
am sure will be admitted by every Member of the Committee, to the efficiency of
our constabulary forces and the good
feeling which, I am glad to say, exists
between the people as a whole and the
members of these two forces.
In this connection, however, there are
some matters which have been causing
no little concern. There has, unfor-
Ministry of Home Affairs 1542
Estimates-
18 APRIL 1935
tunately, been a considerable increase in
the number of cases of burglary and of
breaking and entering within the past
year. Such fluctuations in crime are, of
course, inevitable, but as one of His
Majesty's judges pointed out, a number
of these cases could have been prevented
if the owners of property had taken a
little more care for its protection.
I am glad, however, to be able to
inform the Committee that recent information which I have obtained indicates
that detections have been made by the
police in an increasing number of these
cases, and I have little doubt that the
active measures which are being taken
by the police will have the effect of
speedily checking what I may call the upward curve in the statistics of this class
of crime.
Another type of offence which still
prevails is smuggling. Unquestionably,
smuggling is still being carried on in the
Border counties, although checked and
kept within bounds by the constant
activity of the police. I can only add
my voice to that of the presiding judge
in a recent assizes when he appealed to
all citizens to do everything in their
power to help the authorities to stamp
out this evil. Not only can positive
assistance be afforded by giving information, but I think that what is also
required, and would have even a greater
effect, would be the creation of a healthy
public opinion to show up this crime in
its true light as a serious crime against
the State, just as serious as, say, embezzlement or larceny.
Mr. HEALY: Smuggling arms.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend will have ample opportunity
to develop that argument afterwards.
There is no doubt that this class of crime
is too often condoned by those who should
know better, and the demoralising effect
of such attitude of mind towards such
breaches of the law can hardly be overestimated. In addition, the effect of
smuggling imposes a severe handicap on
the interests of the farmers of Northern
Ireland.
a
In another direction also the state of
crime shows, I am sorry to say,
tendency to increase. I refer to the
increase in juvenile crime. It is hard to
give any one specific reason for this increase. The prevalence of unemployment has been suggested as one of the
causes of this unfortunate condition of
affairs. While, perhaps, this may be a
contributory cause, I am convinced that
the relaxation of parental control is in an
even greater degree to blame. Modern
parents are generally far too much inclined to shake off the responsibility for
training their children, and to regard
this duty as a matter entirely for
teachers. This is a
great mistake.
Nothing, in my opinion, can replace the
moral effect of home influences, and I am
certain that parental control is a far
better remedy than anything that can be
effected by Acts of Parliament or by the
police.
I am satisfied from cases which constantly come under my notice that in
many cases had proper parental control
been exercised, the boy or girl in question
would never have had to appear before
a court.
I appreciate very much indeed the
splendid work that various voluntary
organisations in our Province are doing
in trying to look
look after and train
juveniles and to provide for these interests and occupations which will keep
them out of trouble.
The value and the necessity for such
work is evident from the fact of the
inauguration of the Jubilee Fund by
H.R.H. the Prince of Wales, the proceeds of which will be devoted to such
objects.
I am
sorry that there are still in
Northern Ireland certain misguided
persons who, for reasons best known to
themselves, would, if they had the opportunity to do so, foment disorder and strife
in our midst and endeavour to revive unlawful associations which, as hon. Members will remember, were the cause of
outrage and disorder at the time our
Government was set up. Although I am
glad to say that during the last year no
instances of such outrages of any serious
character have occurred, I am afraid as
yet this is not due to any change of heart
on the part of our enemies, but is attributable solely to the constant vigilance
and energy of police and to the knowledge.
that crime, whether disguised under the
high-sounding but meaningless title of
political crime or otherwise, will be dealt
with with the full rigour of the law. I
Ministry of Home Affairs 1544
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
hope that in due course the futility of
such unreasoning animosity to established
order will become apparent, and that outrage and violence will cease to be used as
weapons to enforce political opinions.
I can only say this, that the Government will not tolerate any such criminal
activities and will continue to take drastic
and stringent measures against any
persons who attempt in any way to interfere with or disturb our Constitution, and
I am fully aware that in doing so I will
have behind me the unqualified support
of every right-minded member of the
community. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) No person who is disposed to obey
the law in Northern Ireland, and keep
the peace need fear any interference with
his personal liberty.
In concluding these remarks on the
general subject of law and order, I feel
that a tribute is due to the members of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the
Special Constabulary for the very able
and efficient manner in which they have
carried out their duties during the past
year. I do not think I can give them
higher praise than to say that they have
continued to discharge their duties with
the same high degree of loyalty and zeal
that we have come to expect from them
as a matter of course.
I now turn to the prisons and kindred
services. The governors of the prisons
and their staffs continued to render most
satisfactory service during the year, and
I have again to record my appreciation
of the valuable work discharged by the
visiting committees and by the boards of
justices. The public-spirited ladies and
gentlemen who act on these committees
and boards discharge their various duties
and carry out their periodic inspections
with the greatest care, and the fact that
the reports which they furnish in regard
to the administration of the prisons are
entirely satisfactory, is an indication of
the admirable manner in which the prison
service in Northern Ireland is conducted.
I should also like once more to pay a
public tribute to the work carried out by
the Discharged Prisoners' Aid Societies.
These societies have one of the most
thankless tasks to perform, and I am
afraid that their work is one which is not
fully appreciated by the general public,
and that they do not get the support from
the public which their good work
deserves.
Although, in every community, there are a few hardened
criminals, yet on the other hand there
are many whose lapse into crime has
really been due to want of employment
or some other similar cause, and if, on
discharge, such prisoners are given a
helping hand it means that in many cases
they are saved from a career of crime.
It is this work of trying to find employment for and to help prisoners on their
discharge that is being carried out
energetically and unobtrusively by the
Discharged Prisoners' Aid Societies, and
I am very glad to think that in many
cases their efforts on behalf of the
prisoners have proved entirely successful.
Last
I have already referred to the increase
which has taken place in juvenile crime,
and the effect of this is shown in the
Estimate for Borstal institutions and reformatory and industrial schools.
year it was estimated that the number of
reformatory children would be as low as
40, but at the present moment the
number is 80. In the Malone Training
School-that is the Borstal institutionthe numbers have risen from 18 to 48.
This substantial rise has been attributed
by the judges to various causes, to which
I have already referred, and it is rather
significant to note, in view of the statement made by one of the judges, that
there might have been too much leniency
shown in the sentences imposed on youthful offenders, to note that a prominent
Belfast welfare worker considers that the
dangerous age for boys is from 11 to 14,
the
age at which many of the more recent
committals expire.
It is highly desirable, therefore, that
such boys who have, in many instances,
banded themselves into gangs, should be
kept under the beneficent supervision and
disciplinary control that obtains in our
reformatories and industrial schools until
they have fully learnt the lesson of
obedience to the law. In the Malone
Training School these boys are afforded an
opportunity to overcome the natural disposition of youth to resent discipline and
to regard lawlessness as something
synonymous with manliness, and are
given the benefit of useful physical and
educational training under the governor
of the school and his very efficient staff.
I cannot too often emphasise how much
we owe the governor of the Malone Training School and his staff for the successful
Ministry of Home Affairs 1546
Estimates-
18 APRIL 1935
way in which they are able to deal with
the boys entrusted to their care, boys who
would otherwise, I fear, inevitably drift
into a life of crime and who would ultimately become a liability, instead of an
asset, to the State. I am glad to say that
many Members of this House have taken
advantage of the invitations sent to them.
to visit the school, and I do hope that
those who have not yet been able to do so
will avail themselves of the first opportunity of inspecting the school and seeing
for themselves what has been and is being
achieved.
The training which the boys receive in
the school is, I submit, an excellent
foundation on which their after careers as
useful citizens of the State may be built,
but the good results of the training which
they receive at the school would be largely
nullified if the boys on leaving were exposed, without some further help and
assistance, to the temptations of their
former mode of life. To meet this difficulty the Borstal Association has taken
upon its shoulders the onerous task of
looking after these boys when they leave
the institution, and the report which that
association sends to me quarterly reveals
that in at least 75 per cent. of the cases
under their care the boys are doing well
in employment which has been procured
for them. This is an eminently satisfactory result and is an indication of the
great value of the work carried on by this
association. We often hear of the bad
cases, but we seldom hear of the good
cases. People when they talk about the
failure of the Borstal institution should
inquire more closely into the results to
find what cases have made good rather
than those who have been failures.
With regard to the local government
services, it will be seen that an increase
of about £48,000 appears in respect of
grants to local authorities. Of this, however, about £39,000 is accounted for by
an increase in the derating grants due
to the carrying forward from last year of
certain final payments in respect of
supplemental grant, so that this year two.
such payments fall to be made. The
other substantial increases are for tuberculosis and housing schemes, of which the
former are percentage grants made on the
basis of the expenditure incurred by the
local authorities.
A year ago I had to refer to a falling
off in building operations under the
Housing Acts, but I am glad to be able
to say that during the past year building
has been resumed on a very satisfactory
scale, and there is every reason to believe
that it will continue throughout the
present year. Last year the number of
houses approved for erection by private
builders was 4,031, as against only 755
in the preceding year, and it is estimated
that at least 3,000 houses will be
approved during the current year. While
private builders are thus active local
authorities have shown a certain
reluctance to embark on housing schemes.
Only 50 houses were erected by local
authorities during the past year, and it
is estimated that about 100 may be built
this year.
As to the question of the administration of roads, I have only to say that the
various road authorities still continue,
with the assistance of the Government, to
put every effort forward, not alone to
preserve the surfaces of roads at a high
standard, but to make such improvements and alterations by way of widening
sharp bends and dangerous corners
will contribute to the safety of all road
users.
as
The number of road accidents, with
the consequent loss of life and injury,
continues to cause a good deal of concern.
In the year 1934 there were 1,835
accidents reported, involving the death of
132 persons, and the injury, more or
less serious, of 1,954 persons. These
figures compare with 1,633 accidents
reported in 1933, involving the death of
141 persons and the injury of 1,757
persons.
an
This state of affairs is sufficiently
serious, but I do not want to exaggerate,
and I should qualify it by pointing out,
in the first place, that there is
increase in the number of fatalities, and
that portion of the increase in the
number of accidents and the number of
persons injured is probably due to more
exhaustive reporting of accidents than
hitherto.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Might I ask the
Minister is speed not a great factor in
connection with these accidents?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I will
deal with that aspect of the question a
little later. It must, of course, be borne
in mind that in quite a number of cases
Ministry of Home Affairs 1548
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
the accidents or the injuries involved
were not of a very serious nature.
We have been analysing the position
with the object of seeing what are the
causes at the root of this casualty list,
and what remedies can be applied, and
perhaps I might give the Committee the
results of our analysis of the total number
of accidents during 1934, as, I think,
hon. Members will find this analysis both
interesting and instructive, and it may,
perhaps, answer the point put to me by
the hon. and learned Member for
Central.
a
As I have already stated, there were
132 people killed on the roads in 1934,
and hon. Members will probably be very
surprised to know that in 24 cases, that
is almost one-fifth of the total number,
there was no motor vehicle involved at
all. This represents an increase of 13 in
this type of accident over the previous
year. Out of the 24, one person,
woman of 71 years of age, was knocked
down by a tramcar, and three persons
were killed by accidents connected with
horse-drawn vehicles. All the rest, that
is 20, were killed in accidents with pedal
cycles. If you analyse this figure of 20
a little further, you will find that twelve
pedestrians were killed by collision with
pedal cyclists, and the remaining eight
people were riders of bicycles who lost
control of their machines and were
fatally injured.
I would ask hon. Members to bear in
mind that these figures do not complete
the toll of cyclists who lost their lives on
the road. There were, in addition, 23
killed in collision with motor vehicles.
It is, therefore, evident that the
tremendous increase in the number of
pedal cyclists using the roads in the last
two or three years has created a further
road problem.
If we deduct 11 non-motoring cases for
1933 and 24 for 1934 from the total
figures from the people killed on the road
for the years 1933 and 1934, we find that
in the year 1933 there were 130 people
killed in accidents in which motor vehicles
were involved as against 108 people
killed in accidents in which motor
vehicles were involved in the year 1934.
There has, therefore, been a substantial
decrease as between the two years in the
number of road deaths in which motor
vehicles were concerned.
In 1933, 38 children under 15 years of
age were killed. In 1934, the number
dropped to 24. An examination of the
circumstances of these 24 accidents leads
me to the conclusion that very few, if
any, could have been prevented by any
legislation.

In 1934, 19 motor drivers were killed,
and of this number
were motor
cyclists. Thirteen passengers on motor
vehicles were killed during the year, of
whom three were pillion riders. Apart
from drivers and passengers on motor
vehicles, 76 people were killed in
accidents involving motor vehicles. That
is a decrease of 16 in the comparable
number for the previous year, 1933.
It is interesting to note that out of the
total number of fatalities 27 persons of
over 60 years of age were killed, and,
to push this analysis just a little further,
22 out of the 27 were over 70 years of
age.
I am not prepared to say that nothing
more can be done by legislation. We
may find it necessary to introduce further
restrictions, and if I do come to the conclusion that any such further restrictive
legislation is required I shall not hesitate
to ask the House to pass it, no matter how
unpopular it may be, but I desire to
avoid it if I can. I am convinced that
the real remedy for the present unsatisfactory state of affairs lies very largely
in the hands of road users themselves.
Greater care and greater consideration
for others is needed from all sections of
the public.
I desire to emphasise that everything
goes to show that the number of bad
and inconsiderate drivers is only a small
fraction of the whole. Some of the bad
driving is due to mere carelessness, but,
on the other hand, some of it is due to
a selfish disregard of the rights and convenience of other people, and I am convinced that the only way to deal with this
small section of the motoring public is to
take away their right to drive. That
does not lie in my hands. The powers
in that respect are vested in others over
whom I have no control. Theirs is the
responsibility and they must answer for
it.
With regard to children, I think that
the most hopeful line of approach is by
arranging that they should be instructed
in regard to the dangers of the road, and
that the risks should be impressed upon
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
18 APRIL 1935
them. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Accordingly, I have arranged with my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Education, for lectures to be given to
teachers at various centres, and also for
lectures to be given to the students who
will ultimately become teachers, so that
they may from time to time in the schools
instruct their pupils as to the proper
behaviour on the roads.
I have been giving very careful consideration to the question of a general
speed limit or a speed limit in particular
areas. I am taking the deepest interest
in the experiment which is in progress in
Great Britain. It is much too soon, in
my view, to form any opinion as to the
value of the speed limit which has been
imposed there. One cannot really judge.
of an experiment of this kind on
results of a month or two's working.
a
the
I trust that it will not be necessary to
impose further restrictions of similar
character here, but again I desire to make
it clear that, should the evidence convince
me that a speed limit of some similar
character is necessary or desirable, I shall
not hesitate to impose it, provided I am
sure that it is going to reduce accidents
appreciably. It seems to me that the
question of whether there should be a
speed limit here or not is, to a very great
degree, in the hands of motor drivers.
If they abuse their present liberty in the
matter of speed then we shall have no
alternative but to introduce further
restrictions.
The police are doing all they can to
eliminate the bad driver or the driver
who travels at a speed that is dangerous
to the public, but the police force is
limited in numbers, and they have many
other duties to perform. Their activities
with regard to motoring are directed to
making the roads safe for the decent and
considerate driver, and for all other persons who legitimately use the roads.
They should, therefore, be able to count
upon the co-operation of all these people.
They have not got that co-operation up
to the present, and without it their
efforts cannot be successful. If they do
not get it, and if their present powers do
not prove sufficient, then motorists will
have themselves to blame when I have to
come to this House and ask for more
drastic powers. One has only to examine
the motoring records of the licence
holders in Northern Ireland to realise
that the vast majority of them are careful drivers. While this is so, one would
have thought it was in their interest to
support the authorities in their efforts to
put down reckless and dangerous driving.
It is due to this small minority of reckless drivers that it has been necessary to
bring in restrictive legislation. It is also
due to them that insurance rates are
increased, and I cannot understand how
it is that the majority of motorists should
not co-operate to a larger extent with the
authorities in their endeavours to reduce
these appalling casualty lists and so bring
about the advantage which must follow
from the elimination of the dangerous
driver.
Further, I am hopeful that the various.
provisions of last year's Motor Traffic Act
will contribute to a lessening of these
accidents. For example, the scheme for
the licensing of goods vehicles, which has
the object of ensuring that such vehicles
are in a fit mechanical condition for the
road, is well under way, and already
more than half of these vehicles have been
inspected and licensed. So far as the
examination has gone it has clearly
demonstrated the necessity for supervision
of these vehicles, and the wisdom of the
provision made by Parliament last year
with regard to them. Provision has also
been made by regulation for preventing
undue overloading of such vehicles, which
removes another possible danger on the
roads, and during the past few weeks
regulations have been brought into operation regulating the hours of driving of
drivers of goods vehicles; it is hoped that
the effect will be to remove one of the
greatest menaces of the road-the tired
driver.
Mr. BEATTIE: When will these regulations come into this House?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think they
are in this House at the present time. I
need not particularly refer to the other.
services, except to say that I should like
to take this opportunity of thanking the
local authorities for the ready co-operation which they are generally willing to
afford to my Ministry in carrying out its
functions in relation to public health and
other matters.

The CHAIRMAN: Only questions of

for these extravagant

Mr. BEATTIE: In discussing the
Estimate placed before the House so ably
by the Minister of Home Affairs I feel
the Minister has a wrong idea in regard
to what the cost of his Department
should actually amount to. He says he
is pleased to note that no increase has
taken place. I am sorry that no decrease
has taken place, because I would expect
a Department that covers the various
services that the Home Office covers, for
1 million people, would require a far
less amount. We all realise that the
making up of a department perhaps
might cost more than when it has got
into smooth running. I think that by
now the Home Department should be in
smooth running and everything worked
into its place. I, at any rate, expected
a very substantial reduction in the cost
of that Department, and I am sorry to
have to state that in my opinion the
Minister consolidated the cost of his
Department for ever and ever, amen.
That is not going to be suitable to the
taxpayers of Northern Ireland, because
the making-up cost of each department
on abnormal conditions, and the income
of the people of Northern Ireland who
have got to pay the final cost-are not
equal to one another. Therefore, the
present cost of Home Affairs, in my
opinion, should be reduced at least 25
per cent. That applies not only to Home
Affairs; it applies to every Department in
accordance with the population. We
have not an expanding ground to operate
upon. We have a limited area to make
our collections from, and we must then
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
make our divisions in accordance with
our area and population.
If we fail to realise that principle we
have failed altogether in the government
of our area. I feel on looking over the
items in the Estimate, and after listening to the Minister very attentively, that
he has treated the important things
lightly and the unimportant things very
seriously. That puts me in mind of the
quack doctor who tries to make his
audience believe that the article he is
selling is one of special quality, one which
could not be got from the medical
practitioner. By that means he is able
to gull his audience and sell his old dud
remedy for a high price. That is really
the picture that has been put before me
in regard to some of the items which I
claim are unimportant. The first important part relates to juvenile crime.
Is the Home Office making any reasonable effort to stop juvenile crime? We
have heard plenty of lip service, but I
have seen no practical service rendered
towards stopping that great evil that
exists in our midst. Has no official made
inquiry into the reason for the juvenile
crime? In my opinion the Ministry have
not thought it worth their while to spend
time on it.
The Minister says that juvenile crime
is due to the lack of parental control.
This complaint cannot be lodged at the
door of the parents. No parent wishes
to see his child led into crime if he can
avoid it. How are we to get the parental
control that we once had? At the
present moment the Home Office pursues
the policy of compelling the father to go
out in the early morning until late at
night seeking employment. They also
compel the mother to go out in the early
morning until late at night either to work
in a factory or mill or some other industry
so that she may make a living and eke out
an existence. Can the Home Office not
get together expert minds and say, "We
must preserve the home and children, and
by that preservation see that the mother
takes her place inside the home and not
be compelled to go out and assist in earning a pittance to feed and clothe the
children." When the mother is compelled to go out the children lose the
motherly care which their parents desire
to give them. Has the Home Office ever
thought of that being the means of
increasing juvenile crime? In my
opinion that is a great factor in the lack
of control which the Minister says is so
important. I hope the Ministry will
assist in removing the mother out of
industry by finding suitable employment
for the father, together with a wage commensurate with the economic requirements of the home. If that is done you
will go a long way to assist in reducing
juvenile crime.
I want to say that in my opinion there
is too much of the inferiority complex in
the Estimates. On every page you find
this staring you in the face. While in
the House I have been looking over
certain classifications. I find that one
man, although he only pays the same rent
as another for the same housing accommodation, has about 50 per cent. more
attached to his classification. Although
he only gives equal value he has anything
up to £200 more in salary attached to his
classification. It comes back once again
to the old story, which is true, and always
will be true-
The Lord made the bees, and the
bees made the honey.
The helpers did the work, and the
platers got the money.
This is true of the R.U.C. The rank
and file do all the hard, grinding work,
but do not get a return commensurate
with the services they give. I say that
fearlessly. I do not say it in disrespect
to any part of the R.U.C. I claim that
the inferiority complex is shown there.
You have sons of Ulster in the force at
the moment who, although they are
common constables, are as good in
classification and outlook as the head of
the force. If comradeship and co-operation were exercised in that force at
present we would have no necessity to
notify police of the secret crime that is
being carried out in Northern Ireland.
If you had hearty co-operation in the
force, if the men were treated as men,
and if none of this inferiority complex
were indulged in, I believe we would
have this evil that exists in Northern
Ireland rooted out very shortly.

lorry drivers,

I want to tell the Prime Minister that

Ulster as good, if not better, than any

I believe that the brick-making industry

I make that point about elasticity in

they drove at the same rate as I do would
perhaps meet with one or two accidents
every day. They are inclined to be
safest when driving at a high speed.
Therefore, a speed limit is not going to
regulate those two factors. I hope the
Home Office will continue to investigate
what is best to ensure the safety of the
highways.
I am now going to make an obeservation which I think I am entitled to make.
I do not agree that policemen should be
employed in certain classes of work which
they are doing at the moment. If there
is anything that the Minister of Home
Affairs should do it is to avoid public
criticism such as is being levelled just
now in connection with policemen having
either to hide behind a ditch or juke
round a corner in order to educate
motorists who violate the line at a corner.
I think it is a very low and mean occupation to ask any man to apply himself to.
The object should be to prevent anything
of the kind happening. I know that if a
motorist coming on the straight to a bend
sees a policeman standing in the open it
would tend to make him pull up and
keep within the line.
Mr. HANNA: Do you suggest a policeman at every bend?
Mr. BEATTIE: No, I do not suggest
that, and I do not suggest that at the
moment you should have two policemen
at every bend. I suggest that to educate
the motorist up to his responsibility on
the road we must have an educator, and
in my opinion a policeman standing at a
corner in the open will do more to educate
the man who is inclined to buzz round a
corner to the danger of others than two
policemen, one at each end, hiding behind
the hedge.

would give a warning for many other

necessary? Having regard to the size

Is it not more reminiscent of the days
when this Province had money to burn?
It had money to burn when this Government was started in 1921. I think the
revenue of the Province at that time was
in the region of £20,000,000. To-day it is
down to about £10,000,000, but, although
our finances are going down and the

like the old antique guard that used to
be kept at Hillsborough Castle by the
Downshire family. Is this Governor's
Guard really a reproduction of that force?
It certainly does seem to me to be superfluous and out of keeping with the present times.
One other matter to which I wish to

that there is to be no going back on the

But, mark you, that £1,100,000 is a

derated and who are faced with a very

The last matter on which I propose to
comment is the question of road accidents.
I do hope and I inferred from his
speech that this will be so that the right
hon. Gentleman will keep an open mind
on this question of a speed limit for
Northern Ireland. I take it that the
right hon. Gentleman has not finally
closed his mind or ended his experience
on that point. There is a feeling-it
may be wrong, and I do not now say
that it is right-among a very large
element of the population in Northern
Ireland, especially among pedestrians,
who constitute by far the largest part of
our population-they are people who have
never had a motor car, and who never
will have a motor car-that a great deal
of the accountability for the enormous
number of road casualties in our area
is to be laid at the door of the motor car
travelling at excessive speed. The
number of lives, young and old, sacrificed
in road accidents every year constitutes
a tragic story. These people do feel that
a great deal of the responsibility for that
is due to the speed of these cars. I am
glad the Minister of Home Affairs has
not closed his mind as to whether or not
there should be a speed limit here such
as has been set up in England. There
is a speed limit in force now in built-up
areas right over Great Britain, and reports go to show that it is working well
and satisfactorily. I am sure the
Minister is watching it carefully, and I
am glad to know that in this matter he
will, for the present at any rate, keep
an open mind.

Ministry of Home Affairs

should be inspected, but individual

or not. I have certainly heard that

It is obvious that the inspection should

of decorative repair. I am quite sure

There is another matter which I
have already mentioned to the right
hon. Gentleman in connection with the
recent regulations for the hours of
work of the drivers of goods vehicles.
There is again another difficulty which
I do not make a subject of complaint,
because I am heartily in favour of any
regulations that would ensure a proper
working day for drivers of goods vehicles.
It is quite proper that drivers of goods
vehicles should drive only a certain
number of hours, and therefore not suffer
unduly from fatigue. We have had experience in court of some lamentable cases
of the results of over-fatigue of drivers.
But in connection with several trades, the
bakery trade and the coal trade, for instance, there are vehicles used for the
purpose of distributing goods over limited.
areas. The drivers of those vehicles are
driving for a very limited portion of the
day, and the greater part of their time is
taken up in actually distributing the
goods or taking orders. They are in a
small way commercial travellers, distributing goods and taking orders for further
goods. I would ask the right hon. Gentleman and the Parliamentary Secretary to
consider carefully whether in connection.
with that type of driver and that type of
vehicle, operating over a limited area,
and, in fact, being driven over a limited
number of miles in the day, some relaxation of these regulations would not be
advisable. It is a difficult matter, and a
matter that will certainly require very
careful consideration, and I think it is a
matter that certainly deserves consideration.
The last matter I would like to refer to
is one in which I have on previous
occasions found myself, somewhat to my
astonishment, in agreement with the hon.
and learned Member for Central. It is
not often that he and I agree on any
subject in this House, but once again I
agree with him in connection with this
much-debated and much-discussed speed
limit. I speak as one who does not drive,
and does not own a motor-car, and therefore possibly my friends who do own and
drive cars might think I am a little oldfashioned. But there are two arguments
in favour of a speed limit, both of which,
to my mind, carry conviction. The first
argument is the number of fatalities in the
city of London, as distinguished from the
number of fatalities in other parts of the
country. In the city of London, where
all traffic necessarily proceeds at an exceedingly low speed, the number of
fatalities is extraordinarily low, notwithstanding the extreme density of the
traffic. That is the first consideration
that affects my judgment in connection
with that matter.
or
The second is this. I think that, while
it would be absurd to suggest that the
average motorist in the city of Belfast
drove recklessly-in fact I think we could
all agree that the number who drive recklessly is relatively small-nevertheless I
venture to think that any person who is
acquainted with either the Lisburn Road
or the Malone Road, and who sees cars
driven into the city in the morning.
sees cars driven out of the city in
the evening on either of those roads, will
say that, not a large percentage, but
certainly a definite percentage of cars are
being driven at a speed which seems to
me as a member of the public perfectly
outrageous. It is for those reasons that,
as an individual, I think that ultimately
the right hon. Gentleman should favourably consider the imposition of a speed
limit. I quite recognise its difficulties,
and that it is a matter that will require
careful consideration, but I certainly
would be very sorry if, in view of the
present situation and the possibilities of
the future, I heard the right hon. Gentleman definitely say that he was opposed
to a speed limit. With these remarks
I will conclude by congratulating the
right hon. Gentleman on these estimates.

TEACHERS ON SCHOOL
COMMITTEES.
1. Mr. STEWART (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education whether the
Irvinestown School Committee have been
given special permission to enable its
teacher members to vote, contrary to the
practice elsewhere; and whether legal
opinion has yet been obtained on the
subject of the advice tendered by the
Permanent Secretary in a letter to Mrs
Hermon on this matter.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): It is not
clear to what the hon. Member refers
under the term School Committee. This
term was employed in Section 3 of the
Education Act of 1923. That Section
has now been replaced by Section 2 of
the 1930 Act and the term used therein
is School Management Committee. Express provision is made in this Section
for the appointment of representatives
of the teachers on these School Management Committees. Such persons have
the right to take part in the meetings,
but not to vote on any question regarding the selection of a teacher.
It is possible however, that the hon.
Member may refer to School Attendance
Sub-Committees.
an
The Application of Enactments Order,
1898, by its terms applies to committees
and joint committees appointed by
County Councils, but it did not appear
to be clear whether sub-committees of
Education Committee come within
the ambit of this order which, read in
conjunction with Section 66 (2) of the
Education Act, 1923, provides that no
public elementary school teacher employed in the area may be a member of
such committee or joint committee. la
the absence of an authoritative interpretation of the Act dealing with this point
the view taken by the Ministry has been.
that membership of such sub-committees
was open to teachers.
In view of the doubts expressed as to
the legality of the position the question
has been referred to the legal advisers of
the Crown, and their opinion is to the
effect that sub-committees of an Education Committee come within the ambit
of the Order.

Transport Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Road and Railway Transport Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Bill, of which
I am to move the Second Reading this
afternoon, is one of the most important,
if not the most important, with which
this House has had to deal since its inception, for at no period of history has
transport had a greater influence on the
life of the community than at the present
time. An efficient, economical, and
comprehensive system of transport, both
for passengers and goods, is vital to the
convenience and prosperity of the community.
The introduction of the internal combustion engine in recent years has provided an additional means of transport
which has exercised a profound influence.
People nowadays are continually on the
move, and the new means of transport
has altered the distribution of population, and it has made many changes in
commercial life and methods.
Transport, therefore, more than ever
before, is an essential public utility
service, like electricity, gas, and so forth,
but in these days it is an even more
essential service than these. It must not
merely be convenient and cheap, but it
must be comprehensive. All parts of
the country must be provided with a
suitable service, and I would like to emphasise this point that our transport
system must be looked at in a broad way
and as a whole. It is a problem affecting
the whole country and it must be dealt
with in a large way, and in this Bill the
Government are attempting to do so. A
solution cannot be found by looking at
individual places, or by considering individual services or districts, and I sincerely hope that hon. Members will not
look at this Bill, and the problems with
which it attempts to deal, from the point
of view of any individual or sectional
interest, but from the point of view of
the community as whole. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
a
I am afraid I shall have to trespass
on the patience of the House for some
little time, and perhaps it would help
hon. Members to follow me if I were to
indicate the way in which I propose to
deal with the matter.
I propose, firstly, to indicate to the
House what the problem is; secondly,
why the Government have come to the
conclusion that matters cannot be left as
they are to-day; thirdly, what attempts
have been made to solve the similar
problem in other places and why the
Government have decided to reject these;
fourthly, to explain in broad outline
what is the solution that we now put
forward; and lastly, the reasons why we
have adopted this solution.
First then, what is the problem? At
the present time in Northern Ireland
public transport for passengers and goods
is being supplied mainly by railway companies operating on rail and road, and
by companies and individuals operating
buses and lorries. In pre-war days the
only means of transport, for other than
short distances, was the railways. Then,
shortly after the war, the comparatively
light and fast omnibus was introduced,
with the result that gradually much of
the passenger traffic hitherto carried by
the railways came on to the roads, and,
in addition, a large additional traffic was
created. People who never, or rarely,
moved from their homes began frequently
to travel comparatively long distances.
Somewhat later haulage of goods on the
roads began to develop, and much goods
traffic left the railways and is being
carried at the present time on the highways.
There can be no dispute that the introduction of road transport has brought in
its train many advantages and conveniences. It can, in certain directions,
perform functions which no railway can
carry out, and in certain respects it has
very much altered the usefulness and
functions of railways. I do not think
that the most bigoted advocate of railways would suggest that it would be an
economic or a proper thing at the present
day to lay down new branch lines. I do
not believe that any sensible railwayman
would contest the proposition that the
usefulness of some of the existing branch
railway lines has been nullified by the
development of road transport, and that
the pruning knife must be applied to the
railway systems.
Another element which we cannot lose
sight of in considering the transport
problem is that in pre-war days the vast
majority of the population had no means
of travelling or moving their goods for
Transport Bill-
Second Reading
14 MAY 1935
any appreciable distance except by the
public carriers, namely, the railways.
Nowadays, of course, the position is very
different, and every owner of a motor-car
can take quite long journeys in his own.
vehicle, and every owner of a lorry can
transport his goods in his own vehicle to
distant parts.
At the present time railways are providing widespread and extensive facilities
for the carriage of both passengers and
goods on rail and road. We have also a
network of bus services all over the
Province providing very good services,
and then there is a very large number of
lorries plying for hire and carrying large
quantities of goods. Why then should
the Government interfere? I may say
at once that if there were the slightest
prospect of the existing services being
carried on permanently or even for a
reasonable period on the present basis
the Government would not for
moment interfere, but we are compelled
to bring forward proposals for a
organisation of the industry because,
after careful examination of the real
position, we are convinced that under the
present organisation the existing services
cannot be continued. This is fully
recognised by everyone who considers the
real facts of the case, but a great section
of the public is living in a fool's paradise
with regard to transport.
one
re-.
The industry, and by that I mean the
transport industry as a whole, is being
carried on on uneconomic and wasteful
lines. It is, to a very considerable
degree, living on its capital, and to this
there can be but one end and that in the
near future. The public would be left
with a broken and ineffective service, and
it is the duty of the Government to prevent this. In some ways it might have
been easier for us to have waited till the
collapse came, but if we had done so we
should rightly have been charged with
lack of foresight and with a disregard
for the real interest of the community.
I know that it has been suggested in
certain quarters that this Bill is being
brought forward in the interests of the
railway shareholders. That is utterly
untrue. I want at once to make it clear
to what extent the Government are concerned with the financial position of the
transport industry. If the only element'
in the situation were that the railway
shareholders, or the shareholders in any
other form of transport, were not receiving dividends, the Government certainly
would not be bringing in this Bill. The
financial position of the industry is vital
because efficient transport services for the
public, without which no country can be
prosperous, can only be provided if the
industry is in a sound financial position,
and if it is in a position to obtain the
capital requisite for the developments
and improvements which are necessary
from time to time if the industry is to
keep up-to-date. It can only be kept in
a position to render efficient service if it
can earn sufficient to pay its expenses,
including the making of proper provision,
not merely for renewals, repairs to rolling
stock, plant, and so on, but, under
the rapidly changing conditions, for
obsolescence.
You cannot have efficient service from
concerns that are losing money, and there
can be no doubt that to-day a very large
proportion of the transport in Northern.
Ireland running under existing conditions is not covering its working ex-
This state of affairs is due, to a
very large extent, to the fact that it is
being run wastefully and extravagantly.
penses.
I do not deny that there are some
individual concerns that are making ends
meet, but this is the exception and not
the rule. Taking the industry as a
whole the position is critical as a result
of uneconomical cut-throat competition,
and there is a prospect of imminent
collapse.
The Government, the House and the
public must face the position that would
be created by the cessation of the railways, which are under legal obligations
to carry any traffic. Such an event
would throw upon the roads large masses
of traffic which have not hitherto been
carried on them. We must face the consequences of the abolition of the railways,
coupled with the fact that we have a road
freight transport system that is badly
organised, wasteful and financially weak.
It is easy to forecast what would be the
result of such a situation unless action
is taken now. If such a situation were
left to develop it would present an ideal
opportunity for the exploitation of the
community. The whole transport of the
country would become a financial
monopoly, worked in the interest of
private individuals and not of the public.
Second Reading
Transport Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Let me first examine the railway
position.
While we as a Government
are not concerned whether or not the
railway shareholder is receiving dividends
on his investment, we have got to face
this fact that for some time the railways
have not been earning sufficient to cover
their actual working expenses. For the
year 1932 the Northern Counties Railway,
which is a branch of the London, Midland & Scottish Railway, actually lost
£33,796; for the year 1933, £81,069; and
for the year 1934, £37,084. It must be
apparent to the thinking public that the
shareholders of this English railway will
not be prepared to go on subsidising out
of their own pockets the Northern Ireland branch, and if anyone questions this
statement I would refer them to the
reports of the last two annual meetings
of the L.M.S. in England.
The Great Northern Railway in
Northern Ireland and the Belfast and
County Down Railway are in an even
worse position, because they have not a
big English railway to support them. In
their cases when their reserves are
exhausted they must inevitably go out of
business.
Therefore, we are faced with thisand the public must realise it--that
either the railways must be allowed to go
out of existence and Northern Ireland
must depend entirely on road transport,
or that some change must take place.
One cannot but think that the critics of
this scheme have not realised the consequences which must ensue from the
closing of the railways. They have not
faced the issue, but, Micawber-like, they
are waiting for something to turn up, but
no responsible Government can adopt
this attitude. We have come to the conclusion that it would be disastrous to the
welfare and prosperity of Northern Ireland if the railways were closed down,
and, therefore, we must take action. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Similar views
were expressed to Sir Felix Pole by
various representative interests. For
instance, the Ulster Farmers' Union,
which represents the greatest industry in
Northern Ireland, stated that they would
view with alarm the abolition of the railway system.
I do not intend to enter into the controversy which has raged for a number of
years as to whether the competition
between road and rail transport is
carried out under fair conditions, or
whether road traffic has been subsidised
owing to the maintenance of the roads
by public authorities with the assistance
of the Road Fund. All these arguments
seem to me beside the point. We have
got to take facts as we find them and
deal with them. But may I say, in
passing, that there is no inherent right in
anybody to use the roads provided by the
local authorities and the State for the
purpose of private profit without control.
The roads have been constructed for the
general convenience of the public, and
not for the profit of individuals.
While the railways have suffered considerable diminution of traffic, partly
through the depression in trade in recent
years, and partly through the competition of road transport, they are to-day
carrying a great volume of traffic, and
still performing functions which, I can
say without contradiction, could not be
carried out by road transport.
During last year the railways carried
more than 13,000,000 passengers,
1,000,000 tons of merchandise, and
400,000 head of live stock. Each morning the railways carry into Belfast from
8,500 to 10,000 passengers. I ask hon.
Members to think what the moving of
that amount of daily traffic would mean
in the number of buses coming into the
city in the morning and going out again
in the evening, and to remember also
that it would mean that these additional
and expensive vehicles could normally be
used only for one run each way per day,
and would be lying idle for the rest of
the time. It does not take any deep
knowledge of transport to realise what
that involves in money.
It is no uncommon thing for trains to
take 5,000 or 6,000 passengers into Portrush in an afternoon, or for 9,000 or
10,000 passengers to be carried into
Bangor on a Saturday. On special
occasions the figure for Bangor rises to
as much as 15,000. In June last in one
day the Great Northern Railway conveyed about 13,000 people into Warrenpoint. On Easter Tuesday, 1934, nearly
16,000 people left Belfast by the Great
Northern Railway trains in the space of
three hours, and on Easter Monday last
that railway carried 26,000 people into
Lisburn.

These figures will give hon. Members
some idea of the amount of traffic still
carried on the railways, and I think that
it is obvious that this means of transport
is essential to the seaside towns, and if it
were to be closed down a severe blow
would be dealt to the prosperity of these
places.
Apart from local tourist traffic, as hon.
Members know, the cross-Channel tourist
traffic has developed in recent years, and
what an important industry it has become
in Northern Ireland. While road transport plays a not unimportant part in
dealing with tourist traffic, it is no
exaggeration to say that under present
conditions the closing of the railways
would largely mean the end of this
traffic which is so vital to Ulster, and
which the Government has done so much
to foster.
The figures of goods traffic and livestock indicate the important part which
the railways still play in commercial and
agricultural matters. If this volume of
traffic were, on the extinction of the railways, to be added to that already on the
roads our present road system would be
entirely inadequate. Vast expenditure
would be necessary for road construction
and road improvement. Where is this
capital to come from? Is it to be provided by the State, or by the local
authorities, or is it to be provided from
the earnings of road transport? I do
not conceive that either the taxpayer or
the ratepayer would consent to subsidise
commercial road transport on this great
scale. I know about the suggested conversion of railway tracks into roads, but
who is going to find the money for it?
Certainly not the people who advocate
these fantastic schemes.
Even those who are the strongest
advocates of road transport admit that
the railways are much more suitable for
handling large masses of passengers and
heavy goods, and that for longer distances
they are more economical and more comfortable than road transport. I do not
think that anyone would suggest that it
is desirable that the main railway lines
between the principal centres should be
abolished, but, on the other hand, I do
not think that any railway man would
deny that the time is ripe for a reorganisation of the railway system in
Northern Ireland as it is to-day, and, as
I shall explain later, one of the main
objects of the present proposals is to
facilitate the re-organisation and to
enable it to take place, not merely from
the railway point of view, but from the
wider point of view of the transport
system of the country.
It seems to be assumed that the only
section of transport that needs saving is
the railways. That, of course, is far.
from being the case, as we shall see when
we turn to the road transport aspect of
the matter. It is true that, so far as the
road passenger transport is concerned,
the position is very much better than it
was seven years ago. Services are being
carried on with regularity and with
safety; the vehicles compare favourably
with those in any country; and the
standard of maintenance is good. This
state of affairs is admitted on all hands
to be due almost entirely to the regulations which were put in force in 1928,
and which at that time received a certain
amount of unfair criticism.
If hon. Members will consult any
responsible person engaged in road
passenger transport, they will find that
in 1928, when those regulations were
introduced, it was on the brink of
disaster, and, while the situation has
greatly improved, it is still far from satisfactory. Loading, if I may use a
technical word, is low, and the average
mileage per bus is bad, and until these
factors, which are vital factors in the
carrying on of road transport, are
corrected there must be a great deal of
waste, and the public must sooner or
later bear the cost of transport which is
inflated by wasteful methods. The waste
is caused, not in most cases by inefficient
management, but by the circumscribed
areas of operation and the duplication of
interests and the consequent lack of cooperation.
While, therefore, the system introduced
in 1928 has served a very useful purpose
and has effected a great improvement,
the point has now been reached when it
seems impossible to effect much further
progress. Further progress can only be
attained by what I might describe a
further fusion of interest, and fusion is
essential if the public are to have an
efficient and economical system of
passenger road transport.

As regards goods transport, it is in a

It is not in the least surprising that
the road goods transport is in this very
critical condition. We arranged-and

was used. To put it another way, for

Who was paying for all this waste space?
Obviously either it was being paid for by

owners' own capital.
Mr. BEATTIE: By the public.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The waste,

drivers to work from early morning until
10 or 11 at night, a state of affairs which
was dangerous, not only to themselves,

With all these considerations in view,
the Government came to the conclusion
that if matters continued as they were
the transport situation was rapidly
approaching a crisis, and that unless
something were done a state of chaos
would arise with disastrous results to the
trade and industry of Northern Ireland.
At the same time, we were convinced
that before a decisive step was taken in
a matter of such vital importance it was
essential that the position should be
thoroughly investigated, and that the
best advice obtainable should be got.
Having realised the gravity of the
situation, the Government did not act
hastily or rashly, although it has been
suggested by certain critics that they did.
We were fortunate in securing the assistance of Sir Felix Pole, a gentleman who
occupied a very high position in transport, but is now the head of a great commercial organisation. He undertook the
work entirely gratuitously, and I would
like to take this opportunity of paying a

of

It is well that we should recognise that
this is not a problem peculiar to Northern
Ireland. It exists in practically every
country in the world to a greater or lesser

which shows the interest that is being

remedy which we propose, it will, I

When the situation of transport in the
Irish Free State became acute, what was
done there was to empower the railway
companies to acquire all road transport
undertakings, and I may say that the
railway companies pressed this Government to adopt the same line. We have
rejected such solution. I am going to
speak plainly. We think that to hand
over the road transport undertakings to
the railway companies would simply
mean that road transport would be
worked as a mere adjunct to railways.
We think that road transport has a wider
function than this. We think that any
such system of working would deprive
the public of advantages from road transport to which they are entitled. Therefore, we will have nothing to do with a
solution on these lines.
In some Continental countries where,
as the House is no doubt aware, the railways are State-owned, severe restrictions
have been placed upon the use of road
transport, so as to prevent it competing
in many directions with the railways.
There are restrictions as to distance; restrictions as to character of traffic, and so
forth. I do not presume to criticise these
regulations in the countries in which
they are in force. They know their own
business best, but I do not think that
action on these lines in this country
would commend itself to this House. It
would not encourage the very necessary
re-organisation of the railways, and I
think that such a system would deprive
the public of service to which they are
entitled, and would prevent the best use
being made of all the available means of
transport.
The only other method of approaching
the problem of which I am aware is one
that requires rather more detailed

already referred. It is one which has
been supported by a certain amount of
advocacy, and it is one which, until I

made some appeal to me. The House

We have come to the conclusion, as a

passenger transport vehicles, it would not

services.
Perhaps I might put it this way. By
far the larger

I also wish to emphasise that it is a
fundamental principle of this Bill that
the transport industry must be selfsupporting. It should not be, and it
will not be, subsidised by the taxpayer
or the ratepayer. There is no reason
why it should be. If the business is
carried on with efficiency and economy,
all essential transport services can be
supplied at a reasonable price to the
public on a self-supporting basis. This
Bill imposes no charge whatever upon
the taxpayer or the ratepayer.
It is, therefore, proposed to constitute
a Board which will take over all road
transport, whether belonging to railway
companies or private operators. In the
first place, therefore, the Bill provides
for the setting up of a Transport Board,
consisting of not less than five and not
more than seven members to be appointed
by the Minister of Home Affairs. The
members of the Board are to be persons
who have had wide experience and have
shown capacity in transport, commercial,
agricultural, or financial matters, or in
the conduct of public affairs. Railways
as such will remain under the present
management, but with important modifications.
The Board will be undertaking a very
difficult task, and one entailing great responsibilities. It is essential, therefore,
that it should be composed of men of
ability and experience. It will not be
representative of any sectional interest,
but the members will be selected solely
with a view to the efficient carrying out
of the functions of the Board.
I want to stress the freedom of the
Board from the control of any
sectional interest. It has been stated by

be issued. If the railways or any other
interest acquired every £ of stock issued
they would be no nearer control, because

to provide proper road services both for
passengers and goods, and, as I shall
explain in a little more detail at a later
stage, machinery is provided for compelling the Board to do so should they
fail in this duty.
We now have the Board providing
road services and the railway companies
providing railway services, and, as I have
said at an earlier stage, the object which
we are aiming at is the provision of the
most economical, the most efficient, and
the most convenient system of transport
which we can obtain by means of the cooperation of the different systems at our
disposal. Therefore, we place an obligation upon both the Board and the railway
companies to co-ordinate their services,
not only as between themselves but as
between other means of transport, so as
to secure the object which I have mentioned. To do that it is necessary to provide some connecting link between the
two principal forms of transport.
The Bill provides, therefore, for the
setting up of a joint committee consisting of three representatives of the Board
and three representatives of the railway
companies, whose duty it will be to consider and report to the Board and to each
of the railway companies first of all, on
proposals for co-operation between the
Board and the railway companies, or any
of them, in the provision or working of
services or facilities; on proposals for
alterations in services, facilities, time
tables, fares, rates, and charges, or the
provision of joint new services or
facilities; and on any other matter
materially affecting the interests of any
two or more of the parties appointing
members to the Joint Committee.
It would in our view, however, be quite
hopeless, having regard to the frailties of
human nature, to expect that the parties
would approach the consideration of the
problem of co-ordination with any degree
of impartiality or with any breadth of
view, unless they could do so with some
identity of interest. No progress will be
made if, when the Joint Committee
approaches the consideration of how a
particular service is to be given, each side
is merely going to fight for its own ends.
To meet that point of view we are setting
up a partnership of a financial character
between the Road Board and the railway
companies, and this we propose to do by
means of a system of pooling of receipts.
This is, of necessity, a very complicated
matter, and I do not think that the
House will wish to be troubled with
details. The House will be concerned
much more with the broad principle. The
pool will deal with the net receipts from
traffic, and it is important to realise what
is meant by net receipts. Net receipts
mean the gross traffic receipts less certain
expenditure. Expenditure required to
Transport Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
earn traffic receipts consists of two items:
first, expenditure which varies with the
mileage run, and, second, expenditure
which does not vary directly with the
mileage. For instance, in the case of a
bus it uses, roughly speaking, twice as
much petrol to run two miles as it does
to run one mile. On the other hand,
whether the bus runs, in a given period,
25,000 miles, 30,000 miles or 40,000 miles
the overhead expenses will be approximately the same. The net receipts, then,
mean the gross receipts less the expenses
which vary with the mileage run.
For the purpose of the pool a standard
year is to be taken. For the road the
standard is to be the year 1932. We
year
have not taken the year 1933, because it
was really an abnormal one as a result of
the railway strike and other factors. For
the railways we are taking the mean of
the years 1932 and 1924. We consider
that it would not be equitable in the case
of the railways to take a recent year
without modification. Each year the
Board and the railways will pay into the
pool their net receipts, and each party
will draw out of the pool in the proportions ascertained for the standard years,
and out of their drawings from the pool
they will meet their overhead expenses,
interest on capital, and so forth.
The effect of these arrangements will
be to give to road transport an interest
in railway receipts and to give to the
railway companies an interest in road
transport receipts. They will enable the
members of the Joint Committee, who
will exercise a very great influence on
the policy to be pursued by the Board
and by the railway companies, to view
the proposal as a whole, and to use the
means best suited to the solution of the
problem in a particular area, unencumbered by the considerations which at
present prevent anything worth while
being accomplished in the nature of cooperation or co-ordination between existing operators.
The Bill provides that both the Board
and the railway companies shall have respectively precisely the same powers and
duties with regard to the charging of
rates and fares, the affording of facilities,
and so on. They will be entitled to
charge such reasonable rates and fares as
they may determine, but they will, at
the same time, be required to afford all
I
reasonable facilities to the public.
wish to emphasise the word "reasonable"
in both connections. They must charge
reasonable rates and they must afford

public must have some means of ensuring that the charges and services are
reasonable.
Therefore, in order to give adequate
protection, we propose to set up a
permanent Appeal Tribunal, to be
appointed by His Grace the Governor,
and consisting of three members, one of
whom shall be a judge or a practising
barrister of not less than ten years' standing, who will act as chairman. This
Tribunal will have extensive powers for
ensuring that the public is receiving
adequate protection. It will take over
the functions of the Railway and Canal
Commission, in so far as it concerns
Northern Ireland, and the functions of
the present Rates and Fares Tribunal,
which was set up by the Government
under the Motor Vehicle Acts.
Tribunal will be permanent in the sense
that it will always be available to sit,
but, of course, it will not occupy the
whole time of its members.

It has often been urged that railways
were at a disadvantage in that they were
common carriers. Now both railways
and the Road Board will, in effect, be
common carriers.
We do not propose that the Tribunal
should fix fares or rates, but that it
should have power, where any charge is
fixed by the Board or a railway company,
to review that charge, and if it is considered excessive to order its reduction.
In the same way, if it is contended that
the Board or the railway companies are
not providing proper facilities, or have
withdrawn a facility which was being
given and which was reasonably required
and ought not to have been withdrawn,
then the Tribunal may direct the facility
to be given, or the withdrawn facility to
be restored. These powers,
as hon.
Members will see from the Bill, are very
wide and drastic, but they afford a protection which the public can reasonably
demand, and they safeguard against any
abuse of power on the part of the transport interests.
I would also direct the attention of the
House specially to the fact that the Bill
ensures that there should be very easy
access to the Tribunal, for it is laid down

that any party shall be entitled to be

There is also the matter of the giving
of undue or unreasonable preference, and
both the Board and the railway companies are prohibited in the most express
terms from giving any undue or unreasonable preference. Further, hon.
Members will notice that where a person

given he is not required to prove that
the preference is undue or unreasonable.
He must prove that there is a difference,
but once he has done so the onus of showing that the difference is neither undue
nor unreasonable lies upon the Board or
the railway company concerned.
I come now to the financial provisions
made in the Bill. The Board will be
entitled to raise capital by means of
borrowing in two forms first, by
temporary borrowings, and, second, by
the issue of transport stock. As I have
already indicated, consideration for the
transferred undertakings will also be
satisfied in part by the issue of stock.
The stock will be in two categories (I
am referring to the permanent provisions
of the Bill) designated "A" and "B."
The "A" stock will be a fixed interestbearing stock, and it will have a prior
charge on the revenues of the Board.
The interest will be cumulative. The
rate for "A" stock, issued in satisfaction
of compensation for transferred undertakings, will be 4 per cent. The rate for
"A" stock issued to the public by the
Board in return for cash will be at such
rate as may be fixed by the Board, with
the approval of the Ministry of Home
Affairs and the Ministry of Finance.
The "B" stock will rank after the
"A" stock. In so far as it is issued in
satisfaction of compensation for transferred undertakings it will bear interest
for the first two years at a maximum
rate of 4 per cent.; for the third year at
the maximum rate of 5 per cent., and
provision is made that in subsequent
years there may be paid a further 1 per
cent.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Why?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
and learned Friend will only listen he

has been paid, half the surplus is to be
applied in payment of a further dividend

at any time. The other moiety of the

has been paid is also to go to reserve.
Mr. CAMPBELL: That depends on

Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think

the money market. "B" stock issued to

of Home Affairs and the Ministry of
Finance.
The total amount of the "A" stock in
issue at any one time is not to exceed the
equivalent of the amount paid in compensation for the tangible assets of the
transferred undertakings.
The Bill, at the same time, makes
certain modifications of a very temporary
nature for the first three years after the
passing of the Act with regard to the
priority conditions attaching to "A" and
"B" stock. For the first three years
"A" stock will be divided into two

stock will be issued in satisfaction of the

of profit-earning concerns. "A2" stock
will be issued in satisfaction of compensation for the assets, that is, the tangible
assets, of non-profit earning concerns,
and for this period "A1" stock will have
priority over "A2" stock. After the
expiration of three years the distinction
between "A1" and "A2" stock will disappear. For the first two years "B"
stock will have priority over
"A2" stock,
but this priority will disappear after the
expiration of the two years.
Hon. Members will recollect that I
mentioned the reserve. Surpluses, after
the payment of a moderate rate of
interest on the stock, are to go to reserve,

Reserve Fund is to be used. They are

for the purpose of meeting any charges

Board to the extent to which those
revenues are insufficient to meet those

The next point on which I would like

There is, naturally, a certain amount of

of the creation of the Board, but there

cannot be given, but I think the

The employees of the Board are to be

machinery for dealing with
dealing with matters
arising in connection with wages and conditions of employment. In framing
these provisions we have kept in mind

the other
hand, we have included the principle of

Where any question arises with regard

of the men is to take place. Should it not

Having regard, however, to the

considerable concern. On the one hand,

parties interested. Accordingly, it will

but I do not think it necessary to go

At an earlier stage in my speech I
referred to various plans in other
countries for dealing with this worldwide problem, and I suggested that the
plan which I am now putting forward
had advantages over them. In the forefront of these advantages I put the fact
that, under this Bill Government interference in the operation of transport is
reduced to the absolute minimum possible. The Board will not be a political
body. It is subject to the general proviso that if it does not perform its
functions efficiently it can be removed,
and to that extent it is responsible to a
Minister, who in his turn, is responsible
to this House. Subject to this, and to
the safeguards in the Bill, the Board is
independent and is in a position to carry
on the business of providing road transport as a commercial undertaking. It
will, in fact, be a board of directors, and
as such I suggest that it is the most
efficient instrument for carrying on what
is essentially a trading undertaking.
But it is also a public trust to be administered in the public interest.
Within the scheme of this Bill, the
reorganisation of the transport industry
is left to those who are responsible for
its operation. The scheme provides the
most effective machinery for eliminating
the extremely wasteful methods of
operation in existence to-day, and it gives
a basis on which a sound economic
structure can be built. The scheme also
provides machinery for making the best
use of every means of transport. I
would like to emphasise that it does not
subordinate one branch to another, but
it puts them on an equal footing.
We have endeavoured to deal with this
problem by applying a thorough and
comprehensive remedy. We do not think
that there is the slightest use in seeking
palliatives which might keep things
going for a year or two, and we have,
therefore, put forward a very comprehensive plan which will enable the industry to be developed consistently over
a long period.
I have seen a good deal of criticism
in regard to our scheme, but not a single
constructive alternative suggestion. It
is evident to everyone who has given
even the most casual study to the problem
that there must be a change if disaster
is to be averted. In such circumstances
criticism that is merely destructive is
perfectly useless."
We are faced with a critical situation
and we are putting before the House
what we think is the best, and indeed the
only, solution, and I believe that, with
goodwill and co-operation, we shall have
a transport system that will later on not
only be a credit to Ulster but an example
to the rest of the Three Kingdoms. I
beg to move, and in doing so I apologise
for the length of time I have taken.

I have risen to voice my opposition to
many parts of this Transport Bill as it
now stands. May I be permitted to ask
at this stage what is the necessity for
such legislation? I mean in all seriousness why should this small area of ours
be the victim of an experiment of such
a kind, an experiment that not even
closely congested districts such as are in
the South of England have ever
sidered? I refer to the London Passenger
Transport Act. True it is that the London
Passenger Transport Board have, by an
Act, linked up the traffic of various
passenger carrying companies, but they
wisely left out the goods and freight
carrying bodies, believing that the competition in freights would largely result
in the survival of the fittest, and what
is more important, that the public benefit would best be served by low rates for
goods in transit by these companies or
individuals, as the case might be.
Why should those conditions not prevail in our area, which is not congested,
but is largely scattered? The Minister
of Finance has often stated in this House
that our large expenditure on roads is
due to our very extensive road mileage,
and I desire to point that out to the
Minister of Home Affairs. The element
of competition has helped the public in
rates and in service. This is another instance of our being out of step with
Mother England. Why not confine ourselves to the passenger carrying transport
if we are to embark on what, after all,
a great many people regard as an attack

increased charges upon the general public

There never was a general request from

Whilst I give all credit to its able chairman, Sir Lynden Macassey, for his work

as we have now in a place like Northern
Ireland, we have got to realise that the
principle is one of unrestricted competition run riot or some attempt to arrive at
co-ordination. If I have to choose
between those two things I stand for the
principle of co-ordination. I will give
one or two reasons later why I believe we

At the moment I am the spokesman of
