His Majesty's Government at Westminster at no distant date. I hope I will
be permitted to say this, that there is a

co-ordination that is proposed in this

charge were to be made this afternoon

Ireland or against the Government the
charge would be that they are about ten

of co-ordination. About ten years ago
an inquiry was set up by the Government. I think the Minister of Labour
had some association with that inquiry.
At that inquiry various schemes of coordination were put forward. Among
others who put forward a scheme were
the people with whom I was associated.
We then suggested that taking the long
view the right thing to do for the community was to aim at the co-ordination
of every phase of transport-road, rail
and canal. We put forward the idea
that road, rail and canal transport ought
to be co-ordinated as a public serviceas a public authority from A to Z-not
only securing the backing and guarantee
of the public authority, but that the
rights of ownerships should ultimately be
vested in the public authority. We said
that the aim ought to be transport for
the welfare of the community as against
any vested interest. That was briefly
the policy put before the Commission on
that occasion.
The Government did not accept that
point of view. As a matter of fact, I
make bold to say that the Government did
not do anything with regard to co-ordination at that particular time, and the
reason they did not do anything in that
direction was in the main, if not entirely,
due to the vested interests as represented
on the railway companies. I was present
at several sittings of the Commission
when the railway directors and managers
appointed one of their number to present
their point of view. I am speaking from
memory and subject to correction, but I
think I am correct in saying that the railway managers' point of view at that time
was that there ought to be no interference
of any kind with regard to transport. As
a consequence of the Government accepting that point of view, and as a consequence of something else, which was the
absolutely callous disregard of the railway companies to the trend of modern
development, things reached a condition
of chaos. It is only a matter of five or
six years ago that for the first time in
the history of Northern Ireland an
attempt was made by the Government to
institute some kind of administrative
authority in regard to transport, and
secure some principles of co-ordination.
That Transport Tribunal, which was
then created, was brought about because
of the chaotic system which grew up in
Belfast and Northern Ireland. I am
happy to look back on the fact that I was
one of the municipal representatives that
stood for sanity in municipal transport
against the unrestricted rights of commercial privateers coming in and taking
advantage of our best bus routes. I
believe it was good policy to stand by the
rights of collective authority and municipal authority, and I apply that same
principle to national authority. If it is
right as a municipal representative to
defend the co-ordinating authority of the
municipality I believe it is also right to
carry it a stage further and extend it to
the Province. I want it to be understood
that I still accept the position that railways are essential services for the wellbeing of the country. I think railways
are indispensable. Railways from the
transport, traffic and passenger point of
view have bestowed many blessings on
the community. I think under wise
administration they are still destined to
play a big part in the development of the
country.
While admitting that, I have also got
to say this, that the railway companies in
bygone days-I do not want to be
unkind to them-were more concerned
with their invested capital than they were
with the day to day requirements of the

travelling public, or with the accommodation of the population generally.
seems to me that it would not have taken

for many years were quite satisfied,
cherishing to themselves the belief that

The end of that was that there began to
arise a new form of transport merchant
throughout the community. They began
to make their appearance here, there and
everywhere. Now that led to unrestricted
competition, and in that unrestricted
competition certain elements were lost
sight of. One of these elements, I am
sorry to say, was that the railways were
restricted by statute, and were also compelled to conform to conditions to which
no other form of transport were compelled to conform.
In the interim between the war and the
post-war period new economic conditions
had grown up. New standards of livelihood had been accepted by the railways,
and in the unrestricted competition which
came about on the roads many of the
people who thought they were espousing
the welfare of the community began, regardless of those conditions and of those
elements of railway transport, to condemn, willy-nilly, the whole railway
system. We ought to try to steer a
middle course in considering all these
elements, though, I believe, and must
express my belief, that the railways did
not always conform to anything like a
decent standard of living for their employees. I am old enough now to
remember the time when at least the
majority of a quarter of a million of
people employed in the railway services
were living under £1 a week in Great
Britain and Ireland.
From the time that railways were first
established it has been handed down to
us that administration, so far as Ireland
was concerned in particular, was very
haphazard, that there were too many
boards of directors, that there were too
many limpets, and that too many
passengers were being carried on the
service. I use that expression, not in its
ordinary sense, but in the sense that too
many people were expecting to make a
living out of the industry without contributing any useful service in return.
When unrestricted competition became
very acute in Northern Ireland there is
not the slightest doubt that that unrestricted competition resulted in a
general lowering of the standard of life
of the people employed in transport, not
only on the railways but on the roads.
In addition, we have got to accept this,
that if you stand for the vindication of
the principle of unrestricted competition,
regardless of all economic consequences,
the end can only be muddle and chaos.
The end may come more speedily in one
set of circumstances than another, but
the end is bound to be the same under
all conditions, and no Government, no
matter what its political complexion may
be, can stand idly by and allow the transport system of a country to get into a
state of complete chaos beyond the hope
of redemption.
I find a vindication of the attitude I
take up in coming to this logical conclusion in the words of the Minister of
Home Affairs yesterday. In the course
of his comprehensive speech he made use
of the following expression:-
"They had got to take the facts as
they found them and deal with them,
but might he say there was no inherent
right in anybody to use the roads provided by local authorities and the State
for the purpose of private profit. The
roads had been constructed for the
general convenience of the public and
not for the profit of individuals.”
Now, I say that that vindicates the
attitude I take up, and which the party
to which I belong take up, in claiming
that transport by rail, road, and sea
ought to be co-ordinated modes of transport and public utility operated for the
public good without, as a first regard, the
advancing of vested interests.
When the first omnibus tribunal was
set up in Northern Ireland it was
apparent to anybody who took the pains
to find out that the conditions which prevailed then should not be tolerated, and
it was incumbent upon every rightthinking public representative in my
opinion to use the collective authority to
see to it that some safeguard was enforced
in regard to public undertakings. We

should be allowed to assume, that is, the

fact, I went further and I said that unrestricted individualism was as dead as
the dodo. I repeat that. We are living
in an age of co-ordination.
We are
living in an age of large scale operations
as against unrestricted individual enterprise. That is the law of economic
development.
If you keep in mind that assertion and
also remember what took place in the
city of Belfast and throughout Northern
Ireland you will, I believe, become convinced that the small man who was in
such abundant numbers in the days of
unrestricted competition has tended to
disappear throughout Northern Ireland.
There are not so many small men in the
business now, or in practically any
business, as there were some years ago.
Larger companies came along and
absorbed those small men.
Many small
men entered business on the credit

them whatever. They thought they
would go into the transport business
while the going was good, as
Americans say, and having reaped as
much as they could they got out again.
Many got out on conditions extremely
detrimental to themselves.

So, in the course of time, for one

Belfast, as hon. Members know, and

What did that mean? It meant that

hoped to produce an Act which would
ultimately meet with the approval of
every section of the community. To do
that you have got to be at pains to allay
the suspicions and fears of various
sections of the community. There is a
fear abroad in Northern Ireland at the
present time that the members of the
community generally, who have enjoyed
certain cheap services in the past, are
going to be unmercifully exploited in the
future in order to protect the investments
of the railway shareholders. I am saying
what a lot of people are thinking. I
would appeal to the Government to introduce additional safeguards to ensure that
under no set of circumstances could anything of that kind take place, so that
ultimately, when this Bill becomes law,
the people will not look back with regret
to the cheap conveniences which they had
and which they have lost for ever.
I
think I have covered everything in this
Bill that is worth referring to in a Second
Reading speech, and I wish to indicate to
the Government that, whilst expressing
approval of the scheme for the co-ordination of transport services, I do so with the
reservations I have mentioned, and in the
hope that ultimately, as a result of the
lesson Northern Ireland will learn in
improved modes of transport, we will
have a great public utility in spirit as
well as in name.
Mr. YOUNG: I should like to congratulate the Minister of Home Affairs
on the way in which he introduced this
Bill, and also upon the fact that it is based
more especially on the lines of Sir Felix
Pole's report. It was implied by some
of the speakers yesterday that this was
the only country in the world where it
was necessary to introduce such a Bill.
I think that in nearly every country in
the world Governments have had to
tackle this question of transport owing
to the chaos brought about by unrestricted
road transport. In Great Britain, for instance, goods vehicles can operate at the
present time only under licence issued
by the Traffic Commissioners. It is not
very long since the Irish Free State
handed over all road transport to the
railway companies. We all know that
in Northern Ireland the competition between road and rail has reached such a
pitch at the present time that there is
no profit being made in transport at all.
The losses of some of the railway companies were mentioned yesterday by the
Minister of Home Affairs in introducing
this Bill. Sir Felix Pole, in his Report,
used these words:
In my opinion.
Acts of Parliament which impede the freedom of
railways should be repealed. In particular, the statutory enactment of a
classification of goods and of maximum
schedules of rates and charges should
be abolished, railway companies to be
as free in respect of charging powers
as are road transport companies, subject to appeal to the Transport Appeal
Tribunal.
As far as I can judge from this Bill this
principle seems to be carried out, and I
think it is only fair that it should be
carried out. After all, the competition
between the roads and the railways has
not been fair to the railways. Take the
hours of labour, the rates of wages, and
the various restrictions under which the
railway companies operate. For instance, I remember seeing in a paper a
few months ago the case of a haulage
contractor who was fined £50 in a Manchester Court. The prosecution in that
case said that the driver was slavedriven. In fact, things were so bad that
when he was in Scotland the driver refused to work any longer and preferred
to give up the job. The employer then
drove the lorry, and at a certain stage
of the journey he was so exhausted that

journey, a potential danger to everyone

And all this is called fair competition.
There is nothing fair, I think, in the
competition between road and rail transport in this country. If the road transport services had got to pay for the
roads on which they run, it would be a

£10,000 a mile. No part of that outlay went to the construction of the road,
the making of enbankments, or anything

Member of this House, no matter on

companies had had to produce that

Mr. MIDGLEY: There are other
people using that road as well as the

Mr. YOUNG: And those transport
companies drive on that road as if they
were the sole owners of it, and no other
individuals had any right to be on the
King's highway at all. My contention.
is that a great many of the road transport services at the present time are not
run on economic lines. A man starts
with a lorry, and so long as the lorry
remains in fair condition and he is able
to pay the petrol bill and the oil bill
he carries on, without making any
arrangements for wear and tear or depreciation. When the motor lorry is done,
the man is also done. In the meantime,
he has reduced the whole of the transport rates for the carriage of goods to a
non-economic basis.
I think that the attitude of the
farmers towards this Transport Bill is
not reasonable. Farmers are quite
willing to accept such Measures as the
Pigs Marketing Scheme and the Milk
Board, schemes which, no doubt, raised
the price of the commodities to the consumer. The argument used in introducing that legislation was that there
should be an economic price for the producers of pork and milk. All that this
Bill purports to do is to place transport
on an economic basis, and it is not on an
economic basis at the present time.
Yesterday the hon. and learned Member for Central Belfast stated that the
position of the railways in Great Britain.
was just as bad as the position of the
railways here. I beg to differ from the
hon. and learned Member for Central
Belfast: the position is not the same.
All the British railways have been able
to pay their debenture interest; in most
cases they have been able to pay their
first and second preferences, and in some
cases even their ordinary dividends.
Compare that state of affairs with the
position of the Northern Counties Committee of the L.M.S., which was
mentioned by the Minister of Home
Affairs. The Northern Counties Committee gross receipts amounted to
£38,000 less than their gross expenditure, and there was nothing for the
payment of interest on capital. If road
transport companies were running their
services at the same rate they would
simply cease to exist. If it were not for
the fact that the Northern Counties
Committee has the benefit of a strong
British Railway at its back it would also
cease to exist.
I ask any Member of
this House if it would be for the benefit
of Northern Ireland that the Northern
Counties Committee should cease to exist.
Some Members have stated that the coordination of transport services may
mean that some men will lose their jobs.
What would be the effect on unemplovment in Northern Ireland if the Northern Counties, the County Down, and the
Great Northern Railways all ceased to
operate?

Mr. NIXON: The hon. Member who
has just sat down concluded by saying he

he announced that if the President of

Yet yesterday we had the Minister of

The hon. and gallant Member for Dock
(Mr. Midgley) has given his blessing to
this Bill with certain qualifications. I
suppose that if I had come into this
House as a Socialist I would have done
the same, but I did not come in as a
Socialist. The Member for Dock said
the Bill was not a Socialist Bill, nor yet
was it a Communist Bill. In a sense he
is right, because Communism means
having all things in common and dividing
with the common people, but this Bill is
going to have all things in common to
divide with the railway directors and the
railway shareholders and the people
interested, but not with the common
people. We do not want a monopoly.
We have had experience of a monopoly.
Go back to the days before road competition, when you were at the mercy of
the railways. As representing a workingclass constituency I am bound to defend
in this House the rights and liberties of
the working people, who want transport
to be kept as it is now.
What was the position ten or twelve
years ago? The Member for Bannside
told us about all the people who went to
Portrush on the Monday of Jubilee week.
I am sure that ten or twelve years ago
Transport Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
the railway fares to Portrush were more
than a 100 per cent. dearer than they
are to-day, and that is the position you
want to create again. But you should
remember that you are introducing a
dangerous element into this Bill. That
element is to pool the receipts and divide
the proceeds. Suppose I suggested to the
Government, "What about the Prime
Minister and all the Members of this
House pooling their salaries and dividing
the proceeds?" It would be turned
down. But remember, that that is the
principle that is introduced in this Bill.
You should also remember this: that if
Communism gets the upper hand in Great
Britain that is the very thing they will
do with all property. That is what they
say they will do, and how can Ministers
stand here and defend that policy in
respect of the railways simply because
certain people have an interest in them.
How will they be able to defend this
principle later on, because they may be
confronted with it far sooner than they
think. It may not arise here, I admit,
but Northern Ireland generally follows
England in the long run.
A short time ago there was a Motion
proposed in this House-I was not
present protesting against Cabinet
Ministers being directors of companies.
In replying to that Motion the Prime
Minister said that no one in Northern
Ireland could say that Cabinet Ministers,
although directors of companies, used
their positions as Cabinet Ministers to
assist the companies they were connected
with. If the Prime Minister had been
at the farmers' meeting in Belfast
yesterday I went because I was invited
he would have heard everyone who
spoke and everyone in the audience you
spoke to make the assertion that this Bill
is brought forward because certain Members of the Cabinet are directors of railway companies. Everyone you meet now
makes that assertion. I am not saying
it one way or the other. I will say that
I have found every Cabinet Minister a
very honourable gentleman, but that is
the charge they are leaving themselves
open to.
There never was anything like this Bill
put forward in any other country in the
world. You might as well say that if
one shop is not doing well you should pool
the receipts of all the shops and divide
the proceeds, or that because Messrs.
Workman, Clarks were not doing as well
as Messrs. Harland & Wolff you should
pool the receipts and divide the proceeds.
You might say the same with regard to
the big factories with which Members
opposite are connected. You are making
a beginning to-day with this principle,
and you do not know where it will stop.
Of course, Ministers and those Members
who support the Bill would like it to
stop at this Bill, but although they have
been there a long time they will not be
there always. How are you going to
defend this principle if you are asked to
extend it to other things. At the present
time the working people of Belfast can,
in the summer time, get a return ticket
to Millisle or Donaghadee for a shilling.
I have no doubt now that the intention
of this Bill is to stop that and all other
similar facilities that are at present enjoyed. The Minister is going to set up
another Board, and any appeal from that
Board will be to the Minister. He will
set up the Board, and if you do not like
what the Board is doing you can appeal
to him.
Northern Ireland is ruled by Boards.
There are Boards in every direction-a
Milk Board, a Bacon Board, a Pig Board
and all classes of Boards. Now we are
going to have another Board and more
officialdom. Long ago I used to be
familiar with the plumb board that bricklayers used to keep things straight, but a
lot of the Boards in Northern Ireland are
to make things crooked. I am not going to
tire myself by speaking any more about
the Bill. It stands condemned on its
own face, and I am going to give Members an opportunity to vote, and I am
going to make them vote. When I
moved the rejection of the Valuation
Bill in this House four years ago I saw
where it was leading. My action on that
occasion seems to have been very popular,
because I am told that the hon. Member
for Mid Antrim claims to have moved the
rejection. I did not hear him say that,
but if he did I would advise him to consult Hansard. I moved the rejection,
and the Member for North Antrim
seconded it. If Members had been wise
they would have rejected that Bill, and
now I am going to give them an opportunity of rejecting this Measure.

The Member for Dock raised the

the Parliamentary Secretary, when he

been responsible for many deaths
throughout the length and breadth of

and Transport Bill is a bad Bill from the

preaches on the hustings about his
Unionism, but where is the Unionism
about this Bill. It is pure unadulterated

know that all the railway magnates are

If the railway magnates had any brains
at all this state of affairs would never

The hon. Member for Bann Side

would be a credit to the country, the

pinched this money and used it for other

to bring the discussion into an atmosphere of seriousness rather than of jest.
I agree with the hon. Member for Dock
that whatever may be said of this Bill

to do without Bills of this character if

to realise there are difficulties that have
to be met, and that, therefore, our business is to deal with facts and not with
fancies or prejudices.
I say that I, personally, if it had been
possible, would have preferred to carry

but could anyone listening to the serious

intervention, and, indeed, if the Minister

down.
I have no

interests in either railway company or

If there had been no railway in what

It would be all right for the people who

to help the farmers of Northern Ireland.

I believe, myself, that the railway companies are very much to blame for the
position in which they find themselves
to-day. Before the bus and lorry came
along the railway companies were very
independent bodies. They had very
little consideration for the public, and
paid very little attention to the carrying
of goods and traffic. Even in the early
days, when the bus and lorry came along,
if the railway companies had taken the
matter up, and had tried to serve the
public in the way the bus and lorry did,
I believe they could have continued to
carry on. But they treated the public
with contempt. Now the Government
have come to the assistance of the railway
companies, and it is the general public
who are going to have to pay.
There are at present very satisfactory
bus services throughout the country, for
instance those run by the B.O.C. A
tribunal was set up and fares and stages
were fixed. Some of these fares were considered to be rather excessive, but I
believe that they were remunerative, and
they certainly have served the public
well. If the B.O.C. is taken over by this
Board does any Member of the Government think that the public will be catered

for in the way in which they are catered

At present you have many evening

I remember some years ago, when the
people were dependent on the railway

different towns along the lines, it was

in three or four hours without any disappointment. That is a great convenience to business people.
As another instance, you have from

fares. Does anyone think that when
there is no competition that half-hour
service will be continued on that route

asked for this Bill in order to regulate
transport? I have consulted several
master hauliers, and they have all

to carry on their businesses as they have
been doing. Many of these people by

prosperous businesses; they have given to
their customers services which never
could have been obtained from any railway companies. Then, I ask myself have
the customers who have been efficiently
served by these hauliers made any
demand to the Government to bring in a

contractor, and speaking for those whom

perfectly satisfied with the arrangements
we have been able to make individually

I think, therefore, I can see running

after the

where there never were tram lines. They

I object very strongly to this business

allowed to control their own business. I

I
ask the right hon. Gentleman now,

companies. I am in the unfortunate

is behind the whole Bill-why should

I have it on very good authority that

This Bill reminds me very much of a

the people who have been engaged in the

Even
Speaking for myself, I was a customer
of a railway company for many years,
and
it was only when competition became so
keen that I found it necessary, if I was to
compete with other merchants, to leave
the railway company because I could no
longer afford to pay them more for transport charges than my neighbours were
paying. If the railway companies are in
low water to-day they are in just the same

was not properly managed and properly
organised, and which did not rise to the

bolster up any other concern in Northern
Ireland. The Bill is going to do a great
injustice to a great many people. There

Some of them, I must confess, are
perhaps not engaged under the conditions we would like, but the Minister of
Home Affairs has already tightened up
very considerably the regulations governing motor transport. By means of
regulations he has regulated the number
of hours that a man may drive a motor
lorry, and there is no reason why the
transport of Northern Ireland cannot be
further regulated.
I see no necessity for such a drastic Bill
as this. In the rural areas there are
to-day many men working in connection

Falls has mentioned the matter, as I

If the Government intend to put this

I think this association ought to get

think possibly his bark is worse than his

Thursday, 16th May, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Question of Privilege.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have now to deal
with the question of privilege raised yesterday by the hon. Member for Pottinger. There is sufficient justification for
this question being brought before the
House. However, the House should, I
think, be very careful to differentiate
between legitimate pressure exercised by
virtue of the people's right to freedom
of speech and illegitimate threats calculated to induce hon. Members to
swerve from the path of duty.
In my judgment, the words complained
of constitute a warning from certain
voters that if Members decide to follow
a particular course of action, they will
forfeit their confidence. The terms of
which
the resolution,
indicate the
intention of withdrawing support at the
next election are in effect merely the expression of lack of confidence, and an
indication of taking such steps as
within the right of any voter.
are
In my opinion, therefore, the question
of privilege does not arise.

DUNGANNON UNION INCIDENT.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received
complaints as to the alleged assault of
an inmate of the Dungannon Union by
a porter in the Institution on the 11th
May, and whether he is prepared to conduct an inquiry into the treatment of
the inmates of this Union.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have received no
such complaint, nor has any report been
made to my Ministry of any occurrence
of the kind having taken place.
I have, however, caused inquiries to
be made, and I shall be very pleased to
inform the hon. Member as to the result
of these. In the meantime, he will
appreciate that no question of ordering
an inquiry arises.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Thank you.

THE LEVY ON GRADE C MILK.
8. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he is aware of the
opposition of dairy farmers to the levy.
of 3d per gallon on Grade C milk, and
whether he will take steps to have the
contribution reduced to the
Grade A.
same as
Sir BASIL BROOKE: No difficulty
whatever has been experienced concerning the levy or the price of milk in
respect of those farmers who supply to a
distributor. I have, however, received
representations from those farmers who
retail their own milk and who seem to
be under the impression that if only
they could secure a reduction in the levy
it would increase their returns. I am
anxious to keep the levy at as low a figure
as possible, but I should like to make it
quite clear that whenever we are in a
position to reduce the levy the reduction
will go towards reducing the cost of milk
to the consumer, as that, I consider, is
in the best interests of all concerned.
For the hon. Member's information I
may say that the levy in question was
reduced from 3d to 13d per gallon for the
summer period commencing 12th May,
and the price of milk to the consumer by
4d per gallon.
I think it is desirable to point out that
the levy on all milk in Scotland for the
winter period was 4d per gallon compared
with 3d per gallon for C milk in
Northern Ireland and 3d per gallon in
Scotland for the summer months compared with 12d in Northern Ireland for
Grade C milk.
A producer of Grade C milk has a
remedy at hand. If he produces Grade
B milk, that is, gives a better service to
the consumer, he can escape with a levy
of 1d per gallon in winter and id per
gallon for the summer period.
To make the levy on Grade C milk the
same as on Grades A or B would defeat
one of the main objects of the scheme,
which is to give the public a clean and
pure milk supply.
FISHERMEN AND THE HERRING
BOARD REGULATIONS.
9. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that the
fishermen of Northern Ireland are
opposed to the Herring Board regulations, and whether he will modify them
to suit the fishing industry in this area.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The hon. Member's
question is based on a misapprehension,
as no regulations have as yet been made
by the Herring Board. The position is
that a scheme, as required by the Herring
Industry Act, was submitted by the
Herring Board for the consideration of
the Imperial Ministers concerned; that
all interested parties, both in Great
Britain and Northern Ireland, were
given the prescribed statutory period in
which to lodge objections against, or to
suggest amendments of, the provisions of
that scheme; and that the scheme, after
undergoing certain modifications by the
Imperial Ministers, is now before the
Parliament at Westminster for approval.
Possibly the hon. Member has in
mind a resolution passed at a meeting in
Portavogie on 6th April in favour of the
exclusion of Northern Ireland from the
area of the Herring Board's jurisdiction.
I would remind him, however, that the
convener of that meeting subsequently,
on being more fully informed on the
matter, admitted in the public Press that
the resolution was based on a misconception of the position.

Financial Statement 1708
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Ways and Means.
Considered in Committee.
Major SHILLINGTON in the Chair.
Financial Statement, 1935-36.
Mr. POLLOCK: I would like to
remind the Committee that this is the
fourteenth year in which it is my
privilege to present the annual summary
of the expected revenue and expenditure of our Province for the year which
lies ahead. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) These fourteen years have been
pregnant with change, much change
indeed, in the world's outlook on affairs
both economic and political. As His
Majesty the King said a few days ago in
that inspiring address delivered in the
ancient Hall of Westminster, we are
living in the aftermath of war and are
still endeavouring to piece together the
broken threads of our national life. And
yet if we in Ulster look back to 1920 and
contrast the conditions of that day with
those obtaining at present, notwithstanding that we have had many a hard
problem to tackle, there is no one in our
community, if he is honest with himself,
will not admit that the future destiny
of this Province is inescapably bound up
with that of the United Kingdom and
the Empire. I am confident that the
present Budget will confirm this view.
Notwithstanding all the chaotic conditions of foreign exchanges, the continued increase in the height of customs
barriers, and the resulting contraction of
international trade, it is pleasant to
report that almost alone amongst all the
nations of the world the United Kingdom
continues to make steady, if slow,
improvement and progress toward normal
conditions of trade. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) The Chancellor of the
Exchequer, when presenting his Budget
recently, stated that 80 per cent. of the
old-time trade of Britain had been recovered, and offered the opinion that the
remaining 20 per cent., if not actually
within sight, would surely follow consistent effort. I should like to hope that
such an optimistic view had warrant for
the opinion that the same improvement
would be manifested in Ulster. Still it
is a fact beyond dispute that Britain's
prosperity is bound to have its reflection.
on our commercial and industrial
interests here. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Although the ugly problem of unemployment still continues to be present
with us, yet we can definitely state
that by every test we can apply, the year
which we have just left behind us on the
31st March has given evidence of marked
improvement on its predecessor. With
this preface I will now proceed to the
more prosaic duty of describing briefly
the outcome of our last year's finance,
showing how closely my anticipations of
a year ago have been borne out by the
results.
I may remind hon. Members that I
am now dealing with the year 1934-35,
and making the comparisons I have suggested. If they will turn to the upper
portion of Table I of the White Paper
which has been circulated, they will find
statements comparing the estimated with
the actual outturn of last year's finance.
My first duty will be mainly directed
to that table, but if hon. Members wish
to see the items in greater detail, they
may do so if they turn to Table II for
the outgoings and Table III for the income.
Expenditure, 1934-35.
I
propose to take the expenditure of
last year, and after so doing I will present to the Committee the revenue of the
Province which was expected to balance
with the expenditure.
CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure, we find that Consolidated Fund
Services, apart from the Road Fund and
the self-balancing item of the Milk Industry Assistance Grant, accounted for
£459,000, or £19,000 below the estimate.
These Consolidated Fund Services are
well known to hon. Members and do not
require any particular elucidation.
ROAD FUND.
The Road Fund payment of £634.000
represents the corresponding receipt
from motor taxation. The Budget
Estimate of £615,000, and which was regarded as rather optimistic, was exceeded
by £19,000, which is a useful addition
to the revenue of the Fund, and also an
evidence of the increasing wealth of the
community in Ulster.

SUPPLY SERVICES.
The Budget Estimate for Supply Services was £8,558,000, to which should
be added £424,000 for supplementaries.
It will be within the recollection of hon.
Members that during the year, by
reason of changes in the conditions of
unemployment payments, we have had
to present important supplementaries.
These, with other things, amounted to
£424,000. This made a total estimated

made by our local authorities towards
the cost of educational services, of
£8,910,000.
a
The actual expenditure for the year
was £8,716,000,
gross saving of
£194,000. The Estimate I made this
time last year was £80,000, so that in
the sum of £194,000 we far exceeded
our original idea of the amount that
might possibly be saved. By reason of
that sum being saved I was able to
defray nearly half of the supplementary
provision required in the year out of
savings made on the various Votes.
DEDUCTIONS FROM RESIDUARY SHARE.
We repaid to the Imperial Government
sums collected by us from the local
authorities in repayment of loans made
before we took over control (£69,000),
and also collections of "New" Land Purchase Annuities, which are the property
of the British Government (£300,000),
amounting to £369,000.
The expenditure of the Imperial Government on the Reserved Services which
they control, such as the cost of collecting Income Tax, Post Office, Customs,
etc., was provisionally fixed at the same
figure as the Estimate for last year,
namely, £1,794,000.

TRANSFERRED TAXES.
The revenue from transferred taxes
imposed by our Government produced
£901,000, that is, £11,000 more than the
Budget Estimate The decline in the
yield of the estate duties, which has been
such a disappointing feature to me in
recent Budgets, in view of the appreciation of capital values, has, I am glad
to inform hon. Members, been arrested.
The receipts in the past year show a
small but welcome increase of £2,000
over the Estimate. Small increases over
the Estimates are also shown by the
receipts from entertainment duty and
stamps duties; reassuring evidence of the
tendency towards a recovery in trade and
employment.
Motor taxation, as I have stated
above, produced £634,000.
RESERVED TAXES.
I now refer to revenue from reserved
taxes. The Budget Estimate for reserved
taxes collected by the Imperial Government was £7,500,000. The receipts are
shown at the same figure, but this figure
is provisional, and I cannot at the
moment say whether there will be any
substantial variation in
the yield
of these revenues. We have not yet
received from the Imperial Government
the actual returns. During past years
there has been some under-estimation
of our revenue, and I express the
hope that this Estimate of £7,500,000
may possibly be increased when a full
examination is made of the returns.
The transferred and reserved taxes
together, therefore, as actually received.
on 31st March last, provided us with
£9,035,000.

Amongst the items of non-tax revenue,
the adjustments of residuary share for
prior years have exceeded the Estimate
by the extremely useful sum of £272,000.

milk industry assistance grant from the
Imperial Government, local loans repayments, "new" land purchase annuities,
and residuary share adjustment, and the
appropriation from the Reserve Fund)
amounted to £3,092,000, bringing the
total revenue available from all sources
last year to £12,127,000.
If we deduct from this the total expenditure for the year, already mentioned
by me, £12,109,000, we are left with a
balance of £18,000 as the provisional
amount available for surplus and Imperial contribution. This £18,000 is
exactly £5,000 more than I estimated last
year.
Although the surplus is not large,
more particularly so in comparison with
the Imperial Chancellor's surplus, yet,
in view of our relatively heavier Exchequer burden on account of unemployment and of the fact that our revenues
are not yet expanding at nearly the same
rate as his, it cannot be regarded as
entirely unsatisfactory. That is the
presentation of our last year's financial
arrangements. Leaving them behind and
trying to forget thèm we come to the
year that lies ahead.

I now turn to this year on which we
have just entered-1935-36— and, as is

will be found in the last column of

CONSOLIDATED FUND SERVICES.
The first category of expenditure is
that of our Consolidated Fund.
The interest on Exchequer borrowings.
shows a small increase of £4,000.
The Sinking Funds take £161,000, as
compared with £217,000 for last year.
The decrease is due to the fact that,
following the precedent of the Imperial
Chancellor, who made no Sinking Fund
provision from revenues, I have decided
to make no provision this year for the
Land Purchase Annuities Sinking Fund.
As hon. Members know, this Fund was
created to reserve in perpetuity the
terminable revenue from land purchase
annuities, which was gifted to us under
the Government of Ireland Act. I
established that principle at the start of
our career and, with one or two exceptions that did not affect either the solvency
or the principle of the creation and continuation of the Fund, that policy has
been continued until the present time,
when, as I say, the amount in the Fund
is £1,600,000 invested in Government
securities. The position of the Fund is
a strong one, and although actuarial calculations imply an annual allocation of
£90,000, a considerable number of uncertain items enter into these calculations which have led me to decide that
I can with prudence make no contribution towards it in the current financial
year. The full reduction of £90,000 is
not, however, fully reflected in the foregoing figures because of an increase in
the provision for the Ulster Savings Certificate Sinking Fund. I should like to
emphasise the point that, as in past
years, I am making full Sinking Fund
provision for Ulster Saving Certificates
repayments.
The other Consolidated Fund Services
take £159,000, of which £150,000 is the
estimated amount in respect of prospective advances which may possibly have
to be made under the Loans Guarantee
Acts.
Hon. Members will be pleased to hear
that included in the £159,000 for the
Consolidated Fund Services there is provision for a sum of £3,000 for a housing
subsidy to assist the Irish Sailors' and
Soldiers' Land Trust's further building
programme for some forty to fifty new
houses in the Province for our ex-sailors
and ex-soldiers. The British Government
were good enough to release a substantial
sum, which has enabled the trustees to
increase the number of houses in the
scheme by forty or fifty. We, following
our early practice, give the ordinary subsidy per house to these schemes in order to
increase the number of houses for ex-
Service men. In order to give effect to
this arrangement I propose to insert a
Clause in our next Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Bill to raise the
existing subsidy limit of £37,000 in
respect of these houses, which is now
exhausted, to £40,000. That will mean
that, speaking from memory, about 1,200
houses will have been provided for ex-
Service men in Northern Ireland.

Naturally, in my opinion, the Exchequer

the proceeds of tax on private motor-cars
and cycles is a luxury tax. In Great
Britain one-third of the tax is retained
by the Exchequer, but, having regard to
the different road conditions obtaining in
Northern Ireland, I am going to content

amounting to about £70,000 in the
present year. I also propose to retain in

per annum in respect of fines for motoring offences, which at present are paid
over to the Road Fund. I am, however,

road works, and this makes the net

The net effect of these changes is,

£654,000 the figure which I have already
given for the payment from the

am going to refer later.
The total Consolidated Fund expenditure, after making the necessary adjustment for the above changes is, therefore,
estimated at £1,058,000.
SUPPLY.
The Estimates for the expenditure on
Supply Services total £9,327,000, which
is over half-a-million more than last year.
This increase is largely due to the
estimated cost of unemployment assistance allowances to the new classes of
beneficiaries coming within the scope of
the Unemployment Assistance Scheme as
from the Second Appointed Day under
the Unemployment Assistance Act, 1934.
In view of the postponement of the operation of this part of the Act, as is wellknown to those who are interested in unemployment matters, money will, alternatively, be required in recouping to
local authorities the expenditure which
they are still bearing in respect of these
persons, and statutory provision to enable
this to be done will be introduced in the
course of the Autumn Session. I hope
hon. Members will bear in mind that
there is a liability on the part of the
Government for any additional expense
that may be incurred under the Act as
from the first day of March last, the
appointed day.

I have now an announcement to make
regarding an important item of receipt.
Unemployment Reinsurance Agreement.
Hon. Members have questioned me
from time to time regarding the working
of the Unemployment Reinsurance Agreement which was concluded between the
Chanceller of the United Kingdom and
myself in 1925. At that time, I was
fully sensible of the advantages of the
scheme which was agreed upon, but since
then conditions have undergone such unforeseen changes that some modification
is now called for. In such circumstances,
I found it necessary to represent to the
Chancellor that the original agreement
required material amendment, and I
should like to add at once that when the
Chancellor was fully apprised of the equitable nature of our claim he was prepared
to consider it in a fair and sympathetic
spirit. This will be found to be the
most important feature of my statement
this afternoon, if for no other reason
than that it serves to bring our net expenditure on unemployment more into
alignment with the British expenditure
and recognises more effectively the
national character of our unemployment
problem. I am not yet in a position to
submit full details of the amended
scheme, but it will be subject to endorsement by Parliament in both countries.
In the meantime, I can assure hon. Members that I am satisfied that our position
in this respect will be adequately safeguarded in the future. Under this
arrangement I estimate that the reinsurance agreement will provide the useful
sum of £643,000 in the current year,
according to the Estimates of the cost of
unemployment benefits.

Now I shall reveal to the House how I
intend to deal with two items of taxation
within my control-motor vehicles and
entertainments. As I have already
stated, the revenue from motor vehicle
taxation has shown great resiliency of
late years, and I now wish to describe
certain reductions of taxation which will
affect the Road Fund alone, but which,
may I repeat, will not impinge upon the
grants made from that Fund to local
authorities.
My first proposal is one which arises
out of the British Budget duty on heavy
oil, that is, to reduce the licence duty
on goods vehicles using this oil to the
same amount as similar petrol-driven
vehicles. This change will take effect as
from the 1st August next. That is only
an equitable adjustment considering that
vehicles using these heavy oils previously
paid licence duty on the same basis as
petrol-driven vehicles. This change will
equalise matters as between ordinary
petrol-driven machines and heavy oildriven machines and heavy oil-driven
vehicles. The loss in revenue to the
Road Fund involved by the proposal is
some £1,500 in the present year.
My next proposal is one which will, no
doubt, be welcomed by farmers. It is
to reduce by 25 per cent., as from the
1st January, 1936, the tax on lorries
owned by them and used for conveying
their own produce.
Representations have been made to
abolish the duty imposed last year on
trailers attached to private cars. I cannot, however, fully agree to this proposal, but have decided to give some
relief. I propose, accordingly, to reduce
the duty by 50 per cent.; that is, from
£4 to £2. This proposal will operate as
from the 1st January, 1936, and will
cost the Road Fund £500 in a full year.
I now come to what, perhaps, will be
regarded as my most popular concession.
Strong representations have been made to
me that the tax on private cars in the
Province should be reduced to the British
rate. Although I am not convinced that
the owners of private cars have a case for
reduction to the British rate, having
regard to
local conditions and
because, to an extent, this is a luxury

Now, let me turn to Entertainments
Duty. I have been impressed by the
representations made to me from time to
time with considerable force, that the
living theatre is at a disadvantage as
compared with the cinema and other
entertainments which do not employ
people in their actual presentations. I
am prepared, therefore, as from the 1st
July, on a somewhat simpler scale, to

The 2d tax I reduce to d, the 3d to ld,
the 4d to 2d, the 6d to 4d, and the 9d to
6d. This scale covers admissions up to
5s, but above that sum I do not propose
to give any remission. Representations.

amateur musical and dramatic societies
in the Province that the entertainments
tax presses heavily on their finances, and
that their work is to a great extent of an
educational character and not conducted
for personal gain, and I am extending
the above concession to these societies,
with the result that, generally speaking,
their entertainment tax will be halved,
which is as far as I feel justified in going.
The cost of these concessions will be
about £5,000, so that the figure of
£130,000 on the existing basis of taxation in respect of Excise revenue, already
given by me, will be reduced to £125,000,

contribution and surplus.

take into consideration the views

With regard to those to whom the Act

now.
I do not object to assistance being given
to the railway companies, but I think the
Government have gone too far. The railway companies themselves are to blame
for the present position of things, for
they had the opportunity, and they did
not avail themselves of it. The Minister
of Home Affairs referred to the great
numbers of people carried to Portrush,
Bangor, Larne and Warrenpoint. If
anybody could be condemned because of
neglect of opportunity in regard to
Warrenpoint the railway company could.
When they had the spending of Government money they could have doubled the
branch line to Warrenpoint, a distance of
exactly ten miles. I venture to suggest
that there are not ten miles of railway
in Ireland over which more goods traffic
passes than the line to which I refer, but
the railway company did not put even a
paint brush on the railway stations in
Newry or on the station in Warrenpoint
for that matter. I say that the railway
company is not free from blame for the
condition of affairs that has been brought
about. It is a mistake for the Government now to give them the right to fix
fares, and to give them the monopoly of
the carrying traffic. I am sure that in
a few years this House and the country
generally will regret what is being done.

Mrs. PARKER: In introducing this
Bill the Minister of Home Affairs, at the
very outset of his remarks, appealed to
the Members of this House, and to those
whom they represent outside this House,
to look upon this Measure in a very wide
and impartial sense one which is
intended for the greatest interest of the
whole community, and he asked us to put
aside any questions of individual concerns, of any particular section or any
particular service, and to try to view the
Measure as one which affects the community as a whole. That was the keynote which he struck in the very opening
sentences of his speech, and I feel that in
asking us to look upon this Bill in that
Transport Bill-
Second Reading
16 MAY 1935
way he raised the whole level of the
debate, and made us look upon it from
the angle of doing the best that we can
for the whole community. That was
emphasised again yesterday by the Prime
Minister, when he said that in practically
every Bill some sectional interest might
suffer, but that the Government were out
for the greatest good of the greatest
number in this Province. We all know
that the Members of the Government
primarily are the custodians of the
security and prosperity of this Province,
and I believe that the ordinary Members
of this House have also a very great responsibility. That responsibility is not
just towards their constituents or towards
any particular section of the community,
any sectional interest; it is towards the
welfare of the whole Province. Those of
us who, perhaps, may receive criticism in
our own constituencies from the electors
or from certain interests, ought to look
upon this Bill from that point of view,
and to forget what may be possibly our
own private interests.
I listened this afternoon to the hon.
Member for Mid Derry. He said that he

sections and of all parties, and that at
that meeting he recognised the tremendous feeling that there was against this
Measure throughout the country. I saw

in support of any Government Measure
or any Government action. I think the

Mrs. PARKER: I am afraid that

is a great deal of feeling against the

Nearly all of the speakers before me have.
alluded to the fact that in the evidence

everybody who gave evidence accepted

heard was the suggestion of a subsidy,
and I could not help thinking to-day,

Finance, of what the feeling would have
been in this House if he had made provision in his Budget for a subsidy for the
three railways with which we are concerned in Northern Ireland.
We know that road transport is in very
great difficulty at the present time. We
must recognise that we are not now really
dealing with either the question of the
interests of the railways or the question
of the interests of road transport. We
are dealing with the general public
interest, and the general public includes
the farming community. I want to
make that perfectly plain. It is possible
that when this Bill is first being worked
there will be dissatisfaction, but I am
quite convinced that time will alter that
and that time will show the people who
are raising difficulties that this Measure
is of very great benefit to the community.
I have listened to hon. Members on the
other side of the House and some on this
side of the House who object to this
Measure, but personally I prefer to follow
the lead of our Prime Minister who, I
think, has never made any mistake in this
Province.

I would very much like to relieve the

There is one other point I want to

the position of road transport if the railways were eliminated. If the railways
were to be eliminated and matters were
to remain as they are, surely the

more serious than the monopoly which is
contemplated under this Transport
Board, with its machinery for appeal.
Apart from that, another question which
has not been stressed is, what would be
the condition of our roads under these
circumstances? It appears to me quite
impossible that the present roads should
stand up to the terrifically increased
traffic, and it would mean not only
enormously increased expenditure on the
present roads, which would have to be
borne by the ratepayers and taxpayers,
but it would also mean that new roads
would have to be built, and I think that
is a matter which the general public
should thoroughly realise.
I am prepared to support this Measure
from a deep conviction that in this case
the Government have shown great vision,
that they have realised there is a small
crack in the dam, and that if that crack
is not dealt with and repaired at once the
waters of the dam will burst and the
whole country will suffer and be submerged in what could only be a calamity.
It is in that belief that I have pleasure
in supporting this Bill.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 21st May, 1935.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMONEY FLAX SCUTCHERS
AND UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether three flax scutchers in
the Ballymoney district were disallowed
unemployment benefit on the grounds
that they were seasonal workers; whether
the Court of Referees which gave the
decision was fully constituted, and, if
not, whether the claimants were informed
of their right to have a full court.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I assume that the hon. Member is referring to the Court of Referees
held at Ballymoney on the 30th April
last at which the claims of a number of
flax scutchers were disallowed on the
grounds that they did not satisfy the requirements of Article 2 of the Anomalies
Regulations, relating to seasonal workers.
The court was composed of the chairman
and a workers' representative, no employers' representative being present. In
accordance with the usual procedure the
applicants when being notified of the date
fixed for the sitting of the court were
informed of their rights in the event of
the court not being fully constituted.
Mr. NIXON: Did the Minister not
give a promise to this House that when
applicants appeared before the court
they would be notified of their rights?
Mr. ANDREWS: The applicants get
notice when they are asked to attend the
court that they have the right to object
to their case being heard if the court is
not fully constituted. Surely that is
sufficient warning.
Mr. NIXON :
The point of the
question is were the applicants verbally
notified of the right to oppose when they
appeared before the court?
Mr. ANDREWS: They were notified
before they attended the court.
Mr. NIXON: I am surprised at you.
PRINTING, BOOKBINDING AND
KINDRED TRADES.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of persons employed in printing,
bookbinding and kindred trades, in the
City of Belfast.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is estimated that
there were on the 15th April, 1935,
about 2,750 insured persons, of 14 years
of age and over, employed in the printing, publishing, bookbinding and photography trades in Belfast..
CHINESE EGGS IN LIQUID FORM.
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he has seen the reports of a recent medical investigation as
to the risks run by people who consume
pastry or bread containing Chinese eggs
in liquid form, and whether he can give
details of the quantity and value of the
eggs, both in shell and in liquid form,
imported into Northern Ireland in the
last four years.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply to this question.
I have seen no such report and I am
not aware of any investigation having
been made into the propriety of using
Chinese eggs, for the purposes to which
the hon. Member refers, with unfavourable results.
I understand from my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Commerce, that
it is not possible to state what proportion
of the total imports of eggs into Northern Ireland are in liquid form, or are
consigned from China.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Five cases of

DUNDONALD WATER SUPPLY.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if the
people residing on Comber Road, Dundonald, have a sufficient water supply;
whether the contractor at present working there has been using the water which
usually supplies the residents; and if the
supply is not sufficient whether the
Minister will take steps to secure an
ample water supply for this district.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that the wells from which the people in
the locality derive their supplies have
been affected by the works in connection
with the new sewerage scheme, but pipes
have already been laid connecting with
the mains of the Belfast Water Commissioners, and it is expected that the water
supply will be available to-day.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
will the Minister assure the House that
he will make representations to the Belfast Water Commissioners to expedite
finding out where the leakage exists that
is preventing the water being supplied
to the homes of people on the Comber
Road?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
done so, with the result, as I have
answered my hon. Friend, that the water
is going to be turned on to-day.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
POCKET PICKING AT TOURIST
TROPHY RACE.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of cases of pocket picking
reported to the police in connection with
the last Tourist Trophy Race, and the
number of persons arrested and convicted in connection with these offences.
No persons have been made amenable
for these offences.
BUS ROUTES TAKEN OVER BY
RAILWAY COMPANIES.
6. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of bus routes taken over by the
railway companies up to date.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would refer
the hon. Member to the reply I gave him
in answer to the same question on the
19th April, 1934. No omnibus services
have been taken over by railway companies since that date.
Mr. NIXON: How many on that
date?
ALLEGED ATTACK ON CHILDREN
CARRYING FLAGS.
7. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state if
it is a fact that on Jubilee Day three
Protestant children going home from
Stewartstown with Jubilee mugs and
miniature Union Jacks, which had been
presented to them, were attacked on the
way back to Mountjoy by two men, and
a Union Jack taken from a little boy
aged twelve years; whether these men
are known to the police; and, if so,
what action he proposes to take to ensure
that children passing along the King's
highway may not be subjected to such
unwarranted attacks.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It has been
reported to me that two persons have
been summoned in connection with the
incident referred to by the hon. Member,
and as the matter is, therefore, sub
judice it is not desirable to make any
further statement.
Mr. HEALY: Perhaps the right hon.
Gentleman would tell the House where
the mugs are now.
Mr. ELLIOTT: On the other side.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Ways and Means (16th May)-Report.
BUDGET RESOLUTION.
Resolution reported:
"That it is expedient to amend the
law relating to Stamp Duty, Inland
Revenue (including Excise) and the
Public Debt and to make further provision in connection with finance."
Question proposed: "That the House
do agree with the Committee in the said
Resolution."
Mr. BEATTIE: After having a few
days' rest from the effect created previous to the Budget being introduced in
this House last Thursday, I feel that the
people of Northern Ireland have now had
ample opportunity to make their minds.
up as to what they think of the results
of the fourteenth Budget presented to
this House. I have endeavoured to get
into touch with many persons of high
standing in the City of Belfast and have
asked for their opinion as to the outcome
of the Budget on Ulster people. I am
sorry to inform the right hon. Gentleman that not one word of praise has been
put to his credit for the Budget which he
so ably presented in this House. I think
the House is entitled to congratulate
him on the manner in which he did present that Budget. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I wish to extend to him those
congratulations. But I feel that if he
was a super Chancellor of the Exchequer,
with all the abilities which a super man
possesses, he could not cover up the
deficiencies that appear in his Estimate
for the year 1935-36.
I knew the day was bound to arrive
when the difficulty of presenting a
Budget would become greater than it
was when I first came into the House. I
certainly paid great attention to the
remarks of the Chancellor concerning the
position of Ulster in the year 1935 in
comparison with that in the year 1918,
which was two years before the Parliament of Northern Ireland was established.
The only conclusion I can come to
is that as the years roll on we are going
to be driven into a particular position,
and we are going to have to make up our
minds as to the direction in which we are
travelling. I believe in selling my goods
in a healthy condition.
I think that at the moment Northerr
Ireland could be patched up to the extent
of saying that everything in the
garden is lovely. We have heard from
the Prime Minister's lips that Ulster is
a little paradise, and I think we could.
come to an agreement perhaps better today than in 1920, when the Six Counties
Parliament was rushed upon the people
without their consent by British
politicians. At that time they knew
perfectly well that the economic position
of the Six Counties was such that it was
impossible to maintain for the citizens
of this area a step-by-step policy with
Britain. I have now come to realise that
it is impossible.
1761 Ways and Means-Report-

I have heard during the week that I
should represent the back-to-the-Imperial
Parliament idea. As a believer in the
management of our own affairs I cannot
see my way to support that in the meantime. I do feel that the Chancellor must
be told plainly in this debate what the
citizens of Northern Ireland are looking
to him for. Are the promises he, along
with other Cabinet Ministers, gave to the
people only figures of speech, or are we
to take it that the Members of the Cabinet
are only political heads enjoying their
positions until the people have to meet
the debt which is gaining headway in the
Six Counties.
I am prepared to face the situation at
the present moment irrespective of whom
it may offend. Our trade is not as it
should be; our outlet is not as it should
be. We have noticed in the Press other
countries fighting for an outlet. We
have no outlet. We are cramped and
held in in an area not bigger than Yorkshire.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): We are part of the United
Kingdom with its 45,000,000 people.
Mr. BEATTIE: We do not seem to be
part and parcel of the great British
Empire about which the right hon.
Gentleman speaks so loudly on political
platforms.
Mr. POLLOCK: We are.
•
Mr. BEATTIE: Now that it has been
admitted by the Chancellor that we are
part of the United Kingdom we demand
from him the same consideration as the
citizens of Britain get, and we are
going to see that we get it. The
Chancellor of the Exchequer is in an
awkward position in not having the
wherewithal to give that equal citizenship to the citizens of the Six Counties.
I recognise that the responsibility does
not rest solely on the Chancellor. First
of all, a Six-County Parliament should.
not have been established. If the wise
heads had been working on behalf of the
people of Ulster they would never have
allowed the British Parliament
establish a Six-County Parliamentto

you have established?
a

Mr. BEATTIE-knowing well that
Six-County Parliament was
uneconomic proposition. I claim that at
that time they did not work in the
interests of the Ulster citizens. I do not
wish to decry the place to which I belong.
I stand for the Ulster people———
Major McCORMICK: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE- -and I am as proud
of Ulster as any Member on the Government side of the House, but those words
are not going to lead me into a garden
of abundance where I am going to feed

we have a standing army of unemployed
for which at the moment the Chancellor
has made no provision-
Mrs. PARKER: No provision?
Mr. BEATTIE: No, and I will prove
it before I sit down. He has made no

fully satisfied with the parity arrangement entered into in 1925 and had full
confidence in it at that time, and that
the British authorities are now going to
give a new parity agreement which will
bring into Northern Ireland a sum of
money to the credit of the Unemployment Insurance Fund. That is
a very flowery statement to make. I
want the money to go into the fund, and
then to go into the homes of the people.
That is where the snag lies in regard to
financial assistance to that fund from the
British Parliament on the reconstruction
of the parity agreement.
I would go as far as to say this. At
one time I was a great advocate of having
control of all our services, but knowing
this unemployment question and the
services that have been given to the
people of Northern Ireland I am prepared
to say that the best thing that can be
done is for representation to be made to
go back into the central fund at Westminster. That is, by the amalgamation
of the Northern Ireland and Great
Britain funds you will save yourselves.
That amalgamation, I claim, was offered
by the present Prime Minister of Great
Britain and rejected by the people now
representing themselves as the Government of Northern Ireland. If there is
that amalgamation, the people here will
have an equal opportunity of getting
subsistence allowance as it is given in
England, Scotland, and Wales. But at

the moment the test and other conditions

Mr. BEATTIE: The right hon. Gentleman can disagree as much as he likes; he

What are we going to do?
Are we going to continue living in
the fools' paradise we are living in at the
moment, forgetting our responsibility to
that large army, or does the Minister of
Finance think that because we are going
to have one aeroplance factory on the

that is going to relieve the unemployment

to-day the tightening-up process is so

Sir ROBERT LYNN: What do you

Mr. BEATTIE: I have made many

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am sorry to
interrupt my hon. Friend. I have
listened to his speeches on unemployment
and I have never heard any suggestions

could cure unemployment. I have been
waiting ever since for the cure.
Mr. BEATTIE: The hon. Member for
North Antrim may try to get me to drift
from my point, but just now I am not
going to give any of the solutions which
I put before the House, and which the
House ignored. At the moment I am

I notice that the Minister of Finance
has suggested a restoration out of the
surplus which he is carrying. I am saying this on my own responsibility. I have
now for eleven years been on four
different Committees of this House without fee or reward. I have acted on Committees on which the Members of the
Senate were paid, and I have never
grumbled. I tell the Minister of Finance
that I do not desire, and I do not think
my colleagues who have been voluntary
workers desire, any payment. Leaving
that payment aside I think the right hon.
Gentleman should live up to his obligations to the Members of this House as a
whole. He told the Members in 1931
that this House would give a lead to
those outside, and he asked them to make
a sacrifice to the extent of 15 per cent.
of the money allowed as expenses.
I ask the Minister to live up to his
word on that occasion, when he said that
as soon as the emergency had passed away
he would restore that cut. He admits,
I am sure, from his own knowledge that
£170 to pay all the expenses attached to
a Member of Parliament is not an amount
which the outside public envies very
much. In the case of some Members it
is recognised that that £170 does not cover
their actual Parliamentary expenses-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I
believe the Minister would be doing
justice to the House if he restored the 15
per cent. cut in Parliamentary expenses
instead of giving the two guineas to the
special Committees.
The next thing I come to, while on the
subject of cuts, is that the Minister of
Finance has a further surplus to disburse,
and so he says, "I am giving a 2 per
cent. restoration of the police pension
reduction," making a 5 per cent. restora-

tion of the police pension contribution."
I do not grumble at that, and no one else

Therefore, I say the Minister is entitled,

5 per cent. which is still outstanding. I
think they were paying 10 per cent. Perhaps I am wrong. Perhaps it was only

Now I am leaving the question of cuts
in salaries for the moment, because I
want to deal first with questions affecting
my own constituents. The next question
I come to is the question of motor taxation. You have reduced motor taxation
to the farmers by 25 per cent. and to
private owners by 12 per cent. I would
have been better pleased if the Minister
had said that private motor-cars are a
luxury.
Mr. POLLOCK: I did say that.
Mr. BEATTIE: You did say that,
although the one I use is not a luxury.
(Laughter.) The right hon. Gentleman
says the private motor-car is a luxury.
Then I say that as a luxury it has no

Budget while there are so many special
cases outstanding. I want to be very
candid with the Minister and to say that
when he makes that statement he either
means what he says or he is talking with

Mr. ANDREWS: He does not do that.
Mr. BEATTIE: He has done it on this
occasion. He has granted a 12 per cent.
reduction on a luxury tax. I am surprised that that position should be presented in Northern Ireland. I wonder
would he give sympathetic consideration
to an instance in which I will show him
that he has not reduced the motor taxation. In the Short Strand, which I have
the honour to represent in this House,
we have the Richardson Chemical Manure
Company, Limited. They have sent a
letter to the right hon. Gentleman pointing out an anomaly that exists in their
industry. There is the picture on the
heading of the firm. The Short Strand
intersects two parts of their works.
Because an electric bogey, which is used
by all industrial firms at the moment,
has to cross the roadway from one building to another with a trailer on it, the
right hon. Gentleman imposes a tax of
£26 on that firm. Railway companies
can use electric bogeys all round their
own premises; Harland & Wolff or any
other concern can use them without any
tax being applied. I leave that view of
the building there to any Member of this
House.
Remember that the reason the tax is
imposed is because the electric bogey has
to cross the street, that it is using the
highway. That is the reason why the tax
is imposed, but if you can reduce the tax
on a farmer's lorry from £4 to £2 why
cannot you reduce the tax on the small
trailer that this bogey draws? At the
moment it stands at £6. Why can you
not wipe that £6 out altogether? A
trailer on a motor lorry is a different
thing to this trailer on an electric bogey.
The trailer on the motor lorry is on the
public highway all the time and you
have reduced the tax on that to £2-but
this small trailer is only behind the
electric bogey crossing the street where no
danger exists. I do not think the Minister is justified in having a tax on the
bogey at all, and I am now asking him
to have that £20 reduced to the minimum
amount. Then he will have done some
useful service to assist not only the
farmers but to assist industry and to help
Ulster through her difficult time. I put
that forward to the Minister in the hope
that he will give the matter the consideration which I expect from him and grant
a reduction of the duty on this trailer
behind an electric bogey.
Then I understood that the Minister
was giving relief to education work that

£700 to £350. I think he said he will

further and to abolish the tax altogether
in the case of these two bodies. I know

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Mr. ANDREWS: The motor industry,
for instance.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I would not call that
a new industry now. It was well established before the Government here was
set up.
It is still in its early stages, I
admit. There are almost boundless possibilities in it yet. I admit that there
are new industries, but the same thing is
happening in the new industries. If you
take the statistics of the number of men
employed to-day in the production of
motor-cars and compare them and their
working hours per car with the number
employed ten or twelve years ago you will
find that there is at least a fifty per cent.
reduction in the working time computed
for the production of a motor-car. You
might wonder where the connection is
with the Budget. It is here. I said a
few minutes ago that the community,
collectively speaking, was not becoming
wealthier, that we were gradually being
pushed by the very development of the
system under which we live into a
position of economic embarrassment.
Our position adds to the difficulties
which confront the Chancellor, and the
Chancellor, therefore, this year produces
a Budget which is the result of subvention, of financial manipulation which
has been challenged by several local
authorities, which is balanced as a result
of finances which have accrued to the
Government because of the violation of
the principles of local government in
Northern Ireland and in contradistinction
to the principles of local government in
Great Britain, and also because periodically for the past few years he has drawn
from reserves to assist in balancing his
Budget. The Minister will himself be
the first to admit that, no matter how
efficacious a reserve fund may be, that
is a process that you cannot maintain for
an unlimited period of years.
It is
bound to come to an end some time.
When you have finished
your reserves,
and have even resorted to the expedient
adopted this year of not providing for
certain aspects of your sinking fundsall these things combined must come to
an end, and then the Minister will be
confronted with a situation in which he
will have to ask the people to shoulder
fresh burdens.
In face of that I submit that the time
is opportune for the consideration of a
fresh policy. Quite frankly, I can see
no way out of the economic impasse except the consideration of gradually but
certainly transforming the face of society
from being a competitive society, in
which the motive is profit, into a cooperative commonwealth in which the
community shall own and control the
means of livelihood. That is the
only way out of the difficulties that
confront the Minister of Finance at
the present time. Whilst I believe that
that ought to be the objective of every
right-thinking economist at the present
time, nevertheless, in the transition stage
of the present state of society to a more
ideal stage of society, it is the duty of
the competent authority to do what that
authority possibly can to ease the burdens
imposed on the largest section of the community in the journey from one stage of
society to another. For these reasons I
want to say that if I were a motor-car
user, if I had reached that state of
affluence which would enable me to run
a car for my own private business-and
I wish I were, because of the convenience
it would be to me I would feel it an
insult to be offered the concession which
the Minister of Finance has offered to
motorists. The Government tell the
people that it is their policy to keep pace
and to keep in harmony with social
developments in Great Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: Social developments.

harmony on this subject, and if I were
one of the people concerned I should resent the concession offered by the Minister
of Finance.
