before the conversation had gone on very
long that it was not so easy to get every
socialistic formula carried out.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Why Lord Snowden?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Because he is
politically alive to your political ally in
front of you.
He is a man who is very
frank in regard to these things, and I
gave him as an example. I do not mind
if my hon. Friend takes the present
Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Neville
Chamberlain. I do not mind either of
them. He will discover it is not very
easy to get the money out of these people.
Therefore, I congratulate the Minister on
the fact that he has been able to get
a sum of £643,000 for unemployment.
If he had not got this amount we would
have had to raise it ourselves. In spite
of all that the Member for Dock says
with regard to new sources of revenue,
I think you would find it very difficult
to get people to agree to extra taxation
at the present time. If he was about
the country as much as I am he would
discover the enormous number of people
who are objecting very strongly at the
present time to such things as the education levy and to revaluation. If he came
along and perhaps put on an extra tax
he might find he was not quite as popular
as he is to-day.
I have an absolutely open mind with
regard to the taxation of land values. If
it can be proved that it is right and
legitimate that a tax should be put on
ground rents I am not raising any objection at all, but do not forget that this
question has been discussed at length for
many years. In fact, Mr. Lloyd George,
in 1909, brought into the Budget something on the lines indicated by the speech
of the hon. Member for Dock. The result
was the slump that took place in building.
I remember one of the first questions I
put down in the Imperial Parliament was
to make inquiries with regard to the
amount that had been spent in making
investigations about these things and the
amount received, and I discovered it cost
far more to work the Act than anything
that was got out of it.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Because it was too
low.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: The question is
one that is worthy of serious consideration, and I have no objection to my hon.
Friend raising it. It ought to be, and
probably has been, explored by the
Minister of Finance. It certainly has
been explored time and again by finance
Ministers of other countries.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Did your party in
England not scrap that policy?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Yes, and for the
very good reason that it was unproductive
and of no advantage whatever. If the
hon. and learned Member for Central
applied his mind to this question with
the care he does to most subjects when he
came into this House he would probably
be the strongest denunciator of the
taxation of land values. I have an open
mind, and I hope the hon. and learned
Member and I will be able to discuss it
across the floor of the House. When he
has studied the question as many years
as I have studied it it will be interesting
to see what his views on the subject are.
Mr. McCARROLL: Your mind does
not seem very open.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: The hon. Member for Dock talked about shifting the
burden. Everybody wants to shift the
burden on to somebody else.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I want to spread it
over.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: The Chancellor
of the Exchequer wants to spread it
equally over everyone. When the hon.
Member for Dock talks about the wealth
of this Province not being as great as it
was, I would like to ask him what he
means by wealth. I have been longer in
the world than he has, and in my short
life I have seen wonderful developments

all over this Province of ours. I have

I do not think it is to the good of any
party, or to the advantage of the country
as a whole, for people to decry their own.
Province in order to make political
capital. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I am ready at any time to take political
advantage of any of my opponents, but
I never want to say anything that is
going to depreciate the value of this
Province, which depends so much for its.
prosperity on other countries. I do ask
hon. Members opposite not to be so ready
to decry Ulster, or to hold Ulster up as
a sort of deserted area with the people
living in a state of semi-barbarism. I
think this Province will compare favourably with any other part of the Empire
or of the world. Therefore, I say to
them: Do not always be so ready to
abuse your own Province.
In conclusion, I would like to join in
congratulating the right hon. Gentleman.
If I have had any difference with him it
has been on the financial side, which is
natural enough. I believe my difference
has been different from those of some
other people, because most people blame
the Finance Minister for not giving
enough away, while my complaint against
him was that he is too soft-hearted and
inclined to give too much away. I want
to see the social services kept up, as the
hon. Member for Dock does, at the
highest possible standard, but like the
hon. Member for Mid Antrim to-day,
and as I said in the first speech I made
in the Northern Parliament, I do appeal
to the Government in spending money to
see that they get value for every pound
they spend.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 22nd May, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
YIELD OF PROPERTY TAX AND
INCOME TAX.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state the
approximate yield of property tax from
Northern Ireland to the United Kingdom Exchequer in the year 1936-37 on
the basis of the recent revaluation
figures, and of income tax at 4s 6d in the
pound, and what was the yield for the
year 1934-35.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As the hon. and learned Member is aware, income tax is a Reserved
Service. I have been informed by the
Imperial authorities that they are not yet
in a position to supply me with an estimate of the yield of property tax in Northern Ireland based on the recent revaluation figures.
In view of this answer, I thought that
the hon. and learned Member would
hardly be interested in the figures of the
yield for the year 1934-35, but if he still
desires this information and will so inform me, I can let him have it in the
course of a fortnight, as it will take this
time for the Imperial authorities to extract the figures.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I am still anxious
for the information.
REVISED UNEMPLOYMENT
REINSURANCE AGREEMENT.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can outline
the main features of the revised Unemployment Reinsurance Agreement with
Great Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: I regret that I am
not yet in a position to give the hon. and
learned Member the information he
desires. As I informed the House when
introducing my Budget Statement, the
arrangement with regard to the Unemployment Reinsurance Agreement has to
be endorsed by Parliament in both
countries, and, therefore, it is not possible for me to give any further information regarding the amended scheme
until I submit it to the House for its
approval concurrently with its submission to the Parliament of the United
Kingdom. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
ENGINEERING DEPARTMENT OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
3. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that
grave dissatisfaction exists amongst candidates applying for posts in the engineering section of the Ministry by reason of
the system by which appointments are
made, and whether the Minister will, in
the interests of economy and efficiency,
only appoint men who have qualified by
a system of examination from a recognised engineering examining body.
Mr. POLLOCK: The general service
system of recruitment is applicable to
vacancies in the engineering staff, and I
am not aware of any dissatisfaction such
as is suggested by the hon. Member. As
he will appreciate, certain of these engineering posts demand practical training
and experience rather than academic
qualifications. To restrict candidature
as suggested would, therefore, not only
.be impracticable but would have the
effect of rendering ineligible for promotion to higher ranks certain existing
members of the engineering staff who
have rendered meritorious service. Such
a result would, I feel sure, not commend
itself to the hon. Member.
Where, however, professional or
academic qualifications are considered
essential for the vacant post, these qualifications are clearly set out in the notice
advertising the vacancy and are strictly
enforced.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman whether he is
satisfied that the present system of
examination for engineering appointments is satisfactory; whether he is aware
that the present system sets out a special
officer from the Civil Service who has no

are a federal State in the United Kingdom and are a part of the United
Kingdom, just as in the United States
are quite a number of New England
States that are not as large as the
Province of Ulster, such as Rhode Island,
Connecticut, Maine, and many others
that I need not mention. All those have

Parliaments such as we have; and all
those have Governments such as we have.
So far as the position of Ulster as a
federal State is concerned, it is, of course,
a new arrangement in the United
Kingdom, but at the same time we have
any number of precedents for the position
which Ulster occupies. It will, therefore, surely be admitted that neither is
our area too small nor is our population
too small for our position as a federal
State within the Kingdom.
I would remind the hon. Member that
a State is not great or small simply by

a great many small States in the world

is very important. In these modern days

in order to exemplify my point? The

is

One other very small matter that was

I have, therefore, decided to follow the
British practice in these matters, that is,
to allow complete exemption to these
vehicles where, on application to the
Ministry of Home Affairs, it has been
successfully established that the vehicles
are used only within or in the immediate
neighbourhood of a factory or works,
etc. The cost of the concession is very
negligible, but I think it is desirable that
that change should be made. (Hon.

There were other points which he touched

I will now touch upon the arguments,

first place, the hon. Member asked, can

other words, he suggested that some

I can say that our social standards in
their relation to British standards will
be maintained and continued as long as
Ulster remains part of the United Kingdom. You cannot divorce this Province
from the United Kingdom by
sophistry. Therefore, the standards
which obtain in Great Britain must
necessarily obtain here. I am now speak-

ing of the social standards-that is the

Mr. MIDGLEY: He did not.
Mr. POLLOCK-when he reminded

Another suggestion my hon. Friend

What would happen, I should like to

and we did not? What would happen to

would necessarily be the natural result, not of course immediately, but
in the course of years. That is how

Summarising all these things and without dealing with the smaller and unimportant matters touched upon by different
Members and perhaps here I should say

Summarising the whole situation, I believe I can say that we have now reached

less difficulty in balancing our accounts in

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,

time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill now
before the House needs, I think, very
little explanation. It is similar in all
respects to that passed by the House last
year and two years previously. The
House, I am sure, will be pleased to know
that we have again been able to secure
for Northern Ireland the International
Tourist Trophy Race. I believe it has
come to be regarded by a very large
section of the community
as
an
institution, and the general community
would be very sorry if it were to pass
away to some other locality, because it
attracts to the Province visitors from all
parts of the British Islands and from
parts of the Continent. Apart from the
financial benefit to the people of Northern
Ireland, I think the House will appreciate that the race imposes upon the
promoters, the Royal Automobile Club,
considerable financial responsibility, and
we propose this year, as we did last year,
to give them power to charge a fee of
half-a-crown for each car entering the
race area towards meeting their expenses.
Provision is again made to give certain
exemptions to persons resident in the
area and persons entering the area for
professional or business purposes.
Mr. BEATTIE: This is an annual
contribution from the people of Northern
Ireland, of which, in the words of the
Minister, the people have got tired. They
have made every reasonable effort to make
this race a success, and up to the moment
it has not come out to the satisfaction
of the people who have given it the wholehearted support which, at the beginning,
they all thought it deserved. Certainly
the race brings Belfast into the limelight
as far as pictures are concerned, and
perhaps gives to the public thrills that
they could only experience at motor races
on the Continent. Nevertheless, I think
we want more than that from the motor
race in Northern Ireland. We want
something that will give Belfast or Ulster
a name in the motor industry.
Up to the moment no maker of motor
cars who takes part in that race and we
provide the finest track in the world to
give them an advertisement that they
could not get anywhere else has thought
it worth while to establish a factory in
Northern Ireland. I supported the Bill
upon the first occasion because I thought
that Morris, or Austin, or the Riley
people, firms of that kind, would have
considered Northern Ireland a suitable
place for the construction of cars, if not
for their manufacture. I believe that
the surplus skilled labour we have in
Northern Ireland is as competent to carry
out work of that nature as any to be
found in Great Britain. The result
obtained in the past has not been to my
liking. I do not want to be called a
killjoy, and I do not wish to say that
we should not encourage a sport which
is enjoyed by a percentage of the community; but as a representative of the
working classes I feel that enjoyment is
not all that we should get out of the race.
We should get better results. I hope
the words I have uttered will be taken
to heart by the Minister of Home Affairs
and conveyed to the proper authorities.
I am not saying that either the Prime
Minister or the Minister of Home Affairs
has neglected that matter in the past,
because I was in their company when it
was mentioned, but I think further representations should be made to see if we
cannot get better results from the motor
race than the thrills and the enjoyment
on the part of those who watch it.
I now come to the raising of the toll
from the motorists who have to go
through that area. That toll is a very
small matter of half-a-crown. I do not
think that any motorist objects to pay
it, provided that the amount collected
in that way goes to the race or what

Mr. BARBOUR: The brief measure
to the Second Reading, of which I now
seek the approval of the House, is selfexplanatory.
Hon. Members will recollect that by an
Act of 1931 authority was given for the
establishment of the Electricity Board of
Northern Ireland whose main function it
is to develop and to co-ordinate the supply
of electricity, primarily in the southeastern part of our area. At that time it
was thought that a number of years would
elapse ere the work of development would
be carried into the somewhat sparsely
populated areas in the western counties of
Tyrone, Fermanagh and Londonderry,
but so energetically have the Board undertaken the task entrusted to them that today not only have they provided the network throughout County Down and
County Armagh, but they have also extended operations as far as Cookstown,
Omagh and Enniskillen. At an early
date their high-tension lines will reach.
Newtownstewart and Strabane, and will
link up with the Londonderry generating
station.
When I introduced into this House the
1931 Measure I emphasised the two principal aims I had in mind, viz., the provision of cheap power for industry and the
improvement of the amenities of life in the
towns and villages to be served by this
new system of supply. Supplies of electricity are now available in some ninety
towns and villages, and if hon. Members
will be good enough to turn to the Report
of the Electricity Board for the year ended
31st December, 1934, they will observe
that the
towns
occupiers of these
and districts are availing themselves
readily of
of the facilities offered by
the Board. These consumers comprise
every class of the community, and the
Board's domestic tariffs being based upon
low standards of charge and high standards of consumption it is not at all
unusual for the householder who uses
electricity for general purposes to find
his quarterly bill working out at under
d. per unit. The rapidity with which
the supply of electricity has been given
to remote country areas, and with which
the cost of that supply has been brought
down to levels within the reach of all
classes of the community, is a remarkable
achievement on the part of the Electricity
Board.

The 1931 Act empowered the Board to

Friend, the Minister of Finance, and

£2,000,000, with power to my right hon.

KING'S JUBILEE MEDAL AND
R.U.C.
1. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state what
qualifications were considered in the
selection of members of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary to receive the award of the
King's Jubilee Medal; whether he is
aware that there is considerable dissatisfaction
among members of this
Force concerning these awards; whether
it is a fact that a member of the Force,
who was punished for unsatisfactory conduct during an attack on the barracks in
which he was serving, and whose general
conduct has been unsatisfactory by
reason of his lack of zeal and efficiency,
was awarded the Jubilee Medal.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): May I remind the
hon. Member that the Jubilee Medals are
awarded by His Majesty the King, and
in these circumstances I suggest it is not
desirable that any discussion should take
place as to the propriety of any such
awards.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman who makes the selection
in Northern Ireland for awards presented
by the King? Surely there is some
authority in Northern Ireland.
R.U.C. AND YORK STREET
TROUBLES.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. Grant:
2. To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he has made any investigation
into the behaviour of a section of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary in the York
Street area, and, if so, what action he
intends to take.
Mr. GRANT: Before I ask this
question I would like to state that the
question that appears on the Order Paper
is not framed in the same way as the
question I handed in at the Table.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think I had better
deal with this forthwith. I came to an
arrangement with the House during the
past eight years that my Department and
myself would so frame the questions
which come in that they should be in
Parliamentary form. I have always explained to hon. Members that should it
be their wish, I am prepared to send the
questions back if they are not in Parliamentary form, but I suggest that unless
there is some radical alteration in a
question it would suit hon. Members
better if we made the alterations.
Mr. GRANT: Question No. 2, to ask
the Minister of Home Affairs.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Following the
representations made by the hon. Member for Duncairn on the 14th May, I
personally, accompanied by the Inspector-
General and the City Commissioner,
inspected the York Street area and investigated the position. Undoubtedly,
damage was done to a number of houses
in Vere Street and Grove Street. The
Inspector-General is continuing his investigations into the matter, and if, as a
result, it is found that any members of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary exceeded
his duty, disciplinary action will be
taken.
I may add that if any further information can be supplied in regard to the
matter the Inspector-General will be glad
to receive it.
Mr.
CAMPBELL: Is it not a
notorious fact that in this area in recent
weeks a campaign of terrorism and outrage has been directed against the
Catholic residents, and will the Minister
inquire why the offenders are not brought
to justice?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not prepared to accept the statement made by
the hon. and learned Member.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the Minister call for an official report on the subject?

For the information of the hon. Member I should mention that potato prices
in Northern Ireland in any particular
year depend on the quantity produced in
Great Britain in that year. If there is
a surplus across Channel, prices fall; if
a scarcity, prices rise.
Speaking generally, when production
in Great Britain is below 4,000,000 tons
prices tend to be reasonable; when production exceeds the four million mark
prices tend to fall below the economic
level, and as the 4 million point is
This
approached the market collapses.
tendency was corrected in the year
1928-29 (a heavy surplus year) by
relatively large exports to Continental
countries.
This dominating factor of
surplus is being corrected by the British
Potato Marketing Board, who are endeavouring to bring supply into line with
demand.
One result of our Marketing of
Potatoes Act has been that even when
there was a surplus and a consequent
slump in prices in Great Britain, Northern Ireland has still been able to ship
potatoes to that country which would
otherwise be unsaleable.
Since the Act came into operation and
during the past few years of heavy supplies and slump prices, we have been
able to sell our potatoes on the English
market when it has been impossible for
English farmers to dispose of their stock.
This is entirely due to the fact that our
potatoes have been graded and to the
successful operation of the Act. I am
sure the hon. Member will have noted
that England and Scotland are following
our lead by the launching of a grading
scheme.

MEDICAL
REFEREE'S DECISION
AND UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if, in
the event of an insured person being declared fit for work by the medical
referee on the day of examination, he is
entitled to receive unemployment benefit
on the following day, although the insured person has not signed at the
Labour Exchange, due to the fact that
he was not aware of the decision of the
medical referee; whether he is notified
on the day of examination, or afterwards, of the decision of the medical
referee; and whether he can state what
the practice is in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): A person is not entitled to
claim unemployment benefit unless he
declares himself capable of work. When
he is drawing health insurance benefit the
decision of the question of capacity for
work is one for his approved society; it
does not rest with the medical referee.
The referee's duty is limited to giving a
second opinion on the matter on the request of the approved society. A copy
of the opinion is sent also to the
claimant's own doctor.
After examination by the referee, a
claimant should consult his own doctor
at once, and I am arranging for insured
persons to be advised accordingly. If
his doctor decides to issue no further certificate of incapacity, the claimant can
attend the employment exchange on the
same day and claim
claim unemployment
benefit. I understand this is what
happens in Great Britain.

not think that this question gives him.
a grand opportunity to follow the stepby-step policy with Great Britain;

in Great Britain on the day of examination gives the applicant his decision there
and then as to whether he is fit for work
or still sick, and in view of that is he
prepared to put that practice into operation on the examination of the insured
person by the medical referees?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am prepared to
look into the question again for the
purpose of confirming in my own mind
what is the practice in Great Britain, and
I undertake to give effect to it.
Mr. BEATTIE: Thank you for that

is supposed to sign.
Mr. ANDREWS: The hon. Member
asked me to follow the practice in Great
Britain. I have undertaken to do so, and
I think that ought to satisfy him.
Mr. BEATTIE: Thank you.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Hon. Members

which has been customary in the past.

and deal with the explanations later.
the Estimates for salaries and expenses of

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, appropriations-in-aid of salaries and wages.
Two items of expenditure call for special

deal with later, and which is covered by
and
appropriation-in-aid,
a general

by appropriation-in-aid. There is also a

£28,000, and which constitutes a payment to the Ministry for various services
rendered.
Hon. Members will recollect that when
I presented the Estimates to the Committee last year I then dealt very fully
with the Pigs and Bacon Marketing
Schemes which had been recently inaugurated and which were giving rise to a
good deal of discussion and some misrepresentation. On that occasion I pleaded for
patience and confidence and a real effort
on the part of those concerned to understand what was being attempted. I am
glad to have this opportunity of thanking
all the Members of the Committee for the
support which they have given me in trying to explain, and get across, if I may
use that phrase, the difficulties to be surmounted. I would like also to thank the
farming community for their assistance.
Some may have thought the various
regulations and orders unnecessary, while
some may have thought they were simply
for pinpricking purposes, but, as a matter
of fact, every order that was made was
made for the purpose of benefiting the
scheme and making the whole thing a
success.
It can, I think, be fairly claimed that
the scheme is now sailing in smooth water
and is developing rapidly. It would be
very difficult to meet the man who to-day
would contemplate with equanimity the
prospect of going back to the old order of
things. Proof that the scheme is working
well can be found in the figures relating
to breeding swine and pigs for bacon and
ham. Every half-yearly census shows a
substantial increase in the number of pigs.
Our population of breeding pigs has
increased by 130 per cent. since 1932, and
our output of pigs for bacon and hams
this year is 100 per cent. greater than in
1932. This benefits not only the agricultural population but also the towns.
During the past year two up-to-date
factories for Wiltshire curing have been
erected and equipped, one in Portadown,
which is now operating, and the other in
Londonderry, which will shortly be in
Ministry of Agriculture
Estimates-

23 MAY 1935
operation. The erection of these factories
cost £40,000 in buildings and machinery.
The new factory in Portadown, when in
full operation, will provide much-needed
employment for 200 hands, and its turnover will be in the neighbourhood of
£500,000 per annum.
That is but one instance, but when you
add to it the new establishment in
Londonderry, and the fact that every one
of the 80 existing roll and ham curing
factories in Ulster has a greater output
than in the past and is doing more
business, it will, I hope, be realised that
the policy which has been so successfully
inaugurated, apart from its benefit to the
agricultural community, is a real asset and
contribution to the urban and city
dweller.
Let me take one other point which will
help to emphasise this benefit. If we consider only the increase in our pig production and assume that only half the feeding stuffs used in their production are
purchased this is a conservative estimate
-then, roughly, an extra half million
pounds worth of feeding stuffs is being
brought into our ports, passing through
our mills, over our transport system, on
lorries from Belfast to our local towns,
creating more trade and more employment
at every one of these stages.
It is most important when dealing with
this subject that we should look at it
not only from a strictly agricultural point
of view but from the view of the community as a whole, both town and
country. I have mentioned this aspect
of rural development and its benefit to
the urban communities because I do not
think we realise the enormous market
for industrial goods which our farming
community provides. I think it is not
often realised that agriculture in
England purchases as much from the
industrial side of Great Britain as Great
Britain exports to the whole of Africa
and Asia combined, or to the whole of
Western Europe. Therefore, I think it
is obvious to hon. Members that if you
decrease the purchasing power of agriculture you decrease the purchasing
power of one of industry's best purchasers.
Before leaving the subject of pigs I
would like to refer to the question of
grading. Hon. Members will remember
that last year that particular aspect of
the pig problem was severely criticised.
There is no doubt that it is only by grading the quality and type of pig required
by the consumer can be secured, and by
paying an increased price for the better
type of pig you are inducing the farmer
gradually to produce the type that is
required. The scheme is now working
very satisfactorily. Our whole time
veterinary officers are carrying it out.
These officers have, in any case, to be in
slaughter-houses and curing establishments for meat inspection work, and the
additional cost of their services is refunded to the Ministry on an agreed
basis by the two Boards.
Now, may I turn to the Milk Scheme,
which I propose to deal with more fully,
because the Committee will be interested
in hearing how the scheme, which has
only recently been brought in, is working. First of all, I will deal with the
manufactured side, because that side is
very much the simplest. Hon. Members
are already aware that the inclusion of
Northern Ireland in the scheme of assistance by the British Treasury in manufacturing milk has enabled us since the
1st of April, 1934, to guarantee to the
farmers supplying our creameries an
average price of 5d per gallon in summer
and 6d per gallon in winter.
To my Ministry has fallen the very
onerous task of operating the scheme,
and hon. Members will be interested to
know that we have paid out to farmers
sending milk to the creameries a sum of
£152,000 during the past financial year.
That is all I need say about the manufactured side, except this, that unless a
scheme had been brought out to help the
manufactured side no scheme for liquid
milk would have been possible, because
with the prevailing low prices there is
no doubt the liquid milk industry would
have been flooded and any prices that
might have been arranged would have
crashed, with the result that winter milk
would not have been produced and there
would probably have been a shortage in
Belfast.
With regard to liquid milk, I would
ask the Committee to realise that this has
been, perhaps, one of the biggest efforts
in public health that has ever been
attempted, and I look on it as one of the
most important aspects-it is not the
only important aspect of the milk
scheme. Every cow which produces milk
is now inspected twice a year by our own
Ministry of Agriculture 1888

[Sir Basil Brooke]
whole-time veterinary officers.
The cost
of that is met by a charge on the local
authorities. As a matter of fact it is the
same sum which originally was paid by
the local authorities for their part-time
veterinary officers, and the difference is
made up out of the Milk Fund. As a
result of that inspection, which only
started a very short time ago-last April
there has been, I am informed, a very
considerable improvement in the general
quality of milk, and I think the farmers
are beginning to realise that without that
improvement in quality the consumption
for which we are all looking will not
increase. I am hoping for a further
improvement, and I should be satisfied
if, in a comparatively short time, we can
see the quality of milk for human consumption rising to at least B grade.
quality and more of Grade A milk being
drunk. We must bear in mind that it
is no use improving and safeguarding the
water supplies of our great cities unless
we can go as far with our milk supply.
If you can improve your milk supply,
which you ought to be able to do, up to
the quality of your water supply and
remove all impurities, then for the community's sake you are producing something that is worth having.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about the beer?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I will deal
with beer, perhaps, in a moment's time,
if the hon. Member will allow me. It is
very peculiar that many people have complained that A and B milk, which is
cooled milk, is not really as good milk
as the old milk, because the cream does
not rise so rapidly. As a matter of fact,
the mere fact that you cool the milk is
a preventive, in a way, to the cream
rising, because you are preventing a
rapid bacteriological growth. The reason
why you cool milk is that it keeps. On
milk that is not cooled the cream will
rise, but the fact of the cream not rising
on the cooled milk does not mean that
it is not as rich in cream as the ordinary
milk. The fact that the cream takes
longer to rise does not mean that it is
not in fact as good milk as it was before.
I have often, myself, heard the remark
made that the present A and B milk is
not as good as the old milk. That, of
course, is quite wrong.
I should like now to say something
about the levies. On this matter there
is considerable misunderstanding, and I
hope to be able to remove some of that
misunderstanding. The Committee, no
doubt, realises that the scheme operating
in Northern Ireland is quite different
from that operating in England. Moreover, it is operated by my Ministry on
the advice of the Milk Council. The Milk
Council have some statutory obligations
and functions, but, in fact, the work is
carried out by my Ministry on the advice
of the Milk Council. This Council is
composed of producers, distributors, and
consumers, with three independent members appointed by myself. I am aware
that there is dissatisfaction in certain
limited quarters on this matter of the
levy, but I should like to emphasise the
fact that it is a very small portion of the
milk trade that is dissatisfied. They,
perhaps, do not fully realise that the
price difference is produced by
graduated levy. In the case of A milk
the levy is small, for B milk it is slightly
bigger, and in the case of C milk it is
bigger still. It is perfectly obvious that
that must be so. A and B producers are
giving greater and better services to the
consumer than the C producers. Therefore, the C producer must get a lower
price than either of the other two producers. I will deal with that a little
more fully later.
a
It is amongst a section, and only a
section, of the C producers that dissatisfaction exists. In the case of C producers who sell their milk to distributors
there is very little complaint, because in
that case the distributor pays over the
levy to the Ministry and the producer,
who is getting his price, equal and comparable to the price in England, is
perfectly satisfied. Where you get dissatisfaction is amongst C retailers, that is
to say, the milk producer who is selling
his own milk in a cart. The reason for
that is chiefly that the C retailer has to
make the physical payment to the
Ministry, and in consequence he thinks,
and perhaps it is a very natural thought,
that if he could only get out of paying
the levy he would be still better off.
The Committee will remember that in
answer to a question by the hon. Member
for Dock (Mr. Midgley) I emphasised
the fact that in the interests of all, not
only of the consumer but of the producer,
it was essential to pass any reduction in
the levy on to the consumer, because it
Estimates-

is only by reducing the price of milk that
we can increase the consumption. Therefore, those gentlemen who are aiming at
what is really the impossible--that is to
say that they should do without any levy
at all-must realise that if that should
happen and if A, B, and C producers.
refused to pay any levy, while all of them
were getting service, the scheme must
fail. The milk in this country would
deteriorate probably worse than it was
before, and the consumer would be losing
the advantages of a real effort in public
health.
I am aware that a further argument is
put forward by the producer-retailer of
C milk to the effect that the retail price
in the smaller urban and rural areas does
not leave him a sufficient margin. My
answer to that is, firstly, that the farmer
in general has complained that the
margin of price between the producer
and the consumer is too high. I do not
dispute that point. But then how can
another section of the farmers proceed to
argue that the distributive price is not
sufficient, because, in fact, these C producer-retailers are not only getting the
benefit of the price, but are also getting
whatever profit there is in the distribution of the milk. They cannot have it
both ways. Either it is a fact that the
producer was getting too much in the
past, or else the farmer who is distributing or retailing his own milk is
doing very well out of it at the present
moment, and has, therefore, no real
cause for complaint.
There is in this section of producers,
who are also retailers, a desire to benefit
by reducing the levy, which in fact would
not go to them, but would have to go to
the consumer, as I have said before. The
cost of distribution in the country is a
great deal less than it is in the town,
and the price that is fixed is a minimum
price. If they can
get an increased
price-well, they can get it. It depends
on how much competition there is in that
part of the world. But it is quite obvious
that I cannot do what they request,
namely, that I should put up the
minimum price for milk in these towns,
because if I do that I then leave B milk,
which is the better type of milk, at the
same price as C milk, with the result that
every person who is prepared to pay the
price would purchase B milk instead of
C milk. And, of course, they are not
particularly anxious for me to do this.
I am not prepared again to put up the
price of B milk, because those people who
are producing that type of milk are perfectly satisfied, and I think the consumers of it are perfectly satisfied as wel!.
Therefore, the claim that these people
put forward will not really hold water.
They have the remedy in their own
hands. Some, I admit, cannot do so,
but the great majority can do as
those milk producers who were prepared
to take advantage of this scheme did,
and go in for the production of B milk,
and they will then be levied at a much
lower rate, d. in the summer time, and
ld., I think, in the winter.
On the general question of the levy on
C milk I would like to point out that the
levy on all liquid milk in Scotland
during the winter months was 41d. per
gallon compared with 3d. per gallon on
C milk in Northern Ireland, and 1d. per
gallon on B milk. In the summer months
the levy on liquid milk in Scotland is
31d. per gallon compared with 11d. per
gallon in Northern Ireland on C milk,
and d. per gallon on B. I do want to
warn all those people who are threatening, as I am informed they are, not to
pay their levies that they will have to
do So. I cannot possibly allow the
scheme, which I am convinced is going to
be of great benefit to the whole community, to be jeopardised by a small
minority who are really claiming the
impossible. There is proof, and quite
definite proof, that the milk scheme is a
success. Otherwise we would not have
had this large increase in milk not only
for liquid consumption, but also for
manufacturing purposes. One has only
to study the price of milch cows at the
present time. That price has gone up
considerably, and, knowing my agricultural friends in this country as I do, I
do not think they would pay a higher
price for their cows unless they thought
the scheme was going to bring them in a
bigger income.
Now, may I turn for a moment to the
consumption aspect. I have often been
twitted that as Minister of Agriculture I
am merely thinking of the producer's
point of view. That is entirely wrong.
Even if I were so narrow-minded
merely to think of one portion of the community, in the interests of all I must
think of all. If you are not giving
satisfactory service to the consumer the
producer will suffer, and on this Milk

Mr. MIDGLEY: In the first place I
wish to intimate to the Committee that I
beg to move a reduction of £100 in the
Vote in order to draw attention to what
I call the callous and scandalous disregard of the interests of the agricultural
labourers throughout Northern Ireland.
I wanted to deal with various aspects of
this Estimate, but I think this opportunity should not be lost to try to focus
attention upon a problem which has been
singularly neglected in the most inhuman
fashion by one administration after
another in the Department of Agriculture since the Ministry was set up.
I hope the people of Northern Ireland
realise that very soon we will be the only
section of the body politic, speaking of
ourselves as a political entity, which has
not provided some safeguards and some
protection for the agricultural labourer.
I want the agricultural Members who are
arrayed in force here this afternoon to
realise that I am not putting forward
this case repeatedly merely to cause
irritation or in a provocative fashion for
the purpose of creating discussion. I am
putting this forward in the hope that the
Minister of Agriculture will at least
indicate that he is prepared to do one of
two things, either to move in line
with the general development throughout the country for the protection
of agricultural labourers, or, if he
is not able to do that because of the
sinister powers arrayed behind him and
the influences which so far have been at
work at least to set up a committee of
inquiry to report to the House as to the
advisability of setting up a Wages
Board.
In Great Britain there is a Wages
Board, and in the last communication I
read in the public Press regarding agricultural matters I saw it is likely that an
agricultural wages board would be set up
in the Free State. Two weeks ago I read
of a case which was quoted in every section of the Press of a farmer in Great
Britain who was prosecuted for not paying the Wages Board return to his
employee, the minimum being 32s. a
week with a guarantee of overtime after a
certain number of hours per week, and
double-time on certain stated occasions as
prescribed in the Act. The Minister of
Agriculture of Northern Ireland has
certainly enhanced his office since he
entered upon it. I will pay the right hon.
Gentleman the compliment of saying
that he is taking a tremendous interest
in his job, and is working very hard.
indeed to make perfect some things which
were formerly full of imperfections, and
I believe that so far as the farming
industry is concerned he is going to
achieve many things.
I also think, even at the risk of
incurring the unfortunate and ill-advised

this House, that taking the long view,
some of the schemes that he has promoted
will ultimately work out to the common
good. In the meantime, the point I

wish to stress is, that while all this is

I am rather reluctant to strike this note,

start operations in the County Down.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!

is made in favour of any firm in the

members of the firm are good Freemasons, or good Orangemen, or good
members of any other semi-sectarian or
political organisation.

Some 30 or 40 years ago the mainstay
of the linen trade was the making of
shirts, shirt fronts and collars, and so
forth. That trade is entirely gone, and
an entirely different trade has sprung up.
It is a sort of trade which Irish flax is
not suitable for.
I would like to say that I think the
Minister is going now on the right lines,
and I congratulate him on doing so.
What he is trying to do is to improve the
quality of flax. He is trying to produce
such a quality that will take the place of
the best Courtrai and Continental flax.
That is what he is trying to do at
present, and to a large extent he has
been most successful. Unfortunately, as
the Member for Foyle has said, it is
impossible to deny the fact that the Irish
flax crop has decreased considerably in
recent years.
Last year there was a considerable increase, and we all hope there

pedigree seeds they are producing-Liral

crop.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) Since the 31st March, 1929,
the debt of the Unemployment Fund, on
the Suspense and Current Accounts
taken together, has been reduced by
approximately £1,300,000.
to
The Suspense debt has fallen
£2,400,000 and is being diminished at
the rate of £100,000 a year. The Current debt, which is maintained in parity
with the debt of the Great Britain Unemployment Fund, is being liquidated by
annual repayments of principal under the
provisions of the Unemployment Act of
1934, and has now been reduced to
£2,321,604.
The proportion of insured persons
registered as unemployed is 25.3 per cent.
in Northern Ireland and 15.5 per cent.
in Great Britain.

common cause in this particular connection. I think the Minister is aware
of the fact that the principal organised
concerns interested are the National
Union of Railwaymen, the Associated
Society of Locomotive Engineers and
Firemen, the Railway Clerks' Association, and the Transport Workers' Union.
It is the unanimous desire of the
executives of all the organisations that
this point of view should be pressed. I
tried, in the speech I delivered on the
Second Reading, to indicate or outline in
my own way what I considered would be
the official mind in regard to a proposition
such as this. I anticipated to a great
extent what the attitude of the Ministry
might be. I think that at that particular time the mind of the Ministry was
that if they gave way to one section of
the community in regard to representation they would have a similar claim from
other sources. That might be the official
point of view.
I want to point out that on nearly
every public board in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland various vested interests,
or sections of the public interested at
any rate, have received representationif not direct from the bodies to which
they were responsible or to which they
owed any service, at any rate from the
point of view of being representative of
the particular financial interests of certain sections of the community. It is
the feeling, no matter what the Minister
may do in regard to the composition of
this particular Board, that certain business interests are bound to be represented
although the Minister may do his best
to avoid giving in to any section that
demands representation. In these circumstances, therefore, it is felt by the
organised movement, particularly the
sections to which I have referred, that
the best interests of the whole Board and
the best interests of the community at
large would be served if this principle
were accepted.
It would give a feeling of confidence
and assurance to those who believe that
their industrial destinies are involved in
the transfer of these undertakings from
public control to a semi-public Board.
It would also give a feeling of confidence
to every working-class section throughout
the community that the legitimate aspirations and desires of these sections would
not be neglected. We do not feel-and
I feel this personally-that this direct
representation which is sought here
would invalidate any principle in
connection with the scheme projected
by the Minister. We think, on
the other hand, that it would give
assurance that it would be beneficial not only to the projects of the
an

Ministry, but would be beneficial to the

beg to move the Amendment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think, in
fact I am convinced, that this Amendment, if it were accepted, would cut
across the principle on which I have
insisted throughout, namely, that the
Board is not to consist of representatives
of sectional interests. From time to time
I have been pressed to agree that provision should be made for the appointment of representatives of various interests, but to that I cannot agree. This
Board is to be a public trust and there
must be entire freedom to select members
solely with the view to the objects of
that trust being efficiently carried out,
not in the interests of one particular
section, but in the public interest. The
rule which applies to one interest must
apply to all, and I cannot accept an
Amendment which would introduce the
principle of sectional representation. I
think the hon. Member might take cognisance of this fact that it is clear that
a person with experience of the regulations in regard to wages and conditions
of employment would come within the
definition contained in this sub-clause.
Amendment negatived.

Mr. MIDGLEY: I beg to move at the
end of Clause 4 to add the following new

(f) The Board shall be under the control of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and shall be responsible to
the said Ministry for the manner
in which the foregoing duties are
executed.
(g) The Minister of Home Affairs shall
have power to veto or alter any
proposal or policy of the Board.
(h) The Minister of Home Affairs shall
be responsible to the Houses of
Parliament for the operations of
the Board.
I do not apologise for putting forward
this Amendment either, because I think
this will consolidate the position from
the Ministry's point of view. I, of
course, need not attempt to camouflage
in this Committee what exactly I am
after in such amendments. I support
the proposition that the Board shall be a
public board in the fullest and truest
sense of the term. At the present time
I do not call it a public board at all.
The Minister was attacked at various
stages during the Second Reading debate
on the ground that the Bill was
Socialism, collective ownership, and all
the rest of it. I stated then, and I
repeat now, there is not a vestige of
truth in that at all. It is not Socialism.
it does not savour of Socialism, and those
who talk about its being Socialism know
nothing about Socialism. God help their
wit that is all I say, when they come
into contact with some direct Socialistic
proposal.
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid that
is going a long way from this particular
Amendment.
Mr. MIDGLEY: With all due respect
it is not so very far from this particular
Amendment.
The CHAIRMAN: Socialism is a very

one.
Mr. MIDGLEY: It may not be a large

I want the Board to be of a public
character, which it ought to be. I am
compelled to travel for illustrative purposes outside the ambit of the Amendment for a moment by quoting a
precedent in support of the Amendment.
We have other Boards operating in
Northern Ireland at the present time,

They

We want to have public guarantees,

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Amendment also would strike at one of the
principles underlying the whole Bill.
This is to be a public trust carrying on a
essential
trading undertaking in an
public utility service. Subject to the

He quoted the Electricity Board, but I

Mr. NIXON: I notice that the Minister said that the success of the Board will

expense of road transport, and road

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mrs. Parker]
fears which are there, and which, I may
say, are not being in any way allayed at
the present moment, but rather are
being worked up by various parties
throughout the Province.
I am not quite sure whether the
Minister really realises the condition of
affairs in practically the whole of the
Northern district at the present moment.
I am not quite sure whether he realises that
the farmers, especially those living in
districts considerably removed from any
railway, are to a large extent depending,
not upon large carriers but upon small local
men, men who have shops and who have
lorries of their own, and who when their
own business is finished are able to serve
the farmers in a way which the farmer
fears he can never experience under the
new arrangement. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
When a farmer needs a load of sand
from Lough Neagh-it may be late in
the evening-these men go down and
fetch it to his yard. If he needs a load
of manure, if he needs any commodity, if
he needs anything at all connected with
his farm, he need not give long notice.
He merely has to go and ask one of these
men whether it is possible to get it, and
it is done within a few hours, sometimes
within even less than a few hours. The
same thing applies with regard to cattle.
At the local fairs there are always a few
lorries available to take two or three
animals and to assist the farmer in every
possible way. Now he is afraid that in
future his interests will suffer. He cannot visualise a system which can possibly
give him the facilities he has enjoyed as
to hours and frequency. He can go at
the present moment to these small
carriers for everything he needs. When
I say carriers I mean these small shops.
Everything he needs can be obtained in
this way. The Minister realises it is
frankly impossible for the farmer to cart
long distances now, and he has to depend
absolutely on the lorries. The railways
did not give them good facilities in the
past, and the farmers have a terrible
fear of being thrown back on the railways. But quite apart from that they
have enjoyed comforts which they cannot do without and prosper.
I am not quite sure whether I have
touched upon every aspect of the question, but I do wish to impress upon the
Minister that this is a vital matter and
if some asurance is not given this unrest
is going to spread. If, when the time
comes and the Board is set up, and these
facilities that the farmers have enjoyed
in the past are no longer available there
will be intense feeling, not to put it more
strongly, throughout the whole Province.
Let an assurance be given now that
nothing will be done to hinder or lessen
the facilities which the farmers enjoy at
present.

I hope is going to be a business

No statement made here by the Minister

and when the Bill receives the signature
of the Governor it is what is in
Clause only that matters. It may be all
right to take out Hansard in order to
satisfy people what was said in speeches
and in the replies to speeches, but that is
of no use whatever. The only thing that
matters is what is in the Clause, and
assurances of Ministers or any other persons are of no use. It has been decided
by the vote of this House that this Board
is going to be free from Parliamentary
control and free from the control of the
Ministry. There is no other Board in
existence that has such a free hand as
this Board is going to have. A board of
directors is subject to the control of the
shareholders, but this Board set up by
Parliament and subsidised to a certain
extent by Parliament with the peoples'
money, is going to be responsible to no
person.
The speech of the Minister to-day was
rather contradictory when compared with
his speech on the Second Reading. If
the Minister is going to have nothing to
do with the Board he cannot give
assurances, and if he is not going to have
anything to do with it, why did he tell
the House on the Second Reading that
he had already been negotiating with
certain companies for the purchase of
buses. He tells us to-day that the Board
is not going to be subject to any political
or other influences outside its own
operations, and yet he himself, on his
own showing, has already made a bargain
on behalf of the Board before it is
appointed and before this Bill is passed.
When this Board is set up, as it will
be by this subservient House, there will
be no Board like it in the United Kingdom. Every other board of control is
subject to some authority, but this Board
is going to be subject to no authority.
Four or five years ago I would not have
ventured to express an opinion on any
financial matter, because there were such
Transport Bill-
Committee
28 MAY 1935
things as financial super-men, but Hatry,
and Kruger, and Jimmy White, and such
men, have convinced me that most of
these people who pose as financiers have
spurious reputations, and there are some
of them in Northern Ireland. I would
advise the House to be careful what they
do this afternoon in regard to this Board.
Mr. BEATTIE: Reject the Clause.
Mr. NIXON: Reject it or pass it as
you like, but do not whinge about it afterwards. In my opinion the Clause should
be rejected, because this Board is going
to have unlimited powers. There is no

Therefore, the whole Bill should be

the Bill because the whole Bill is bad
and I want it rejected. Just imagine
what is going to happen all over Northern Ireland. If you read this Bill you
will find that it is to be operated in

They are of paramount consideration at
every turn. Why am I taking such an
interest in the operations of this
Transport Board? It is for the reason

own private motor-cars, I am satisfied in

irresponsible Board, is in operation they
will not get the convenient facilities for
travelling that they now enjoy. I am
satisfied that fares will be put up, and
that these cheap excursions will cease to
exist, and I am further satisfied that the
cost of living to these people will also
be increased because they will not have
the same facilities for cheap transport
from the farms. Eventually the consumer has to pay for all these things.

moment that this is the last word on the

transport undertakings to the Board).
(1) The Board shall, within a period
of six months from the day on which
this Act comes into operation or within
such longer period as the Minister of
Home Affairs may allow, acquire every
road motor undertaking operated for
hire or reward in Northern Ireland,
including the passenger and freight
road transport services of any railway
company operating in Northern Ireland, but not including-
(a) The tramway and omnibus undertaking of the Belfast Corporation; or
(b) the passenger and freight road
transport services of the Londonderry and Lough Swilly Railway
Company; or
(c) any road motor undertaking, so
far as the same was carried on
immediately before the passing

CLAUSE 6 (Consideration for transfer
of undertakings).
In the case of any undertaking
transferred to the Board under this
Act, the following provisions shall have.
effect: :-
(a) The Board shall pay or issue to the
owners of the undertaking, as consideration for the transfer, such an
amount as may be agreed upon by
the Board and the owners, or, in
default of such agreement, determined in accordance with the provisions hereafter contained in this
section;
(b) Where the amount of the consideration agreed upon or determined as aforesaid does not exceed
five thousand pounds, that amount
may be paid in cash;
(c) Where the amount of the consideration exceeds five thousand
pounds, the Board shall issue to
the owners transport stock of a
nominal value equal to so much of
the consideration as exceeds five
thousand pounds, unless special
circumstances exist which justify
the whole or any part of the said
excess being paid in cash;

their suggestion is very unfair to the ratepayers of the city of Belfast, because they
say the Corporation can ask for powers to
build buses for themselves. That would
mean they would be compelled to build
in their own factory, and the cost could
be whatever they liked. Surely that is
not a businesslike suggestion for the right
hon. Gentleman to make. I, personally,
do not want the Corporation to set up
any department to build buses, but as we
have a factory in our midst building for
the whole of the Six Counties they ought
to be allowed to go into the market and
compete for the buses the Corporation
require.

about that. There never was, and never

Therefore, the Bill provides for equal

The Committee will have important

scheme and with matters affecting the
pooling scheme, and hon. Members will

having regard to the varying circumstances, elastic provision will be
necessary. For instance, one type of
difference might probably be settled by
reference to the auditor; another class
of difference might be settled appropriately by reference to a technical
arbitrator agreed on between the two
sides; while yet a third type might be
proper to be submitted to the Appeal
Tribunal. Therefore, it is more
appropriate to provide machinery of an

to the varying circumstances that may

reasons the Government cannot accept

Mr. O'NEILL: I beg to move, in
Clause 15, page 21, after the word
"guests" in paragraph (f) to insert the
word "mainly." The Parliamentary Secretary has said that the Government are
very anxious to foster the tourist traffic,
and by this Amendment I hope to test
how anxious they really are. The next
Amendment I have put down is to the
same effect. The object of these Amendments is to secure that hotels which cater
for tourists should have the right to drive
their guests to various places of interest.
At the present time I do not think it is
the intention of the Government to give
hotels this power, and if that is so I do
not see how it can be held that the Government are in favour of tourist traffic.
Hotels have been mainly responsible for
creating and encouraging tourist traffic to
Northern Ireland. What makes the present position all the more ridiculous is that
the Government are prepared to allow
hotel proprietors, who own a bus, to drive
their guests from or to the station, or
from or to an aerodrome, but they are not
at liberty to take tourists to other places.
I am informed that that is the position,
and if it is it is one of the most unfortunate things that could happen to the
tourist traffic. Hotel owners can cater
for this traffic much better than can the
Board, because I cannot believe the Board
will do any canvassing for tourist traffic.
Why the hotel proprietor should not be
permitted to carry his guests anywhere at
any time I do not know, because he is to
be allowed to own a bus to take them from
or to the station. That is a ridiculous
state of affairs, and it is very unfair, and
I honestly believe it will kill the tourist
traffic in Northern Ireland if it is not
altered in the way I suggest. The reason
I have included the word "mainly" in the
Amendment is because in the case of
a hotel owner who has a party
of perhaps forty tourists one bus would
not accommodate them, and he would
have to engage a second bus, and I have
put in the word "mainly" to enable that
hotel proprietor to take other tourists
who were not guests in his own hotel,
but were staying in the town. I
hope the Parliamentary Secretary will
accept this Amendment, because it is only
fair that a hotel proprietor who has gone
to the trouble and expense of canvassing
for tourists and bringing them to his
place should be allowed to carry them in
his own bus to places of interest, instead
of finishing with them when he has
brought them from the station to his
hotel. The Board cannot take them
about as cheaply as he can, nor will the
Board organise parties in the same way,
and I think the Government will be
making a huge mistake if they decline
to accept this Amendment.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 29th May, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
THE TROUBLE IN YORK STREET
AREA.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether any precedent exists for the recent visit by him
to the York Street area, following upon
representations made in the House by a
member of his party relating to attacks
made by the police on certain houses;
whether on this visit he communicated
with persons of that party only;
whether any proceedings, disciplinary, or
other, which may arise out of his investigations will be open to the public or the
Press; and whether he will lay on the
Table of the House the official reports
relative to the disorder in that area
necessitating the recent imposition of
Curfew.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As I have previously stated, I am prepared to receive
and investigate any information which
may be brought to my notice, and this
offer is certainly not confined to any one
party. Should the police investigations
which are at present continuing result in
proceedings, disciplinary or otherwise, I
can
assure my hon. Friend that these
will be carried out strictly in accordance
with the law and the regulations on the
subject.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the negative.
Mr. GRANT: May I ask whether it is
not the duty of the Minister to make
personal inquiry into grave complaints
made against a section of his Department, and whether the best way of discovering the facts and finding out what
really took place is for him to inspect
the damaged dwellings and interview the
persons who were attacked and injured?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I believe in
personal investigation into every complaint which can possibly be of help in
elucidating the facts.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Was part of that
information supplied to the Minister by
the hon. Member for Duncairn?
Mr. GRANT: Is it not a fact that
when there is a visit of any member of
the Royal Family to Northern Ireland
the co-religionists of the hon. and learned
Member attempt to create all the disturbance they can?
Mr. CAMPBELL: It is absolutely
untrue.

AUTHORITIES
POWERS) ACTS.

2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister whether he has seen the
Declaration just issued by the British
National Council for Civil Liberties composed of many Englishmen of eminence,
including ex-Cabinet Ministers, which
states: In Northern Ireland liberty has
almost ceased to exist, that habeas
corpus has been suspended by the Civil
Authorities (Special Powers) Acts, that
the people of England will not tolerate
restrictions upon the liberties of those
who are subjects of the British Parliament, and whether he will give due consideration to
British
this weighty
Declaration.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have not
seen the Declaration referred to, but I
may say that any
such statement as that
quoted by the hon. Member is so far
removed from the actual fact, and indicates such a complete ignorance of
conditions in Northern Ireland, as to
render it unworthy of serious consideration. As the hon. Member is well
aware, the operation of the Civil Authorities Acts in no way interferes with the
liberty of anyone who is prepared to
obey the law, and who does not seek by
unconstitutional means to subvert the
Constitution.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Prime
Minister care nothing for an expression
of enlightened English opinion?

The

distance may be exceeded. The likelihood is that in some of those areas we
are going to have a combination

carrier combined. For a considerable

There are no more persistent people in
demanding what they consider justice,
but what I often interpret as privilege,
than the agricultural representatives in
this House. They have won concession after
concession, and to have heard some of
them speaking this afternoon would have
justified one in imagining that the chief
function of the Northern Parliament was
to meet periodically and consider what
concessions they could give to the agricultural community. That is on the employers side, but not on the workers side.
They have not done anything yet for the
purely working-class section, and I am
going to ask them to do something now
by inviting the agricultural Members to
come into the Division Lobby with us
in favour of this Amendment. The time
is opportune, indeed it was opportune
years ago, for making a reconstruction of
transport in regard to working conditions.
and wages.
This Bill has provided us with an
opportunity that does not often occur in
Northern Ireland, to gather up the
tangled skeins that there are at present in
relation to transport, especially in the
agricultural area, where men like the
agricultural labourers are scandalously
paid. It was the way in which transport conditions were carried out in agricultural districts that was responsible for
the chaos that has occurred. This is an
opportunity to regularise the whole conditions of employment in regard to transport, so that when the Board begins its
operations here we will be able to see
that the activities of this branch and of
that branch, whether in town or country,
are covered by some phase of this Bill
which will then be an Act.
This is not a new idea in regard to
wages and conditions in this area. In
the Road Traffic Act (Great Britain),
1930, there is the following Clause:
The wages paid by the holder of any
road service licence to persons
employed by him in connection with

Clause 15 provides that:
"A person other than the Board

public highway for the conveyance of

reward, except with the consent in

of the Ministry of Home Affairs."
Then we come down to the exceptions,
which are to be found in sub-Clause (4)
(e) (i), which enables the owner of a
lorry to continue to carry his own goods.

formally move them and say what I want
to say. I want to tell all the die-hards

proposed yesterday in regard to the
public' ownership of these services, that
it was only out of respect for the time of
the House that I did not present my
claims at much greater length yesterday.
I want to assure the House and
Press of Belfast, which seems to have
felt that the public services of Northern
Ireland were in danger
danger of being
nationalised, that there is no justification
for that fear. I wish to assure every
such section of the community that a
magnificent case can be made out for
making this a public service, and these
Amendments which I formally move in
order to get speaking were designed to
secure the financial side being public.
The Amendments which I moved yesterday were designed to get public control
by Parliament by leaving the service
open to criticism by public. representatives in the House of Commons.
I repeat now that I am not going to
press these Amendments in view of the
decision of yesterday. I wish to state

case could have been made for the acceptance of the principle of social ownership
and control, which my Amendments

benefit of the community. The airy way

yesterday that a full conception of what
public ownership is was not likely to
receive the consideration in this House
which it was justified in receiving. I
think also on financial grounds alone the
provisions embodied in my Amendments
are better than those in the Bill, because
for time and for eternity, so far as I can

an assurance that when these obligations
have been liquidated, which are going to
be incurred by the Board, the system of
private bond holding will be perpetuated

It seems to me that for time and
eternity, in so far as one is justified in
using that expression, the people of
Northern Ireland are going to be saddled
with a burden which is a heavier contribution than they should be asked to bear
in respect of those who are going to hold
the stock of an undertaking which ought
to be publicly owned. During the past
two or three years everything that has
been done in Northern Ireland in regard
to traffic has increasingly focussed the
eyes of the people on a co-ordinated conception of the whole service, and this Bill
is intended, in a semi-public way, to bring
some sort of order out of chaos. I want
to assure Members of the House, who
think that there is no case for financial
and public ownership, if they wish to dispute that at greater length I will be glad
to provide them with an opportunity. I
feel I was justified at the moment in outlining to the House very briefly, very
imperfectly and very inadequately, the
point of view which was expressed in
these Amendments, which, I do not
think, received the consideration yesterday they deserved from the general
public point of view.
It seems to me that we have reached
that mental condition in Northern
Ireland when to use the word "socialism"
or the term "socialisation" is tantamount
to waving some kind of coloured flag in
front of an infuriated animal, and the
result of which is only to infuriate that
animal still further. There seems to be
no conception at all on the part of the
masses of the people. I notice every time
the element of Socialism enters into the
consideration of any question in this
House that is going to result in benefit to
some section of the community, certain
sections of the House are ready to rally
to the defence of the case put forward,
but let them realise that it is inherently
part of the Socialist conception of society
-the minute you use the term
Socialism," which means social ownership, it brings to their minds bogus fear,
gross irregularities, and grotesque caricatures, which scare them into the opposite
camp. I have said sufficient to justify
my point of view and to say,
intellectually constituted, neither this
House nor the mass of the public is
capable of any conception of social ownership.

this is so and while, therefore, the interest
should be quite secure, we can hardly be

assets.
I know that statements have been made
that the stocks are in some way guaranteed, and that the income thereon is
guaranteed. That, of course, is entirely
wrong. The interest on these stocks is
dependent on the earnings of the undertaking and there is no guarantee behind
it. Four per cent. is a moderate and
proper rate of interest in the circumstances.
The effect of the next two Amendments would simply be to inflate the
amount of capital required to pay compensation. It is a much sounder method
of finance to issue capital at a rate which
may be reasonably expected to keep the
price of the stock at or about par, rather
than to issue at a rate that must put it
to a discount.

(1) The Board may, with the

or mind or old age upon their resigning or otherwise ceasing to hold office
or to serve. The scheme shall also

be authorised by sub-section (2) of this
section.
(2) A superannuation scheme under
this section may contain special provisions for including previous pensionable service in the service which may
be reckoned for the purpose of a
superannuation allowance or gratuity
under the scheme, and for applying
sections two and three of
Superannuation Act, 1909 (as amended
by the Superannuation Act, 1914) in

enactments were applicable before their

Board.
the
In this section the expression "previous pensionable service" means service rendered (previously to his service
under or on the Board) by a person
who, immediately before he became an
officer, servant or member of the
Board, was-
(i) employed upon conditions enabling
a superannuation allowance to be
granted in respect of his service
under former undertakers whose
undertaking has been transferred
to the Board under Part II of
this Act; or
(ii) serving in an established capacity
in the Civil Service of Northern
Ireland.
(3) Employment under or on the
Board shall be approved employment
for the purposes of section four of the
Superannuation Act, 1914; and where,
in pursuance of that section, a superannuation allowance, additional allowance or gratuity is granted by the
Ministry of Finance in respect of previous pensionable service, any superannuation allowance, additional allowance or gratuity which may be granted
in pursuance of a scheme under this
section shall be abated to the extent of
the amount granted by the Ministry of
Finance as aforesaid.
(4) Notwithstanding anything in
this section, where any person becoming an officer, servant or member of
the Board was, immediately before he
became such officer servant or member,
a member of any railway superannuation fund or railway pension fund, that
person may continue to be a member
of such fund if he so desires and if the

fund. is managed agrees, and in that
case the Board shall have power to
make contributions to the fund, in respect of that person, equivalent to the
contributions which would have been
made thereto if that person had continued to be a member of the fund
otherwise than by virtue of this subsection.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to

(1), and insert instead, "shall within a

This Amendment relates to the Clause
dealing with superannuation. Under
the Bill, as it stands at present, the
Board is enabled, but not compelled, to
establish a superannuation scheme for its
employees. Having regard to the
character of the service, I think it is
reasonable that there should be an obligation on the Board to establish a scheme
within a reasonable time. This is provided for by the Amendment.

Mr. MIDGLEY: I beg to move, in

"(1) The Board shall, with all

prepare and submit to the Ministry of

number of persons appointed by the

may be approved or modified by the

Under the present proposal it is only
suggested that those whose health is
broken up by infirmity or old age should
be covered, whereas superannuation, as
generally envisaged, should embrace every
section of the work people in the whole
service and make provision for superannuation at a definite retiring age. The
experience of the past with regard to
superannuation schemes, especially in
Great Britain, leads us to the belief that
it would be a good proposition to offer the
co-operation and assistance of the trade
unions in the drawing up of such a
scheme. I am given to understand, with
regard to the superannuation schemes of
the British railways, especially the
L.M.S., and Southern Railway lines, that
the machinery is along the lines suggested
in this Amendment.

(1) The wages paid by the Board to

persons, shall not be less favourable to

payable and the conditions which

of any resolution (passed by the House

or the House of Commons of Northern
Ireland) for the time being in force
and applicable to contracts with
departments of the Government of
Northern Ireland.

of employment or other conditions of
employment in the case of persons

(a) The matter in dispute shall in the

unions of which the employed persons concerning whom the question
arises are members (in this section
referred to as "the trade unions
concerned') for settlement by
direct negotiation between the
Board and the trade unions concerned;

concerned are unable to reach an

to a negotiating committee consisting of equal numbers of
representatives of the Board and
representatives of the trade unions
concerned ;
(c) If the said committee is unable to
reach agreement as to the matter
in dispute, that matter shall be
referred to a tribunal consisting of
three members, namely:-

I have been asked by the executive of

The unions have the feeling that this

Furthermore, I understand from the

take it that the wages that will be paid

The only point I have to advance in

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid the
hon. Member misunderstands the effect of
this. The machinery that will be set up
is, first of all, negotiating machinery consisting of representatives of the Board
and representatives of the men. If they
