CLAUSE 34 (Compensation to persons employed in transferred undertakings).
(1) Where an undertaking or part
of an undertaking is transferred to the
Board under this Act, compensation
shall be payable by the Board to any
person who, immediately before the day
of transfer of the undertaking or part
of an undertaking, was employed by
the former undertakers as a whole-time
Transport Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
officer or servant in connection with the
road transport service of the undertaking, and-
(a) was so employed continuously
for a period of three years ending on
the day preceding the day of transfer,
and
*
*
*
(2) The compensation payable to a
person under this section shall be as
follows:
(a) in the case of a person who is
not offered employment by or on the
Board, or is dismissed for any cause
other than misconduct or incapacity,
being a person who had been at least
ten years in such employment of the
former undertakers as is specified in
sub-section (1) of this section, an
annual allowance calculated on the
basis of one-sixtieth of the amount
of that person's annual remuneration
for every completed year before the
day of transfer during which he was
continuously employed in such employment as aforesaid;
(b) in the case of a person who
is not offered employment by or on
the Board, or is dismissed for any
cause other than misconduct or
incapacity, being a person who had
been for less than ten years in such
employment of the former undertakers as is specified in sub-section
(1) of this section, a gratuity calculated on the basis of one-twelfth of
the amount of that person's annual
remuneration for every completed
year before the day of transfer
during which he was continuously
employed in such employment as
aforesaid;
(c) in the case of a person undergoing a reduction in his annual remuneration for any cause other than
misconduct, incapacity, or retirement
on pension from employment by or
on the Board, such lump sum as will
reasonably compensate that person
for the said reduction.
(3) The annual remuneration of any
person shall, for the purposes of this
section, be taken to be the total remuneration and emoluments paid to
him during the calendar year next
preceding the day of transfer.
(4) If any question arises as to the
right of any person to compensation
under this section that question shall
be referred to and determined by the
Transport Appeal Tribunal established
by Part VI of this Act.
Where a question is referred to the
said tribunal under this sub-section in
relation to any person, the tribunal
shall consider any representations which
may be made to it by a trade union
of which such person is a member.

This whole Clause should give great
satisfaction to everyone. lt not only
recognises the rights of those who have
been engaged in the transport business,
but goes far beyond any recognition of
legal rights, and recognises certain moral
rights which the employees will have if
they are not taken over by the Board. As
the Clause stands at present employees
who are not taken over by the new Board
and who have been in the transport service for three years will have those moral
rights recognised and will be compensated
to some extent. That is a very generous
gesture, but at the same time it does
not seem to me to go far enough. Recognition of rights might be extended
even beyond the three years. The
rights and honourable expectations of
those who have been engaged in the
transport business for less than three
years might be recognised. I suggest
that any person who has been in the
transport business, and whose position
has been confirmed by his ability to retain his post for three months prior to
the date of the printing of this Bill,
should have his rights recognised He is
Transport Bill-

being thrown out of employment at a
time when the labour market is overstocked, and I do not think the burden
thrown upon the Board by this Amendment would be very serious. I should
say that the new Board will take over the
great majority of the employees who are
at present in the transport business,
and we hope that the activities
of the Board will be SO extended
that they will be able to retain these
employees. If it is said that three
months is too short I would point out
that it is three months prior to the 18th
April, and by the time of the transfer
these people will have been in employment in the transport service for upwards.
of a year.
I do not suggest that I would

man who is employed in the transport
service for, say, two years, and who is
then thrown out of employment, is suffering a great hardship.

are employed for two, three and four

PIG INDUSTRY COUNCIL.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
total number of meetings held of the Pig
Industry Council, the annual salary payable to the Chairman, the allowances to
other members, and from what fund
these emoluments are payable.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, to reply to this
question.
Four meetings of the Pig Industry
Council, and two meetings of a subcommittee of the Council have been held.
Members of the Council, other than the
chairman, are entitled to an allowance of
two and a half guineas a day in respect
of attendance at meetings of the Council.
No remuneration has yet been fixed for
the chairman of the Council. All expenses of the Council are paid out of
the Pig Industry Fund in accordance
with the provisions of Section 14 of the
Agricultural Marketing (Pig Industry)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1934.

Mr. ANDREWS: I understand that
my right hon. Friend, the Chief Whip,
in his jocular way, gave an undertaking
yesterday that I would speak for at least
sixty minutes. Well, that is an ordeal
that I have seldom asked hon. Members
to endure, but I hope, under the circumstances, I will have the forgiveness of
hon. Members on both sides of the House
if I endeavour to fulfil the undertaking
which the Chief Whip gave.
This is the one occasion in the year
that I have an opportunity of telling
hon. Members of the policy which directs
the efforts of the Ministry of Labour;
the reason for the adoption of that policy
and for the Government's adherence to
it. It is also my duty to-day to justify
the large expenditure of the Department,
which, when account is taken of the income derived from the contributions of
employers and employees under the three
insurance schemes and of sums derived
from certain miscellaneous sources, as
well as from Exchequer grants, will
amount, I estimate, this year to no less
than £6,480,242. I also desire to refer
to the many activities of the Department which are far more widespread than
is probably generally known.
Our policy is to ensure that our industrial classes here are treated similarly
to those in the rest of the United Kingdom. No other course could, in the
opinion of my colleagues and myself, be
justified as regards the individual, and
also because our Parliament is so closely
linked up financially and in other ways
with the Mother of Parliaments across
the Channel.
The most serious problem that we have
had to struggle with during the last 14
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
30 MAY 1935
years has been that of unemployment.
It is encouraging to know that the
pósition has considerably improved.
When the Government came into
existence here, the number registered as
unemployed was just over 100,000, while
the number registered to-day is under
70,000. The improvement in the position
is greater than these figures indicate,
because the field of insurance has been
extended, and for various reasons registration, as hon. Members know, is much
more complete. I remember that some years
ago unemployment was looked upon by
many as a local problem which could be
cured by local effort; if that had been
so, my colleagues and I would have solved
the problem long ago. It is now, however, recognised to be a world problem,
which is mainly caused by world conditions and which probably can only be
completely solved by world effort.
ex-
It is true that our home trade has
been considerably improved by the
various fiscal measures taken by the Imperial Parliament, which have to a considerable extent prevented dumping.
Our foreign trade, however, still remains
seriously affected by industrial conditions
in other countries, and by tariffs, quotas,
currency restrictions, fluctuating
changes, insecurity and the development
of an ever-increasing degree of economic
and commercial nationalism the world
over. Another factor which is all too
apparent is the replacement of human
power by machinery, and by scientific
methods of production. Again, we here
in Northern Ireland have been seriously
affected by the fact that emigration to
our Dominions and the United States has
not only stopped, but many who migrated
in years gone by are returning home,
generally owing to depression and the
high cost of living in those countries.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Is that peaceful
penetration?
Mr. ANDREWS: I will deal with that
matter later on if the hon. and learned
Member desires me to do so. As our
population in Northern Ireland must be
increasing by at least 8,000 per annum,
due to the fact that this is the difference
between the birth rate and the death
rate, it will be clear to hon. Members
that this is another important factor
which has got to be reckoned with.
I think I have said sufficient to show
to what a large extent unemployment is
a world problem, and that, while there
is an ever increasing supply of labour,
the consuming power of the inhabitants
of the world appears to be unequal to the
world's power to produce. While we in
the United Kingdom cannot obviously
afford, from a competitive point of view
to go in advance of other countries, I
cannot help but feel that the nations
may, sooner or later, require to give
serious consideration to the subject
of working hours and the possibility
of bringing closer together the ages
when persons normally enter industry
and leave it.
to
It appears
also that an Imperial effort should be
made to develop gradually those sparsely
inhabited parts of our Empire which are
awaiting development to-day.
me
In the meantime, this Government can
only deal with the matter on a local
basis, for obvious reasons, and I feel that
I am justified in claiming that no other
Government has consistently done
much to encourage industry and provide
employment during the last fourteen
years as this Government has done.
Mr. NIXON: Question.
Mr. ANDREWS: The work of the Ministry of Labour can be conveniently considered under four main headings. First,
there are its duties in connection with
employment; secondly, its services to
assist the unemployed; thirdly, its responsibilities under the National Health
Insurance scheme; and lastly, its
administration of the Contributory and
Non-Contributory Pensions Acts.
I will deal with employment services
first. Hon. Members will be glad to
know that the last five months have
shown continuous improvement in the
employment position. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Comparing them with the
corresponding months of 1933 and 1934,
we find that the volume of employment
has been on a steadily rising level, the
average number of persons in employment, between the ages of 16 and 65 in
the industries insured under the Unemployment Insurance scheme for the
first five months of this year being just
under 187,000, as compared with a figure
of about 186,000 for 1934, and 176,000
for 1933.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. Andrews]
I think that the monthly returns that
are published of registrations at the
employment exchanges are commonly
misunderstood by many members of the
public, who appear to imagine that they
represent a solid block of people undergoing the misfortune of prolonged unemployment, and in danger of becoming unemployable. Such, of course, is not a
true conclusion at all. On the day in
each month, on which the count is made
of registrations, many persons are simply
standing by between the completion of
one spell of work and the beginning of
another-a normal incident in industry.
Others are temporarily on short time, and
in the case of those whose normal working week is less than a six-day one, many
are on their off day on the day of the
count.
I am glad to know that most of the
insured population present no unemployment problem at all. They are in
regular work, year in, year out, and
have no occasion to rely on their insurance benefit. The proportion of the
population which made a claim at some
time or another in the course of 1934 was
not much more than one-third, and for
the great majority of these the problem
is not so much one of prolonged unemployment as of irregular employmentnot one of having no prospect whatever
of a job to go to, but of following an
occupation, which, for a greater or less
period during the year gives intermittent
work.
This problem can only be satisfactorily
dealt with by a general improvement in
trade, not only in this country, but
throughout the world. This brings us
into that domain which I have already
indicated, and we in Northern Ireland
are fortunate indeed to have our interests
in international affairs entrusted to the
safe keeping of the Government of the
United Kingdom.
During the last twelve months over
26,000 placings in employment were
made through the employment exchanges.
The local employment committees still
continue to be of great service in maintaining touch between the Department
and the public in all matters relating to
the employment position in their respective districts. We are indebted to
these committees also for the part which
they continue to take in the administration of the King's National Roll scheme
for disabled ex-Service men, and to the
local authorities as well for their cooperation in the promotion of schemes of
public utility to give employment in
their areas. I hope they will continue to
do what is possible in this direction.
The schemes in operation at present
number 37, of which 22 are in Belfast
and 15 in the country. In addition, 25
schemes have been sanctioned, but not
yet commenced, of which the total
estimated cost is over £100,000. The
work that is being done consists mainly
of harbour and dock improvements, water
supply and sewerage schemes and hospital
extensions.
As regards those who are in work, the
Ministry is responsible for ensuring
healthy and safe conditions of employment in the 7,000 factories and workshops of Northern Ireland through its
administration of the Factory and Workshop Acts, and its supervision of the
Workmen's Compensation Code. Bv
regular contacts with employers the
Ministry ensures that the standards
which Parliament has laid down, and
which employers generally recognise are
necessary, in the interests of the workers
and of efficient production, are observed
throughout the industries of Northern
Ireland. Considerable improvements
have been effected both as regards safety
and ventilation. It is particularly
gratifying that many employers are not
content merely with observing the
minimum standards laid down by the
Acts, but are anxious to go in advance
of the standards prescribed by Parliament in order to ensure that their
workers are employed under the best conditions practicable.
There are two points in this connection,
however, that I wish to emphasise.
First, although trade is not what we
should like it to be, there is still a good
deal of overtime being worked. I fully
realise that employers usually only resort
to overtime in cases of emergency, but
I appeal to them to use every effort to
spread their work among as many workers
as possible, and the Department will be
glad to facilitate them in this direction
by authorising the working of two shifts
in preference to overtime.
The second matter to which I would
again call attention is the number of
industrial accidents. The number of
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
30 MAY 1935
casualties on the road is arousing public
opinion, and rightly so. But do we
realise that if we exclude fatal accidents,
almost as many are injured in our
factories, the number in 1934 being over
1,800? It is true, I am glad to say, that
many of these factory accidents
slight, but even so they are misfortunes
for the victims and costly to their employers. Safety devices, guards for
dangerous machinery and improved
are
machine designs are constantly being
investigated and provided with the object
of reducing accidents, and much has been
done in this direction. The personal
factor, however, will remain the dominant
one, and I would like to take this opportunity of emphasising to all concernedemployers, managers, foremen and
workers the importance of anticipating
and then of making adequate provision
against the day to day risks of factory
life.
The preservation of helpful and happy
relations between employers and workers
in the adjustment of wage problems is
another service performed by the Ministry in connection with employment.
During the year 54 trade disputes were
reported to the Department, of which
many were settled without dislocation of
work. The only serious dispute was the
one affecting brickyard workers in
Belfast. There were twelve variations in
the rates of wages of groups of workpeople that came into effect last year,
the chief changes being the increases to
workpeople engaged in the spinning and
weaving branches of the linen trade,
brickmakers, dockers, municipal employees and those engaged in the tobacco
manufacturing industry.
I feel I am entitled to take advantage
of this opportunity to pay a tribute to
both the employers and employees in
Northern Ireland for their very evident
desire to accommodate each other with
the object of preventing industrial strife,
which obviously settles nothing and
injures both.
I now come to the Department's
services for the unemployed. The most
important changes in connection with the
Unemployment Insurance scheme during
the year were those made by the Unemployment Act of last session. Part 1 of
that Act made certain far-reaching
changes in the Insurance Scheme, and
Part 11 of the Act brought into being
the new
scheme.
Unemployment
Assistance
Dealing briefly first with the insurance scheme, the amendments have
all been in operation for many months
and few persons now could be found to
The
express disapproval of the scheme.
restoration of the cuts in the rates of
unemployment benefit was made as from
the 1st July, and from the same date also
came into operation the provisions under
which persons having good employment.
records in the past are entitled to qualify
for additional days of benefit, which
would give them a possible maximum of
12 months' insurance benefit. It is
interesting to note that as a result of
this concession the proportion of persons
signing the unemployed register who are
in receipt of insurance benefit has
increased considerably. In addition, the
age of entry into insurance was lowered
as from the 3rd September from 16 years
to the school leaving age, and, as a consequence, between the 3rd September and
31st March over 20,000 insurance books
were issued to juveniles in employment
under 16. I am glad to say that
dependants' benefit is being paid to less
than 140 unemployed juveniles between
the ages of 14 and 16, and that employment in this group is undoubtedly satisfactory.
The first portion of the Unemployment
Assistance scheme came into operation on
the 7th January, and it embraces about
260,000 of the working population.
When the scheme comes fully into operation on the second appointed day-I am
not in a position to say when that will
be beyond stating that it will be on the
same date as in Great Britain-about
another 100,000 of the working population will be brought within the scope of
Unemployment Assistance. From that
date the scheme will therefore apply,
broadly speaking, to all persons who
ordinarily obtain a livelihood by working
for an employer, irrespective of the
amount of their remuneration if they are
manual workers, and up to a limit of
£250 per annum if they are non-manual.
The principles for assessing the needs.
of applicants and their resources are laid
down in regulations as provided by the
Act. In the application of these regulations certain difficulties emerged. In 70
per cent. of the cases the application of
the regulations resulted in the assessment
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
of allowances at amounts equal to or
exceeding the old transitional payments
basis, but in the remainder of the cases
the allowances fell below the scale of the
former transitional payment scheme. In
view of this it was decided that the
regulations both here and in Great
Britain required to be reviewed, and
pending the completion of this review the
Temporary Provisions Act was passed
this year to give applicants for assistance
the right to have their needs assessed on
the basis formerly adopted by the Public
Assistance Committees for transitional
payments as well as under the Regulations, and to be paid at whichever is the
more favourable rate. This, I think it
will be agreed, is a generous temporary
arrangement to rectify an admittedly.
unexpected difficulty.
The classes for unemployed juveniles
are continuing to give entire satisfaction.
In Belfast this instruction is given at the
Juvenile Instructional Centre in Alfred
Street, which has proved to be such a
remarkable success, and to which there
has been a total of 14,800 admitted since
it was opened; the present daily average
attendance is 521, made up of 295 boys
and 226 girls. In other places with the
co-operation of the local education
authorities, technical school classes and
elementary continuation classes are being
provided as a condition for the receipt of
benefit where facilities for holding the
classes are available. Last year there
were 19 class centres outside Belfast and
91 classes attended by almost 2,000 boys
and girls.
The last matter to which I would like
to refer in connection with our Employment Services is the successful establishment of certain welfare schemes for the
unemployed in some of our country
towns as a result of the interest in this
movement shown by our Local Employment Committees and the public-spirited
support of the inhabitants of the
localities. I would like to mention, in
particular, the splendid work in this
connection which is being done at
Carrickfergus, Lurgan, Portadown and
Newtownards; and I hope very much
that this excellent movement will extend
to many other towns.
The National Health Insurance Scheme
continues to work smoothly with every
evidence of satisfaction. The 370,000
persons within its scope are members of
some 74 approved societies, of which 19
have their headquarters in Northern Ireland, and 55 elsewhere in the United
Kingdom. The majority of the members
are in mutual insurance with their fellow
workers in the rest of the United Kingdom, and the Northern Ireland societies
linked financially to the United
Kingdom scheme through the Central
Fund, which is administered by the
statutory Joint Committee, composed of
representatives of the Ministry of Health
in England and Wales, the Scottish
Department of Health and my own
Department.
are
The medical service, which is now provided for almost one-third of the population of Northern Ireland, is one of the
most important features of National
Health Insurance. Nearly 500 doctors and
433 chemists are co-operating with the
Department in providing medical treatment and medicines. It is particularly
gratifying that there has been a complete
absence of friction in the provision of this
service. I would like to thank the members of the medical profession for the
invaluable assistance they have given to
the Department in this matter. I am
very pleased that the post-graduate
course for insurance practitioners that
was arranged in 1933 with the assistance
of Queen's University was followed up by
another course in 1934, attended by 45
doctors. It is hoped that it will
possible this year to arrange for another
course, which for obvious reasons is very
desirable.
be
I am convinced that the medical benefit
service is becoming one of the most
important factors in promoting the
general health, for it makes skilled attention available at the on-set of illness; and
by providing untrammelled access to
medical advice and treatment it is
securing for our people an opportunity of
being instructed in the principles of
healthy living.
The improved state of the health of
the insured population is reflected in the
reduced expenditure on sickness benefit.
I am glad to say that the usefulness has
been amply proved of the co-operative
scheme for visiting members who are on
sickness benefit, which the
which the approved
societies set up in September, 1933, for
the country areas outside Belfast, on the

of which my hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Gordon) was

An important reform in the administration of dental benefit came into operation in June 1934, when a Dental
Benefit Council was established, consisting of a chairman appointed by myself
and six persons on each side to represent
the dental profession and the approved

treatment, and a part-time dental referee

I now wish to refer briefly to our pensions administration. The number of
pensions of all kinds in payment has
increased during the year by over 1,700
to a total of 84,151, and in addition
allowances are being paid
being paid to almost.
10,000 children. Those who enjoy the
benefits of these schemes are of all ages;
they include five centenarians, one man
and four women, two having been
born in the year 1830, when King
George IV. was on the Throne. The
rumber of separate payments made to
this big family in the course of the year
is between four and a quarter and four
and a half million pounds.
Fresh claims to pensions that had to
be investigated and decided last year
were not far short of 11,000, the
majority having been made under the
contributory scheme; in addition almost
1,000 current pensions under the noncontributory scheme were reviewed. The
volume of work that this entails can be
readily appreciated. The total amount
paid out in pensions under the two
schemes in the year ended March of this
year, exclusive of all administrative cost
was approximately £2,226,000.
The benefit of these pension schemes
to the individual pensioners is easy to
realise, because within the personal
knowledge of us all are many homes
where the granting of a pension has
kept penury from the door and misery
from the minds of those within. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) There are still
a few old-fashioned people, however, who
appear to imagine that our social services
are, to a considerable extent, a waste
of public money. I believe them to be
absolutely necessary, both from the
human and the public points of view.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Their
importance in this latter respect, I feel,
is not so widely appreciated as it deserves
to be. These schemes ensure the distribution of a most valuable amount of
purchasing power among large numbers.
of persons who, from their circumvery
stances, must put this power into
immediate use in the purchase of
essential commodities, and thereby
stimulate demand and production from
which our entire community benefits.
This fact undoubtedly has helped largely
to modify in the United Kingdom the
effects of the crises in the world's trade
and commerce, and to gain for us our
relatively greater economic stability.
I now wish to give a brief analysis of
the financial position as I see it. It is
of interest to recall in this year of His
Majesty's Silver Jubilee that the three
great social insurance schemes, and the
national unemployment assistance scheme
which was inaugurated by the Act of last
year, have all come into existence within
the span of His Majesty's reign. I desire
to bring to the notice of hon. Members,
in a few figures, a picture of the
estimated receipts and payments for the
current financial year under these four
schemes and also the non-contributory
old age pensions scheme.
Taking the receipts side first, the total
estimated receipts for the year are
£6,378,000, of which £1,741,000 will be
derived from the contributions of employers and workers; £264,000 will
come from miscellaneous sources; and
£4,372,000 from the Exchequer.
This
last figure, I should explain, is a gross
one, and will be abated by a substantial
contribution from the United Kingdom
Exchequer under the re-insurance
arrangement. On the current estimates
of unemployment in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland, the existing reinsurance agreement would produce a
contribution from the United Kingdom
Exchequer of an amount ranging from
£250,000 to £300,000. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, explained in his Budget Statement that
negotiations are now proceeding for a
revision of the existing agreement, which
will supplement its yield and increase the
expected contribution this year to the
sum of £643,000, which my right hon.
Friend said that he anticipated on the

basis of the present estimates in both

The revision of the agreement will also,
of course, produce an increased yield in
future years, as compared with the existing agreement, of amounts which will be
regulated by the unemployment position
here and in Great Britain. It is, in my
opinion, altogether wrong to look upon
these re-insurance contributions as subsidies in the sense that has been applied
to them by some hon. Members. It is
obvious that unemployment finance is
really a United Kingdom liability, and,
subject to reasonable security being given.
as regards equality of administration
throughout the Kingdom, adjustments of
costs between the two Exchequers accord
with our position as a unit of the United
Kingdom. Seven-eighths of our taxation.
is imposed at Westminster, and the
promised revision of the agreement, for
which, on behalf of the Government, I
thank Mr. Chamberlain to-day, is the
expression of his evident desire to assist
in the matter along lines of justice. I
wish to remind hon. Members on this
subject of certain principles which the
late Lord Balfour enunciated, and they
are as true to-day as when he uttered
them. He said:-
:-
"I think that the true position of
the United Kingdom is that it should
be treated as a whole, and that we
should not look too minutely to see
whether this or that part gives as much
to the general Exchequer as it gets out
directly or indirectly."
And Lord Balfour added:-
"That is the Unionist view of
finance."

Lieutenant-Colonel MITCHELL (who
was received with general cheers): I do
hope that the right hon. Gentleman will
not be under any misapprehension that
I crossed the Floor of the House in the
ordinary sense of that term when I
went to sit on the opposite benches for a
time this afternoon. I did so because it
gave me an opportunity of seeing the right
hon. Gentleman's face and the expression
on his countenance while he was delivering his very interesting and lucid statement, and because my position on this
side of the Committee makes it extremely
difficult for me to hear the Minister's
words and also makes it impossible for
me to see his face.
The first thing that strikes a new Member on entering this House is the extraordinary monopoly that appears to be
possessed by certain Members on the
Opposition side of all sense of sympathy
with those who are in distress or suffering
from unemployment. I venture to state.
that I know something of the conditions
of these people, that I have a good idea
of the suffering and distress of the unfortunate people who are unemployed,
and of those whom I may call the under
dogs. My life has been spent amongst
them, and no one has any higher opinion
than I of the remarkable bravery and
courage they display under extraordinary
difficulties in times of serious distress,
sickness, or sorrow. But I did feel
amazed at the accusation against men on
this side of the House that they had no
feeling for people of that kind.
It occurred to me that no one on this
side of the House would envy the Minister of Labour the extraordinary difficulty
he had in dealing with this greatest of
all problems that Governments had to
face in this world-the problem of unemployment and all the sequelæ that follow.
The fascinating and picturesque brain of
the Member for Dock, the passionate
eloquence of the Member for Shankill,
and the oratory of the Member for
Pottinger, cannot alter stern, hard facts,
and the difficulty is you cannot give away
money that you have not got. As far
as I know it is not in the power of the
Minister of Labour or the Minister of
Finance to coin money and hand it out.
I do not wish to deal with subjects with
which I am not personally in touch, and,
therefore, I propose to deal only with two
points in connection with the extraordinarily interesting speech of the
Minister of Labour. And might I say I
would like to congratulate him and his
Department on the great immunity
Northern Ireland has enjoyed from
serious difficulty or labour troubles
during his administration of the office.
I do know that there is a strong feeling
amongst the working classes all over the
country that he is their real friend, that
they are really a large family of his, and
that he has a very much bigger heart
than the hon. Member for Woodvale
appears to think. They know that he
regards them as a great family of his
own and that his one earnest desire is
to see their social position elevated and
these men helped in every way conceivable.
One of the greatest problems of unemployment is the question of the boy
leaving school and having no work. I do
not imagine that anything is more calculated to undermine his sense of independence and his use to the community
later in life than the fact that at that
early impressionable age he gets the idea
that money can be obtained without work
and for nothing. Let him start two or
three years with that impression and it
is very easy for it to become fixed in his
mind. He is at the age when character
is formed and on it his whole after life
depends. I am very glad, therefore,
that it is proposed to deal with that. It

Sir ROBERT LYNN: The Member for
Duncairn (Mr. Grant) referred to the
fact that he has listened to all speeches
which the Minister of Labour has made
in introducing his Estimates in this
Parliament. I have missed very few of
them. The debate to-day shows that as
near perfection as it is possible for a
Government Department to be is that run
by my right hon. Friend. In one of the
first speeches, if not the very first, that
I made in regard to the Ministry of
Labour I pointed out to the right hon.
Gentleman that his duty was to make the
crooked ways straight and the rough
places smooth for the unemployed and for
those who came under his Department.
Looking back over those fourteen years
I can say truthfully that he has done
that. He has done his duty faithfully
and well for the people. Indeed, all the
speeches we have listened to to-day have
been of a congratulatory kind, because,
although here and there individual points
have been raised, on the whole Members
on both sides of the Committee have had
nothing to say regarding the administration of the right hon. Gentleman's
Department except that it has been done
very well. The hon. Member (Mr.
O'Neill) who has just sat down was complaining that there was nothing but.
sympathy and kind words given to them.
The best answer to the complaint of the
hon. Member for Mourne is the figures
that have been given by my right hon.
Friend. Those figures have grown
enormously in the fourteen years, and I
think, on the whole, the money has been
well spent. It is something on which we
may congratulate ourselves that our unemployed, our old-age pensioners, and all
the other people who come under the
Ministry of Labour are getting the same
treatment and the same amount
benefits as are accorded by the wealthier
country, Great Britain. Hon. Members,
instead of sneering at the Government for
being able to get our share out of Great
Britain, ought to congratulate them.
They should encourage them rather than
blame them. I have listened very carefully to practically every speech that has
been made this afternoon, and I agree
with the hon. Member for North Armagh
(Mr. J. Johnston) that there is no readymade solution for unemployment.
Politicians sometimes, carried away by
their own enthusiasm, may think they
have found a solution. I remember a
good many years ago my hon. and
respected Friend, the Member for
Pottinger (Mr. Beattie), assured the
House that he had got a cure for
unemployment.
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes. He has.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Every time
there has been a debate on the subject
ever since I have been trying to get him
to put that cure before the public, but
I have never got it yet, and do not
expect to get it this evening.
Mr. BEATTIE: You got it two or
three times. It is in Hansard.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: If it is in
Hansard the printer must have obliterated my copy, because I have looked in
vain for it. There is no use in shutting
our eyes to the fact that this is a worldwide problem and that it is not going to
be solved in the way some people would
have us believe. It is not by any means
a local problem. Indeed, so far as Northern Ireland is concerned, we are in a
better position than some parts of Great
Britain, and I must say that, instead
of blaming my right hon. Friend, in all
fairness hon. Members opposite should
join in giving him encouragement and
in helping him to make the lot of those
who are suffering easier than it is to-day.
There is one thing that I would like to
point out to hon. Members on both sides
of the Committee, and that is that there
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
30 MAY 1935
are more people in employment to-day in
Great Britain and Northern Ireland than
there were before the war. A good deal
of our trouble is due to the fact
mentioned by the Minister of Labour,
namely, that avenues of migration have
been closed to our people and that the
surplus that formerly went either to the
Dominions of our own Empire or to the
United States of America cannot do so
now as those doors have been shut.
Therefore, we are accumulating a surplus
of labour at home for which it is impossible
at the present time to find employment.
There is no justification whatever for
the statement that has been made
and made again on the other side of the
Committee that the Government have
done nothing to encourage industry.
The Government have done as much and,
indeed, more than any other government
in the world to encourage industry as a
whole.
I would just like to drop this hint to
hon. Members opposite. I give them
credit for the best intentions and for
wanting to do the very best they can,
though they will not give us that credit.
I would like them when dealing with a
question like shipbuilding to be careful
with regard to their words, because words
that are spoken here-sometimes spoken
very lightly may be taken very
seriously on the other side. We have
had trouble in the Imperial Parliament
already with regard to this shipbuilding
question. Hon. and right hon. Gentlemen in dealing with a question of this
sort ought to be very careful, and ought,
if possible, to do nothing that is going
to embarrass the Government in their
desire to bring work to this Province.
It is encouraging to hear from the
Minister what any observant person can
see for himself, that during recent
months there has been an improvement
in the matter of employment. And
might I say this? The hon. Member for
Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) was talking about
confidence. Confidence plays a very big
part in the industry of our country. You
are not going to create confidence or to
get people to start new industries in this
Province if you go about complaining
that you are in a bankrupt state. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) If the idea gets
abroad that a man is on the verge of
bankruptcy, believe me, he has great
trouble in finding money. I do say to
hon. Members that I hope they will
weigh their words carefully and not use
language that is likely to disparage or

AEROPLANE FACTORY IN
BELFAST.
the
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state what developments have taken
place, and are taking place, in establishing an aeroplane factory in Belfast; and
could he state whether the Government
are giving any assistance to secure this
new industry.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): Whilst I am aware that
negotiations have been proceeding with.
a view to the establishment of an
aeroplane factory in Belfast, they have
not yet reached a stage at which anything more than a provisional application for assistance could be made to my
Ministry under the New Industries
Development Act. I can, however,
assure the hon. Member that if and
when a definite application materialises,
it will receive every consideration at the
hands of my Department.
SLAUGHTER OF PIGS IN BELFAST
ABATTOIR.
2. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state if he has seen the recent letter
from the Pigs Marketing Board to Mr.
McClean, Veterinary Surgeon of the
Belfast Corporation, threatening to kill
no
more pigs in the Belfast Abattoir
unless he agreed to allow the pigs out of
the abattoir without inspecting them for
tuberculosis, and, if so, what steps he
proposes to take to protect the consuming public.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, to reply to this
question.
The Pigs Marketing Board have
shown the Minister a copy of the letter
to which it is presumed the hon. Member
refers. The Minister does not think that
this letter calls for any action by him.
There can never be any question of such
pigs escaping inspection for tuberculosis, or any other diseases, because all
pigs entering curing establishments in
Northern Ireland are inspected by
veterinary officers of the Ministry.
PIGS SEIZED AS UNFIT.
3. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state the number of pigs seized as unfit
for human consumption in the abattoirs
and stores outside the City of Belfast
since the Pigs Marketing Board was
established; and whether he can state
what was done with any pigs so seized.
Oral Answers
Transport Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. GORDON: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Agriculture, to reply to this question.
Three hundred and seventy-one pig
carcases were seized in Northern Ireland,
excluding the City of Belfast, as unfit
for human consumption in accordance.
with the provisions of the Agricultural
Produce (Meat Regulation) Act, 1930,
from the establishment of the Pigs
Marketing Board on the 1st October,
1933, until the 31st May, 1935. The
proportion of seizures within and without the city is approximately the same.
Any carcases so seized were dealt with
under the provisions of Section 9 of the
Act, i.e., treated by the Inspector in
such a way as to render them incapable
of use for human consumption or handed
over to the appropriate sanitary authority
to be dealt with in accordance with the
provisions of the Public Health Acts.
THE STRIKE AT
MESSRS. COWDY'S, LOUGHGALL.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he would take immediate steps
to put under arrest all those employed in
Messrs. Cowdy's, Loughgall, who are in
possession of revolvers without permits;
whether he is aware that three nonunion men named George Walker, Irwin,
and S. Farquhar, appeared on the Loughgall Road on Monday night, 3rd June,
under the influence of drink, armed with
revolvers, and threatened five strikers
that if they made any conversation with
them they would shoot to kill; whether,
in view of this outrage, the Minister will
have the persons mentioned put under
immediate arrest; whether he can state
who provided these revolvers and ammunition to the non-union men employed in
Messrs. Cowdy's, Loughgall.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I regret that owing
to the short notice given I have at the
moment no information whatever in
regard to the matter referred to by the
hon. Member, but I will cause immediate
inquiry to be made, and the hon. Member may rest assured that appropriate
action will be taken.
Mr. BEATTIE: Thank you.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Road and Railway Transport Bill.
As amended, considered.
CLAUSE 5 (Provisions for transfer
of transport undertakings to the Board).
*
*
*
In this sub-section the expression
"operated" means operated immediately before the passing of this Act
and then providing a road transport
service which had been commenced
before the first day of June, nineteen
hundred and thirty-four.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to
move, in page 6, line 3, at end (nineteen hundred and thirty-four'') add-
"and for the purposes of this subsection an undertaking shall be deemed
to be a road motor undertaking if it
consists mainly of the business of receiving, storing and forwarding merchandise
in connection with road transport services provided by any undertakings to be
acquired by the Board as aforesaid."
The purpose of this Amendment is to
deal with a type of undertaking which is
essentially a transport undertaking, but
which might not be held to come within
the definition in the Bill.
There are very few of these undertakings, which consist of a depot for the
purpose of receiving and forwarding
goods by road transport, and this is
practically the sole purpose of these undertakings. Such an undertaking maintains a depot and collects and receives
goods and forwards them by specified
carriers.
They are really part of a
carrier's undertaking and they perform a
necessary transport service. The Amendment provides that they should be
treated as transport undertakings.
As
I have said, there are only a few of them
-probably not more than 5 or 6 altogether-but we think it would be an
injustice to leave them out.
Amendment agreed to.

on the rapidity with which information
can be collected, and at this stage it is
not possible to say when it would be
practical to put the pooling scheme into
operation.
It has been represented, however, that
something more definite should be put in,
and accordingly we propose to limit the
general power by stating that it shall not
be later than twelve months from the date
of the passing of the Act.
Amendment agreed to.

(8) All or any part of the Northern

Stock may be redeemed at par at the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
in Clause 19, page 27, line 13, leave out
"such stock" and insert "'A' Stock."
The Bill provides that the Board may
redeem the stock at any time after the
expiration of thirty years from the date
of issue, and it also provides that all stock
shall be redeemed within a period of sixty
years. Hon. Members will, of course,
appreciate that this provision necessitates.
the establishment of a sinking fund, and
it has occurred to us that the compulsory
redemption of the "B" Stock within a
period of sixty years might impose too
heavy an annual charge upon the
revenues of the Board, which, of course,
would not be in the interests of the
travelling public. While, therefore, we
think that the options of the Board should
be preserved so that they can, if they so
desire, redeem all stock within the period,
we are of the opinion that it is better not
to make it compulsory upon them to
redeem the "B" Stock within that period,
lest it should cause too heavy a charge on
the revenues of the Board.
Amendment agreed to.

Has that position been improved by this
Bill? In my opinion no improvement is
taking place at all. The farmer has the

That to me is certainly not satisfactory.

carriers are being protected, so far as

would deny that knows nothing about
economics or the development of
industrial history. This small man, this
mythical, small man, is everywhere being
wiped out of existence by larger combines. Already there are not nearly so
many of these small men in Northern
Ireland as there were half a dozen years
ago, in the days when they invaded the
rights of the municipality of Belfast and
when the Belfast Corporation had to ask
for legislative powers to preserve their
revenue. The small men have been
absorbed by larger companies, and your
transport life to-day has been remodelled
along the lines of co-ordination.
But that co-ordination, in the opinion.
of the Government, has not been
sufficient to yield the results that it
ought to yield to a community like
Northern Ireland. Therefore, the Government has decided to go a step further,
and although that step is the opposite
to that I would have liked them to have
taken in regard to ownership and
financial control, nevertheless, realising
that thousands of transport employees in
Northern Ireland, both road and rail,
who have been working very long hours
and living under very arduous conditions,
are going to be provided with machinery
which, if properly utilised, will result in
a higher standard of life, I cordially
support the Bill. I am optimistic
enough to believe that in the days which
lie ahead many of the fears which have
been conjured up in this House by
speakers on both sides will, in actual
reality, be found to have been present
only in the minds of the people who expressed them.
Of course, everything may not work
perfectly smoothly at first. Someone
may discover that a bus which used to
pass a certain point at five minutes to
eleven passes at a quarter past eleven,
and in a certain country district it may
be found that whereas four or five buses
used to pass daily, a lesser number are
operated by the Board, simply because
the former system was uneconomic. But
have we here any right to defend uneconomic conditions and claim that
certain services should be maintained all
the time, irrespective of whether or not
they were economic? I say we have not.
We have the right only to look into the
resources and potentialities of the
Province, and co-ordinate them to the
end that every section of our community,
from the humblest to the highest, shall
be guaranteed the greatest possible
security; that our transport services shall
be operated with the sole object of securing the greatest good for the greatest
number; and that a decent standard of
conditions and life shall be the first duty
and consideration of those in whose
charge our transport is placed.

Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): This is a
small, and I hope a non-controversial Bill
in which the Ministry seeks from Parliament power for the amendment of certain
matters that have developed in the course
of the administration of the Act as it
stands at present. The Clauses are
independent of one another, and probably
the simplest plan for me would be to go
through them one by one.
Clause 1 arises in this way: As the
law stands at present an education
authority, which is the county council of
a county or the corporation of a borough,
works through an education committee,
and the education committee is restricted
in certain matters. The education
authority must retain to itself the raising
of money by rate or loan and the acquisition, holding, or disposal of land.
Hitherto all negotiations leading up to
the acquisition of sites for schools were
performed by the education committees.
The land itself was conveyed to the
education authority-the county council
or the corporation-but all the work in
connection with the selection of the site,
negotiations, and everything of that sort,
was in fact done by the education committee, and in some cases they incurred
expenses in connection with that work.
Recently the auditor has pointed out
that, in fact, the education committee
should not have paid for those things, but
that they should have been paid for by
the county council. The county councils
and the education committees have found
it more convenient, and they say it will
be more convenient for them in the
future, to preserve the existing arrangement. Accordingly, this Bill seeks power
in connection with the acquisition, holding, or disposal of land, and the disbursal
or applying of money in discharge of any
expenditure or cost incurred on account
of such negotiations, and the disbursing
or applying of money in repayment of
any loan raised by the education
authority or in payment of interest
on such loan. The Clause provides
that the education committee shall
continue to do those things and that
there shall be no difficulty with regard to
their powers to do them. The Clause
expressly reserves to the county council
its right to retain any matter it chooses
within its own power, and that nothing
shall operate to enable land to be
acquired otherwise than in the name of
the county council.
The second Clause deals with a small
matter. Borrowing powers are given to
education authorities by the Act of 1992
for the execution of works. It has been
pointed out that works do not include the
acquisition of a site for a school, only the
Education Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
building of the school and that sort of
thing, and that consequently when an
education authority acquired a site for a
school it could not pay for the site
out of the loan raised, although it could
pay for the building put upon the site.
In many cases it was found very convenient to include the cost of the site in
the amount raised by loan, and it is to
cover that omission that this Clause is
proposed.
Clause 3 deals with two small matters.
It enlarges the powers of an education
authority, firstly, to include power to
provide playing fields and opportunities
for physical training. The second part is
a little different. In some cases it has
been found that if the education
authority could have provided or contributed to the provision of a foot bridge,
or the repairing of a footpath, it would
have provided an easier and sometimes
safer access for the children to the school
concerned. They had no power to do
that, and one or two cases have arisen
where it would have been a great
advantage if a footbridge which had
fallen into disrepair could have been
repaired by the education authority as it
would have enabled the children to reach
their schools more conveniently and sometimes more safely than if they had to
cross the public roads.
The fourth Clause deals with a somewhat different matter. By that the
Ministry may by regulation provide that
such officers of an education authority as
may be prescribed by the regulations shall
not be appointed or removed from office
without the concurrence of the Ministry.
At present the Ministry have ample
power over the personnel of the teaching
staff of a school, but they have no power
directly with regard to the approval or
disapproval of the appointment of particular persons as officials or officers of an
education authority. The Ministry think
it advisable that they should be given
that express power which they would
exercise directly, rather than the indirect
powers which they have already. Accordingly sanction is asked for that in
Clause 4.
Clause 5 deals with the parents' representatives on school management committees. As the House is aware, where
in a transferred or provided school a
teacher had to be selected that was
hitherto done by the school management
committee. The school management committee is composed as to one half of
representatives of the transferors of the
school, and as to one quarter by parents'
representatives. Occasionally it has
happened that when a parents' meeting
was called a quorum did not attend, or
that when they did attend they failed to
agree upon a nomination. In those two
cases this Bill seeks power for the education authority to fill those vacancies.
There is a proviso that a period of twentyeight days is to be allowed after the
failure of a meeting to nominate representatives, within which if the failure is
made good the education authority must
under the powers given to them accept
the nominations of the parents' meeting.
The
Clause 6 groups together a number of
cases where it is proposed that the
ordinary procedure with regard to the
appointment of a teacher in a transferred
or provided school shall not apply.
system at present is this: Where a
vacancy occurs the education authority
must advertise the vacancy in the Press;
a list of the applicants is sent down to
the school management committee, the
school management committee sends three
names from that list back to the education authority, and the education
authority may appoint one of those three.
Sometimes it happens that where
scheme of reorganisation of schools is put
into operation there may be a superfluous
teacher.
You may have, say, one school
with a set of three teachers and another
school with a set of three teachers, and
you amalgamate them so that you can do
with five teachers. One teacher is superfluous. That is the case dealt with in
paragraph (b) where power is sought for
the education authority to appoint that
superfluous teacher to any school under
their control in which they have a
vacancy.
Sometimes it also happens that, owing
to falling attendance in a school, one
teacher in that school becomes redundant.
It is proposed in that case also that the
education authority shall have power to
appoint that redundant teacher to any
other school under their control where
they have a suitable vacancy. Paragraph
(d) deals with the appointment of a
temporary teacher without going through
the process of advertising, and paragraph
(e) deals with the case where a school

management committee does not within
the prescribed time send forward the
names of the qualified candidates to the
education authority. Paragraphs (b) and
(c) are cases where the school management committee are not given the opportunity which they have had heretofore of
nominating candidates for appointment
in a school as teacher to the education
authority. In those cases, (b) and (c),
where you have a superfluous teacher
transferred to another school which is not
part of a scheme of reorganisation, in
order that no hardship may be inflicted
upon the school management committee,
who might object to a particular teacher
being appointed to a school under their

is given. If there be any
teacher
appointed who in their opinion is unsuitable they may appeal to the Ministry,
and if the Ministry find that their appeal
is well grounded the ordinary procedure
will be reverted to in that case.
Clause 7 deals with yet another matter.
There is a scheme
scheme on foot whereby
teachers in the United Kingdom are
exchanged for teachers in other parts of
the Empire, or indeed on the Continent.
Power is sought here so that the Ministry
can by regulation provide that teachers.
in our area may, where opportunity
occurs, take the same advantage of this
scheme as teachers in other parts of the
United Kingdom. Those are the provisions of this small and, I hope, uncontentious Measure, and I beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
COLLECTION OF RATES.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state the
total rates collected by local authorities
last year and the Exchequer grants to
those authorities in the same year to
make up to them the losses in rates due
to (1) the complete derating of farm
lands and buildings; and (2) the 75 per
cent. derating of industrial and freight
transport premises; and (3) the 40 per
cent. derating of fisheries.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply to this question.
The total rates collected by local
authorities during the year ended 31st
March, 1935, amounted to approximately
one million and seven hundred and fortyeight thousand pounds (£1,748,000), and
the grants paid under the provisions of
the Local Government (Rating and
Finance) Act (Northern Ireland), 1929,
in respect of that year amounted to one
million and forty-three thousand four
hundred and twenty-seven pounds
(£1,043,427), being £928,130 in respect
of farm land and buildings, £114,323 in
respect of industrial and freight transport
hereditaments, and £974 in respect of
fisheries.
It is anticipated that further sums of
£43,000, £11,000 and £40, respectively,
will fall to be paid on the completion of
the audit of the accounts of the local
authorities for that year.
DANGERS OF ROAD TRAFFIC.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he proposes
to take any steps to lessen the dangers of
the road traffic to school children.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would point
out to the hon. Member that steps have
already been taken to deal with the
matter raised by the hon. Member.
Since 1933 lectures on traffic dangers
have been given by uniformed police
officers to school children in the city
schools. I am satisfied that this method
of instruction is having valuable results,
and, accordingly, I have been in consultation with my right hon. Friend, the
Estimates-
Ministry of Finance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Minister of Education, with a view to
extending the area in which instruction
to school children shall be given. The
hon. Member will, no doubt, realise the
impossibility of sending uniformed police
officers to every school in the Province;
therefore I am arranging, with the cooperation of the various educational
authorities and of the teachers' organisations, that lectures for teachers on this
important subject shall be given in various
centres by police traffic experts. These
lectures will enable teachers to bring before
the children in their charge, the most important sources of danger and to impart
instruction on how to avoid traffic
accidents. In this way it is hoped suitable instruction in safety principles will
be imparted to all school children.
In addition, the police devote a good
deal of time and attention to securing
the safe passage of children across the
streets on their way to and from school.
I think everyone must be impressed with
the kindliness and patience exercised by
the members of the force in carrying out
this duty.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to give
notice that I will raise this question on
the Motion for Adjournment.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In presenting this Estimate for the administration expenses of
the Ministry of Finance, I do not propose
to enumerate the diverse activities of the
Ministry or to touch upon policy in any
direction. The performance of the
statutory functions of the Ministry in
the regulation of the service as a whole,
in the collection of revenue, in the
administration of works services, to
mention only a few, require large blocks
of staff and I shall confine my opening
statement to giving information in regard
to changes in staff organisation necessitated for one reason and another.
On page 16 it will be noted that the
total number of staff has had to be increased
by 10, but despite the increase in the
money provision arising from the consolidation of salaries, it is satisfactory to
note that the staff readjustments which
have been carried out have had the effect
of limiting the additional money provision to a sum of £1,000.
Owing to an increase of work in the
land purchase collection branch consequent on the increased number of
annuities in collection, four additional
writing assistants are required, but this
is offset to some extent by a reduction
in the number of clerks. It is not expected that any further increases of staff
will be necessary here, as the vesting of
holdings under the 1925 Land Purchase
Act is now completed.
In the Works Division the work of rebuilding at Government House, Hillsborough, and the number of barrack reconstruction schemes on hand account
for an increase in temporary architectural

school
new

It is not possible, in moving an Estimate of this character, to give any
general review of the Department's work,

perhaps the nearest approach to such a

Custom House, the two large buildings
in
Ormeau Avenue occupied by the
Valuation Division of the Ministry of
Finance, the Unemployment Assistance.
Board, and certain other staffs, and

work, which includes the cleaning of

performed by 55 disabled ex-Service men,
only persons of this description being
employed. With a few exceptions, the
men work throughout the night, from 11
p.m. to 8 a.m. with a meal interval of one
hour; and they deal with a total floor
space of approximately 280,000 square
feet, or 6 acres. A number of the
cleaners are employed as watchmen and
all are trained in fire protection duties.
A special tram service is arranged to
bring the men to Stormont at night. No
special tram is required in the morning,
since the service starts at 7-30 a.m. It
will interest hon. Members to know that
the change from the earlier practice of
carrying out the cleaning work in two
shifts one before and one after office
hours-was made in the interests of the
men themselves when this building was
first occupied, since the continuance of
morning and evening shifts would double
the time and expense of travelling to and
from Stormont; but even the later
cleaners prefer night work, and indeed
requested that they might be placed on
a par with the Stormont cleaners in this
respect. I think that hon. Members will
agree that the way the work is carried out
is highly creditable to these men, many
of whom suffer from physical disabilities.
If I may be so ungallant as to say so, the
machine for employing 50 men cleaners
works more smoothly than it would if the
same number of women were employed
-(Hon. Members: Oh!)—and I am sure
that the results are equally satisfactory.

The money provision for the office of
the Registrar General-on page 18shows practically no change from last
year, but a few remarks about the work
of this office will, I am sure, be of general
interest. The principal matter of
interest in 1934 has been the gratifying
co-operation of the medical profession in
the collection of vital statistics.
The
standard of registration of births, deaths
and marriages continues to improve,
although progress is unavoidably slow
and there are still a number of births and
deaths which escape registration.
An outstanding feature revealed by the
vital statistics is the decrease in the
number of deaths from tuberculosis.
These numbered 2,100 in 1922 and have
steadily decreased to 1,400 in 1934, that

certain grants and some extra allowances
in regard to forage, as they were expected
in the old days to have a horse to go
about on. Now there are a number of
resident magistrates appointed under the
old law, but the policy of this Government has been as far as possible to give
a comprehensive salary in respect of these
offices though there may be a certain
amount allowed for travelling expenses.
I think in that lies the reason for the
differentiation between the seven and
the four resident magistrates.
Mr. BEATTIE: I think it has been
consolidated as far as the police are concerned.
Mr. HANNA: Not in respect of those
appointed earlier.
Mr. BEATTIE We have the
allowances consolidated wiping out the
forage allowances and motor allowances.
We consolidated the two into one in the
police. I want to see what I am speaking of carried right through. Unfortunately, for some reason or other four
of these resident magistrates of Northern
Ireland have not received allowances
which the other seven have received. I
think the Government should remove
that anomaly. The other point, the
maximum amount they receive is going
to hit them very hard if additional work
is going to be placed on their shoulders.
Question put, and agreed to.

PUBLIC RECORDS AND ANCIENT

Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £4,465 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charges that
will come in course of payment in the
year ending 31st March, 1936, in respect
of the salaries and expenses of the Public

the cost of the administration of the

V (N.I.), c. 12.)-(Note-£1,000 has
been voted on account.)
Mr. BARBOUR: This estimate will be
found on page 45. Apart from the new
Sub-head I, in which provision of £500
is made for grants for archæological investigation, this estimate shows practically
no variation from last year, and does not,
I think, require much explanation. I
should, perhaps, draw the attention of
the Committee to the fact that the provision under Sub-head C is a revote, as
the final details of the scheme for carrying
out the work at Carrickfergus Castle have
not yet been agreed between the Ministry
and the Urban District Council; it is
hoped, however, that the work will be
carried out in the current year.
Turning now to Sub-head I, page 47,
Archæological Investigation, a sum of
£500 has been set aside for excavation
works undertaken under the control of
the Ancient Monuments Advisory Committee in connection with archæological
research. Very meritorious work has been
done by various individuals and learned
bodies from their own limited resources,
and the Government has thought well to
play a part in this important and interesting work. As Members know,
archæology has now, to a large extent,
become a matter not of the library, but
of the spade, and there seems to be no
Estimates-
Public Records
5 JUNE 1935
limit to the possibilities to be revealed by
this means. Hitherto, owing perhaps to
a lack of wealthy institutions, Northern
Ireland, despite its wealth of antiquities
calling for research, has been outstripped
in this respect by other countries.
The grant will be issued in the form
of a contribution not exceeding 60 per
cent. of the total wages of unemployed
men specially engaged for these works.
Every workman engaged in these excavations will thus cease to draw unemployment benefit, and accordingly the
resultant net charge to the Exchequer
should be much less than the figure
which appears in this Estimate. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
The House may be interested to hear
of the bodies which are likely to operate
these schemes. An international body,
the Prehistoric Council, has, under encouragement from the Belfast Municipal
Museum, conducted several valuable
local excavations, and, with the increased
resources available to it under the
Estimates provision, should be able
greatly to extend its work with proportionately good results. Then, that
very old-established institution,
the
Belfast Natural History and
and Philosophical Society, which has a special
Archæological Section, and has been
associated in the past with such good
work as the excavation of Nendrum and
many other ancient sites, may be expected
to utilise this opportunity for further
work, and it is not unlikely that the
Belfast Naturalists Field Club will do
the same. Some of the other Field Clubs
in the country, which are doing such
good work in the scientific study of their
neighbourhoods, may also wish to take
part. Private individuals will not be
excluded if their proposed schemes, like
the others, meet with the approval of
the Ancient Monuments Advisory Committee, and investigators of repute from
foreign countries will also be welcomed
if they similarly comply.
It is hoped that the Harvard
University Archæological Mission may
continue and extend the good work which
they did, entirely at their own charge,
in Ulster last year when they excavated
the neighbourhood of the diatomite beds
near Toome, and a raised beach near
Glenarm, and made a most elaborate
study of a sand and gravel cliff near
Cushendun, which they cut through
from its summit down to the level of the
river Dun, which flows round its base.
It is understood that this year they may
seek to investigate a large fort in Northern Ireland with a tradition of
occupation since the Bronze Age.
These projects are expected to account.
for £400 of the provision. The remaining
£100 is set aside for assistance, on a
similar basis, to an extremely interesting
and scientifically very promising investigation being conducted by the Committee
for Quaternary Research in Ireland, in
conjunction with a foreign scientist, Dr.
Jessen, of Denmark, into the composition
and history of Irish bogs. This matter
of quaternary research is now world-wide,
and it is thought that the examination of
the various stata of Irish bogs wil! throw
valuable light on the early botanical
history of this region, and consequentially
on the period from which objects of
antiquity found in Irish bogs date.
Previous investigations of this kind have
proved fruitful not only on the Continent,
but in the fen country of England, and
so recently as last year in the Irish Free
State. We have set aside £100 this year
for contribution towards the wages of
unemployed labourers working under Dr.
Jessen, and it is hoped that the work may
be conducted in an extensive Ulster bog
in which objects of known date have
already been found.
I feel confident that hon. Members will
entirely approve this modest contribution
towards the investigation of our country's
history, which also will help to maintain
Ulster's place in the foreground of
scientific research. I beg to move.
Mr. CAMPBELL: This Vote seems to
me to be the Cinderella of the estimates
to-day. I think the Committee will
regret anything in the way of stingy
treatment by the State of a department
of this kind. I am quite free to admit
that from the Parliamentary Secretary's
statement it is evident the Ministry are
making some progress, and I for one am
very glad to know that the Government
are moving forward in this very important
department of public activity. But when
one looks at the actual figures it does
strike one that we are very far behind
the times. All that we spent on the purchase of historical documents last year
was £75, and all we spent on archæological objects was £10. For a territory
Estimates-
Public Records
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Campbell]
like ours, so rich in antiquarian objects,
and with so very many historical associations, that does not seem a very generous
contribution by the State. It almost
amounts to something on the stingy side,
and I do think the Minister might be
more generous in this direction. We have
had a very entertaining lecture from the
Financial Secretary regarding archeology
and its development in Northern Ireland,
but if this Vote is any test we are about
as far advanced in regard to archæology
as they were in England when Mr. Pickwick set out on his archæological travels
one hundred and seven years ago.
There is another item I want to draw
attention to. The receipts are only £225.
I take it that that represents the entrance
fees charged to beautiful castles like Dunluce, Carrick, and Ardglass. The total
is negligible, and I suppose it would
hardly suffice to pay the running expenses
of these places. But I would represent
to the Minister that the people who visit
these castles and other ancient monuments
are not the riff-raff. They are very
often poor men, but they have a keen and
deep interest in those beautiful antiquarian surroundings. I believe the
charge for admission is sixpence per
head. If you take a working man
of Belfast who has an education
sufficient to develop a feeling and
a respect for these buildings, and he
wants to bring his family of perhaps
three or four children to see one of these
places, when he has paid his railway
fares and other expenses to Ardglass or
Carrick it is a trial for him to produce
his own and three or four other sixpences for admission. He cannot do it,
and, on behalf of that class, I appeal to
the Minister and to the Committee to
consider if it would not be well to reduce
the fee of sixpence to a nominal sum
for an adult, with perhaps free admission for the children. In London
they used to charge for admission to
beautiful places like the Abbey and
Hampton Court, and when it was pointed
out that they were depriving a very
large part of the population from enjoying these beauty spots the authorities.
gladly withdrew the charge. I know
the interest the Minister and the
Financial Secretary take in this matter,
and I would make an appeal to them to
see if they can agree to the abolition
of any entrance fee in the case of
children accompanying their parents, and
to make the fee for the parents as low
and as nominal as they possibly can.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: It is not often
that I am in such complete sympathy
and harmony with the hon. and learned
Member for Central as I am in this
matter. I would like to congratulate
the Minister on the start he has made in
regard to this important department of
his activities. We have a large number
of historical monuments, and it would
be an advantage to all classes in the community, irrespective of their political
beliefs, to know their history. In yesterday's or to-day's papers I noticed that
some considerable finds were made in
what used to be my old constituency and
is now part of Bann Side, where remains
have been found that go back 2,000 B.C.
That shows how important it is that we
should go into this matter thoroughly,
and now that the Minister knows he has
the sympathetic backing of the whole
Committee, I am sure he will take a
greater interest in the subject than he
has already done. He has certainly done
a great deal in preserving Dunluce
Castle which, without his interference,
would have disappeared in the course of a
few years.
There is yet an enormous
amount of work to be done in this
direction. I would like to get a great
deal more information with regard to the
invasion of the Celts when they drove our
Irish people out of the country, and I am
sure the hon. and learned Member for
Central is interested in that, too. There
is an enormous field for development here,
and I am sure the Minister will lend a
sympathetic ear to all that has been said.
Mr. McALEER: I agree with all the
previous speakers have said, and I would
suggest to the Minister that when these
archæological excavations are being riade
there should be placed in charge a person
who has had experience, and is competent
and trustworthy and responsible, because
it is really nothing short of vandalism
that when tombs are being excavated and
explored rough workmen come along and
smash urns, food vessels, and other valuable relics. I support the plea of the hon.
and learned Member for Central that
there should be far more money devoted
to the acquisition of historical documentз
and articles of archeological value, and
that we should make our collection a more
general one.

Mrs. PARKER: I should like to add
a few words to what has been said on this
subject. I am in complete agreement
with what hon. Members have said with
regard to this Vote. While I would like
to congratulate the Minister on what has
already been done, I feel that even more
might be undertaken. As has already
been said, if the Minister realised how
many people there are in this Province
who take a great pride in their ancient
monuments and a great interest in them,
he and his Advisory Committee would be
encouraged to proceed more quickly and
more generously on the lines already
adopted. I would like to draw the
right hon. Gentleman's attention
to
a matter which, I dare say, is
connected with the small amount asked
for in this Vote. That is, that in a great
many of these ancient churches scheduled
as ancient monuments there are burying
grounds inside or outside the ruins of
those churches which are in a terribly
dilapidated condition. I am very greatly
interested in all the ruins and ancient
monuments in this country, and I have
been particularly struck, going into one.
or two in my part of the country, by their
very forlorn appearance; the high rank
grass and the dilapidated condition generally of the paths and grounds. I do not
think it is calculated to impress the
visitor or the tourist who takes an interest
in these wonderful relics of a great past,
of which we are all so very proud. I feel
sure if the Minister thought it necessary
on a future occasion to ask for a larger
sum this Committee would be only too
glad to grant it for the purpose of preserving these valuable relics of a great
and an old civilisation in which we take
as great a pride as do hon. Members
opposite.
