Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
a
Mr. CAMPBELL: I addressed
question to the Minister of Home Affairs
to-day in regard to the danger on the
roads to school children. I am not at
all satisfied with the reply given, and I
submit to the House that the Minister
does not sufficiently realise the gravity
and urgency of the question of the death
and mutilation of school children which
is going on week by week and month by
month. The number of children killed
or injured in this area annually is distressing. On the average it is something
like one or two deaths every week, and
ten or twelve are injured every week.
That is a very doleful picture. The
peculiarity is that our view of the
sacredness of human life is such in recent
years that this thing is allowed to go on
without remedy or cbservation of any
kind.
In England last
year of 3,517
pedestrians killed by motor traffic onethird, or to be exact 1,172, were
children. What this means in human
Dangers of Road Traffic 2262
Adjournment-
5 JUNE 1935
""
suffering, perhaps depriving the children
of learning and livelihood all through
life; and in agony to the relatives, one
can easily visualise, yet the officials seem
to take no note or account of it. Are we
to take it that this terrible toll of the
roads is to be treated as a thing of no
importance? Are these lives to be
sacrificed as an inevitable concomitant of
the craze for rushing for pleasure or profit?
Must we take it as part of the fate of
our present mechanised system of civilisation and say Kismet, what must be
will be"? I feel very strongly on this
subject. I do feel that the children of
the poor, who are the children most
affected by this motor traffic, were not
born to be fodder for motors any more
than fodder for cannon. In the
administrative county of London last
year 4,500 children were either killed or
injured. That is the average year after
year. How many of these young lives
were victims of the Moloch of speed?
The speed limit in built-up areas in
England is 30 miles. The responsible
Minister says that this is working well.
It is very satisfactory. Members on the
other side of the House would not question
the accuracy of a responsible Minister of
the Crown at Westminster. We have no
such protection here, while that scheme
has been in operation in England for
almost three months.
Among the remedies suggested by the
London County Council Education Committee are playing places to keep the
children off the streets, the reservation
of side streets from motor traffic, and
the instruction of the children in traffic
sense. Those may be very potent
remedies, but even beyond that children
will be children to the very end of the
verse. The present appalling mortality
cannot continue indefinitely. The
public conscience will be stirred sooner
or later. Public sentiment will not
allow this thing to go on without check
or restraint. The Government should
take some steps to devise some root and
branch remedies to try to meet this great
new peril, because the people will not
allow young life to be crushed out as it
is being crushed out at the present time.
In Belfast, in the central areas of the
city, children are swarming on to the
main roads as well as the side roads.
There is one great belt covering part of
the Central Division running from the
Shankill Road on the one side to Limestone Road on the other, and in all that
large and thickly built area children are
in every street by the score. I cannot
find one playing ground in that area.
In one school in that constituency, I am
instructed on good authority, two of
the children attending are injured
by motor cars every week. That makes
200 a year injured in respect of that
particular school.
and
Of course, motor trade and progress
must be maintained, and motor cars must
go on. They are progressing by leaps
and bounds year by year. Somebody
has said that the unfortunate pedestrians
are saving their lives by leaps
bounds. I was delighted indeed to hear
the Minister of Home Affairs pay a
tribute to the police to-day in regard to
this matter. It is a well deserved
tribute. It is a very pleasant spectacle
indeed to see the police near the large
central schools all over the city, even
when they are off duty, guiding the little
children to safety from one kerbstone to
the other. It is a very pleasant sight,
and one appreciates it, but there is a
very unpleasant sight parallel to it, that
is these large commercial lorries rushing
along our main streets at the rate of an
express train flashing through a station.
Sometimes you shudder to think what
would be the fate of a little toddler if
he came out of a side street and got in
the path of
these weapons of
one of
destruction and death.
One trouble is that motor cars are so
cheap and are so easily got nowadays,
either second-hand in the open purchase
market or on the hire purchase system.
That is leading to the result that a group
of irresponsible people are now getting
control of motor cars who should not be
in control of motor cars at all. They
have no sense of responsibility. Possession of a motor car is now no more proof
of responsibility than a tall hat or a fur
coat was a guarantee of solvency twenty
years ago. I do say the time has come
when officialdom as represented by the
Ministry should get a move on and stir
itself into life instead of slumbering
along in Sleepy Hollow.
Mr. HANNA: In so far as the speech.
of the hon. and learned Gentleman
suggests that we on this side of the House

upon the great number of our motorists

Oral Answers to Questions.
THE STRIKE AT MESSRS.
COWDY'S, LOUGHGALL.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
the number of policemen doing special
duty at Messrs. Cowdy's Works at
Loughgall; what is the cost of this
special duty; whether, in view of the
fact that this strike arises out of the
failure of Messrs. Cowdy to put into
operation an award made by an officer
of the Ministry of Labour, he will inform
the firm that they will in future only
receive ordinary police supervision; and
whether he will charge Messrs. Cowdy
with the bill for the total cost of the
additional police protection.
The following questions also stood on
the Order Paper in the name of Mr.
Beattie :-
7. To ask the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware that Messrs.
Cowdy, Loughgall, evicted all their
tenants from their homes on Saturday,
1st June, whether he is prepared to
amend the Rent Restriction Act to prevent action of this kind being used as a
lever against the workers, and whether
he is aware that Messrs. Cowdy refused
to apply an arbitration award as agreed
upon by them and their employees.
8. To ask the Minister of Labour
whether Messrs. Cowdy, Loughgall, are
paying a living wage to their workers,
and, if not, whether he is prepared to
establish a Trade Board for the Irish
Bleaching Industry.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked to reply
to this question. I hope my reply will
cover the other questions asked by my
hon. Friend in this connection.
I am glad to be able to inform the
hon. Member that, as a result of conferences which I had with the parties.
yesterday, an agreement was reached
which will be submitted to the workers
to-morrow, and which I hope will be
ratified. In these circumstances I am
sure the hon. Member will not desire any
further statement in reply to the three
questions on this subject which appear
in his name.
Mr. BEATTIE: Failing any settlement of the dispute to-morrow and I
hope there will be a settlement-would I
have the right to put on the Order Paper
these particular questions?
Mr. ANDREWS: I think that is
quite fair.
WAGES OF CONSTABLES IN R.U.C.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
what wages will be paid from July, 1935,
to constables of the Royal Ulster Constabulary who joined the force since July
of 1932, after the completion of three
years' service.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Government
have had this matter under consideration
for some time past, and I hope to make
an announcement in due course.

entrants joined knowing the conditions

Sir DAWSON BATES: That statement is made entirely without foundation. The men, when they joined, knew

PUBLIC HEALTH IN BLACKSTAFF
RIVER DISTRICTS.
3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware of the menace to the public health
of the community adjacent to the Blackwater River, especially in the Donegall
Road and Grosvenor Road districts,
during the present summer
weather;
and whether he will make representations
to the proper authority to have this
grave danger attended to.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I presume
the hon. and gallant Member refers to
the Blackstaff River. I am aware that
complaints have been made with regard
to the matter to the Public Health Department of the Corporation and that it
is being investigated by them.
Accordingly no necessity for any repre
sentations on the part of my Ministry
arises at this juncture.
Major McCORMICK: Is the Minister
aware that this is a long-standing complaint not of a month or two months?
Reference has been made to it in the
Belfast Corporation,
Corporation, and small
small and
tentative efforts only have been made in
regard to it. That is why I draw
attention to it.
NARROWING OF COUNTY DOWN
ROADS.
4. Dr. WILSON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware of the
dangerous policy being pursued by the.
Down County Council in allowing the
narrowing of 1st and 2nd class roads in
County Down; and whether he will take
steps to have the roads maintained to
the fullest possible width.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can assure
the hon. Member that the policy of the
Down County Council, far from tending
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
towards the narrowing of roads, is
definitely in the direction of road widening. They are, however, pursuing the
policy of aligning roads to uniform widths,
and this course, which has been pursued
for the past two years, is in conformity.
with most modern practice in Great
Britain and elsewhere and is generally
accepted as tending to promote safety.
In some cases the new alignment involves a slight narrowing of the width of
the carriageway; in others it means a
widening.
At the same time, when resurfacing
is being undertaken, the camber of each
road is reduced and the flattening of the
surface in effect provides an additional
two feet of effective carriageway.
Except on roads within 10 or 15 miles
of Belfast, the re-alignment is providing
for at least two traffic lanes on each road,
ten feet being allowed for each lane.
Dr. WILSON: May I point out to
the right hon. Gentleman-
The
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
hon. Member must ask a supplementary
question.
Dr. WILSON: Is the Minister aware
that this policy of narrowing the roads.
has the effect of creating corners where
none previously existed?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would be
very sorry to think the hon. Member is
under that impression. What I tried
to point out was that the county councils
are trying to ensure a fixed limit for the
whole road.
R.U.C. AND CUSTOMS PATROL
DUTIES.
5. Mr. McCARROLL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he possesses any disciplinary
control over the members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary whilst engaged in
Customs patrol duties, and, if not, what
officers exercise this control and where
can local complaints be lodged.
Sir DAWSON BATES: All members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary,
whether engaged on Customs duties or
otherwise, are under the direct control
of the Inspector General and subject to
the disciplinary code of the force.
I shall be glad to look into any complaints which the hon. Member may wish
to bring under my notice.

6. Mr. McCARROLL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of prosecutions of lorry owners or drivers in
Northern Ireland between January 1st
and June 1st this year, with the corresponding figures for 1934; the number
of prosecutions instituted in the January
to June, 1935, period against bus owners
or drivers; whether any special instructions have been issued to the police
to watch for buses exceeding the speed
limit in recent months.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the
hon. Member's permission I propose to
circulate a tabular statement giving particulars as to the number of prosecutions
for exceeding the speed limit, and, also,
in the case of omnibuses, for overcrowding.
With regard to other prosecutions, I
regret that in the time at my disposal
it would not be possible to obtain the
figures for which the hon. Member asks.
In February last I issued a general instruction to the police to exercise still
with
greater vigilance in connection
motoring offences, particularly with regard to negligent driving, but no special
instruction was issued with regard to
omnibuses exceeding the speed limit.

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
reason for such an increase in the amount
for Government hospitality. Is it a fact
that the hospitality extended to distinguished visitors was paid out of this
public fund? If so, what right have the
Government to use this money for their
own political ends? This is one of the
Estimates not presented before the Committee, and I feel I am entitled now to
discuss it.
Mr. BEATTIE: In connection with
the Jubilee ?
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
had better proceed with his speech.
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not wish to proceed with my speech if I am on wrong
lines. At the same time, this Estimate
is now increasing every year. When it
was going down I kept quiet, but now
it is going up. I feel the Government
are using this money wrongly, and if any
other political party were in power they
would direct attention to the manner in
which it is spent. When the Government want to entertain political friends
they should do so out of their own pockets
and not out of the public purse. That is
really what is happening to-day. In my
opinion this House is being abused. When
I came into the House a reading and writing room was provided for the Members.
To-day I find the Milk Board or some
other Board domiciled in the room set
apart for the Members of this House.
Mr. GRANT: Not the Milk Board.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am informed the
Milk Board is also included. It is time
the rights of Members of this House were
protected. No room set apart for them
should be used by outside bodies.
Mr. SPEAKER: As a matter of fact,
I may state for the information of the
hon. Member for Pottinger that the
person responsible is the Speaker of the
House of Commons. If he wishes to raise
the matter and gives me notice, I shall be
only to pleased to explain to him at any
reasonable time, either inside or outside
the House, the reasons why various rooms
have been taken over.
Mr. BEATTIE: Circumstances alter
cases often. The only thing I desire to
speak about is the accommodation provided for Members of Parliament, which
is taken over by outside bodies. I do not
want to put down a Motion against Mr.
Speaker. I feel he is in the position of
having to accommodate certain persons
and that he had no accommodation other
than the rooms he gave them. I would
like to impress upon the Government that
Mr. Speaker should not be placed in a
position like that.

Mr. BEATTIE: We have to battle

Members of this House and we have

do not want for one moment to reflect on

Member.

The PRIME MINISTER : As I
happen to know more about the proposals
of the Government for the present financial year with regard to entertainment,
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) has
asked me to explain to the House that,
amongst other arrangements, we have
coming into our midst the British Pharmaceutical Congress and the Auctioneers'
Society Congress. Both these associations meet in various capitals and other
large cities from time to time, and on
this occasion the Government have made
arrangements to offer them hospitality
and to help them while they are here to
see as much as possible of our Ulster
area. Over and above that, I happen to
know that the International Girl Guides
will be coming, and, as has been done in
every country in which the International
Girl Guides' meetings have been held,
the Government propose also to extend
to them some hospitality. The estimate
here, of course, covers a little more than
usual on account of the Royal Silver
Jubilee celebrations. Those celebrations,
and the other events, make up, approximately, what it may cost the Government
in the way of entertainment this year.
Of course, anything that is over will be
carried on to next year.

does more to advertise Belfast than any

It is very disagreeable for one to have to

who profess to be patriots make some

As I say,
the Prime Minister has a castle to live

free house. The only thing the Prime

even occupying the
the minds of local

you have the upkeep of the driver, I

the great cost to the taxpayers of Northern Ireland in keeping up the Prime
Minister's residence. I hope the Minister of Finance, at the earliest opportunity, will do his utmost to economise

the Prime Minister received £2,500 or
£2,000 a year, a house, a motor-car, and

Mr. POLLOCK: The main purpose of
this Bill is to give legislative effect to the
proposals relating to the taxes within our
control, which I brought before the House
when presenting my Budget Statement.
As hon. Members are already familiar
with the nature of these proposals it will
not be necessary for me to speak at any
length on this Bill.
Clause 1 gives effect to the various proposals I made relating to motor vehicle.
duties. The new rates of duty are set
out in the First Schedule to the Bill.
Part I of the First Schedule sets forth
the new rates of duty for motor-cycles,
which have been reduced by 12 per cent.
As this concession did not extend to motor
tricycles the rate of duty for these
vehicles remains unaltered. Part II of
the First Schedule shows the duties pro-

made, as formerly, between the rates of
duty payable by hackney carriages using
light oil and those using heavy oil, the
same rates of duty applying in both cases;
thus giving effect to the Budget proposal,
so far as it affects hackney carriages, to
reduce the duty on heavy oil-using
vehicles to the same level as vehicles using
as

light oils.

corollary to Mr. Chamberlain's proposal
to increase the duty on heavy oil. Part
III of the First Schedule sets forth the
rates of duty for the various classes of
lorries and trailers. The new rates of
duty for farmers' lorries are given in
sub-division 1 of Part III of the First
Schedule. These rates are 25 per cent.
below those shown for the other goods
vehicles in sub-division 2, except in the
case of vehicles not exceeding 12 cwt.
This gives effect to my Budget proposal
to reduce by 25 per cent. the duty paid
by farmers on their lorries used in conveying farm produce.
As hon. Members will again observe,
no distinction is made in Part III between
goods vehicles using heavy oils and those
using light oils, which gives effect to the
Budget proposal to which I have already
referred, so far as it affects goods vehicles,
to reduce the duty on heavy oil-using
vehicles. Sub-division 3 of Part III of
the First Schedule also gives effect to the
Budget concession regarding the taxation
of "articulated" vehicles. It is proposed
to treat these vehicles as a single unit for
taxation purposes; at the moment they
are subject to double taxation. Part IV
of the First Schedule gives effect to the
Budget proposals to reduce the duty on
private cars by 12 per cent., and to
reduce the duty on trailers used by such
cars by 50 per cent.
As
Hon. Members will observe that no provision is made either in Clause 1 or the
First Schedule for the further motor
vehicle duty concession which I announced
in my reply to the Budget Debate.
hon. Members will remember, I then
announced that I had decided to follow
the British practice regarding the taxation of certain bogeys and trailers used,
for example, in crossing a road from one
part of a works to another. The British
practice is to remit the duty in full on
such vehicles where it is proved to the
satisfaction of the Ministry of Transport
that the vehicles are used in such manner.
As this is, in effect, a technical remission
of duty rather than an exemption from
duty, no legislative authority is required.
All the changes in motor vehicle duties,
with one exception, will take effect as
from the 1st January, 1936.
The exception is the change in the duties on
heavy oil-using vehicles, which takes effect
from the 1st August next.
Clauses 2 and 4 give effect to my
Budget concession to the living theatre.
The new rates of duty, which will take
effect from the 1st July next, are set out
in the Second Schedule. Clause 3 gives
effect to a very minor concession in
entertainments duty. Under the existing law the performance of music by a
band at an entertainment, consisting of
certain indoor games or sports would
render the entertainment ineligible for
exemption from duty, even though all the
other necessary conditions were fulfilled.
This pressed rather harshly on such entertainments as military and police boxing
tournaments. Clause 3 will, therefore,
enable a band to perform at such tournaments without rendering the entertainment ineligible for exemption.
Clauses 5 and 6 deal with the two very
minor matters in stamp duty law
mentioned in the Budget Resolution.
Clause 5 makes provision for the payment
of stamp duty upon receipts in respect
of certain vesting orders made by the
Ministry of Home Affairs under the Local
Government Act (Northern Ireland),
1934, to enable local authorities to
acquire land for various purposes. The
purpose of Clause 6 is to remove doubts
as to the proper amount of duty payable
upon certified copies of entries in the
Adopted Children Register.
Clause 7 gives effect to my various
Budget proposals relating to the Road
Fund. Hon. Members will remember that
I announced my intention to follow the
British practice and retain in the
Exchequer a proportion of the revenue
from motor vehicle duties as a luxury tax.
The percentage to be retained is fixed at
25 per cent., as against 33 per cent. in
Great Britain. In addition, the Clause
gives effect to the proposal to retain in the
Exchequer the sums collected as penalties
and fines in respect of motor offences. The
amount to be retained in the Exchequer
annually, resulting from the foregoing
proposals will, however, be diminished by
£50,000, until the debt due from the
Road Fund to the Exchequer, under
Section 4 of the Exchequer and Financial
Provisions Act, 1933 (i.e., for Distress
Relief Road Works), is extinguished.
Clause 8 authorises the extension of the
Second Issue of Ulster Savings Certificates for six additional years. I would
remind the House that in 1931 it
authorised a somewhat similar extension

to be paid on these certificates during the
extended currency sought for will be fixed

Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to ask
the Minister of Finance a question with
regard to stamp duty. During the past
few months, in Belfast particularly, we
have had an outcry against the infliction
of the charge in respect of copies of birth
certificates. I have tried to trace this
imposition to its source, and I am now
informed by the educational authorities
that the people responsible are the Ministry of Finance, and that they are taking
advantage of the parents of the city of
Belfast by mulcting them to the extent
of 3s 7d, instead of the usual sixpence in
respect of stamp duty. It is done in a
manner such as this. I understand that
when the local authority announces its
secondary school scholarship examination
there are always many hundreds of
children who apply to be admitted to the
examination. The custom is that each
one must supply proof of age.
Mr. POLLOCK: Secondary schools?
Mr. MIDGLEY: No, children in
elementary schools entering for scholarships admitting them to secondary schools.
The custom is for a child going into an
elementary school to get a copy of his
registration of birth, which is provided
for sixpence. If that certificate has been
lost, or perhaps was never obtained, the
child is compelled to seek a further one
or one for the first time, as the case may
be, and the Ministry, I understand,
impose a charge of 3s 7d for that document. It is claimed that because this is
an examination of elementary school
children for admittance to a secondary
school that they are perfectly entitled so
to do. I wish to say that in my opinion
it is a shameful evasion of the responsibility which the Ministry owe to the
people to safeguard their economical
affairs as far as they possibly can.
Let
me tell hon. Members how this works out.
I know-it is beyond doubt that actually
some people in Belfast have been deprived
of the right of entering for the examination because of this imposition of 3s 7d.
Mr. POLLOCK: That is very remarkable, surely.
Mr. MIDGLEY: There is nothing very
remarkable about it if people have not
got 3s 7d. If they do not get a copy of
the birth certificate, the education
authorities sent back their application to
be admitted to the examination, stating
that the child is not eligible for admittance because the form of application has
not been accompanied by a certificate of
registration of birth. That is not hearsay.
I have seen that myself.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is quite natural;
they want the certificate.
Mr. MIDGLEY: In one breath the
Minister of Finance says it is rather remarkable, and then when the case is
actually proved he says, "Well, what can
you expect?" In other words, the Minister of Finance has it both ways. He is
the best living embodiment of backing a
principle both ways that I have ever come
across. What I want him to do is this.
I want the Minister of Finance to give
an assurance to this House that the poor
people of the city of Belfast, or of any
part of the Six Counties, are not going
to be held up to ransom to the extent of
3s 7d in regard to a matter which is
normally procurable for sixpence.
No poor children in the city of
Belfast or Northern Ireland should be
precluded from entering any educational
examination simply because the parents
cannot afford the money. If a man is
on the bureau and in receipt of benefit
it will be admitted that he has not got
any surplus three and seven pences to throw
away on copies of registration. I went
to the Corporation and I fought this out
on the Education Committee. I went
to another committee and assailed a body
of people there. Some of these are members of the board of guardians, and I
thought the responsibility lay with them.
I was told that the matter of stamp
duty rested with the Ministry of
Finance. My opinion is that some
definite understanding or law ought to
be laid down to cover all schools. It is
not right that children on entering the
elementary school should be compelled to
pay 6d, for a copy of registration, and
that the brothers and sisters of the same
children when they require the same
thing on entering a secondary school
examination should have to pay 3s 7d.
I ask the Minister to see that with the
usual meticulous care he expresses and

National Health Insurance and Contributory Pensions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.

Mr. GORDON: A Bill has been introduced in the Imperial Parliament to
amend the law relating to National Health
Insurance. It is not expected that this
Bill will reach the Statute Book until
after our Parliament has risen, and as
certain of these new provisions will
operate from July, 1935, it is necessary
that we make provision for their coming.
into operation at the same time as the
provisions become operative in Great
Britain. There are several reasons why
this uniformity of legislation must be
maintained, and although our Bill is
short, it is important, and I propose, even
at the risk of wearying the House, to
give a wide interpretation of its effect.
The National Health Insurance scheme
is an entity for the whole of the United
Kingdom. Many of its funds, such as
the Central Fund and the Reserve
Suspense Fund, are common to both
Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
British societies recruit members in
Northern Ireland. It follows, therefore,
that the law governing Health Insurance
must be identical in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. The Parliament of
Northern Ireland could not legislate in
respect of the common funds to which I
have referred, namely, the Central Fund
and the Reserve Suspense Fund, except at
the risk of destroying their United Kingdom character.
This position has previously been
recognised when Health Insurance amending legislation has been required in this
House, and in 1928 and 1932 power was
conferred by our Parliament on his Grace
the Governor to apply, by Order in
Council, the British Health Insurance
and Pensions Acts of those years to
Northern Ireland, with such adaptations
and modifications as were necessary. Our
present Bill proposes to confer similar
power. The United Kingdom Bill provides that in the event of the Parliament
of Northern Ireland making provision to
that effect the United Kingdom Act shall
extend to Northern Ireland. It further
stipulates that the provisions in it relating to the Unemployment Arrears Fund,
to which I shall refer later, shall not be
extended to Northern Ireland unless substantially corresponding provision is made
by the Parliament of Northern Ireland,
in which case an Order in Council may be
made under the United Kingdom Act to
provide that approved societies in
Northern Ireland may receive payments
from the Unemployment Arrears Fund.
The new proposals are designed to make
permanent provision for insurance
during genuine unemployment on conditions which, on the whole, are substantially more generous than any that
have been given before. The proposals
meet three needs of the unemployed
insured person, and I feel sure will meet
with approval from all sides of the House.
The unemployed insured person will no
longer have to pay arrears of contributions which have arisen through unemployment, and if he has been an insured
contributor for ten years he will be entitled to both medical benefit and full
pensions cover for life. This should dispel the gloom that overshadows the worker
who becomes unemployed, when he realises
that full provision is being made for him
in respect of pensions.
Under our present legislation an insured
person, on becoming unemployed, is entitled to a free period of insurance
amounting on the average to 21 months.
This right will continue in operation. I
should like to emphasise that the concession which at present is restricted to
persons aged 58 on becoming unemployed, will now be extended to all
persons irrespective of age, so that a man
who has ten years of insurance behind him
will be entitled to free insurance for
pensions purposes, and to medical benefit
for life during genuine unemployment.
He will also get any additional benefits,
such as dental or optical treatment given
by his society. The only condition is that
he shall produce evidence from year to
year that he has been genuinely unemployed.
The new provisions will impose an
additional burden on the Contributory
Pensions Fund. The cost will depend on
the future trend of employment, but it
is thought that the amount may rise from,
roughly, £2,000 in 1936/37 to between
£20,000 or £30,000 in 1942/43. We propose to remove a further burden from our
unemployed. In recent years insured

persons have been required to pay half
their Health arrears during unemployment. Under the new proposals these
payments will be abolished, and in order
to recoup societies for the loss involved a
fund will be created, know as the "Unemployment Arrears Fund."
Half of the income of the Fund will be
derived from societies themselves, by
means of deductions from contributions at
the same rate as in Great Britain, which
it is expected will be one-third of a penny
for each weekly contribution in the case
of a man, and one-ninth of a penny for
each weekly contribution in the case of a
woman. The other half of the income of
the Unemployment Arrears Fund will be
provided by an Exchequer grant, equal in
amount to the total deductions made from
contributions during the year. The
scheme, so far as the societies' contributions are concerned, may be termed a reinsurance scheme, towards which the
societies with the least unemployment will
pay the most.
Societies will receive grants from the
Fund at the rate of 3d for each week of
genuine unemployment of each member.
The societies which suffer most by unemployment will benefit the most from the
proposed scheme. The Bill now before
the House, in addition to providing for
the extension of the United Kingdom Act
by Order in Council, provides for the
Northern Ireland income of the Unemployment Arrears Fund. The permanent
provision is identical with the provisions
of the United Kingdom Bill. In the
British Bill, however, it is provided that
the surplus in the Navy, Army and Air
Force Insurance Fund shall be drawn on
in relief of the payment which the
Exchequer would be due to make.

Two minor matters are dealt with in

the

I now come to a matter of particular
interest to the hon. Member for Pottinger.
Our Bill also provides for the making of
reciprocal arrangements in regard to contributory pensions between Northern
Ireland and any part of His Majesty's
Dominions administering a similar

Member for Pottinger is aware.
Having presented the case for the Bill

Motion made, and Question proposed,
That in the opinion of this House, as

hundred and thirty-five, provision
should be made for the payment at the

twenty-three:
Provided that the total of such payments of two guineas per diem made to
any member in pursuance of this resolution shall not exceed the sum of fifty
guineas in any one year.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is unnecessary for
me to enlarge upon this Resolution, which
is self-explanatory. In fact, it has been
referred to in the course of the previous
debate this afternoon. It gives effect
to the Budget proposals of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Finance to pay
to hon. Members the sum of two guineas
for expenses in respect of attendances
at Special Committees of the House or
Joint Committees of the Senate and the
House. I beg to move.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I desire to oppose
this Motion, and I shall do so as briefly
as possible. I object entirely, as far as
I am personally concerned, to the payment of Members of this House for
attending Committee meetings. I do so
for several reasons. The first is that
they are paid a certain amount of money
which is considered suitable for their
expenses, and they ought to attend meetings of Committees, in my opinion, without any extra money being paid to them.
In order to make myself clear, I would
like to say that I opposed the payment
of Members from the very first. When
I became a Member of this House I
considered it sufficient honour to be a
Member without receiving any remuneration. The services rendered by Members
of this House before remuneration of
any description was given were quite
equal to the services rendered since.
I object on principle to such payments.
I consider £170 sufficient to meet the
expenses of Members. If we commence
to pay in this way we will do away with
voluntary service to a tremendous extent
throughout the country. In connection
with county councils, where the work is
much more onerous and the committee
meetings more numerous, the members
get nothing at all. In many cases applications have been made by those responsible for carrying out the financial
arrangements, and the applications have
been turned down. Now, if they are
brought up again I do not see how they
can be refused, because the people concerned will naturally say, "We look to
the House of Commons as our guide in
these things, and they pay their Members not only a certain amount for expenses but in addition they now pay
them for attending Committee meetings.
If they, the wisest people in the country,
the people who are appointed to govern
our State, do that then it must be right,
Payment of Members
Payment of Members

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Crawford]
and there is no reason why you should not
pay us too." The result will be that they
will have to be paid, and they have as
good a right as the people here. Boards
of guardians, rural district councils,
urban councils, all the administrative
bodies throughout the whole country will
be doing the same thing, and they can all
claim for their members equal right to
payment with the Members of this House.
It would be a tremendous mistake.
Then it would do away with all voluntary service. I am one of those who believe that voluntary service has been and
is of immense value to this country. Indeed, in my opinion, it has not been considered nearly valuable enough by a great
many people. I know men who have
given years of public service voluntarily,
who have done great and very useful work
without ever asking for a single penny of
expenses, and who are willing to continue
to do that voluntary work. If this is
passed all that will be done away with.
If the Minister had been looking round
for some way of spending a little money
it would have been much better if he had
cast his eyes on the people who are
regularly summoned to attend as jurors,
and had considered the question of paying their out-of-pocket expenses. Many
of the people who are called upon to serve
as jurors are men in poor circumstances,
who have to come from remote districts of
the county. They are brought in here to
answer their names and to serve as jurors,
and have to go back home and pay all
their expenses out of their own pockets.
I think that is a most unreasonable thing,
and if the Minister had included in his
Budget some amount to pay these people
their out-of-pocket expenses I would have
supported it with great pleasure.
When I commence to think of how we
are now doing away with all voluntary
service, putting paid officials in its
place, I am realy alarmed. The pensions.
committees, which gave their services
voluntarily, have been done away with;
insurance committees have been done away
with; public assistance committees are
going to be done away with, and paid
officials put in to do the work that formerly was done voluntarily; and now the
magistrates are going to be done away
with also and paid officials are going to
do a great deal of the work they used to
do. My belief is that soon nobody in
I
Northern Ireland will be asked to do anything without getting money for it.
regret that very much, and, as far as I
am concerned, I am going to vote against
it.

The PRIME MINISTER: The Cabinet
gave this matter very careful consideration along with other matters prior to
the introduction of the Budget. We felt
that it would be the desire of the House
not to ask for the restoration of the cut
in Members' expenses until all others outside the House had first of all been treated
in the same way.
We still hold that
opinion. We think that for Members
and Ministers to vote for themselves a
restoration of the fifteen per cent. cuts
prior to restoring the other cuts that have
not been restored would not be welcomed
by hon. Members on any side of the
House. But then we came to where there
was an inequality, and what appeared to
us to be an unfair discrimination between
Members of this House and the Members
of the Senate. We thought that, as we
claim to be, and are, a very democratic
assembly, Members should be entitled to
a fair remuneration for the work that
they do.
We felt that those who are rich
enough to avoid drawing any of their
salaries or allowances, or these fees
which we now suggest, need not do so,
but undoubtedly there are Members in
this House, of whom we know, who experienced a certain amount of financial
difficulty as a result of the recent cut in
their expenses.
This Resolution has
been brought forward by the Government
in the hope of solving the problem in the
meantime. It has been done with the
best intentions. The Government have
no wish whatever to press it on the House,
and what I suggest is that we should
leave it to a free vote of the House to
do what they think right in the matter.
My colleagues and myself will support it,
because we think it is right, and just,
and fair, but any other hon. Member
can take whatever course he likes.
Mrs. PARKER: We have just been

the same time I do feel very strongly.
with the hon. Member for Mid Antrim.

POMEROY WATER SUPPLY.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL (for Mr. Stewart)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware that the east and
west portions of the town of Pomeroy
have no water supply for domestic or
sanitary purposes; whether the lack of
water is a very serious menace to the
lives of the people who reside there, and
prevents milk producers from complying
with the requirements of the Milk
Board; whether he is aware that the
local authority, the Cookstown Rural
District Council, have arranged a scheme
to remedy this state of affairs, and what
steps he has taken to provide funds to
carry out this scheme.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I understand that
in some parts of Pomeroy, owing to the
level of the reservoir, the water supply
is deficient. I am aware that this has
caused inconvenience to milk producers
and others, but it would not appear from
the reports that have been received that
the situation is so serious as the hon.
Member suggests. The Cookstown Rural
District Council, which is the sanitary
authority for the town, some time ago
directed its engineer to prepare plans
for improving the supply, and these are
being awaited.
I have not been asked to provide funds
for carrying out the work, but an application for a loan will receive favourable
consideration when the plans are ready
and the estimated cost is known.

4. Mr. McCARROLL (for Mr. Healy)

whether his attention has been directed

John Curry, Aghintra, Derrylin, Co.

Kinawley, cycling from an opposite
direction, after midnight on 11th May,
and that Constable Blaney was riding
some yards behind the sergeant on an
unlighted cycle; whether Dr. Kidd
proved that death resulted from a wound
on the back of the head at the base of
the skull, which could hardly have
arisen from such a collision; whether
there was no mark on the sergeant's
bicycle; and whether he will hold a sworn
inquiry into this affair, as well as into
the manner in which Sergeant Stewart
discharges his duty generally.
Mr. SPEAKER: Is the hon. Member
sure that the hon. Member for South
Fermanagh wishes him to ask this particular question? Has he his authority?
MCCARROLL:
Mr.
authority.
I have his
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen
the depositions taken at the inquest on
the unfortunate young man referred to
by the hon. Member.
The facts are, briefly, as follow:-
The deceased, who was cycling without a
light, came into collision with Sergeant
Stewart, who was cycling in the opposite
direction, but whose bicycle was properly
lighted. As a result of the collision, the
deceased sustained a fracture of the base
of the skull, which proved fatal. Sergeant Stewart received slight cuts on his
face and left leg, but no injury of a
serious nature. Neither bicycle was
badly damaged.
The deposition of Dr. Kidd was not
to the effect suggested by the hon. Member, the doctor's evidence on the point
being merely that "the injury he (the
deceased) had could have been caused by
falling from a push bicycle on to the
road," and in answer to a question on
cross-examination the doctor stated "the
bruises were on the back of the head and
The
on the right side behind the ear.
head must have come into contact with
something."
There is nothing whatever to indicate
that this occurrence was anything more
than a most regrettable accident which
offers no grounds whatever for the suggestion that an inquiry should be held
into the sergeant's conduct.
It is a fact that Constable Blaney, who
was cycling behind the sergeant, had no
light on his bicycle. This matter, which,
however, had no connection with the
accident, is being inquired into.

(Northern Ireland), 1933, which came
into force on the first day of October,

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): Under the provisions of Section 1 of the Agricultural
Marketing Act (Northern Ireland),
1933, my Ministry was, subject to certain
conditions, empowered to frame agricultural marketing schemes. In the exercise of this power the Ministry framed
the Pigs Marketing Scheme (Northern
Ireland), 1933, which was approved on
the 6th September, and came into operation on the 1st October of that year.
This scheme has subsequently been
amended by the Ministry under the provisions of Section 1 (3) of the Agricultural Marketing Act. A copy of the
scheme in the form in which it exists
after these amendments is in the hands
of Members.
In sub-section 5 of Section 1 of the
Agricultural Marketing Act it is provided
that:
""
'A scheme approved by the
Ministry shall in any event cease to
have effect upon the expiration of a
period of two years from the date upon
which it came into force, unless at
some time before the expiration of
that period it has been approved by a
resolution passed by each House of
Parliament."
It is the purpose of the resolution which
I am submitting to the House to continue
the Pigs Marketing Scheme in force after
the 30th September next. I feel that
few words of mine will be necessary to
commend the resolution to the House.
2339 Pigs Marketing Scheme

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment
[Sir Basil Brooke]
Every hon. Member is familiar with
the striking increase in our pig population which has occurred during the past
three years.
It may be of interest to
the House to know that during the
eighty-five years from 1847 to 1931, the
greatest number of pigs ever recorded in
Northern Ireland at the June census was
296,000 in 1871. In 1932 the number
was 219,000. A year later they had
increased by 50,000, and two years later
by 160,000. At a census taken at the
1st December, 1934, the pig population
just exceeded 400,000, while a sample
inquiry taken at the 1st April this year
showed that the number had further
risen to 430,000. Within three years we
have expanded our pig production by
almost 50 per cent. above the highest
level ever previously attained. Whereas
in 1932 our output of pigs for bacon
curing was under 300,000, in the current
year the Imperial Government in its
arrangements for the reduction of
imports of bacon from abroad is allowing
for an output of 542,000 bacon pigs from
Northern Ireland.
The figures which I have quoted are,
I think, striking. They show that by
concentrating upon the pig question in
this country my Ministry has tackled the
question which gave the largest
possibility of expansion. But, of course,
an expansion of this magnitude could
not be carried out unless it was organised
in an efficient manner, and it is here that
the Pigs Marketing Board has played a
most important part. The increase in
pig production which has occurred has
outrun the ability of our existing bacon
factories to deal with it, and it has been
necessary to export large numbers of
pigs to Great Britain for curing there.
Such an increase in our export trade is
only a temporary development, I hope,
for the Government, and in fact all concerned, are aiming to have all the pigs.
cured in this country rather than ship
them to the other side. For obvious
reasons it gives more employment, and,
further than that, the cost of exporting
pigs to England is quite a considerable
amount. Hon. Members are aware that
two new factories for Wiltshire curing
have now been established in this country
-one at Portadown and the other at
Londonderry. If the latter is not
actually working, it will be working very
shortly. But during this difficult interim
period the Pigs Marketing Board has
accepted at the standard prices from producers all surplus pigs which cannot be
absorbed by the existing curing establishments, provided they are sold alive. The
Pigs Marketing Board, I think everyone
will admit, has established marketing
methods second to none. It has reduced
marketing costs. The Board, to put it
in the shortest possible way, has
established a great marketing organisation which exists to help the producers to
market their pigs to the best advantage.
In its early days the Pigs Marketing
Scheme provided that the Board should
also exercise certain functions in regard
to price fixing. By the Pig Industry
Act which was passed by Parliament last
autumn, however, these price fixing
powers were transferred to the Pig
Industry Council, which consists of three
representatives of producers and of
curers together with three independent.
members nominated by me. In consequence of the creation of this new body
the Pigs Marketing Scheme has been
amended so as to delete or modify certain
provisions in regard to price fixing.
I do not propose at this stage to submit a resolution continuing the existing
Bacon Marketing Scheme. The House
will recollect that under the recent Pig
Industry Act the functions which the
Bacon Board were created to perform
have been vested in either the Pig
Industry Council or the Ministry. In
these circumstances there is clearly no
need to continue an overlapping organisation, and indeed I have received
request from the Board to prolong the
scheme.
Question put, and agreed to.
Adjournment.

That they had considered Scott's Divorce

Resolved: "That notwithstanding any
Standing Order or Custom of the House
the remaining stages of the Appropriation

Adjournment of the House (Summer).
Resolved: "That this House at its
rising this day do adjourn until Wednesday, 10th July, for the consideration of
Senate's amendments, and at its rising that
day do adjourn until Twelve o'clock noon
on Tuesday, 16th July, and that after
the Report of Royal Assent to Bills
agreed to by both Houses, Mr. Speaker
do adjourn the House, without Question
put, until Tuesday, 8th October, provided always that if, during any of these
adjournments of the House, it appears to
the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the Government, that the
public interest requires that the House
shall meet at any earlier time, Mr.
Speaker may give notice that he is so
satisfied and thereupon the House shall
meet at the time stated in such notice
and shall transact its business as if it had
been duly adjourned to that date."—
(The Prime Minister).

including Ulster, and we had to do all
we possibly could to get a share of the
British market. Had we not got this
Act upon the Statute Book, I say with
every confidence, that we could not have
sold a single apple in England at allnot one.
The hon. Member says that we have
compulsion here, and that in England
they have got only a voluntary manner
of dealing with the same thing. It is by
the expressed wish of the great majority
of the apple growers that we have compulsion here. I am quite sure that if we
had the voluntary method here, and if

topped apples or inferior apples, they
would immediately bring down disgrace
upon the Ulster exports, which would be
prejudicial to all those who really play
the game.
The same thing applies to potatoes.
Some years the price soars to £5 a ton;
in other years we see the price down, as
it has been recently, to even 15s. I may
be exaggerating; I have not got the exact
figures, but I know that that was so when
I was a boy. You cannot foretell these
things, but what you can foretell is this,
that if it were not for the grading system,
and rigid adherence to that system, our
market across the water would simply
vanish altogether. Why should it be
otherwise?

Mr. HEALY: Yesterday I had on the
Order Paper a question concerning the
death of a young man named John Curry,
at a place called Derrylin, in County
Fermanagh. It concerned a head-on
collision between this civilian and a sergeant of police. The sergeant of police,
Sergeant Isaac Stewart, of Kinawley, was
proceeding towards Derrylin from a place
called Teemore, and behind him a few
paces was riding a police constable named
Blaney. At the cross-roads there was
standing that night the brother of the
deceased boy. He had a clear view of
the road, and he swore at the inquestand I do not think there was any doubt
that he was telling the truth-that the
deceased had a lighted bicycle. The deceased was proceeding in the direction
from which the two policemen were
coming. According to the sergeant's
evidence deceased approached him with
an unlighted bicycle, although the only
civilian witness in the case swears that
deceased had a lighted bicycle. The
civilian witness, again the brother of deceased, swore that looking down the road
he did not observe any light approaching,
which he would have quite easily
observed if the sergeant had had a lighted
bicycle. It is curious in this connection

our own commonsense would tell us that

mark on the deceased, on the sergeant,
or on the bicycles of both of them. But
there was nothing of the kind. This is
one of those cases that deserves a little
more consideration than it received at.
the inquest. The inquest was held in
Enniskillen town, about ten miles from
where deceased came. He died in hospital, and practically never recovered
consciousness.
The people in the district believe that
there is something to investigate, not
merely in relation to this matter, but in
relation to the way Sergeant Isaac
Stewart discharges his duties generally
on the Customs patrol in this area. He
is a very zealous man, and my information is that even on suspicion he can
become very aggressive with the people
in the locality. There was a suspicion
in his mind, I think, that the deceased
was engaged in smuggling and that his
brother was, perhaps, also engaged in that
enterprise. But the amazing thing is
that when this accident occurred, if the
story which the sergeant told is true,

there was nothing of the kind. It is
also significant that the deceased did not
fall off his own bicycle at the point where
the collision occurred, but was able to
proceed eight yards further down the
road and then dropped unconscious.
The people of the district are not satisfied that Sergeant Isaac Stewart is a man
who ought to be discharging the important duties which fall to his lot at the
present time.

PROVIDED AND VOLUNTARY
SCHOOLS.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether his attention has been
directed to the statement in the Imperial
Parliament last month of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Education
on the Vote for that Board to the effect
that by general agreement the time has
come for the co-operation and sinking of
differences between the provided and the
voluntary schools, and for placing the
interests of the children in front of everything else.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): I have seen
the statement of the President of the
Board of Education to the effect mentioned
in the hon. and learned Member's question, and I earnestly commend it to the
attention of the managers of voluntary
schools in Northern Ireland.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask if the
Parliamentary Secretary would earnestly
commend it to the Minister?
REPAIRS TO VOLUNTARY
SCHOOLS.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state how many
of the seven hundred voluntary schools
which are not under County Council con-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Campbell]
trol are in urgent need of repairs, and
the sum total of public money spent on
repairs of the schools under County
Council control since the Education Act,
1923.
Mr. ROBB: In reply to the hon. and
learned Member, I would point out that
the number of voluntary public elementary schools was 1,173 on 31st December,
1934, and not 700, as suggested in the
question.
No precise figure can be given as to
the number of schools in this total which
are in urgent need of repairs, but, with
the exception of 81 school buildings which
are vested in, and maintained by, the
Ministry, it would appear from the reports of the Ministry's inspectors that
there is a large number which urgently
require attention.
In reply to the second part of the
question, I regret that I am unable to
state the amount spent upon repairs as
distinct from enlargement and improvement in the case of transferred schools,
as such information is not available in
the Ministry. The cost of repairs is not
shown separately from the cost of enlargement and improvement of schools, but it
may be of some assistance to the hon.
Member if I give him the total amount
spent upon the enlargement, improvement
or reconditioning of transferred schools
where the cost in any one case did not
exceed £100. This total, up to 31st
December, 1934, was £21,874.

BAND'S PARADE THROUGH YORK
STREET.
6. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
on Sunday, June 23, a band named the
Lord Carson Flute Band paraded on two
occasions through York Street in the face
of police warnings, and in breach of his
order banning such parades, and whether
the issue of an order, which can thus be
openly flouted, is calculated to bring the
law into disrepute.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As prosecutions arising out of the incident referred
to have been directed by the Attorney-
General, the matter is sub judice, and
it would, therefore, be improper for me
to make any further statement in regard
to the hon. Member's question.
DISTURBANCES IN BELFAST.
7. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of persons who have sustained
injuries arising out of street disturbances
in Belfast since 1st May last; whether
during that period damage has been done.
to the houses of over 40 Catholic citizens
during parades of irresponsible bands
accompanied by their followers; whether
the recent recrudescence of disorder is
not in a large degree attributable to the
action of the Government in issuing an
order prohibiting band parades and
immediately afterwards revoking such
order.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Since the first
of May last 26 persons have sustained
injuries in street disturbances in Belfast.
I am glad to say that none of these
injuries was fatal, and most were of a
minor character.
During the same period a considerable.
amount of window breaking and other
damage to property was caused, but this
was not confined to the property of
citizens of any particular creed.
Most of this disorder took place prior
to the issue of the order referred to by
the hon. and learned Member, and I cannot accept the suggestion contained in the
last paragraph of the hon. and learned
Member's question.
Mr. CAMPBELL: In view of the unsatisfactory nature of the reply, I will
call attention to this matter on the Motion
for the Adjournment.
Mr. MURPHY: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if it is not a fact that
these disorders in Belfast are to a large
extent attributable to the disloyal and
mendacious manifesto signed by, amongst
others, the hon. and learned Member for
Central.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Undoubtedly
statements such as that referred to by
the hon. and learned Member for Derry
City are factors in the situation, and I
deplore them very much.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman seriously suggest that as an
answer for the consideration of the House?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do. I did
not understand the hon. and learned
Member intended to put that supplementary question.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE

In submitting men for work on relief
schemes the Department gives first consideration to those unemployed men who

until these men have been absorbed, to

scutchers, who are ordinarily employed f -
a considerable portion of the year in uninsurable agricultural work, and the

account uninsurable work towards the
fulfilment of conditions for benefit in
respect of insurable work.

JUVENILES IN INDUSTRY.
12. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Labour whether it is a fact
that juveniles are in increasing numbers
displacing men in important industries in
Northern Ireland, and whether he can
state the number of youths of, or about,
16 years of age who are available for
employment according to the latest
returns.
In putting this question to the Minister
of Labour will you allow me to say that
he has general sympathy in the accident
which has befallen him. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. GORDON: I will take the earliest
opportunity of conveying the sympathy of
the hon. and learned Gentleman to the
Minister of Labour.
The statistics compiled by my Department do not show that there is any increasing tendency of recent years towards
the displacement of men by juveniles in
industries in Northern Ireland.
In 1931 the average of the monthly
figures representing males employed in
insurable occupations was, approximately,
114,500, of whom 8,750 were boys aged
over 16 and under 18, and 12,500 were
aged over 18 and under 21. The corresponding figure for 1934 was 119,500 males
employed in insurable occupations, of
whom about 7,000 were aged over 16 and
under 18, and about 13,200 were aged
over 18 and under 21. The monthly
averages for the first half of the year
1935 show no change from the 1934 position.
The number of youths over 17 years of
age and under 19 years of age available
for employment is about 1,450.

aware that there are at least 4,000 or

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have had enquiries

Member's question and am informed that,
following on Press advertisements and
subsequent interviews with a number
of candidates, the Electricity Board
appointed on 1st November, 1934, Mr. A.

in the Board's operations, and to a decision to use their headquarters' stores
as a distributing centre for consumers'
appliances, the Board appointed Mr. W.
J. Ferguson to take charge of that department. This appointment is additional to

of stores since August last, but who, I am
informed, had no wide experience of, or
training in, such matters. I am advised
that in making the later appointment the
Board sifted the many applications before

large number of applications before them,

Mr. CAMPBELL: It behoves one to
speak with restraint upon a situation of
gravity, aggravated as it was by the
vacillation and blundering of the Government. I hope no voice will be raised
in this House except in denunciation of
recent outbreaks of mob ruffianism which
are disgracing the city and hurting the
trade of the city and disgusting decent
citizens. In these outbreaks the York
Street area was the storm centre. For
some time past that area has been infested with nests of armed gangsters.
Outrage has followed outrage there without detection. Intimidation of traders
and workers has been rampant. An inoffensive and esteemed Catholic gentleman was murdered in the main street,
and the murderers have never been
brought to justice. The Catholic population is comparatively weak, and in parts
of the district is grouped together in
clusters of streets for mutual protection.
They have been experiencing mob law for
weeks; yet Catholic police are being
transferred from the district.
Onslaughts have been made on their
homes, which bear signs of deliberate
planning. In one particularly stormy
quarter the police drove off the attackers,
who fled into adjoining houses, and from
their fastnesses, through open windows
and even roofs, stoned the police. It is
alleged that police in the conflict damaged
some of these houses. I am very glad
to say, from the information which I
have, and in which I believe, that not
one solitary Catholic member of the force
was on duty on that occasion.
Mr. HANNA: That is not so.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I repeat it.

What was inevitable followed. Provocative parades by the brisk lads whom

Attacks on Catholics and Catholic houses

quarter was being rapidly reduced to the

riots of Lord George Gordon. We are
coming back to the state of civilisation

The situation became
so bad that the Minister found it necessary last month to issue an order prohibiting parades and processions in the
city.
Within a few days-on Sunday, 23rd
June-an incident happened, but as the
Minister said to-day a prosecution had
been directed. I am precluded by the
rule of debate from saying anything about
it. The Grand Master next indulged in
quixotic mock-heroics, and boasted that

Twelfth, order or no order. The Minister climbed down-slid down with
rapidity. He revoked his order in
haste. This haste was strange in a
Minister who, like Richard Brinsley
Sheridan, never does in these matters
to-day what he can put off till to-morrow.
What followed this weak and panicky
surrender? Irresponsible bands swarmed
out over the streets. The riff-rafi
re-emerged, bent on loot. Rioting,
stone-throwing, and attacks on property
marked the passage of the band parades.
On July 2 a most deplorable incident
occurred. Three men were shot during
disorder in the vicinity of Upper Library
Street.
On 3rd July a mob, blind to Christian
charity, halted, danced and jeered,
shouting party cries and foul expressions
in front of the Mater Hospital. Passing
down the Crumlin Road they hurled
stones in whatever Catholic houses they
could identify. They went up the
Antrim Road, blazing a trail of shattered
windows on their way. No baton
charges were made. No arrests were
made. Vigorous action on the part of
a few police would have scattered the
mob to the winds. But nothing was
done. So recently as Monday, and again
last night, there was an orgy of disorder
around Annadale Street a Catholic
quarter. The bands were still abroad.
The Minister was happy. The Catholics,
indefensible to a large extent, knowing
the odds against them and knowing the
official forces on the other side, endured
in patience in the face of the grossest
provocation. But for their forbearance
matters would have been much worse.
How is it that so many of these rioters
are armed? It is a most deplorable thing
that in poor quarters of the city of
Belfast, where the people are hardly able
to get dinner or breakfast, there should
be this profusion of firearms to the deadly
danger of innocent people. Why are so
many firearms abroad in this city? Whe
are they not taken from these people? Is
it because of the weakness of the Executive, or is it that the crowd in Belfast is
the law? Is the mob the law? The
Minister of Home Affairs, as I have said.
badgered and menaced by the crowd,

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): I think that if there was
anything needed to show the difficulties
of the Government and the difficulties
that confront the police force from the
Inspector-General down to the latest
member of that force one would have it
in the two speeches the House has just
listened to. The hon. and learnd Member
for Central asked were the police neutral.
I wish to say on behalf of the Government, on behalf of the Inspector-General,
and on behalf of the police force as a
whole, that the police force are neutral
under very difficult circumstances, and
that they do their best, as they are bound
to do, with the assistance of the Government behind them, to preserve law and
order in this city. I must say that some
of the things that have been said in this
House this afternoon are not going to
make it any easier for the police or for
the Government.
It is unnecessary to point out that you
have, on the one hand, the hon. and
learned Member for Central complaining
that the people who belong to his political
party and his political faith are murdered
in the streets of Belfast; while, on the
other hand, the Member for Duncairn
complains that the dice has been loaded
against the party to which he belongs. I
can assure this House that so far as the
administration of the police force and of
justice is concerned, the Government does
its best to see that justice is meted out
with an even hand to both parties, and
they will continue to do so. May I say
that from my knowledge, which is perhaps not so perfect as it might be, of
recent happenings in Belfast I agree with
what has been said by the Member for
Duncairn, that there has been a great
deal of exaggeration both in the Press
and elsewhere. At the same time, no
Member of the Government who has any
responsibility for the maintenance of law
and order; no Member who has any responsibility to his constituents, and no citizen
can lose sight of this fact, that behind a
lot of this sporadic disorder there are
people in this city on both sides who are
armed with lethal weapons. It
is
immaterial for the purposes of this debate
to say whose fault it is.
We all know that up to the year 1907
arms were proscribed in this country, and
that it was the leader of the party to
which the hon. and learned Member for
Central belongs who got that embargo
withdrawn. I always thought that that
was one of the worst days in the history
of this country, and that has since been
proved to be true. Whoever is responsible, the Government and the police know
that arms are there, and that at any
moment what in the old days might be a
mere riot may nowadays take on a complexion very much more serious, and one
which it would take the whole of the
armed forces of the Crown to deal with.
Therefore, it is not a matter the police or
the Government can play with, and they
are bound to do the very best they can
to see that these disorders do not spread
throughout the city.
These disorders broke out, and in an
endeavour to preserve the peace of the
city certain steps were taken by the police.
I am not going to refer to matters in
controversy; I am dealing with matters
of policy and not detail. Certain matters
had to be dealt with by the police, and
certain orders had to be made. The
Member for Duncairn has said that he
approved of the order made by the
Minister as regards the imposition of
curfew and keeping the people in a certain
area inside their houses during the night.
We all know, and the Member for Duncairn knows as well as I do, that these
orders are only temporary, and are made
only for the purpose of preserving order,
and that when it seemed that things had
settled down, and that the necessity for
these orders had passed away they would
be withdrawn, because the Government
does not wish to interfere with the rights
and liberties of the citizens either of this
city or any other except so far as is necessary for their own protection and the preservation of order. But it was found
that that was not sufficient. Unfortunately there were some shooting episodes,
Adjournment-
Belfast Disturbances
10 JULY 1935
which looked as if they might develop
into something more serious.
One of the things which gave rise to
trouble was processions, and they were
temporarily suspended. It was said by
the Member for Duncairn that this was
an insult to the party which he represents, but it was an order that was made
not as an insult to any Order or any
party. It was not directed against any
body of individuals. It was merely an
order made, whether rightly or wrongly,
in the interests of the citizens as a whole
and in an attempt to preserve peace, and
I am glad to say it has been abundantly
successful. I hope there will be no
further outbreak of trouble in the city
or elsewhere. In some places the making
of these orders has been construed into a
confession of failure on the part of the
police. It is suggested that they were not
able to maintain order by their own force
and by their own power, and that therefore, they had to have these orders made
to assist them. I think the citizens at
large realised what lay behind all these
troubles and the possibility of very much.
greater disturbances than actually took
place, and they will agree that the
measures taken by the Government have
had the necessary effect. The city has
now, I sincerely hope, settled down once
again to a state of peace and tranquillity.

This debate has taken two lines.
is criticism of what has happened in the
city, and the other goes back to the
causes which lay behind all these troubles.
It is necessary to keep the two distinct.
I deplore the speech we have listened to
this afternoon from the hon. and learned
Member for Central. If there is any
speech that could have been made here
that is calculated to lead to further
trouble it is that speech, because while
complaining that the party to which he
adheres was treated by the police in a
partial manner, which I, as representing
the Government, deny-
Mr. CAMPBELL: I never made such
an allegation, not for one moment.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: When
he said that the anti-Catholic hatred was
fomented by people who are in high
quarters he was only throwing further
oil upon the flames. That speech of his
this afternoon is calculated to have the
very opposite effect to that which he
would have the House believe he desired
in his heart, namely, to attempt to preserve the peace of the city. The hon.
and learned Member has, if I may say so,
been fishing in troubled waters. He
would be much better advised to try to
assist the forces of the Government in
maintaining peace than in attempting to
rake up ancient matters which, while
they may or may not be true, are at any
rate not going to help the Government
or the police to maintain the peace of
this city.
When the hon. and learned Member
gave us the dissertation he did this afternoon upon loyalty and disloyalty, I could
only think that he was deliberately
attempting to use these very awkward
situations which arise from time to time
in this city for political purposes, while
at the same time pretending he was endeavouring to assist the Government and
the police force in maintaing order in
the community. His speech is one which
should never have been made. I think
that, whether it was intended or not, it
will have an effect which is very detrimental to the peace of the community.
I certainly think that at this time, when
the police are endeavouring to preserve
the peace of the city, it is improper to
endeavour to make party and political
capital out of what may turn out to
affect the peace and the life of the city
which the Government are endeavouring
to preserve.
The peace of the city, I hope, is now
secured. So far as the police are concerned, I think that throughout the
whole of the trouble they have behaved
with exemplary forbearance. It is all
very
well to talk in this House about
what happens in these disturbed areas,
but I can assure hon. Members that if
they were down in these areas while the
trouble is on, when at any moment men
may appear out of a side street armed
with lethal weapons, while people are
running out of one street into
another, and it is impossible to identify
them in the crowd, the position
of the police is not an enviable one. They
deserve the support not only of every
Member of this House but of every loyal
citizen. If this debate has served any
purpose at all it shows that so far as
the police are concerned they have an
unenviable job to perform, and I am

Mr. NIXON: I would like to say at
the outset that there is one thing we
can all say about the Attorney-General,
and that is that he is one man occupying
a high political position in Northern
Ireland who never made a speech outside
or inside this House or elsewhere that
was calculated to incite the people or
lead to disturbance. If everyone modelled
their speeches on those of the Attorney-
General I think there would be less
trouble. I can say the same about the
Minister of Commerce and the Minister
of Finance, and I will stop there. There
is nothing so painful as to make a speech
calculated to lead unthinking people into
committing excesses, and then arresting
and prosecuting them for it. I hope
that any speeches to be made here this
afternoon-of course, I have no control
over them-while they may contain
straight criticism, will not be calculated
to make things worse than they are.
The Minister's reply to my question
about the police excesses in Grove Street
and other streets was fair enough up to
a point. But this occurred on the 11th
May, and it is time something definite
was done. It happened two months ago.
I want to say that the section of the
police that misbehaved on that night
do not represent the police force as a
body. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
By no means do they do that. Since I
became connected with the police I have
never seen any policeman do anything
improper, and this is the only time I
have had occasion to take exception to
what the police have done.
But I will try to give you some good
advice before I go any further. It was
slightly touched on by the hon. Member
for Duncairn (Mr. Grant). What has
largely led up to all the trouble has been
the policy of transferring useful policemen that has been going on for the past
three years.
The policeman who comes
into the city may be as good a man as
the man who goes out-he may, indeed,
be a better man-but he does not know
the people, the people do not know him,
and human nature does not respect new
authority. When I came to this city
first I was in Dover Street-it was a very
disturbed area at that time and the
senior head-constable would not trust any
man alone until he had had two years' experience in the city. From my own
experience I quite agree with that. When
a strange head-constable stands up in
front of a lot of men to send them out
to duty, he does not know where to
send them, he does not know the right
man to send to the right place, but the
man with experience stands up, looks at
his men, and with the whole locality in
his head he knows the sore points, he
knows the people, and he says "Constable
Brown, go you to such a place," and
so on, and so he tells off his men.
One sensible man with good local know
ledge is worth twenty without that
knowledge. The man without local
knowledge, instead of keeping the peace,
may raise a row. The man with local
knowledge goes along, meets someone
whom he knows to be a respectable man,
and has a friendly chat with him, while
the man without local knowledge may
meet the same man and say to him, "Get
away home out of this.” And so he gets
that man's back up, as well as the backs
of a lot of other people. I am sorry for
the present Commissioner, because I know
him to be a very efficient officer, but he
has to deal with a situation for which
he is not responsible. I am as sure as
I am standing here that if these transfers
had not been going on for some years
we would not be debating this subject
this afternoon at all. I am sure of that,
and I have a right to know.
When the Attorney-General states that
the police did everything with great forebearance I disagree with him in regard
to this one event. I disagree with him
in regard to that entirely. Here the
people were in their own houses. There
was curfew in the area. The police had
an armoured car, so that if the people
had tried to throw anything at them,
which I deny, they could not have done
them any injury if they stayed in the car.
