Now what about the ban-the one a.m.
ban on all processions except funerals? As
a matter of fact there must be something
peculiar in the minds of the people who
drafted that, because it was not necessary
to except funerals. No one ever regarded
a funeral as a procession.
You never
heard a man who was at a funeral saying,
"I was at John Thompson's procession
to-day." It simply shows the panicky
state of mind of the Minister and the
Inspector-General on the occasion. The
hon. Member for Duncairn says it was
not the Minister who drafted it, and I
myself do not think the Minister would
call a funeral a procession.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is quite common.
Mr. NIXON: A funeral is a procession?
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes, quite common.
Mr. NIXON: Not in our part of the
town. At all events, why should all processions be banned simply because some
people misbehave themselves? If I do
anything in this House contrary to the
Standing Orders or regulations, or if I
defy Mr. Speaker, I will be ordered out,
and if I do not go out I will be put out.
But are all the Members of the House to
be put under restriction or restraint for
what one Member does? And are all
processions in Belfast to be banned and all
the people in Belfast to be restricted because something happens down York Street?
Nothing happened on the Shankill. Why
should processions be banned there? Now
listen. There is an old saying that "Wide
will wear and tight will tear." If you are
too ready with your bans in Northern
Ireland you will get the people to break
them. The Minister of Home Affairs
himself has often commended the attitude
of the late William Johnston of Ballykillbeg in defying the Party Processions
Act and in going to jail for two months,
and in going from jail to Parliament and
thereby securing the repeal of that Act.
I wonder did he think of that when he
was putting on the ban at one a.m.

[Mr. Nixon]
No, the ban will not do in this city.
I will not stand at this Table, or any
other place in this House, to defend anyone who does wrong or who does any overt
act to break the peace. Under no circumstances will I defend such a person. But
I say it is a bad policy to try to curtail
the liberty of everyone because of the
actions of a few. Civil and religious
liberty. Civil liberty includes the right
of law-abiding peaceful men to march the
streets of Belfast. This is a Protestant
Parliament, we are assured by the Prime
Minister, for a Protestant people, and I
submit as an argument against the ban
that if this is a Protestant Parliament for
a
Protestant people, as the Prime
Minister says it is, it should be competent
for a Protestant band to march the Protestant streets of the Protestant city of
Belfast playing "The Protestant Boys"
in front of a Protestant procession going
to a Protestant place of worship to hear
Divine service celebrated according to the
Protestant ritual by a Protestant clergyman.
Mr. HENDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mr. NIXON: I submit that that
should take place in this city without a
permit, and, moreover, it will take place.
But, although I say all that, I still say
that if anyone does wrong there is a way
to deal with him. Now, the Attorney-
General made a somewhat alarming statement about arms in the hands of parties
on both sides. I really do not think
there is at the moment any very sinister
influence behind it. I hope the Attorney-
General is mistaken in that, because if
his statement be correct it discloses a
very serious situation. At all events,
the way to deal with that is to deal with
the people who have those arms, and
there is a way of getting at them. You
do not gain anything by antagonising
law-abiding people by refusing to allow
them to walk the streets in an orderly
well-behaved procession. A short time
ago I am telling this for what is it
worth-a very respectable man was complaining about the police. As I say I
have no complaint to make except in this
one instance. He said, "If you want the
police you will have to go to the golf
links for them. If you look at the
pictures in the papers now you will see
the police all over the show playing golf."
Then, during the trouble, when things
were at their worst, the Commissioner had
to go to England to attend a golf competition. Well, there was not much golf
in my time. There were three people
shot at Carrick Hill-I think, perhaps,
two or three speakers have referred to
this-and the shots came from Carrick
Hill. I know a man who was at a
window looking out; he saw the shots
being fired, and there were no policemen
there. Someone was at fault for that.
There should have been police there.
There should have been cars at Carrick
Hill and other dangerous points, and if
that had been done there would not have
been half the trouble. The authorities
have in these cars a weapon that was not
dreamt of in the old days. I would
sooner have a car than a hundred policemen it demoralises the people who wish
to create disorder. People know there
are guns in the car; there is nothing
better than a car for dealing with a mob.
I hope I have not said anything to
make things worse. I do think that if
the Minister of Home Affairs would
attend to my remarks about the transfer
of police and also about using these cars
more freely, without waiting until the
situation gets out of hand altogether,
good would result. Do not be in a hurry
putting on bans on processions, because
when
you do that you are up against
people who are not inclined to do any
harm, you are antagonising them, you are
There is no good in
making trouble.
looking for trouble. We get plenty of
trouble in our lifetime without looking
for it. At any rate I hope the position
will improve. I think it has improved.
I may just go back for a moment to
say this. This matter of what happened
in Grove Street has been under consideration for two months. Nothing has been
done, although there is promise in the
Minister's reply that something will be
done. I know that orders have been
issued to prosecute the band for something that happened on the 23rd June.
There was not much time lost there. The
Government might have acted with a
little more promptitude-not that I want
to see anyone victimised to any great
extent, but I want to see something done
on the lines of justice, something that will
give confidence to the people that when
they are locked in their houses at night
nobody will be allowed to bludgeon them
in their own homes. That is all.

Mr. BEATTIE: I want to say that I
deplore the discussion that has taken place
in the House to-day, and that I deplore
it from two points of view. I am a representative of the working classes of all
religious beliefs, and when I came into
Parliament I tried to the best of my
ability to represent both Catholics and
Protestants. The hon. Member for Duncairn, who is now proceeding outside,
would be well advised to remain in his
seat, because the Member for the Division
in which the trouble first broke out has
not yet mentioned anything about the
trouble. Hearing of the trouble and the
difficulties that had arisen, I made a personal visit to the area, and I saw for
myself the grave difficulties of anyone who
had control of the lawful authority. But
to-day's speeches from the hon. Member
for Duncairn and other hon. Members will
not help to ease off the situation in other
areas, apart from the area first referred
to. There was an occasion on which a
transfer took place from Mountpottinger
Barracks. I am going to justify that
transfer, for it led to peacefulness in the
area. For the hon. Member for Duncairn
to say that the transfer of a head-constable
from Mountpottinger was the cause of
some trouble in Grove Street is a very farfetched statement.
Mr. HENDERSON: I am sure that
every Member of the House regrets
that the hon. Member for Pottinger has
lost his voice. I think he was on the right
lines. What has happened here to-day
has not been a credit to this House.
Everyone has lost sight of the fact that
the Prime Minister himself brought the
heads of some of the English newspaper
syndicates over here to advertise Ulster.
Those people have been responsible during
the past two or three months for doing
terrible harm to Ulster, owing to striking
headlines such as "Cloud Over Belfast,'
and "Armoured Cars in the Streets."
Those are the people the noble Lord
brought over to advertise Ulster. Instead
of doing that, those newspaper magnates
have practically destroyed the tourist
traffic of Northern Ireland.
I am
sure it will interest the hon.
Member who represents one of the constituencies of Antrim to know that in one
of the principal hotels there last year
there were from 200 to 300 people. When
I was there at the beginning of last week
I was told by a responsible authority that
there were only 15 tourists coming on
Monday. That is terrible. We have
spent thousands of pounds in advertising
Ulster, and all the good that was done by
the Tourist Development Association has
been undone. The Gentlemen who are
responsible for this are sitting on the
other side of the House. Did you ever hear
such an indictment as that which came
from the hon. Member for Duncairn this
afternoon. The indictment made by the
hon. Member for Duncairn would justify
the electors in asking the Government to

hooliganism has been rampant in parts of
Belfast. We have a responsible Minister,
the Attorney-General, making the alarming statement in this House that the forces
of disorder have more guns, practically

anxiety of those who have guns to use
them I do not know what would.
Actually you have the
have the Attorney-
General admitting to this House that the
people who are responsible for law and
order cannot combat the people who have
the guns. I think that is a terrible admission. It is the duty of the Government
of the country to see that ample protection is given to the citizens who behave
themselves. I take very strong exception.
to the conduct of the Minister of Home
Affairs in putting a ban on the loyal

people. On every platform in the country.
the Government have prated about their

—
I should like to ask - Did the
Minister in an unthoughtful moment give
a promise to the hon. and learned
Member for Central Belfast that this
Protestant band would be prosecuted in
order to please him? Could any Protestant in Northern Ireland realise that
a band going out from its headquarters
to take part in a procession to church
would be prosecuted? I think that is too
terrible for words. I think the Minister
of Home Affairs and the Parliamentary
Secretary have been guilty of something
Adjournment-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
that is going to do untold harm in Northern Ireland. That does not come well
from the boosters of Protestantism, from
the people who prate about their Protestantism, and who got into this House
on the backs of Protestants and Orangemen.
Now they are going to prosecute
a Protestant band. I say it is a shame.
I am strongly opposed to any section
of the community being interfered with
by anyone. The police are there to defend them. But what are the facts today? Is it not true to say that the police
deliberately went down into Grove Street,
broke the windows of the houses, battered
in the doors, and reduced the children in
those homes to a state of absolute terror.
Just picture the Minister of Home
Affairs and the Parliamentary Secretary
living in one of those homes in Grove
Street. Picture the policemen coming in
with their batons, breaking the windows,
and bursting open the doors, and the
heads of the houses standing with their
wives and children clinging to them. It
is unthinkable that this could have
happened in Belfast, especially in view
of the fact that you had imposed curfew,
that these people's doors were closed, and
that they were in their own homes. I,
like other hon. Members, regret what has
taken place here to-day.
In so far as the Orange Order is concerned, they have nothing to do, good,
bad, or indifferent, with the trouble that
has taken place. They do not countenance it in any way, and I hope that if
any Members of this House think the
Orange Order had any responsibility for
those disturbances they will disabuse
their minds of such a thing. At the
same time I want to protest strongly
against the people being denied the right
to walk through the streets of Belfast.
The Attorney-General made a terrible
admission when he suggested that the
forces of the law were almost afraid to
take action. You would think Belfast
was Chicago. The Attorney - General
stated that irresponsible persons of both
religious beliefs had so many arms that
the Government were almost afraid of a
revolution breaking out, although he did
not use the word "revolution." It is the
duty of the Minister of Home Affairs and
the police to see that no unauthorised
person possesses a revolver or a gun, just
as it is the duty of the police to see that
every citizen of Northern Ireland is given
ample protection. I have the greatest
confidence in the police force, although I
resent what was done in Grove Street.
I believe this is an opportune time for the
Minister of
take
Home Affairs to
immediate action. The present state of
affairs cannot be allowed to continue much
longer, because in the event of any Protestant or Catholic or anyone else being
killed or injured through shooting, the
persons I will hold responsible will be the
Minister of Home Affairs and the
Inspector-General.
The Inspector-General has ample power
and ample forces for searching homes for
firearms, and I believe the police force
in Northern Ireland is strong enough to
protect the people against irresponsibles
who come into the country with revolvers
and rifles. This has been going on for
some time and no action has been taken
by the Government other than putting a
ban on processions, which made
the Minister of Home Affairs the
laughing stock of the whole of
Northern Ireland. First of all he put

visited Ulster, and then he put on this

placing them almost in the centre of
Royal Avenue. I believe that a great

Even the Government's staunchest supporters have turned against them on this
question. It would have been all right
if the Government had placed a ban on
those responsible for the disturbances,

Orange processions is absolutely terrible.
Could the Parliamentary Secretary or
the Deputy Speaker of this House justify
the Government's action on any Orange
platform during the coming Twelfth
celebrations. What made them do it I
cannot understand.
I, like other hon. Members, hope we
have seen the last of these troubles,

prosperous,

hope the Government will see that no

STAFF CONGESTION AT STORMONT
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he is now in
a position to inform the House of the steps
which he has taken to relieve congestion
in the accommodation of the staff at
Stormont due to the newly-established
Agricultural Marketing Schemes, and to
other developments in the Service.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
I have been asked to
(Mr. Barbour):
reply on behalf of my right hon. Friend.
The Ministry of Finance has entered.
into an agreement to purchase the block
known as "Berrington's Buildings" in
Ormeau Avenue, for the purpose of
relieving the congestion in the accommodation of the staff at Stormont.
The House will, however, be glad to
know that actually no expense to the
Northern Ireland Exchequer is involved,
as the cost of purchase and of adaptation
will be met from the surplus in the Capital
Building Fund originally handed over by
the Imperial Government.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of that reply, could the Minister state the
amount of the surplus in this Capital
Fund No. 2 and the cost of this building
they have just bought?
Mr. BARBOUR: The purchase price
of the building was £7,650. The purchase
price and the estimated cost of adaptation
together amount to £20,000. After this
expenditure has been met, the balance left
in the Capital Fund will be approximately
£14,000.

Oral Answers to Questions.
CHEAP MILK FOR SCHOOL
CHILDREN.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he can
state when he proposes, in conjunction
with the Minister of Education, to introduce a scheme for the provision of cheap
milk to school children as promised a
year and a half ago.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I dealt with this subject very fully when presenting the Estimates in May last, and I have little to
add to what I then said.
The hon. and gallant Member is aware
that milk is being provided to school
children in England and Scotland at a
cost to the children or their parents of
3d per quart, compared with the retail
price of 6d or 7d per quart. The
difference in cost is found by the English
and Scottish Milk Marketing Boards.
In April last I elected to deplete the
Milk Fund by reducing the levies and
thus enable milk to be sold in Belfast
to all who desired it at 3d per quart,
compared with 6d or 7d in England. I
came to the conclusion that it was far
sounder policy to make milk available
to the unemployed and the poorest of
the poor at practically the school children
rate than to use the funds available for
an experiment, especially as extra staff
and administrative expense would be involved in organising and running any
scheme of milk to school children.
I have no intention of abandoning the
proposal to supply milk to school children at specially cheap rates. Such a
development is an important part of any
publicity campaign which has as its
object an increase in milk consumption.
It would, in my view, be a mistake to
embark on any such campaign until we
have perfected the running of the scheme
and until our efforts to clean up byres
and herds, which, after all, only began
in May last, have had more time to
materialise.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is it to be
inferred that the price of milk is not
being reduced in spite of the promise
made on 22nd November last year that
it would be reduced at the earliest possible moment?
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think I made
it plain to the hon. and gallant Member that though a scheme would not be
drafted, it might be adopted as part of
a publicity campaign if conditions rendered that necessary.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: When does
the Minister expect those conditions to
arise?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I could not
give the hon. and gallant Gentleman an
accurate answer.
ALLEGED EXCESSIVE FOOD
PRICES.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Agriculture if he has read a statement
of the Chairman of the Public Health
Committee, at the meeting of the Belfast Corporation on the 2nd September,
to the effect that the working man had
now to pay an excessive price for bacon
and pork; that he is further taxed by
a system of levies on milk; that the
price of milk had reached a level which
only the well-to-do citizens can afford to
pay; that two years ago milk was at
least 50 per cent. cheaper, and judging
by the standard adopted for Grade C the
quality was often better than Grade B;
whether this statement is accurate, and,
if so, what steps he proposes to take in
the matter.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have read
Press reports of the statement in
question. The suggestion regarding the
price now being paid by the working
man for bacon and pork is inaccurate.
It is interesting to note in this connection the following index figures relating to the retail prices of bacon in
Belfast supplied by the Ministry of
Labour. The average minimum retail
price for 1933 was 103d per lb., and the
average minimum retail price during the
expired portion of the present year was
83d per lb., representing a decrease of
2d per lb., as compared with the year
1933.
The suggestions regarding milk are
likewise inaccurate. As the hon. Member is aware, the current price of Grade
C milk in Belfast is 5d per quart
delivered and 4d per quart if collected.
So far from milk being 50 per cent.
cheaper two years ago than it is now.
the ruling price of milk in Belfast was
then 5d per quart delivered, though it
is true that some milk was then sold at
5d per quart. It is, therefore, apparent
that there is in fact no truth in the
suggestion that the imposition of the
levies has involved an increase in the
price of milk to the consumer.
I need only add that Belfast has the
cheapest milk supply of any city in the
United Kingdom.
Fortunately or unfortunately, I am
not in a position to control the statements of members of the public, however
inaccurate they may be, and I do not
therefore propose to take any action in
the matter.
TAKING OF BIRDS' EGGS IN
RATHLIN.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether robbery of rare
wild birds' eggs by strangers took place
on Rathlin Island last June on a considerable scale; and whether anv
measures have been taken to check such
depredations.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is not a fact, as
suggested in the hon. and learned Member's question, that there were extensive
robberies of wild birds' eggs by strangers
in Rathlin Island last summer.
The fact
is that an ornithologist of repute, under
licence issued under the Wild Birds Protection Act, 1931,
Mr. CAMPBELL: I did not catch
that.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. ani
learned Friend knows the designation of
the gentleman I am referring to did visit
Rathlin Island this year for the purpose
of obtaining eggs of a certain species
of wild bird, and, incidentally, for the
purpose of studying the habits of these
birds. I am satisfied, however, that this
gentleman did not and would not do any
act which would be inimical to the interests of wild bird life in Northern Ireland.
It is also a fact that in former years
strangers have undoubtedly visited places
in Northern Ireland, including Rathlin
Island, for the purpose of unlawfully
Oral Answers

8 OCTOBER 1935
obtaining wild birds' eggs, but with the
helpful co-operation of the Ulster Society
for the Protection of Birds, of which
society the hon. and learned Member is
vice-president, steps have been taken
which I am satisfied will make it increasingly difficult for unauthorised

Mr. CAMPBELL: Thank you.
LIMITATION OF SHOP HOURS
FOR JUVENILES.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he proposes to
introduce legislation in the present
session to provide that no person under
18 years shall be employed in a shop for
more than 48 hours in a working week.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question
of introducing legislation to bring the
law relating to shop hours in Northern
Ireland into closer conformity with the
corresponding law in Great Britain is at
present engaging the attention of my
Department.
The views of the various associations of
local authorities and of other representative bodies have been sought in the
matter, but I have not yet received
replies from all of these.
I am not, therefore, in a position to
give any definite undertaking as to the
introduction of legislation in the
direction indicated.
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman when he is considering
legislation will his Bill prohibit all
adults and juveniles from working more
than 48 hours a week?
Sir DAWSON BATES: All these
matters will come under consideration
when we are considering the whole
question of introducing legislation dealing with this matter.
SUGGESTED LIMITATION OF
MOTORS.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he can state whether,
having regard to the increasing number
of motor vehicles and the distressing frequency of deaths and accidents on the
roads, he will consider the advisability
of a temporary limitation of the number
of motor vehicles so far as compatible
with the due maintenance of public and
private activities.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
and learned Member is aware, steps have
already been taken under the authority
of Parliament for the regulation and
control of
certain classes of motor
vehicles in connection with their use on
the public roads in Northern Ireland.
It is hoped that the measures already
taken will conduce to a considerable
degree towards a reduction in the number of accidents on the roads, and I am
not prepared at present to consider the
question of further restrictions in the
way of limitation of motor traffic.
It may be of interest to the hon. and
learned Member to know that on the
basis of population and of motor vehicles
the number of road accidents in Northern Ireland is comparatively lower than
the corresponding numbers in Great
Britain.
Taking the year 1934, for every
100,000 population in Northern Ireland
the number of road accidents was 147,
whereas in Great Britain the corresponding number was 455.
Similarly, for every 1,000 motor
vehicles in Northern Ireland the number
of road accidents in the year in question
was 46, whereas in Great Britain the
corresponding number was 85.
SHOOTING OF JOHN MCKIERNAN.
6. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he can state whether
with reference to the shooting of John
McKiernan in his licensed premises in
Great George's Street, on Saturday
night, 21st September, an intimation was
conveyed to the police barracks in York
Street that afternoon that this man was
in danger and a request made for his
protection, and, if so, what steps were
taken to protect him.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a
fact that an intimation was conveyed to
police in York Street on the afternoon
in question that Mr. M'Kiernan was in
danger, nor was any request made to the
police for his protection.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
were
It is a fact, however, that a communication was received at 9-45 p.m. by the
police authorities requesting that a policeman should be sent to the public-house
in question. Three constables
immediately dispatched to the premises
and on arrival there at 9-50 they were
requested by the publican to wait in
York Street until he would be ready to
go home.
The police moved away as requested,
and a few minutes later, hearing the
sound of shooting, they immediately
rushed round the corner to the publichouse only to find that the murder had
been committed.
I need hardly add that every effort is
being made to render the guilty party
amenable.
UNEMPLOYMENT IN SHRIGLEY.
7. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can state
if, as a result of his visit to the Shrigley
area in May, he is able to give any
information as to the possibility of finding employment for those who have had
no regular work since the closing down
of the mill five years ago.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I have had the benefit to-day
of discussing the possibility of finding
additional work for the people of Shrigley
with a deputation from the district,
which the hon. and gallant Member
accompanied.
The Downpatrick Rural District
Council has almost completed a water
supply scheme, on which a number of
Shrigley men obtained employment, and
I have authorised an unemployment relief
grant for a sewerage scheme, which I
hope the Council will start in the very
near future, and which will give employment to about 50 men for 35 weeks.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Will the
right hon. Gentleman urge on the Rural
District Council the necessity of expediting this sewerage scheme? As the
deputation told him to-day the people in
that area are starving on 21d a day.
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes, I shall do
everything in my power. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
THE RECENT DISTURBANCES IN
BELFAST.
8. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Prime
Minister whether he will consult the

directed to inquire into the origin and

that ought to be taken for the better
preservation of the public peace and the
prevention or prompt suppression of riot
and disorder, and to the giving to such
court the powers of the High Court of
Justice vested in the Riots Commission
appointed under the Belfast Commission
Act, 1886.
The PRIME MINISTER: No, sir;
the answer is in the negative. Under
the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
the responsibility for the maintenance
of law and order in this part of the
United Kingdom is a matter which falls
within the sole competence of the Ulster
Government, and the necessity for any
consultation with the authorities in Great
Britain does not arise.
There is no need for any special court
of inquiry, as the origin and all the
circumstances surrounding the recent unfortunate disturbances in the city of
Belfast are fully known and cannot be
disputed. They are found deep-rooted
among a certain section in our national
life who are disloyal to the Throne and
Constitution of these realms.
My colleagues and I are fully satisfied
with the tact, forbearance and efficiency
of our police force, including the "B"
Special Constabulary, from the Inspector-
General down through the various ranks,
and I feel sure that this House will be
ready to congratulate my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
in his handling of a most difficult situa
tion at a time of very grave anxiety,
and desire to bear testimony to the many
public-spirited citizens who, by their
influence, were largely instrumental in
allaying the high tension then existing.
I am particularly anxious that no word
shall be uttered in this House which
might again arouse public feeling. Peace
and goodwill cannot be fostered and preserved unless there is a whole-hearted
determination among the itizens of all
classes to promote good feeling and to
support lawful authority.

The PRIME MINISTER: As I stated
in the answer, the facts are well known.
We know that an attack was made on a
peaceful procession. We know that a
man was captured by one of our very
gallant Royal Ulster Constabulary. We
know that the miscreant is now undergoing, I think, five years in jail, and
what further facts could an inquiry bring
out other than those which I have just
mentioned? The only thing I would say
is that I hope all Members of the House
will, in view of what has happened,
realise that an ill-spoken word, even in
this House, may possibly cause further
trouble, which I am sure everybody
desires to avoid. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): Hon.
Members will remember that in 1925
when we passed the Drainage Bill it was
made a condition that when the scheme
was examined and approved of it had
the force in itself of an Act of Parliament. The effect of that was that when
difficulties which were not anticipated
arose it was not within the power or province of any department or person to
alter that scheme in any particular.
Amendments from time to time have
taken place since then, but at
request of, and after consultation with,
the Advisory Committee on Drainage it
was thought well that this short Bill
should be introduced so that county
councils if they commenced a scheme and
found that some alterations were necessary could in the middle of the scheme
without the expense of introducing a new
scheme have the alteration made.
the
the
The first Clause vests power in
Minister of Home Affairs, after proper
and due examination. to make such
alterations as may be found necessary so
that the work of drainage may be carried
out. It will be noted by hon. Members
that any scheme of alteration must be
initiated by the council concerned. We are
all appreciative of the necessary and good
work that has been done in connection
Drainage Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
with drainage, and it would be a pity
now that the local authorities are acting
in the best interests of the people they
represent that this House should prevent
them from getting on with that good
work.
The remaining Clauses of the Bill deal
more particularly with the situation that
has arisen in connection with the Bann
drainage. It was necessary to dump the
cleanings from the river on the lands
adjoining the river. It was not in the
first instance considered necessary to take
over the land and it was intended that
compensation should be paid for the disturbance caused by the dumping of this
material on the land. It has now become
apparent that it would be cheaper to
take over the land entirely, as owing to
the dumping produce will not now grow
on it. Therefore, the second Clause of
the Bill has been introduced to enable
the Minister of Finance to arrange compensation on a uniform basis. It is proposed to use this ground for the growing
of trees where it is found suitable. The
House, therefore, will note that this Bill
will give the local authorities, in the first
place, an opportunity of proceeding with
these beneficent drainage schemes and,
in the second place, will facilitate the
transfer of this land to the Ministry of
Finance. I beg to move.

It was then realised that these two
different types of unemployment to which
I have referred required to be dealt with
by two different schemes-one an insurance scheme, and the other a scheme in
which the money was provided entirely
by the State, except for a small contribution given by the local authorities.
Our Act of 1934 placed insurance benefits
on a sound foundation, and, much as
that Act was criticised when it was introduced-and, as I have frequently said,
very unfairly criticised-it not only
placed the payment of benefit on a sound
foundation, but it enabled the cuts to be
restored, and the period of benefit in
thousands of cases where the record of
employment was good continued to a very
considerable extent. Through this Act
the State accepted the responsibility, subject, as I have said, to this small contribution from the local authorities, of
the financing of what is known as the
transitional payments side of the scheme.
Now I wish to point out that this Act
requires the needs of an applicant for
unemployment assistance to be assessed
in accordance with the regulations made
by the Ministry of Labour. Under the
Act such regulations cease to have effect
at the end of twelve months from the
date on which they come into force, unless approved in the meantime by a
Resolution of each House of Parliament.
It is to obtain this approval that this
Resolution is submitted to-day.
The Unemployment Assistance (Determination of Need and Assessment of
Needs) Regulations (Northern Ireland)
1934, which are identical in their terms
with corresponding regulations in Great
Britain, were made by my Ministry for
this purpose on 31st December, 1934,
and came into operation on 7th January,
1935, the First Appointed Day. In both
Great Britain and Northern Ireland the
Regulations have been modified by the
Unemployment Assistance (Temporary
Provisions) Acts, the effect of which is to
provide that those entitled to Unemployment Assistance allowance shall be paid
in each week either at the rate assesed
under the regulations or at the rate payable on the former transitional payments
basis, whichever is more favourable.
That, in effect. is giving those entitled
to this form of assistance the better of

opinion at any rate, with success.

I would like to know whether the

it would indicate that we here in Northern Ireland are not on the same level
as the people in a corresponding state of

Unemployment Insurance (Anomalies)
(Seasonal Workers) Order (Northern
Ireland), 1935.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): -I beg to
move, "That the Order made by the
Ministry of Labour on the 23rd August,
1935, under Article I of the Unemploy
ment Insurance (Economy) (No. 3)
Order (Northern Ireland), 1931, as extended and amended by Section 12 of the
Unemployment Act (Northern Ireland),
1934, for the removal of anomalies in the
operation of the Unemployment Insurance Acts in relation to seasonal
workers be hereby approved."
I am asking the House to approve of
this very important Motion, which deals
exclusively with a type of insured persons
known as seasonal workers. Time after
time questions have been raised in this
House, and raised with me privately, as
to the conditions that are laid down for
seasonal workers in order that they might
obtain benefit. The Order, a copy of
which every Member of the House has
received, is known as the Unemployment
Insurance (Anomalies) (Seasonal Workers)
Order (Northern Ireland), 1935.
The provisions of the Order are identical with those of a corresponding Order
in Great Britain, and are based on recom-
2505 Unemployment Insurance-

8 OCTOBER 1935
Seasonal Workers
mendations made by the Unemployment
Insurance Statutory Committee. The
Order revokes certain Anomalies Regulations which governed the payment of
benefit to seasonal workers, and at the
same time introduces amending provisions
of an important and helpful character to
seasonal workers in their off-season. The
effect of this Order, which operates from
29th August, 1935, and which, under our
existing law, requires approval of Parliament within twelve months, is to make
it easier for a seasonal worker to qualify
for benefit in his off-season.
Hon. Members are aware that a seasonal
worker has to satisfy certain special conditions for the receipt of benefit. He will
no longer be required to satisfy these
conditions if he can
prove that the
seasonal occupation which he follows
amounts to 29 weeks in the year, or, if
he can prove the payment of 150 contributions in any period of four out of five
consecutive insurance years within the ten
insurance years before the date of his
claim to benefit. If he can prove any
of these conditions he will be excluded
from the scope of the Order.
Mr. BEATTIE: Why put the onus of
proof on the man or woman? You should
be able to prove those things.
Mr. GORDON: The onus of proof
always rests with the individual who is
making the claim for benefit of any kind.
We will examine and investigate the proof
to decide whether or not it is satisfactory.
This provision is the most important
change made by the Order. A seasonal
worker who does not possess these new
qualifications must still prove employment during his off-season in order to
qualify for benefit.
The new conditions will be much
easier to satisfy. Previously, a claimant
had to prove insurable work in his offseason. Credit will now be given for
non-insurable work performed in his
off-season. Under a previous Order an
applicant was required to show a substantial amount of employment in his two
off-seasons preceding his claim to benefit.
Under the present Order he must still
show some work of an insurable or noninsurable character over two test periods
of off-season, and if his aggregate of work
amounts to a quarter of his two test
periods he will be entitled to receive
benefit, provided he satisfies all the other
requirements of the Act.
Another point to which I would like to
draw attention is that the test periods of
off-season will be reduced by any spells
of proved incapacity occurring in them
through illness, and consequently a
claimant can qualify for benefit by a
shorter period of work in the off-season
in which the illness occurred. The
change will prove a great boon to the
seasonal workers, and, I feel sure, will be
accepted as an honest endeavour to remove some of the difficulties which prevented seasonal workers from qualifying
for benefit.
Mr. BEATTIE: This Order is really
an attempt to get rid of a very anomalous
position, a position that has become so
aggravated as it affects seasonal workers,
that it will take more than a small
Measure of this kind to make the regulations acceptable to those concerned. The
first thing you have got to do is to
identify the occupations that are classified
as seasonal. If seasonal occupations are
to be determined by the payment of 39
contributions in four years a lot of shipyard workers are going to be classified as
seasonal workers.
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Member has
misunderstood the position. It is not a

question of making an effort to remove
a seasonal worker from the category of
seasonal worker and placing him on the
same basis as an ordinary insured person.
Mr. BEATTIE: That enlightenment
leaves the matter just as dark to me as
it was previously. The conditions you
are introducing to remove the seasonal
worker from that category are exactly
the same as the conditions that would
have removed him from that classification
previously.
Mr. GORDON: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was the Umpire's
decision of 1927 or 1928 that brought in
the two off-seasons. I fought that
strenuously. I still adhere to my opinion
that you are bringing shipyard workers
in as seasonal workers. Let me inform
you that the man who is going to have
39 weeks' employment in the year will

ment. I want a guarantee that those

to

MISCELLANEOUS EXPENSES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£1,200 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending on 31st
March, 1936, to pay certain miscellaneous
expenses, including certain grants in
aid."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This estimate provides for a
grant in respect of the expenditure incurred by the local Committee in holding
the International Tourist Trophy Car
Race in Ulster in September last. Their
expenses were heavily increased by the
cost of the prize money, which this year
resources.
had to be met from local
Shortly before the date of the race an
appeal was made to the Government for
assistance, as private benefaction had for
the first time failed to provide the prize
money, and local subscribers had already
contributed towards the general race
expenditure. In deciding to respond to
this appeal the Government had regard
to the great difficulties in which the promoters of the race would have been
involved if the prize money had not bee
forthcoming at such a late hour.
£1,500 was accordingly advanced to
the Ulster Tourist Trophy Car Race
Committee. Of this, £300 was subsequently returned to the Government as
certain prizes were not awarded. It was
clearly pointed out at the time the grant
was made that it was not to be regarded
as a precedent, and that the Committee
would not be entitled to look to the
Government for aid if a similar situation
arose next year. In addition, the two
conditions which hon. Members will see
at the foot of the Estimate were attached
to the grant.
The accounts of the race are not yet to
hand, and therefore it is too soon to say
whether anything will accrue to the
Government after the accounts have been
wound up. If any profit emerges, it is
not, however, likely to be of any substantial amount. I beg to move.

for themselves, so as to give themselves
an advertisement on political platforms
throughout the country.

off for other necessary purposes. Therefore, the date this year had to be different
from that on other occasions. The
hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) mentioned the
question of discussing the matter with
the ratepayers in County Down. Fortunately the Down County Council have
it in their own hands to decide whether
the people of County Down desire the
race to be held there, and they would
be the first to complain, I am sure, if
they found that the closing of the roads
was such an inconvenience. If that were
the case they would not stand it any
longer. County Down is my own county,
and I know the County Down people
Supplementary Estimates
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
well. They have a sporting instinct, and
they are quite prepared to suffer what is
undoubtedly a great inconvenience on the
day of the race and during the period of
the trial runs that are necessary in such
a contest. They have always been most
obliging, they have been self-sacrificing,
and they have in every possible way
helped Ulster to retain what is known
as the blue riband of motor-car racing
throughout the world. I may say that reports from abroad always tend to show that
there is no other place where the contest
is more fairly run, where the drivers and
mechanics are more welcome, and where
fair play is absolutely the order of the
day. I say we have got a reputation
which it would be extremely unfortunate
to lose in any way.
This Estimate refers to what has
happened this year in exceptional circumstances, and I cannot go into the future,
but we may take it it is the wish of the
Government that this race should be retained in the Ulster area. There is just
one other point. The hon. Member for
Pottinger said that the race was of no
advantage to the working man. Very far
from that being the case, there are very
large numbers of men occupied for a con
siderable time, not only in erecting the
grand stand but in preparing the roads.
There are also the waiters who attend in
the tents. It is not the wealthy who are
making anything out of it; the money
has been spent on those who are deserving
of all the help we can give them to obtain
temporary employment of a suitable
nature. I hope it will be recognised that
this was forced upon us at the last
minute, as it were, and that it was the
only step that could be taken in order
to save the race to Ulster.

PROTECTION OF FISHERIES.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if it
is a fact that the Toome Eel Fishery
Company is making undue demands on
the resources of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and whether he will see that
the members of this force are not used
by this company as unpaid water bailiffs.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The duties of
the police in this respect are limited to
taking such measures as they may consider necessary for the protection of the
company's water bailiffs from molestation
in carrying out their lawful duty.
The police cannot, and do not, as
suggested by the hon. Member, act as
unpaid water bailiffs in the private interests of the Fishery Company, but they
will continue to take every possible step
to ensure the preservation of the peace.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Might I ask whether
it is not a fact that the patrol boat,
which is the property of Toome Eel
Fishery Company, has invariably one or
more members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary aboard, and is that not making
use of the members of the force?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think my
hon. Friend is aware that on several
occasions bailiffs have been fired on by
certain persons, and it is the duty of
the police to furnish every protection
they can to these people carrying out
their lawful duties. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)

REARRANGEMENT OF PETTY
SESSIONS DISTRICTS.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will take
into consideration the resolutions which
have been passed by the different local
authorities in connection with the proposed rearrangement of petty sessions
districts.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have
already given an assurance that before
any changes in petty sessions districts
are made, full consideration will be given
to any representations made by local
authorities or others interested, and the
hon. Member may rest assured that no
alteration in any petty sessions district
will be effected unless I am satisfied, after
the fullest inquiry, that such change
would be of general advantage.
I am glad of this opportunity of being
able to explain that the tentative suggestions which I had received, and which
were circulated to local authorities and
other bodies for the purpose of ascertaining their views, were not in any way
intended to represent the considered
scheme of the Government.
I may add that before any final decision is taken I shall, if so desired, be
very glad to discuss with the hon. Member, or with any other Member, the
question of any particular petty sessions
in which he may be interested.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Might I just thank
the right hon. Gentleman for that reply?

Sir DAWSON BATES: The gentleman referred to in the hon. Member's
question made application some time ago
for a cadetship in the force. From the
particulars submitted by him as to his
educational and other attainments it
appeared that he possessed prima facie
the qualities which are desirable for a
cadet in the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
There was no vacancy at the time and
Mr. Wolseley joined the force as an
ordinary constable. During the period
of his training as a constable he gave
entire satisfaction to the authorities and
confirmed the opinion which they had
formed as to his competency to discharge the duties of a district-inspector.
With regard to the last part of the
question, the rule which the hon. Member probably has in mind is that under
which half the appointments to the officer
rank are filled by the promotion of headconstables, a condition which has been
fully observed and which it is not proposed to alter in any way.

Diseases of Animals (Therapeutic
Substances) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Therapeutic Substances Act, 1925, gives control over the manufacture, importation
and sale of medical therapeutic substances. There is, however, at present
no similar control in the case of therapeutic substances intended to be used
solely for veterinary purposes. The
necessity for regulation in the case of
veterinary therapeutic substances be
comes increasingly evident. The absence
of such control presents a very serious
obstacle to the treatment and prevention
of animal disease. Provision has been
made in legislation recently passed by
the Imperial Parliament for the control
of the manufacture, importation and
sale of veterinary therapeutic substances.
The Act, however, applies to Great
Britain only and does not extend to
Northern Ireland.
In these circumstances the need for
Northern
legislation in
Ireland on
parallel lines is of a double-barrelled
nature. The conditions under which
such substances as tuberculin, antiabortion vaccine, and similar preparations
may be imported into Northern Ireland,
or produced or sold here, are far from
satisfactory. It is consequently of the
utmost importance that, as in Great
Britain, power should be assumed whereby the potency and purity of substances
of this character may be ensured.
Furthermore, complementary legislation here is essential if the position of
the United Kingdom as a whole is to be
Unless
safeguarded.
action is taken
here Northern Ireland might easily be
a loophole through which spurious
veterinary preparations, not allowed to
be manufactured in or imported into
Great Britain, might flow into the United
Kingdom as a whole. I may say that
the British Act visualised such legislation in this Parliament, and the object
of the Bill now before the House is to
place Northern Ireland in regard to this
matter on exactly the same footing as
Great Britain. I beg to move.
Question, "That the Bill be now read
a Second time," put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for Tuesday next.

10 OCTOBER 1935
Motion for Adjournment.
POLICE PROMOTION SYSTEM.
CASE OF DISTRICT-INSPECTOR
W. D. WOLSELEY.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn.".
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. HENDERSON: As I pointed out
I am entirely dissatisfied with the answer
given by the Minister of Home Affairs
to my question regarding the appointment of a district-inspector from the
ranks of the police. I think this has
been the cause of a great deal of the
trouble that has taken place in Northern
Ireland, and a considerable number of
very valuable lives have been lost
through the action of the Government,
or of the Ministry of Home Affairs, in
appointing district-inspectors with
absolutely no knowledge of police work.
In the part of the town where the
trouble broke out that trouble was due
entirely to there being placed in charge
of that district a district-inspector without any knowledge of police work at all.
Here you have another glaring example
of that, and it is demoralising the whole
police force in Northern Ireland. Here
is a young man-whether he is a friend
of a political hack or not I do not know,
but it rather strange that a young man
only eighteen months in the police force
should be appointed to this position.
After all a painter or a joiner-and all
craftsmen are looked upon as very
humble persons in the right hon. Gentleman's eyes-has to serve six years to his
trade, but here the Government of the
country, who are responsible for law and
order, place a young man in the important position of district-inspector-a
young man who has practically no knowledge of police work at all.
This is absolutely preposterous, and
on behalf of those constables who have
given great service to Ulster, and who
have served through such troublesome
times I ask the Government if they think
that justice is being meted out to them.
If the constable concerned was some one
who had been in the police force for ten
or twelve years, who had a thorough
knowledge of police work, and who knew
the mentality of the people of this
country, I would agree that he was
entitled to promotion. Does not the
Minister of Home Affairs think the time
has come when district-inspectors should
be appointed from the ranks?

CONDITION OF A DROMORE P.E.
SCHOOL.
1. Dr. WILSON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he is aware of the
condition of No. 3 Public Elementary
School, Dromore, Co. Down; that it is
impossible to heat the school owing to
defective grates; whether it is a fact that
this was brought to the notice of the
Down County Regional Committee some
months ago, and that no action has been
taken by them to remedy the defects
before heat is necessary in this school.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The Ministry was not aware of the difficulties
referred to by the hon. Member, but,
upon inquiry from the Down County
Regional Education Committee, finds
that they have already been dealt with
and that the new grates were installed
in Dromore No. 3 Public Elementary
School last Saturday.
DECREASE IN THE NUMBER OF
SCHOOL CHILDREN.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the decrease in 1934-
35 of nearly 5,000 pupils in the numbers
enrolled in the public elementary schools,
due to a falling off in the child population, is mainly in the county council
schools or in the voluntary schools, and
in what counties the decrease is most
noticeable.
Mr. ROBB: As the number of provided and transferred schools varies from
year to year it would be difficult to
furnish exact figures, but the information available does not suggest that the
fall in the average number of pupils on
the rolls is greater in the county council
schools than in the voluntary schools, or
vice versa.
In reply to the second part of the
question, however, I may say that the
decline is somewhat more noticeable in
the city of Belfast and in the Counties
of Armagh and Fermanagh than in the
other areas.
ARRANGEMENTS FOR MEALS IN
SCHOOLS.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education what steps the Ministry have
taken to encourage arrangements in
schools for the pupils to secure some
warm food at mid-day.
Mr. ROBB: In each of the last four
years the Ministry has referred to this
matter in its annual report. Last
November a circular was issued to education committees, managers and teachers
of public elementary schools strongly
urging that steps should be taken to
inaugurate schemes for the provision of
hot mid-day meals for those pupils
attending country schools who are unable to return home for lunch and who.
as a rule, have nothing to eat but a piece
of white bread from possibly early morning until late afternoon.
In the same circular the Ministry furnished information regarding
regarding simple
schemes that are operated voluntarily by
the teachers, and other persons interested, in a number of the schools and
which provide a very simple meal for all
the pupils in the school.
It was further pointed out that the
preparation and serving of a simple
meal, or even of such dishes as soup,
porridge, cocoa or hot milk, need involve

RECONSTRUCTION OF THE
DURHAM STREET BRIDGE,
BELFAST.
5. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the reason for the delay in the
reconstruction of the Durham Street
Bridge; whether he is aware that
hundreds of workers and shopkeepers in
the district are suffering great inconvenience through this delay.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have caused inquiries to be made into this matter and
am informed that the contract for the
work was entered into on the 13th September, 1934, the basis of the contract
being that the work should be completed
within fifteen months from that date
(i.e. in December next).
Unfortunately, however, certain difficulties in connection with the foundations, which could not have been
foreseen, have arisen and have delayed
the progress of the work. These difficulties have been overcome and the work
is progressing, but it will not, under the
circumstances, be possible for the contractor to complete the work for some
little time after the stipulated date.
The contractors are being pressed by
the Corporation to expedite the completion of the work.
Major MCCORMICK: Is the right
hon. Gentleman aware that in the
original estimate for this bridge the calculations of the Improvements Committee, owing to the great inconvenience
caused by the closing of the thoroughfare, were that the bridge would
be completed in the middle of the
summer?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I really fail
to understand what my hon. and gallant
Friend wants, and until he puts down a
question I am not prepared to answer.
Major McCORMICK: I am asking
the question now and I want an answer.
I am asking is he aware that in the
calculations of the Improvements Committee, made for the purpose of the building of this bridge, the bridge would have
to be completed by the summer.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir. I
am not aware of anything in regard to
the calculations of the Belfast Corporation. I only told my hon. and gallant
Friend the terms of the contract.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the right
hon. Gentleman say whether this bridge
will be built ready for the Twelfth of
July?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps the
hon. Member would go to the Belfast
Corporation, of which he is a member,
for that information.

6. Mr. HENDERSON asked

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Mr. Pollock): In the absence of my

In answer to similar questions on the
same subject which the hon. Member has
put from time to time the Minister of
Commerce has confined himself to those
industrial undertakings which were

date, have since extended their operations to products additional to those

thus give must not be taken as official
in the ordinary sense of that term since
they have been obtained from outside
sources for the special purpose of replying to the hon. Member's question.

which I have mentioned is 30, employing
in all 781 persons. I regret that I have

Unemployment Assistance (Temporary

CLAUSE 1 (Grants to local authorities in consequence of postponement of
Second Appointed Day).
Question proposed: "That the Clause
stand part of the Bill."
Mr. BEATTIE: I think I intimated
that I would ask one or two questions
in connection with this Clause. Owing
to the failure of the National Government in not applying itself to the needs
and requirements of the unemployed in
Great Britain, the Northern Government
now bring in a similar Clause to tide
them over a period of waiting. I do not
think, as I said before, that it is good
enough to be neglectful of your responsi
bilities. The Second Appointed Day
means for many thousands of people in
Northern Ireland the fruits of lifesomething to sustain them during the
cold winter days. Your failure to apply
yourselves to setting out the Second
Appointed Day on the pretence that you
would be going out of step with Great
Britain is no justification to me at any
rate for the starvation of many thousands
of people on a meagre income. I was
rather suspicious when the Second
Appointed Day was put off, because I
saw then there was a danger of it never
applying. We have got the physically
fit unemployed who have run out of all
claim to any unemployment insurance
benefit. I cannot understand the conclusions that have been arrived at as far
as the basis of cost of living is concerned.
By the method adopted you are giving
into homes sums of money far below
what some residents would pay for the
keep of a dog or cat in the Dogs' and
Cats' Home during their absence.
I think we have got to take our
courage in our hands and say to the
United Kingdom, "You have failed in
your obligations to the physically fit unemployed, and we are now preparing ourselves to appoint a date for the coming
into operation of Part II of the Act."
If you do that I think you will get a
certain amount of return both from the
United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. I
2549 Unemployment Assistance Bill-

15 OCTOBER 1935
Committee
think the position is so desperate here that
you must declare the Second Appointed
Day to be the 1st November. If you
do that you will have the whole Committee with you, and I believe that representations at Westminster would be
sympathetically considered. Although
this Bill only provides crumbs from the
table, I am not prepared to sweep away
those crumbs. In view of that, I have
to accept the majority decision of the
Committee.
My second point deals with the local
authorities who have to be compensated
in accordance with the responsibilities
which they shoulder during the postponement period. It cannot be denied in
any quarter-Ballymena, I believe, did
stand out by itself that Belfast has
borne the brunt of the cost of maintenance of the unemployed in Northern
Ireland. The responsibility of Belfast
has been far in excess of that of any
other local authority in this area. The
Government should have set out a special
allowance towards the Belfast authorities
for their splendid services and heavy
responsibility in the maintenance of the
unemployed during the transitional
period we have passed through.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: They have done
that.
Mr. BEATTIE: The other counties
who failed in their responsibilities-
Sir ROBERT LYNN: No, no.
Mr. BEATTIE- -are, I believe, now
going to get something which, in my
opinion, they do not deserve. Belfast,
Derry and Newry were the only three
places who applied themselves in real
earnest to assist the down-and-outs.
They put into operation Section 13 of the
Act. I know that Londonderry did not
live up to the expectations of Belfast.
I was in Derry, and I found that that
city had to be compelled to apply the
special section giving authority to give
outdoor relief to the able-bodied.
Belfast applied that section right from
the commencement, and set up a basis of
calculation. The demonstrations that
took place in Belfast as to the under
purchasing power of the people were of
such importance that the Minister of
Home Affairs and Guardians had to reconsider that scale. I say that that scale
is yet too low to give any decency and
comfort. If we are going to continue the
policy of having a half-starved population we are going to have very serious
trouble ahead. I could apply myself to
recent happenings, but I do not want to
be throwing up anything like that.
have heard many ideas as to why the
troubles originated in Belfast. I could
offer reasons which I believe are nearer
the truth than many I have heard.
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid that
would lead us into a debate.
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not want to do
that. I want to assist to the greatest
possible extent. If you are compelled
to violate the step-by-step policy with
Great Britain you will find that good will
follow. I feel we cannot justify the
present period of uncertainty. I hope
the Government will give the matter reconsideration. I also hope they will give
the claim of the Belfast Corporation the
consideration which it is entitled to.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: I hope
nothing that could be said on either side
of the Committee will be the means of
making the Minister consider the matter
of getting out of step with Great Britain
on this question. By doing that we
might cut across the Reinsurance Agreement which has been such a great boon
in the past and, as far as one can read,
is likely to be of even greater benefit in
the future than it has been in the past.
Having regard to the fact that unemployment is decreasing at a greater rate
on the other side of the Channel than it
is here, the result will be that the percentage of unemployment will be greater
in Northern Ireland than it is in the
United Kingdom. Therefore, I think we
are under a deep debt of gratitude to
the Minister for the Reinsurance Agreement which he was able to carry out in
conjunction with the Imperial Parliament a few years ago.
I think one must
be very careful that we do nothing that
would in any way prejudice our claim
under that Agreement.

NEW CLAUSE (Additional powers
of county councils in relation to watercourses).
"In any case where, notwithstanding
that a watercourse has been scoured
out and cleansed in accordance with
the provisions of section five of the
Drainage Act (Northern Ireland),
1933, the proper flow of water in the
watercourse continues to be obstructed
by reason of the existence of any rock,
boulder or other like obstruction in,
or projecting from, the bed or sides of
the watercourse, the county council
may, with the consent of the occupier
of the lands on or through which the
watercourse flows or of which it forms
a boundary, enter upon any such lands
for the purpose of removing any such
obstruction and may execute all such
works as are necessary for that purpose.
"Any expenses incurred by the
county council under this section shall
be defrayed out of the county fund,
and shall be raised by means of the
poor rate as a county at large charge."
(Mrs. Parker.)
Brought up, and read a First time.

little explanation on my part. Under
the 1933 Act the duty is imposed on
occupiers of agricultural land adjoining
a watercourse of keeping that watercourse scoured out and cleansing as
much of it as possible. In the pursuit
of that object by the occupier it is quite
possible that he may come upon some
obstruction such as a boulder or gravel,

be done. At the present moment it

damage as it did before he started the
cleaning out and scouring.. This Clause
will enable the county council, with the

this is a point which requires considerable stressing-with the permission of the

to come in on that land and remove
any obstacle which may be found in that
particular stream or watercourse. And
when that is done the cost, according to
this Clause, will be defrayed out of the

rate as a county at large charge. I think

2607 Superannuation Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 16th October, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Superannuation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This Measure is in the main an
attempt directed towards bringing our
Civil Service conditions into harmony
with those existing in the United
Kingdom.
Those changes were the result of
exhaustive consideration by the Royal
Commission on the Civil Service, which
reported in 1931, by the Imperial
Treasury and by the Civil Service Staff
Associations.
The major changes to be effected by the
Bill will be found in Clauses 1 and 2, and
I think it would be convenient, perhaps,
if I dealt categorically with the more
important Clauses.
Clause 1 applies the Superannuation
Act, 1909, to women. Heretofore the
superannuation of female civil servants
has been calculated in accordance with a
scale laid down by the Superannuation
Act, 1859. In 1909 revised arrangements
were applied to male civil servants, which
accorded to these officers, in place of
pension as prescribed in the Act of 1859,
pension on a smaller scale, together with
a lump sum on retirement or death. The
Act of 1909 was, as I have indicated, confined in its operation to male civil
servants and it is now proposed to
make the provisions of that Act
applicable to female civil servants,
a change which will have the advantage of securing a measure of
uniformity. I should add that existing
female civil servants will be allowed to
retain their present benefit under the Act
of 1859 if they so desire. So much for
the first Clause.
Clause 2 of the Bill provides for the
surrender by a civil servant on his or her
retirement of a portion of the pension to
which he or she would be entitled, in
return for which the officer will be
assured of the payment of a pension to a
dependent in the event of that dependent
surviving the pensioner. As hon. Members are no doubt aware, the Superannua
tion Acts make no provision for the
payment of pensions to dependents, and
the provision made in this Clause will,
therefore, give an opportunity to retiring
civil servants, who so desire, to make some
provision for their widows or other dependents who may survive them.
Clause 3 lays down a uniform rule for
the reckoning of unestablished service given
by officers who subsequently become established. Hitherto the amount of credit to
be given in respect of such service has
varied in accordance with the particular
circumstances of each case, though the
practice has more and more tended in
recent years towards allowing one half to
count for superannuation purposes. The
proposed statutory provision will, therefore, be a confirmation of existing practice
and does not connote the introduction of
any new principle.
When we come Clause 4 it will be found
that it relates to the basis upon which
superannuation benefits will, in future,
be calculated. Under existing legisla
tion the benefits are calculated in some
cases on the actual rate of salary payable
to the officer at the date of retirement.
and in some cases on the average amount
of salary received by him during the three
years preceding his retirement. Under
this Clause the superannuation benefits
will, subject to the preservation of existing rights, be calculated in all cases on
the average amount received over the
three years preceding retirement. As
this will result in some saving in pension
charges, the proposal is accompanied by a
small increase in the amount of additional
allowance payable on retirement. It is
calculated that the benefits payable under
the New Clause will be actuarially equivalent, taking the Civil Service as a
whole, to the benefits which would be payable under existing legislation.
I come now to Clause 7, the two intervening Clauses not being of much moment.
Clause 7 concedes a slight improvement
of superannuation benefits in the case of
2609 Superannuation Bill--

16 OCTOBER 1935
Second Reading
civil servants transferring to approved
employment outside the Civil Service.
com-
Clause 9 allows more generous
pensation to civil servants who may be
injured in the course of their duty. The
present provisions in this respect are
based on the Act of 1887, and contain
limitations which give rise under present
day conditions to hardships in individual
cases.
Clause 10 is designed to provide, in
respect of certain officers who had given
unestablished service in public departments prior to the establishment of the
Northern Ireland Civil Service, power to
reckon this prior service in calculating
their superannuation allowances.
As regards Clause 11, I need not
enlarge upon that because it has been
decided that it shall be eliminated pending further examination of the case.
Clause 12 gives the necessary statutory
authority for applying to certain existing
pensions the arrangements recently arrived
at in respect of the consolidation of basic
and bonus.
pay
The consolidation
arrangements are very much to the convenience of the whole of us.
The other Clauses of the Bill are of a
formal nature and it is, I think, unnecessary for me to dwell upon them. This
Bill simply places our Civil Service on a
basis something analogous to that of the
United Kingdom, and the effect upon the
Exchequer is so negligible that it is not
necessary to make any calculations in
respect of it.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

Mr. CAMPBELL:
I would like to
make one or two remarks upon this Bill.
I am perfectly certain that any Measure
that will tend to benefit the Civil Service
of Northern Ireland will be welcomed in
this House. Politics apart, the Civil
Service is very efficient and effective, and
at all times most courteous. The Bill is
a further step in what we might call the
enfranchisement of women. It puts the
female civil servants for all practical purposes on the same basis as the male civil
servants. As I understand the Bill-the
Minister will correct me if I err-it safeguards the female civil servants who
entered the Service after the commencement of the Act, and it equally safeguards the female civil servants who were
already in the permanent Civil Service.
There is one Clause in the Bill which I
think, and which I am sure the general
public will think, is very meritorious.
and that is Clause 2, which introduces a
new principle in the superannuation
system. This is an entirely new
departure, and, I submit to the House, a
new departure for good. It enables a
retiring civil servant to surrender, as from
the date of his retirement, in return for
the benefits he gets under the Act an
amount not exceeding one-third of his
superannuation allowance, and thus to
obtain for his dependents a pension of
equivalent value to that surrender. The
only drawback I see in the matter is that
one would like it to have been more
stringent. Many civil servants live up
to the last penny of their income; sometimes they live beyond their income.
Then death comes and very often you find
the family, wife and children as the case
may be, more or less helpless and stranded
on the world. So far as this Clause is
optional in giving civil servants the right
to make this surrender it is altogether to
the good, but I would like if the Minister
could have seen his way to go even
further and make it obligatory. I am
sure the general public will
see the
wisdom of that, and I believe very many
civil servants will think it wise also.

The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF
THE
SECRE-
MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): The main
object of the Bill is covered by Clause 1,
which provides for an extension of the
scope of the scheme made under Section
1 of the Unemployment Act passed by
this House last year, whereby unemployment insurance contributions may be
credited to children who have continued
to receive whole-time education for at
least a year after attaining the age at
which compulsory elementary education
ends. Section 1 of the 1934 Act enables
regulations to be made by the Ministry
for crediting unemployment insurance
contributions in such cases in accordance
with a scale laid down in the First
Schedule to the Act. The object was to
ensure that boys and girls who continued
their education would be credited with a
certain number of contributions in respect
of their continued education since attain.
ing the school-leaving age.
The object of the first Clause of this
Bill is to enable the scheme to be
extended so as to bring in boys and girls
who had left school at the beginning of
the summer holidays, and who had been
continuously attending school for at least
one year after attaining the normal
school-leaving age.
The wording of the Clause enables the
scheme to apply to any such child who left
school at any time within the period of
four months immediately preceding 4th
September, 1935. The change in this
respect is identical with an Act passed
through the British Parliament last July.
There are three separate and distinct
types of procedure laid down in the Unemployment Insurance Acts according as
the rule-making power is exercised, by
way of Order, Special Order, or Regulation. The distinction between these
various Orders, under this Bill, will be
abolished, with the specific exception of
the Orders and Special Orders relating
to special schemes and supplementary
schemes where there is good reason for
preserving the existing procedure.
In all other cases the procedure to be
followed in future will be exercisable by
regulations under this Bill. Such regulations must be presented to Parliament
immediately they are made, and if either
House, within the statutory period of ten
days, five of which must be days on which
Parliament is sitting, resolves that the
regulations be annulled, the regulations
become void as from the date of such

Labourers' Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): This is a simple
Bill which requires little explanation. It
is intended to enable rural district
councils to resume operations under the
Labourers Acts which, as the House is
aware, have been suspended during the
past four years owing to financial considerations. While the Acts were in
operation they were very successful in
securing the erection of cottages for
labouring people in rural districts. From
the initiation of the Acts in 1883 up to
the transfer of services to the Government of Northern Ireland in 1921, some
6,000 cottages were erected, while during
the short period from 1921 to the suspension of operations over 2,000 further
cottages were erected.
It was hoped that the financial assistance provided in connection with the
Housing Acts would, to some extent,
make up for the suspension of work under
the Labourers Acts, and such has been
the case. Some 6,200 houses have been
built in rural districts under the Housing
Acts, but the bulk of these houses have
been erected in the neighbourhood of
Belfast and other large towns like Lisburn
and Lurgan, or at the seaside, so that
only about one-half of the number have
been built in what may be described as
the purely rural areas.
Representations have been received from
hon. Members in all parts of the House
-you, yourself, Mr. Speaker, have been
very insistent in making representations
along the lines for which this Bill now
provides as well as from many of the
rural localities, urging my Ministry
to do something more to improve housing
conditions in the rural districts, especially
in the direction of providing better
accommodation for persons living in
unsanitary houses. Accordingly the
Government have come to the conclusion
that operations under the Labourers Acts
should be resumed, and in conjunction
with the local authorities it is proposed to
have a survey of housing conditions with
a view to ascertaining the number of
families living in houses which are unfit
for habitation and to concentrate, in the
first instance, on the provision of houses.
for these people.
The Government propose to continue to
local authorities, carrying out housing
schemes under the Acts, the assistance
provided in the Labourers Act of 1927;
that is to say, a grant of 40 per cent. of
the loan charges, subject to certain conditions designed to limit the cost of the
houses erected and the rate of interest
paid for loans.
It is estimated that the cost of erection
of a labourer's cottage should not exceed
£300, and it may possibly not exceed
£250. Assuming the former figure as the
maximum cost, the financial position, on
the basis that the loan is repayable in 40
years with interest at 4 per cent., would
be as follows:-

Against this the tenant may be expected
to pay a rent of 2s 6d per week or
£6 10s per year, leaving a net burden on
the rates of £8 4s per house. These
figures, of course, represent the charges
for the first year of the loan, and will
diminish annually until the loan is extinguished at the end of 40 years.
The position, therefore, is that in the
first year the Government pays £7 16s,
the local authority £8 4s, and the tenant
£6 10s, and as I have indicated, these
figures will be reduced annually as the
loan is paid off. This appears to me to be
a very equitable arrangement, and I hope
that the local authorities concerned will
take full advantage of the assistance

are really needed.
Without any further words I do wish

schools while, at the same time, the
proper housing of those children was
neglected owing to the financial
stringency. In conclusion, I again congratulate the Government on their action
in presenting this Bill for the approval
of this House.
