HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 17th October, 1935.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
WAGES OF GROUND STAFF AT
STORMONT.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has received
representations from the Amalgamated
Transport and General Workers' Union
on behalf of the ground staff at Stormont, and, if so, whether he is prepared
to increase wages to all the men involved
in conformity with the application.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It is true that some time ago
an application for an increase in wages was
made by the Secretary of the Amalgamated Transport and General Workers'
Union on behalf of our ground staff, and
the matter is under consideration.
BANNING OR SEIZURE OF FILMS.
2. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
how many films have been banned or
seized under the order made some three
or four years ago giving the police
authorities the right to seize and destroy
any films which they consider unsuitable,
and, if no seizures have been made,
whether he will revoke the order.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The position is that
a regulation was made on the 2nd May,
1930, in pursuance of the Civil Authorities Act empowering the civil authority
to make orders prohibiting the possession
or exhibition of any cinematograph film.
It has not been found necessary by the
civil authority to make any order under
this regulation, but, at the same time,
the power to make such order is regarded
as being a valuable if not necessary one,
and it is not proposed, therefore, to revoke the regulation.
It is to be clearly understood, however, that the powers given under this
regulation are exerciseable only in the
case of films which are considered subversive of law and order. The regula
tion has no relation whatsoever to
suitability or unsuitability of films from
the moral point of view, in which case
the Belfast Corporation-of which the
hon. Member is a member-is the cortrolling authority.
Mr. HENDERSON: Would the right
hon. Gentleman state whether it would
not be advisable, in the interests of the
people of Northern Ireland, that a film
censor should be appointed?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir. Not
if the Belfast Corporation did its duty.
CONTROL OF RENTS.
3. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minis
ter of Home Affairs whether he will consider the necessity of introducing
legislation controlling the rents charged
for dwelling-houses built with the help
of public subsidies; and whether it is a
fact that the rents charged for these
houses are often excessive and unreasonable.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would
remind the hon. and learned Member
that local authorities are already empowered by the Housing Act of 1933
to impose, if they think fit, a limitation
on the rents of the subsidy houses for a
period of three years as a condition of
making grants towards the erection of
such houses.
The hon. and learned Member is also
aware that no grants are payable by the
Government unless the local authority
makes a contribution of £25 or allows
exemption of rates to a corresponding
amount.
This principle has already been adopted
in Belfast and other places, and in the
case of Belfast the Corporation have fixed
maximum rents of 7s and 7s 9d a week
according to the density of the houses
per acre.
Under these circumstances there is no
necessity for introducing further legislation dealing with the houses at present
being erected, and apart from any other
consideration, it would be impossible at
this stage to impose limitations of rent
on houses which have already qualified
for subsidy.

Mr. POLLOCK: The purpose of the
financial Resolution which is on the Order
Paper to-day is to authorise the payment
out of voted moneys of the grants payable
to local authorities under the Bill now
before the Committee. The proposal in
the Bill is to continue the Labourers Acts
for a further period of five years; the
assistance to be given to rural district
councils under these Acts will consist of a
grant from Government funds amounting
to 40 per cent. of the loan charges

Under the Labourers Acts there was a

Exchequer grant being 33 per cent. of the

contradicted, and I would like to assure

They are houses. They are not henhouses or pigeon-houses such as have been
built under the subsidy. The Prime

to the hon. Member's question is in the
negative. I would remind the hon.
Member that local authorities have
powers in connection with the censoring
of films which have proved entirely
adequate, while the existing law in regard
to obscene books, pictures and representations provides ample power to deal
with any cases of publication or exhibition of such objectionable matter.

The PRIME MINISTER: In rising to
move the Resolution standing in my name
on the Paper, I am sure the House will be
aware of the dramatic and sudden
calamity that has overcome the country
in the death of Lord Carson. I venture
to make an appeal to the House when I
explain that this Motion will entail the
postponement of the Private Members
Notices on the Paper. I can give hon.
Members, however, a guarantee that at
the earliest date possible these Motions
will be again placed on the Paper and
can be debated as fully as the House
desire.
The Government are foregoing their
business out of respect to the memory of
our departed friend and leader. It means
that the House will meet later on in the
autumn-before Christmas-arrangements
for which meeting I will announce
as soon as possible. At the moment it
would be inappropriate to give a forecast
of the actual dates which are in the
minds of my colleagues and myself. The
permission of the House will be asked,
and has been obtained, to pass this Bill.

When I refer to that I will ask for

me personally owing to the position in
which I find myself to-day. The task
before me is the most difficult one I have
had to face in my political career. Over
and above the general loss not only to
Ulster and Great Britain and the Empire
of a great statesman, I have lost my
dearest friend. It is very difficult in a
few words to express my feelings, but I
am comforted, at all events, by the knowledge that I have around me some of
those who from the earliest days, when
Lord Carson was elected the leader of
the Ulster people, worked with him and
worked with me to the one end. If there
can be solace in reflection in connection
with this great man's passing it is that
his life was a pure one, it was an honourable one, it was a lesson to all of us for
straight dealing, and, above all, for sincerity and simplicity. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).

The old friends who are around me

when he was first elected to the leadership of the Ulster people he took upon
himself what appeared at the time to be

- behind him the name and reputation of

In the few moments that were available before the House met I thought
"What will the loss mean?" I am sure
the working men, especially in the yards,
who had an overwhelming feeling of
affection for him, reflected as it is by
the people of Ulster, will realise that a
sudden void has taken place, and they
may feel that one of the securities upon
which they counted during his lifetime
has been taken away. I know I, myself,
thought that whilst he was alive nothing
possibly untoward could happen to our beloved Ulster. Others may think the same
thing. Therefore, I can only say in all
sincerity and humbleness that as long as
I have the position I hold to-day I will
not allow the ideals for which that great
man fought to be lowered in the slightest
degree, but will maintain them to the
end. Indeed, I will endeavour
to
cement even still further the bonds that
bind us to Great Britain and the Empire.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I am sure that all those who came in
contact with Lord Carson from day to

extend to his beloved wife and family
their very deepest sympathy, and hope
that the softening effect of the flux of
time will allow nothing to remain in
their memory, as in our memory, except
that of a man to whom we have already
paid the highest tribute that we can by
asking and obtaining their permission to
have the care of his body for all time.
Immediately this disaster overcame us we
got in touch with the Dean and Chapter
of the Cathedral in the City of Belfast,
and they most willingly have agreed that
the body should be placed in that sacred
edifice where Ulster people can reverently
from time to time pay tribute to his
memory. We can think of nothing more
dignified or more fitting, and Lady
Carson, with whom I was in personal
communication this morning, desired me
I would close by saying that Lord
Carson and I were like David and

We of this Province will never forget the

and we certainly will never forget the

Hear, hear.)

EFFECT OF CUT ON TEACHERS'
PENSIONS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the total
number of public elementary school
teachers who have retired on pension
since the first cut in teachers' salaries
in 1926, and the total amount saved
thereby to the Exchequer; whether it is
his intention to reimburse to these retired
teachers the total amounts thus withheld
from them and take steps to ensure that
the pensions of teachers in future will
not be diminished by the operation of
the salary cuts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The number of public elementary teachers who retired on pension
between the 1st April, 1926, and the 30th
September last is 927. The aggregate
reduction in pension charges due to the
cuts in teachers' salaries could not be
ascertained without a great amount of
labour, which I do not think I would
be justified in instituting.
There is no question of any part of
his pension having been withheld from
any teacher, for under the Rules the
amount of pension is calculated on the
actual salary paid, and this principle has
been adopted throughout.
I am unable to hold out any hope that
the pensions can be re-calculated on the
basis of salaries received before the reductions took place.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
right hon. Gentleman whether he is aware
that teachers who retired since April,
1929, and who had contributed the percentage amount on their total salaries are
now in receipt of reduced pensions, and
whether in view of that serious loss to
those pensioned teachers he is going to
continue this grave injustice which he inflicted on teachers who retired in that
period?
Mr. POLLOCK: I think the hon.
Member, speaking as he does on behalf of
the teachers, fails to remember what the
Government has done for the elementary
school teachers. When we took over the
Pension Fund from the Imperial Government the deficiency in 1932 had amounted
to £4,356,000. It was so helplessly bankrupt that the Government, representing
the taxpayers of Northern Ireland, with
extreme generosity, took over the whole
liability of that fund and secured the
teachers absolutely in respect of these
pensions. The teachers are not in any
different position from that of all the
other servants of the Government, that is
to say, the pensions are paid on the basic
salary of the pensioner at the time the
pension was granted.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the basic salary of
the teachers was the only salary interfered
with in Northern Ireland, and in view of
the basic salary being changed does not
that make a great difference in the pension

THE CONTRIBUTORY PENSIONS
ACTS.
9. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of cases of
hardship to widows and orphans having
arisen under the Contributory Pensions
Acts, involving denial of all pension rights
through deceased contributors' cards being
two or three stamps short of the requisite
minimum; and whether he would consider
sympathetically an amendment of the law
to avert such hardships.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I am aware that cases necessarily arise where claims to pensions fail
because the applicants are unable to
satisfy the qualifying conditions, but I
would point out to the hon. and learned
Member that this is bound to happen
under any scheme, whether statutory or
voluntary, which is founded on rules
requiring observance.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the
Minister of Labour if he would give the
matter his own personal consideration?
Mr. ANDREWS: No. It is not possible to prevent hardships in connection
with legislation of this kind where statutory conditions have to be conformed to,
which statutory conditions have had the
approval of Parliament.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman not bring in a Bill to provide
pensions for all widows?
TRIAL OF ROMAN CATHOLIC
PRISONERS.
10. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Attorney-General whether in view of the
want of confidence induced among many
people in Northern Ireland by reason of
the trial of Catholic prisoners in party
cases by juries consisting exclusively of
members of a different persuasion he will
direct that the systematic stand-by for the
Crown of Catholic jurors in such cases
shall be discontinued.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): The Crown do not stand-by
jurors on the ground of religion, and if
the hon. and learned Member will
scrutinise the results of recent trials he
will find that the Belfast jurors have
acted with conspicuous impartiality and
solely on the evidence presented to them.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

answer of the right hon. and learned
Gentleman, may I ask does he deny that
in party cases of recent occurrence
Catholic prisoners have again and again
been tried by juries exclusively non-
Catholic owing to Crown stand-bys, and
in the interests of fair trials and of
general confidence in the fairness of trials
will he undertake that this system of
winnowing out Catholics from juries will
be discontinued?
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: 1 do
deny it.
In a case of a felony an accused
person has twenty peremptory challenges
which can be exercised without assigning
cause, and it would be inconsistent with
this right to inquire how it is exercised.
The Crown has no peremptory right of
challenge, but has a right to have the
panel exhausted, and here again to state
on what basis this right is exercised would
be obviously improper. I am not to be
drawn into an answer further than to
say it is not exercised on sectarian
grounds. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
CLOSING OF BELFAST PIG
MARKETS.
1. Major
HALL-THOMPSON (for
Lieut.-Colonel Gordon) asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware that
the closing of the livestock markets in
Belfast for the sale of sows, boars, overweight pigs, porkers and cutters has
deprived the farmers of an open market,
as the Pigs Marketing Board does not
buy pigs of the above description, and
whether he will consider the re-opening
of these markets at the end of six weeks'
quarantine, as is the practice by the
Ministry of Agriculture in England.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I assume the hon.
and gallant Member is referring to the
closing of the three livestock auction
marts in Belfast for the sale of live pigs.
So far as I am aware, this very necessary
action by my Ministry has not deprived
farmers of an open market for pigs of
the description mentioned. Farmers are
still perfectly free to dispose of such pigs
in any way they please through other
channels, and are presumably doing so.
Oral Answers
Diseases of Animals Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
Before dealing with the latter part of
the hon. and gallant Member's question,
I would like him to know that the action
which we have taken was, if anything,
overdue, and we have had ample evidence,
including that given in two recent_prosecutions, that the closing of the Belfast
auction marts for live pig sales was absolutely necessary to prevent the spread of
swine fever, which is a menace to our
rapidly developing pig industry. That
no hardship to producers is involved is
clearly proved by the fact that our action
has been highly commended by the Pigs
Marketing Board, representing the united
producers.
With regard to the question of reopening the marts for pig sales, as a
representative of an agricultural constituency the hon. and gallant Member
will, I hope,
hope, appreciate that the
disease aspect of the question and the
welfare of the agricultural industry are
the paramount consideration. The restrictions cannot be withdrawn until I
am satisfied that such action will not
endanger the safety of the pig population.
I cannot, moreover, promise to do so at
the end of six weeks or of any other
specified period, nor am I aware that such
a course would, as suggested, be adopted
in Great Britain, because obviously the
removal of restrictions of this nature
must depend entirely on the disease
position, and quite clearly each particular
case must be considered on its merits.
Mr. MINFORD: Arising out of that
reply, can the Minister tell us if fat sows
cannot be sold in the open market?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The difficulty
there is there is no guarantee that these
fat sows would be killed. They might
be bought by the vast majority of
farmers for breeding purposes and distributed through the country, and so the
danger might be increased.
Mr. MINFORD: Will the Minister
guarantee that every pig sold in Belfast.
market will be killed immediately? No
farmer is going to buy a fat sow to take
home.

nary Surgeons Act, 1881, either in the

Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Senate's
Amendment is designed to extend for the
purposes of the particular section the expression "animals" so as to embrace all
animals that might be subject to professional veterinary treatment. For instance,
by virtue of the Amendment it would be
possible for a registered veterinary surgeon
to prepare without a licence a therapeutic
substance for the treatment of a captive
lion or a captive tiger under his care.
The object of Clause 3, Sub-clause (2),
of the Bill is to remove any restrictions
that might arise in consequence of the
Act upon the rights and powers of veterinary surgeons to prepare therapeutic
substances in the exercise of their professional duties. I think, therefore, that no
reasonable objection can be made to an
Amendment, which will have the effect
of still further reducing the possibility of
such restrictions. I beg to move, "That
the House do agree with the Senate in the
said Amendment."
Question put, and agreed to.

over 55 was not entitled to a pension under
the Widows', Orphans' and Old Age
Contributory Pensions Act, 1929, in
respect of the employment of her late
husband.
The husband had been employed in Dublin, for three years before
his death in 1905, as a solicitor's clerk
at a salary under £160 a year, and the
question involved was whether employment in Southern Ireland before the
coming into force of the Irish Free State
Constitution Act, 1922, was employment
to which the Widows', Orphans' and Old
Age Contributory Pensions Act, 1929,
applied. The Widows', Orphans' and Old
Age Contributory Pensions Act, 1929,
Section 1 (1) provides:
A widow shall . . . be entitled to a
widow's pension, payable in accordance
with the Widows', Orphans' and Old-
Age Contributory Pensions Act, 1925
.. if she has attained the age of 55
and is the widow of a man-
(a) Who died before the fourth day
of January, 1926, and as respects whom
it is shown
(ii) That his normal occupation was
at some time within the period (i.e.,
three years before his death) employment in respect of which contributions
under the principal Act would have
been payable if that Act had been in
force at the time.
Mr. Justice Roche, in giving judg
ment, said that the Act of 1929 provided for pensions becoming payable
not merely to widows whose husbands
were contributors under the earlier Act,
but also, by means of what might be
described as a relationship back, to
widows whose husbands would have
been paying contributions if the principal Act had been in force at the time
of their death.
The Acts of 1925 and 1929 had both
been passed after the Irish Free State
came into being, and the argument was
that the matter should be treated as if
they had been passed before that
event. That argument was fortified by
the further argument that the deceased
man would have been an insured person
within the National Health Insurance
Act, as that Act did relate to Ireland.
But the real point for decision was
whether the husband was between 1902
and 1905 employed in an employment
in respect of which contributions under
the Act of 1925 would have been payable if that Act had been then in force.
In his view the Act of 1925 could
only be extended back in point of time
and not in point of place. To hold
otherwise would be to make applicable
to Ireland an Act which Parliament did
not intend should apply to that country.
He, therefore, thought the decision of
the Minister was correct. The appeal
would be dismissed.
In this case the Minister of Labour
through his accredited officials has denied
the right to participation in the 55 or 60
pension to all those widows whose husbands were employed in the Irish Free
State prior to 4th January, 1926. That
was the case of a man who returned to
Northern Ireland on the setting up of
the two Governments. His residence
qualification commenced from the inception of the Northern Ireland Government,
but his widow cannot be treated as a
person who would qualify for the pension.
I think that in itself would justify me in
asking for an extension of the Pensions
Act to cover all widows and orphans here.
If we do not do so then it is only, in my
opinion, a farce and a fraud on those who
are looking for the assistance which is not
forthcoming from our present Government.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech on behalf of his Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
were 80
It is a matter of great satisfaction to
me as his Majesty's representative in
Northern Ireland, at the inauguration
of the third session of this Parliament,
to record the tributes of affection which
widely and spontaneously
addressed to their Majesties the King
and Queen on the celebration of their
Silver Jubilee. This year will long be
cherished as having afforded a unique
opportunity to the people of Northern
Ireland of demonstrating once again
their unalterable loyalty and devotion
to the Throne.
I am gratified that we continue to be
free from industrial disputes, and I wish
to commend the reasonable spirit shown
by both the employers and the workers'
representatives in maintaining their
relationship on a harmonious footing.
The unsettlement of foreign markets,
due to international causes, led to a
curtailment of employment during the
summer months, but I am glad to learn
that since then the situation has been
more than restored, and that there has
been a reduction in the number of
persons registering for work at the
Exchanges of some nine thousand.
It is a source of great satisfaction to
me to observe that the improvement in
Northern Ireland's industrial position,
to which I called attention a year ago,
has been maintained, and especially
that the shipbuilding industry has
King's Speech
Debate on the Address
26 NOVEMBER 1935
enjoyed a degree of activity approaching
that of pre-War years. It is equally
gratifying to find that there is an increasing demand for linen goods in the
Dominion markets, and that, mainly
as a consequence of improved conditions
within the Empire, the exports of linen
piece-goods during the first nine months
of 1935 were slightly greater in value
than those during the corresponding
period in 1934.
Experience of the National Health
Insurance Scheme points I am glad to
say, to a considerable improvement in
the health of those falling within its
compass, due no doubt in great part to
the absence of serious epidemics, as well
as to the beneficial effect of the Medical
Benefit arrangements which have
operated for five years, and now cover
over 370,000 persons. I am also
gratified that the results of the latest
quinquennial valuation of Approved
Societies, in so far as they are already
disclosed, indicate that during the
coming five years there will be no
lessening of those additional benefits in
the form of dental and other treatments
now enjoyed by a substantial part of
the insured population.
A measure will be laid before you
extending until the 30th September,
1936, the scheme of subsidy payments
by my Government and by the Local
Authorities, should they so desire, in
connection with the provision of houses
for the working classes.
It was found impracticable last
session to consider proposals for the
amendment of the Derating Code in
relation to Government grants, and a
Bill for this purpose will be submitted
for your consideration.
You will also be invited to consider
proposals for the amendment of various
statutes consequential on the changes
in the valuation of properties in
Northern Ireland, which take effect
from 1st April next.
Legislation will be submitted for your
consideration amending the Marketing
of Dairy Produce Act, 1929; the
Marketing of Eggs Acts and the Agricultural Produce (Meat Regulation)
Act, 1930.
Other Bills will be introduced dealing
with Miscellaneous Law Reform, the
principles of Arbitration, the Superannuation Rights of Civil Servants and
Markets and Market Tolls.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The marked progress which continues
to be made in the electrification of the
rural and urban districts throughout
Northern Ireland, and the increased
welfare in those areas, which has come
about as the direct result of the legislative Measures taken by Parliament to
bring about a co-ordination of the public
supply and distribution of electricity
are most satisfactory.
I am glad to observe the gradual improvement in the position of the agricultural community, which has been
brought about through the operation of
the various Measures which have been
passed in recent years with the object
of improving the methods and organisation for the marketing of agricultural
produce. In particular, I am glad to
note the success which has attended the
efforts which have been made to improve
the position of the pig producer, as a
result of which the number of pigs in
Northern Ireland has doubled since
1932.
It is also gratifying to note the success
which has been achieved under the Milk
and Milk Products Act, and to know
that in addition to securing a reasonable price to the farmer who produces
milk for the liquid milk market, this
Measure has resulted in the payment of
over £272,000 to creamery suppliers
since the 1st April, 1934.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your deliberations.

That a humble address be presented to his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland as followeth :
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Lynn]
Northern Ireland, in
Parliament
our
assembled, beg leave to offer
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
The most notable event in the annals
of our country this year was the Silver
Jubilee of our beloved King and Queen,
and it is in keeping with the feelings of
our people that the first paragraph in
the Gracious Speech should refer to it.
You will search the pages of history in
vain for such a widespread exhibition of
loyalty to the Throne. As one thought
of the extent and variety of the rejoicings
it was possible to draw a mental picture
of the British Empire and the unique
position which our King holds as the
head of the greatest Commonwealth of
Nations the world has ever seen. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
a
To be the head of such an Empire
means great responsibility. By common
consent it is agreed that in our "rough
Island story" we have never had
Sovereign who has discharged his duties
more faithfully or with greater ability
than has King George, and, as for his
gracious Consort, she has long since
established for herself the position of
perfect woman and Queen, who shares
with the King the unbounded love of
tens of millions of loyal subjects.
We in Northern Ireland yield to no
part of his Majesty's vast Dominions in
loyalty and devotion to the Throne, and
to each one of us it was a matter of deep
pride that our Prime Minister and Lady
Craigavon formed part of that historic
procession to St. Paul's last May. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) In paying their
tribute to the King and Queen they were
expressing the feeling which is deep in
the heart of each one of us.
Our earnest prayer is that their
Majesties may be long spared to rule over
us.
Reference is made in the Gracious
Speech to the fact that during the year
our community has been free from industrial disputes. Strikes and lock-outs are
relics of a barbaric age when Might was
always Right. Our employers and employed are to be congratulated on their
wisdom in using Reason rather than Force
in settling their differences. In the ultimate result it is always Reason that has
the final word. Why not let it have the
first word as well?
I have never known a strike or a lockout to benefit anyone.
In the last forty years more money
has been wasted on coal strikes than would
have bought out half the coal mines in
Great Britain.
In other spheres as well as the industrial
we can only hope and pray for the development of the sweet spirit of reasonableness. It is not in keeping with the
teaching of Him whom we call Master
that we should try to enforce our opinions
on others by resorting to brute force. We
should never forget that we profess to
serve one King, and that His injunction
to us is to love one another. When we
realise our duty to obey this command
strikes, riots and bitter feelings will disappear for ever.
It is a matter for thankfulness that
the industrial position of Northern Ireland continues to improve. Not for a
considerable time has shipbuilding been
so active, and for this satisfactory state
of affairs no small amount of credit is
due to the Northern Government. I have
no hesitation in saying-and I speak with
a good deal of inside knowledge of the
shipping industry-that had it not been
for the help and influence of the Northern
Government many of the shipbuilding
orders that have come to Belfast would
have gone elsewhere. The linen industry
is also on the upgrade.
It is gratifying to note that there is a
gradual improvement in agriculture.
There is no doubt that the marketing
schemes have had a beneficial effect.
They are in the nature of an experiment,
and, I am sure, that where weak points
are revealed, the Government will be
ready to remedy them. The measure of
the success of these marketing schemes
must in the long run depend largely on
the people concerned, and I would appeal
to them to co-operate wholeheartedly with
the Government. It is not possible to
produce a scheme that will please everyone, but in a democratic community like
once a measure has been passed,
even though we may object to some of
the details, we should do our best to help
its successful operation.
ours

Debate on the Address
26 NOVEMBER 1935
The dog-in-the-manger policy is not
consistent with democratic Government,
nor is it helpful to the community. With
cordial goodwill on the part of all concerned, it is always possible to enhance
the value of any piece of legislation.
People who have no other mission in life.
but faultfinding rarely achieve anything
tangible. Criticism, where it is of a
constructive character, is always helpful,
but mere faultfinding is worse than useless.
With regard to the paragraph about
health insurance, I feel that no one is
better qualified to deal with it than the
hon. and gallant Member (Colonel
Mitchell), who is to follow me, and I shall
content myself by saying how deeply
grateful we all are to the medical profession of which he is such a distinguished
member. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Most of us owe more than we can ever
express to members of that profession.
As you will see the Bills to be introduced this Session are few in number,
and I doubt if any of them will provide
much food for controversy. This does
not cause me any personal regret, because for many years at Westminster,
and here, I have been urging the slowing down of the legislative machinery.
I am not among those who believe
that all
our ills can be cured by
Parliament, and I am, therefore, grateful to the Government for reducing
legislation to a minimum this Session.
One of the Bills to be introduced
reminds us of a fierce controversy which
raged over revaluation a few months ago.
If we had believed some of the more vocal
of the critics it was to be the end of
all things. We were assured that the
Courts would be engaged for years in
hearing appeals. What has really
happened? In Belfast, out of 110,964
valuations, the learned Recorder has had
to deal with less than 300 appeals. The
only conclusion I can come to is that there
was no very serious grievance, and that
most of the agitation was what the
Americans call hot air. Local councils
were afraid that they were going to suffer,
but their fears have been removed by the
agreement which Parliament will
asked to ratify in a short time.
be
In this connection may I say that the
general public are under a deep debt of
gratitude to the Minister of Finance (Mr.
Pollock) and my hon. Friend the Member
for Mid Antrim (Mr. Crawford), who
were chiefly responsible for carrying out
this amicable arrangement.
They have
provided us with another object lesson on
the value of sweet reasonableness, and
they have routed an army of critics.
As tradition on this occasion prevents
me from entering the controversial arena
I am anxious to make way for those who
wish to measure swords, but before doing
so I desire to express my deep thankfulness for what we in Northern Ireland have
achieved in the past, and I wish to express
the hope that with courage, confidence
and unity we may achieve even greater
things in future. I beg to move.
Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL (in morning dress): I have the honour of rising
to second the vote of thanks so ably
proposed by the Member for North
Antrim. The loyalty of Ulster is traditional. If one travelled the whole world
over one could not find anything comparable to our Royal Family. The
Prince of Wales, the Duke of York, the
Duke of Kent, and our Earl of Ulster
form a battalion characterised by
nobility, dignity, uprightness and diplomatic tact which constitute an impregnable defence for the British Crown.
The people of Ulster hope that the time
is not far distant when one of the Royal
Family will
to reside amongst
them.
come
The questions of unemployment and
increased business prosperity have been
so fully dealt with by the hon. Member,
who has just spoken, that I propose to
pass on and deal as suggested by him
with the next question, the health of
the community. It is now a recognised
fact that the Governments in all civilised
countries have a responsibility for the
health of the people whom they govern.
It is interesting to note that the first
attempt to make any regulations bearing
directly on the health of the people dealt
with a single disease-smallpox.
refer to the legislation following the
discoveries of Jenner regarding compulsory vaccination, which
was introduced about 130 years ago. As a result of
that legislation the dreaded disease of
smallpox, with its heavy mortality and
pock-marked victims, has with the help
of better housing and other conditions
practically disappeared from our midst.
I
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Mitchell]
The battle against disease has been long,
slow, and extraordinarily expensive.
There is, indeed, nothing in this country
to be compared with its costliness, either
to
the nation or to the individual.
Fortunately, the battle is being waged
very successfully, though very slowly.
Typhoid and typhus fevers, which were
rampant in former days, are now almost
a rarity. The white scourge of tuberculosis is also being dealt with with
extraordinary success, and there is every
reason to hope that in the life of the
present generation our country will be
free from that dreadful disease.
The National Health Insurance Acts,
which were introduced in Northern
Ireland some years ago, have been of
considerable benefit, and it may interest
some people to know-I do not know that
it is understood enough-the large amount
of money that is distributed amongst the
people as a result of this arrangement
made by the Minister of Labour. During
the past year no less than £258,000 was
distributed for medical benefits and
medicines. In sickness benefit no less a
sum than £418,000 has been distributed
amongst the homes of the poorer people in
this Province. That sum included maternity
benefit. I often wonder how we manage
to provide the money, but it is done. I
look forward to the Acts being further
extended. As at present arranged no
special provision is made for insured
people when they become seriously ill.
When they require hospital treatment
they have to fall back on our great
voluntary hospitals. I look forward to
the time when the right hon. Gentleman
in charge of this Department will be able
to arrange for some recognised hospital
accommodation for these unfortunate
people when they require it.
I appreciate very much the reference
in the Speech to the prosperity of the
farming community. Numbers of energetic
young men in later years have rushed to
the cities dreaming of regular employment, wealth and pleasure only to find
themselves up against concentrated
unemployment, misery and vice.
As
soon as the farming community can
make a competent and comfortable living
that rush will stop. These young men
will remain on the land, provide homes
for themselves, and rear their families in
pure air, surrounded with all the beauties
of nature. Wireless and transport conditions have together improved the
amenities of country life, and I do hope
that this improvement will continue, and
that more and more all these people will
stay on the land. "Back to the land" is
a useless and stupid suggestion unless it
can be shown to the people that they
can make comfortable livings and happy
homes in the country. Once that is
recognised the independence which characterises the countryman will ensure
loyal citizenship in this country.
a
The hon. Member who moved the
Address in Reply to the King's Speech
referred to the legislative programme of
the Government. Excessive legislation is
an undesirable thing. However we may
look at it, it must clearly be understood
that every Act of Parliament, every new
piece of legislation, inevitably interferes
with the liberty of somebody. It curtails
his liberty and rights, and, while it is
necessary to have some uniform arrangement by which people will live in comfort
and happiness with one another, it is very
undesirable, in my view, to undermine
the independence and the rights of the
individual. I have, therefore, great
pleasure in seconding this Motion..

Ireland into such an unsettled state that
the Government of Northern Ireland
was on the verge of being once and for
all left on the shelf.
In 1929 I came forward as a recruit
into politics. I certainly glorified my
entry by heading the poll for East Belfast. The hon. Member for Shankill
(Mr. Henderson) also glorified himself
by heading the poll in that division.
Every Member in opposition to the
Government at that time came out with
flying colours, due to the propaganda of
the hon. Member for North Antrim, who
is now coming down to lecture the
Opposition on their duties to the Government and to Government legislation,
which will be passed and which has been
passed for the guidance of the people of
Northern Ireland.
I always liked the hon. Member for
North Antrim, and I always respected
and honoured the seconder of the Motion,
but I do not put them in the same class.
I put the mover in one class as a parliamentarian, and I put the seconder in
another class as a humanitarian. The
seconder to-day has proved beyond the
shadow of a doubt that he is desirous of
assisting and relieving the pains and
sufferings of the down-and-outs.
He
did so by his reference to hospital accommodation and the treatment necessary for
the poor, unfortunate, people who have
been struck down in life through no fault
of their own, but through depression in
trade and through circumstances over
which they have no control. He has
certainly my most hearty support in his
efforts to relieve the difficulties and
troubles of that class.

But I must come back again to the
old parliamentarian. (Laughter.)
must say that if he wants peace, contentment, love, comradeship, and good feeling in Northern Ireland, he will have to
get inside the Cabinet and assist them to
realise the needs and requirements of the
people, and put those requirements into
the King's Speech at the next opening
of Parliament. I regret to see no reference to the needs and requirements of
the people in the Speech. There are one
or two little palliatives which will relieve
a certain section of the community in
their difficulties with legislation already
passed, but I can see nothing to assist
the many thousand unemployed in Northern Ireland, the many thousand widows
who are denied the right to widows'
pensions, and the many thousand
juveniles who have attained the age of
twenty-one years and have not got a
place in industry yet.
I find nothing in the King's Speech
and nothing in the remarks of the hon.
Member for North Antrim to outline the
policy of the Government in regard to
these questions, which I think are allimportant. The nation's assets lie in the
human element. That is the principal
thing, and in this Speech it has been
forgotten. It is quite true to say that
the shipbuilding and engineering industries have improved, but it is not
true to say the improvement can absorb
into employment all those who previously
were in those industries.
In 1914 shipbuilding employed upwards of 22,000 men, but with the same
amount of tonnage on the stocks to-day
what is the number employed? The industry does not absorb 11,000, due of
course to the output being expedited by the
introduction of new machinery and newer
methods of constructing ships. I do not
put the responsibility for that on the
employing class, nor yet do I put it on
the Government; but I do put on the
Government and leave at their door the
blame for having made no provision for
that half of the shipbuilding and engineering workers who will no longer find
employment in those industries. That
means we are going to have a continual
unemployment figure from that source
alone.
The next thing I come to is the linen
industry, where an improvement has been
shown. In normal times people would
regret an improvement in industry when
the causes were those which have brought
about the improvement in the linen industry, that is the threatened world-wide
war. There is an improvement in many
industries due to that threatened war over
the world. I do not think any of us
would agree that any nation should apply
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
itself to war, but I can say that we in
Northern Ireland are reaping the benefits
of a threatened war. I cannot justify
employment of that kind. Perhaps the
Members of the Government would endeavour to justify it. However, our
linen industry has got that little fillip,
and it can be stated in the King's Speech
that there is an improvement in our linen
industry. There is, unfortunately, a
larger percentage of linen workers in
Northern Ireland out of employment now
than there was ten years ago.
Then we come to the most vital problem,
that is that of the boys of to-day who
I will be the men of to-morrow. I have
made reference to those between the ages
of 14 and 21. I have perused the King's
Speech, and I find nothing in that Speech
setting out the policy of the Government
in regard to making provision for the
youth of our country. Is it their
intention that the younger generation
shall loaf and lounge about and not be
fit for any useful employment? Is that
the intention of the Government? According to this document which I have in
my possession they are bankrupt of any
ideas in so far as the juveniles of Northern
Ireland are concerned.
I thought I might have found a reference to the raising of the school-leaving
age, so that if we could not find work for
them we might find them education. But
now I see we cannot find them work,
and we are not willing to find them
education. Therefore, I would like to
know what is the intention of the Government with regard to the juveniles in
Northern Ireland who have attained the
age of fourteen years. Every Member of
the House recognises, if not publicly at
least privately, that it is nearly impossible
to place the juveniles who are leaving
school in employment. The omission of
any reference to this matter would justify
any Member on this side of the House
in condemning the Government for their
slip-shod methods of applying themselves
to the real issues that require attention.
Then in the Speech we have mention
made of national health insurance? Such
a misnomer I never heard in my life.
The scheme should be applied to every
member of the community, but to-day it
is applied only to a particular class which
is brought under the Minister of Labour,
and which follows an insured occupation.
To-day 370,000 people are enjoying the
rights of national health insurance. What
is the population of Northern Ireland? It
is 1,250,000. Upon what do the remainder
of the people depend for health, unemployment, and old age? What right has
the Government to place itself on the side
of one class of the community and say:
We will give a State grant for the upkeep
of national health insurance under
friendly societies and deprive the remainder of the community of the right
of participating in that scheme.
Once again I say the name is a misnomer when applied to the scheme as
run by the State. I have advocated time
after time that society ownership of
national health insurance must cease, and
I am proud to see that my way of thinking
is being taken up by politicians in Great
Britain. The time has arrived when
there must be a stocktaking in regard to
national health insurance. National
health insurance must be applied so that
it will cover all workers, whether of hand
or brain, who require the assistance of
the scheme.
I come now to the sorest point in connection with national health insurance.
We have at the end of this year 3,500
widows denied the right to pension
because of the conditions of membership
which those private companies placed
upon those deceased who were at one
time insurable. Neglect might not be
the proper word to apply, but I feel that
the harsh regulations applied by the
various societies operating in health insurance have been the means of denying
the right to pensions to anything from
6,000 to 7,000 widows in Northern
Ireland.
That may be challenged, and it may be
said that national health insurance only
conforms to the law or to the regulations
made by the Ministry of Labour. That
is quite true, but I can administer a
thing in a Christian way, and I could
administer it in an unchristian way. The
regulations could be used very sympathetically or they could be used
very severely. But to-day no Member of
the Government could justify the denial
to 7,000 widows in Northern Ireland of
the right to participate in the pensions
scheme under national health insurance.
I feel that we have to remedy that
position, and we have to remedy it in
such a way as to provide for that 90 per

.
cent. of those widows whose husbands, if
employment had been anything like
decent in Northern Ireland, would have
been in employment at the date of their
death. Owing to the depressed state of
the employment market their husbands
were put out of employment for periods
of three to five years, and at the end of
five years their insurability connection
ceased altogether. Then, due to malnutrition caused by unemployment and
financial difficulties, ill-health beset the
home; that ill-health attacked the weak
spots of the father's body and took him
away, leaving his widow and orphans
without their breadwinner.
Because of the defects of the system
under which he lived, and which prevented him from complying with the
insurability conditions under national
health insurance, his widow and orphans
are now denied the right to pension. I
say that is not Christian. That never
really was the intention of the originators
of the widows' and orphans' pensions
scheme. The Government of Northern
Ireland would be justified in travelling
along the lines of the Motion moved by
the hon. Member for Shankill (Mr.
Henderson) and myself and in providing
pensions for all widows whose husbands'
earnings did not exceed £260 in any one
year. That would be justifiable and
would relieve some of the hardships under
which some of the widows and orphans
who are not in receipt of pensions to-day
are suffering.
As I say, unemployment, pensions,
juvenile employment, and the school leaving age are not going to be affected by
the King's Speech. The Minister of
Finance, through the hon. Member for
North Antrim, has tried to justify the revaluation of Northern Ireland. He
justified it on the ground that only
300 appeals had been lodged before the
Recorder of Belfast. But he did not give
us the number of the first appeals
lodged before the Commissioner.
believe I would be right in saying that
out of a population of over 400,000 there
were upwards of 300,000 appeals to the
Commissioner. Because of the heavy
penalty that is placed upon an appellant,
because of the necessity of placing down
£5 before he can appeal, because of the
expense of engaging counsel and of bearing the heavy costs of an appeal, out of
those 300,000 appeals to the Commissioner
I
you only had 300 appeals presented to
the Recorder. One reason for that is that
there are many thousands of people waiting to see the results of the appeals
brought before the Recorder by those who
had the money at their disposal to fight
their cases.
And the results of those
appeals so far certainly have not been
very satisfactory. But valuation in
Belfast is by no means settled. There is
a very heavy sledge hammer hanging on
a very slender thread. Some day it may
fall and, perhaps, give the knock-out to
the Minister of Finance. I would not
like to see it. Of course I mean that
politically. But I feel that you will
have to do something further than just
give people the right to appeal to the
Recorder. Financial difficulties have
prevented many people from appealing to
that court.
Now I have to come back to this little
lecture which the hon. Member for North
Antrim gave us.
He says:
-
"I express my deep thankfulness and
I express the hope that we may live to
achieve greater things."
I have lived in that hope since I first
entered this House. This is now 1935,
but to-day I am as far from seeing that
hope realised as I was when I first came
here. Right well does the hon. Member
for North Antrim know that the achievement referred to will never be accomplished while we have facing us a party
who are prepared to sacrifice the real
assets of the nation and to keep themselves in the seats of the mighty by handing out little palliatives to the farming
community. Before I finish I feel that I
might be permitted to read a speech
delivered in Ballymoney Orange Hall by
the hon. Member for North Antrim and
to compare it with the speech he has
delivered here to-day. On one occasion
I said to the hon. Member for Coagh that
the conversion of Paul on his way to
Damascus was as nothing compared with
the conversion of the hon. Member for
Coagh judging from the speech he then
made. This is another extreme conversion.
Mr. ELLIOTT: You will be getting
turned yourself.
Mr. BEATTIE: I hope I have not expressed myself in a manner that would
convey that I was converted to the politics
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
of the hon. Member for Coagh or the hon.
Member for North Antrim. If he has
taken that from my remarks he will be
disappointed.
"Speaking at Ballymoney Orange
Hall last week Sir Robert Lynn, M.P.,
an Orangeman and a supporter of the
Craigavon Government, said-
"We are becoming, if indeed we
have not already become, the most
official-ridden community in Europe
outside Russia. Civil servants control the Cabinet, the Cabinet control
the Members of Parliament, and the
public pay and suffer. Public
opinion as we once knew it is almost
dead. Our opinions are now made
for us on the mass production
system."
That is a glorious contribution to make
towards the Government in 1925. As an
old parliamentarian you knew that would
be on record against you, but, nevertheless, you get up to-day and make a statement eulogising the Government for the
good work they have done and for the
independent spirit they have shown. You
make that speech in Ballymoney Orange
Hall to the raw farmer, the fellow you
think you can gull at every turn and
corner. I wish I were in Ballymoney
Orange Hall for five or ten minutes with
the farmers. Then, perhaps, they might
not be as raw as some hon. Members on
that side of the House think they are.
Then we come to another speech of the
hon. Member. This is not a case of just
an odd speech here and there, such as
some Members of the Government make.
To keep themselves in the limelight they
get up now and again and make outrageous speeches, and one cannot find
fault with them for that. Like the shopkeepers, they have to keep their windows
dressed for the next election. The
Government have to dress their window,
and I raise no objection to that. I am
only trying to show the consistency of
the hon. Member for North Antrim in
his pursuit of the Government. At this
other meeting he said:
:-
"They in Northern Ireland had set
up an administration large enough and
costly enough to run a wealthy State.
In days of old, when we were more
prosperous than now, one Cabinet
Minister was sufficient to manage the
affairs of the whole of Ireland. To-day
we have seven Cabinet Ministers and
five or six Parliamentary Secretaries in
the North. Our population is only
equal to that of Glasgow, but one
Secretary of State and one deputy
suffice for the whole of Scotland."
Do I take it from that speech delivered
in 1925 that the hon. Member for North
Antrim desired an all-Ireland Parliament, that he believed that on the basis
of an all-Ireland Parliament the needs
and requirements of the people of
Northern Ireland could be fulfilled?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Certainly not.
Mr. BEATTIE: I certainly feel that
no one outside an asylum could read anything else into it, because you were asking for the abolition of the Cabinet and
suggesting that one Secretary of State
should be set up in its place. I feel that
those speeches read in conjunction with
the speech of the hon. Member to-day will
not raise him in the minds of the people
in his constituency. I would have congratulated him if he had gone on the four
points which I have raised and had dealt
with the most important things for the
State, namely widows' and orphans'
pensions, unemployment, the juvenile
question, and the school leaving age. If
he had based his argument on what the
Government have done for those classes of
the community I certainly would have
given him credit where credit would have
been due.
I make this my last point. I do not
know whether it has reference to the
King's Speech or not, but we will try it.
The King's Speech does not contain anything in regard to the improvement of
unemployment in Northern Ireland. We
are still waiting for the Second Appointed
Day. We are waiting to hear that the
100,000 able-bodied unemployed
in
Northern Ireland are going to get some
humane treatment, as far as the necessaries
of life are concerned, by being taken away
from the poor-law and being placed under
Ministry of Labour administration. Up
to the moment I have not heard one
solitary word as to what the date is likely
to be, but I have heard in the past the
Minister of Finance say that he is compensating Belfast and other local authorities for providing for these people under
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
26 NOVEMBER 1935
the poor-law. I do not want provision
made under the poor-law. I want provision made under the Unemployment
Insurance Act that is likely to give them
that decency and comfort which they
deserve. And I will not be satisfied until
every man, woman, and child in Northern
Ireland is getting that condition of life
which we all desire to have ourselves.
My next point is that the economy cuts
on all salaries in Great Britain have been
restored by the Chancellor of the
Exchequer there. There is not one
person in receipt of a salary in Great
Britain now who is suffering any reduction as a result of the economy cuts of
1931-32, but we in Northern Ireland are
still subject to that economy cut.
There
is a class of the community-the school
teachers who lost £150,000 by the 1926
and the 1931 cuts. That was taken away
from their basic salaries. They were the
only profession in Northern Ireland who
lost anything from their basic salaries.
By the reduction of their basic salaries
their pensions were affected if they
retired within the period of the operation of the cut. In England the pension
cut and the cost of living bonus cuts have
been restored. Not only has that been
done, but a Commission has been set up
to establish a new salary scale for the
teaching profession in England as from
March next.
The Minister of Finance and the other
Members of the Cabinet have not thought
it worth their while to recognise the
services that this class of the community
has rendered through the cut, representing £150,000, and through its contribution to the erection of new schools
throughout Northern Ireland. Not one
contribution has been given by the
Government towards that great service.
The Government have done the opposite.
They have added insult to injury. They
have brought in a Superannuation Bill,
which is mentioned in the King's Speech,
to cover civil servants. What is wrong
with the teaching profession that the
Government have not included them in
this Superannuation Bill which it is
hoped to put into operation in 1936?
Are the civil servants in the happy
position of regulating the Bill that the
Government bring in, and deciding what
the Government will do, and what the
Government will not do? Are those outside this House only permitted to receive
what the civil servants think is good for
them? The hon. Member for North
Antrim has said that the civil servants
run the Cabinet. When he made that
remark he must have been thinking what
I am saying now, that the mind of the
Cabinet is regulated by highly-paid civil
servants. I object to that. If this
Superannuation Bill is good for civil
servants, it must also be good for other
classes of the community in that grade.
I hope the Minister will not forget that
the grade I am speaking of is living in
hope of his pronouncement on the cuts
in their salaries. They hope that their
conditions of service and their superannuation will be regulated with
equality of civil servants for whom the
Minister is making provision in this Bill.
the
I have now dealt with the points which
I wished to bring forward. I have every
sympathy with those broken down in
health, who were referred to by the
seconder of the Address. Throughout my
industrial career I have endured many
insults and suffered much abuse by going
round the shipyards and engine works
collecting a shilling per month from each
man for the upkeep of the Royal Victoria
Hospital and other institutions of that
kind. I should like to say that I stand
for the State being responsible for the
upkeep of those hospitals. They are a
State responsibility. I am not aware
that any man deliberately goes out of his
way to meet with an accident. I feel
that if the hon. and gallant Member for
the University (Colonel Mitchell) would
come along with me and advocate State
responsibility for the hospitals in
Northern Ireland, we would make more
headway than we are doing by depending
upon charity for the upkeep of such
important institutions as those referred to
by the hon. and gallant Member. That
is all I want to say so far as the general
discussion of the Address is concerned,
and I hope that the Minister of Finance
and others will pay strict attention to the
points I have made.
The PRIME MINISTER: My duty on
an occasion of this sort is more or less
prescribed by long practice. The first
and most pleasurable part of that duty
I have to perform is to congratulate the
mover and the seconder of the Address
to the Throne. My old Friend the Member for North Antrim, of course, is

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
our
[The Prime Minister]
familiar with the procedure in the Parliament at Westminster. He has had
almost as long a Parliamentary career as
I myself have had, and although, as has
been pointed out in somewhat glowing
language by the hon.
by the hon. Member for
Pottinger, in the early stages of
career as a young Parliament he and I
may have differed from time to time, I
think that probably on many occasions
there was very little between us on one
question or another. Still I think that
on the whole this House will realise that
the great good the hon. Member has done
to his native country in presiding for a
very protracted time over the Committee
that has laid the foundation stone of our
educational policy in Northern Ireland is
a debt that we all owe to him, a debt,
if I may say so in all sincerity, quite
large enough to wipe out everything else
that he has ever said. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The hon. Member for Pottinger twitted
him with window dressing. There is not
a Member on this side of the House who
could not take a lesson in window
dressing from the hon. Member. I think
he prides himself upon it, and I am sure
any young Member who desires a hint on
that subject knows exactly where to go.
With regard to our very distinguished
Friend, the Member for the University,
I was delighted with every word he said.
Our hearts are as generous as his is
where the health of the community is
concerned. He has given due praise
where praise should be given, and I can
assure him that my colleagues and I are
with him in still striving to better all
those who are not so well able to look
after either their health or their pockets
as others are in the community.
The second duty that falls to my lot
is to answer as well as possible the speech
that is made by the Leader of the
Opposition, and to restrain myself as far
as possible from travelling outside that
particular duty. The hon. Member for
Pottinger complained that in the present
King's Speech there is no reference to
unemployment insurance, old age pensions, or widows' and orphans' pensions.
That is very easily explained. We intend
to maintain our unemployment insurance,
our old age pensions, and our widows'
and orphans' pensions on the same satisfactory basis as has been the custom in
the past, and at the same time, if any
improvement in those services takes place
at any time in the legislation of the
Imperial Parliament, we shall not be very
many days behind them in giving the
citizens of Northern Ireland full advantage of any increase that may take place.
I cannot say more. At the same time
the people themselves will rightly realise
that more than that would be impossible
for Ulster as against the wealthy community in the rest of the United Kingdom.

inspector. We would not dream of it."

I have always looked on Ulster as
garden. I think I have called it the
garden of Eden on some occasion when
my heart was joyful and my feelings were
much in the air with regard to the love
I have for my own part of the world.
A garden runs down very easily unless
it receives intensive care. I am sure you
have all seen a beautiful garden in the
spring and the occupiers of the house
to which it belonged have had to go away
for some reason or other. I do not know
anything more sad and regrettable than
to look at what was a beautiful garden
becoming in a few months like a wilderness. I always feel with regard to the
garden of Ulster that if we allow it to
stagnate even for a month or two it would
be very difficult to catch up, and the
bounden duty not only of the Government and Members on all sides but those
who live in the garden outside is to keep
it free of weeds and do what they possibly
can to make two blades of grass grow
where only one grew before, and to pull
together so as to make this garden the
most perfect garden inside the Empire.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

[Mr. Henderson]
I am absolutely amazed at the part played
by our Cabinet Ministers in trying to
bring prosperity to this country. They
have failed miserably. The Prime Minister, in answer to the hon. Member for
Pottinger, who asked for better pensions
for widows and orphans and pensions for

that in this Parliament they could not
do that, even if they wished to do it?
Would that not be true?
Mr. ANDREWS: No.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the Minister

orphans in Northern Ireland who are not
receiving them at the present time? He
has said that he has power to do that.
I want to tell the right hon. Gentleman
that he cannot throw dust in the eyes of
the people.
While I am very proud of the electors
of Shankill for returning me to this Parliament, it is rather unfortunate that we
are not in a position to do anything for
our industries which are declining at the
present time. Is it not true that in the
home of linen, Northern Ireland, many
mills have been closed during the past
few years? They have been closed in
Shrigley, in Whiteabbey, and in places
in Antrim-in fact you could not single
out any part of Northern Ireland where
there has not been some small factory or
mill closed during the past six or seven
years without anything being done to
provide the neighbourhoods concerned
with new industries.
The Government have failed miserably
in their effort to establish new industries
in order to absorb the ever-growing unemployed population of Northern Ireland.
The Minister of Labour will tell us, and
I am delighted to hear it, that there has
been a little bit of a fillip so far as the
shipyards are concerned, but the Government were not responsible for that. They
always take credit for doing what the
directors of the shipyard do. The Prime
Minister referred to shareholders in the
shipyard. Why did the noble Lord and
his friends not try to become shareholders
in some new industry? I, myself, have
not the money to become a shareholder
in any industry. I am kept occupied
fighting for the people who sent me here.
I do not wish to be pessimistic in this
matter, but I feel that as far as our
Cabinet Ministers are concerned that they
have become absolutely hopeless. If the

for Falls (Mr. Byrne), or even myself,
we would take him into districts where
the sights to be met would strike horror
into his heart, even in my own neighbourhood up the Lisburn Road.
young man came to me the other night,
and through the apathy of the Minister
of Labour in not compelling bookmakers to stamp the cards of their clerks
he can receive no benefit when out of
work. These men can receive no benefit
and some are receiving no out-door relief.
They are practically on the verge of destitution. Nothing has been done for them
and their families by the Minister of
Labour.

How does it come that every effort

to increase the number of pigs reared in

It is not my intention to take up
more of the time of the House-I know
there are agricultural Members who are
anxious to take part in the debate-but
I want to say this: The hon. and gallant
Member for Queen's University referred
to the fact that the terrible scourge of
tuberculosis was being combated in
Northern Ireland. I wish it were. I
wish that were true. I am glad to say
there is a huge attempt by the Belfast
Corporation, whose intention it is to build
one of the largest tuberculosis hospitals
in the Kingdom. I am delighted to
know that. But even when it is built
there are thousands and thousands of
children all over Northern Ireland
diagnosed as suffering from tuberculosis,
and there is no place to treat them at all
in some of the agricultural areas. (Hon.
Members: No.) You have not the supervision that you ought to have over those
children, and you are going to have more
children and adults suffering from tuberculosis if something is not done for them.
Everyone who takes an interest in the
subject realises that tuberculosis is
caused chiefly by bad housing conditions
and by people not being able to procure
proper nourishment. And, despite all
the elation that has been raised by the
Prime Minister and Members on the
other side of the House, let me tell them
that on the verge of Christmas all over
this small country of ours you could find
hundreds and hundreds of people who
do not know what to do to secure tomorrow morning's bread.
This is a fertile country, and I feel
that if I had the power-and some day
we hope to have the power in this House.
Yes, we. The Minister of Labour and
myself may not be here to see it, but
there will be young men spring up in
Northern Ireland who will be more
active in their efforts to make this country
a country fit for heroes to live in. The
present Members of the Cabinet have
done good service for their country.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I would
be the last to say they have not done good
service for their country, but I feel that
we want younger men to follow in their
footsteps and to give greater service. It
can be done, and I believe that the rising
generation will have the will to do it. I
hope I will live to see the day when the
Government of this country will see that
no person in the country is hungry, and
that every person in the country is
properly housed. That is the duty of a
Government. I do not believe in
dictators, but dictators in other countries
have done that. We do not want a
dictator here, but a Prime Minister who
will put into operation legislation of a
similar nature.

[Mr. Henderson]
That is not the way to talk.
What we
want to do is to make Northern Ireland
a place where any person in the world,
if he comes to Northern Ireland, is going
to be at home and happy, and where he

It is regrettable that I have to raise
this matter on the King's Speech. Mr.
M'Kibbin was building 2,000 houses on
the Crumlin Road. He has been kind
enough to hand me these accounts of conversations that took place between the
Ministry of Home Affairs and himself.
Mr. M'Kibbin is a great Unionist, a
great Protestant, and a follower of the
Prime Minister. He went to the
Ministry of Home Affairs because some
hooligans had attacked the workmen who
were employed in the erection of his
houses, and had destroyed the houses.
In many instances Protestant people were
driven out of their homes. It is quite
true to say that there were Catholic people driven out of their homes too. I
know that the Prime Minister is ruthlessly opposed to anybody being driven
out of his home. I am satisfied that the
Prime Minister, like myself, wants to see
the people living in happiness and at
peace with one another.
We want to see the country prosper.
The country cannot prosper if politicians
are going to keep the people fighting with
one another. On this occasion Mr.
M'Kibbin went to the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I will not weary the House by
reading his letter to the Minister. Did
he get satisfaction from the Minister of
Home Affairs? No, he did not. Every
time he went down to see the Minister
no one was in. When they were in, he
was told they were not in. What did he
want? He wanted this Government to
give protection to the Protestant people
living on his estate at Glenard, and the
Government refused to give protection.
What happened then? Mr. M‘Kibbin
went to the parish priest of Ardoyne,
and according to Mr. M'Kibbin he got
members of the Irish Republican Army
to give protection to the Protestant
tenants. So you see that the Protestant
Parliament for Protestant people did not
provide protection for the Protestant
tenants, and that Mr. M'Kibbin had to
go to the parish priest, who got members
of the Irish Republican Army to provide.
protection. Is that not rather amusing?
Mr. ANDREWS: It is very sad.
Mr. HENDERSON: It is sad to think
that the Government let down one of
their most loyal defenders who has built

They had to go to the parish priest
at Ardoyne and to the Irish Republican

There should be no call for anything like
that. It is rather surprising that these

M'Kibbin protests against is this: he

Speech regarding the police, but I hope

for the people to live at peace with one
another. I am going to conclude now.

people. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I will briefly deal with two or three

touch on is as regards the shipbuilding
and linen industries. I am pleased to
note that the shipbuilding industry has
improved. There are other speakers
more capable of dealing with that point.
than I am. As regards the linen industry, I would like to put forward one
or two things affecting the agricultural
end-I mean the production of flax.
would draw the attention of the Minister
of Agriculture and Members of the
Cabinet to the fact that several times a

not at a loss. I would again urge the
Minister to take this matter up with a

about 10s per stone, so as to give a fair
return to the agriculturist for his labour.
I
There is another thing that it might
be worth drawing the attention of the
Minister to, and that is the procuring
of pure line seed at a cheaper rate for
sowing purposes. During the last number of years there has been too much of
a margin between the price the grower
receives for the seed he produces and the
price paid by the farmer to the retailer
for the seed bought. If pure line seed
were put on the market at an ordinary
competitive price more flax would be
grown, more labour would be given to
agricultural labourers, and mor money
would be circulated, thus adding to the
wealth of the Province.
One would think in listening to the
speeches yesterday of the hon. Member
for Pottinger and the hon. Member for
Shankill that the Government were altogether blind to the wants and require-

ments of the poorer classes of working

We are

One thing is specially mentioned, and

to be. The last thing mentioned in the

my view it is very necessary that a Rent

in houses to which the Government

exorbitant rents with which

People who are also suffering very

We have in this city many people who

and either asks a very heavy fine or a very
large increase in the rent. I know of
one case where the rent charged for a

the lease the landlord demanded £200
for the same house. Now, I think the
Government will agree that it is unfair
to allow such a state of things to continue.
Then other matters were mentioned by

Shankill (Mr. Henderson). They spoke

Another matter that has been mentioned is revaluation. According to the

The seconder of the Motion touched
upon a matter in which
I am very
interested, namely housing. Tuberculosis is a great scourge, and I am glad
to see what has been done in order to

I pleaded that the subsidy of £140

It is very small, and that

on all occasions to protest-

Having said so much I would like to
say, in regard to this King's Speech, in
a few broad words that it is the pregramme of a Government bankrupt in
policy and void of vision, a Government
just as feeble in legislative output and

That prosperity in which we are asked to
believe is, I do submit to the House,
shadowy to a very large degree, unreal to
a very large degree. The people in these
Six Counties are getting tired of being
cozened and humbugged by this constant
repetition about prosperity where there
is no prosperity and all this talk about
Northern Ireland being a garden of
paradise.

And what is the reason? One great

that they are beginning to take you at

British people. It seems to be a very

I regret very much that the Gracious
Speech is silent about slums. From

Four or five years ago this Parliament

10s, or 12s a week. They are compelled

The Bill promising a continuance of the
