The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Basil Brooke): There are only two
or three points raised in this debate
to which I would like to reply. The hon.
Member for Shankill, as representing the
consumers, complained that as a result of
the pigs marketing scheme the poorer
people in Belfast were unable to obtain
bacon at a reasonable price. The House
will, no doubt, remember that during the
last Session this question was raised and
figures were given. Unfortunately I am
not able to give the exact figures, but I
can state quite definitely that the price
being paid for bacon and ham at the present time is less than it was in 1933 before
any pig scheme came into force. I am
again speaking from memory when I say
that the average price during the previous
ten years-from 1923 to 1933-was
slightly higher than is being paid now
during the operation of the pigs marketing scheme. I do not think the hon.
Member for Shankill has much to complain of.
The hon. Member for North Tyrone
and the hon. Member for Antrim raised
the question of flax. The former drew
my attention to the question of a minimum price for flax. That again was
debated last Session, but I should like to
repeat that great difficulty is experienced
in fixing any minimum price for a commodity in this country competing against
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
an overwhelmingly large supply of the
raw material from foreign countries.
The actual amount of flax produced in
Northern Ireland is only one-fifth of the
total required by the spinners. It will
be quite obvious to every Member that if
a minimum price were fixed for flax
grown in this country we have no power,
and could never obtain any power if we
wanted to do so, to compel the spinners
to buy that flax at the minimum price
and ignore all the flax offered in the
world markets. There can be no doubt
that if a minimum price were fixed and
the price of flax in foreign countries
dropped below that minimum price the
result would be that the farmers in this
country would be placed in the position
of having a flax crop with a minimum
price which the spinners would refuse to
buy.
The whole of this flax question is a
most complicated and difficult one. I
should like to assure the House that it is
not through any lack of sympathy on the
part of my Ministry or the Government.
If we could help the farmers to grow
more flax it would be done, but as the
bulk of the raw material comes from
abroad and the bulk of the finished
article is sold abroad it is obvious that no
marketing such as has been inaugurated
for other commodities could possibly be
brought into force.
With regard to the pure line seed
which the hon. Member for North Tyrone
mentioned, and with which the hon.
Member for Antrim wished to associate
himself, the Ministry and the Linen
Research Institute have for many years
been working on those seeds.
The present practice is, as regards the seed in
this country grown in the plant breeding
establishment at Stormont, to produce
seed up to a weight of roughly one ton.
That is sent across to Canada and becomes
a commercial article and is sold back to
this country as seed for those who wish to
sell flax. The difficulty is that again it
is impossible for us to compel the farmer
in Canada to
grow seed if it is an
uneconomic proposition. It is always
after a series of years when flax has been
a profitable crop here that you find the
bulk of seed increasing in Canada until
such time as the acreage of flax in this
country falls below its highest level.
Then the next year there is a lesser
demand for flax seed from Canada and
there is a consequential less sowing of
flax. The matter is purely governed by
the law of supply and demand.
I am sure both hon. Members will
realise that the Government cannot set
itself up as seed merchants. All we can
do is to work on the seed which is producing the greatest bulk of fibre and is
giving the biggest yield. I think I am
right in saying that the Stormont cirrus
and Gossamer seeds have practically
doubled the amount of flax that can be
grown. It used to be 30 stones to the
acre in the old days, it is over 50 at present. I am much afraid that the
position cannot be altered until we get
other countries, or Canada itself,
increasing their supply of pure line seed.
We have tried a new venture this year
and are sending some seed to Denmark so
as to get a greater bulk of seed. One
other point raised by the hon. Member
for North Tyrone-the question of drainage-I have noted.

make certain changes in the law relating
to Civil Service superannuation. The
proposed changes involve certain principles, and, therefore, require a Money
Resolution as a necessary preliminary,
but I am happy to state that the

Committee stage was dropped owing to
pressure of other business. The Bill now
before the House is identical with the
Bill previously presented, as it was
amended in the Committee stage. It will
not, therefore, be necessary for me to
weary hon. Members with a recapitulation of the detailed objects of the Bill.
In any event, hon. Members will have an
opportunity for discussion on the details
of the Bill in the Second Reading. I am
sure, therefore, that the Committee will
agree that the present Resolution should
be adopted formally. I beg to move.

similar question. I have nothing further
to add to that.

ORGANISATIONS.

of Commerce whether he can state the

members who are registered; whether he
can state the names of teachers' organisations in Northern Ireland who pay

to organisations who comply with the

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE

organisations registered in Northern Ireland either as friendly societies or as
trade unions. The Irish National
Teachers' Organisation, a trade union
registered in the Irish
the Irish Free State,
renders certain returns to the Northern
Ireland Registrar of Friendly Societies
and also furnishes a list of persons resident in Northern Ireland who are

the trade union. This union pays benefits
to its members.

Member's question, I presume that by
referring to recognition he has in mind

without a political fund are concerned,
the Registrar has no jurisdiction. A
registered trade union which has a
political fund is under obligation to
render certain returns to the Registrar.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Superannuation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Mr. POLLOCK: This Measure which
I am now about to submit to the House
for Second Reading is absolutely
identical in its character with the one
which I had the honour of submitting
in the month of October. This Measure
that I refer to passed through all its
stages up to the end of the Committee
stage, but owing to the interruption.
which then took place it was necessary
to drop the Bill. It also rendered it
Superannuation Bill-
28 NOVEMBER 1935
Second Reading
necessary that we should ab initio consider it to-day. It may be said that
having discussed the Measure six weeks
ago any detailed explanation may perhaps be unnecessary, but I think possibly
Members may expect, in order that their
memories may
may be refreshed, that I
should refer in some detail to the more
important Clauses and proceed with the
explanation which I gave six weeks ago.
The Bill in the main is an attempt
directed towards bringing our Civil Service conditions into harmony with those
existing in the United Kingdom. Those
changes were the result of exhaustive
consideration by the Royal Commission
on the Civil Service, which reported in
1931, by the Imperial Treasury and by
the Civil Service Staff Associations.
This was followed by a Measure passed
in the Imperial Parliament in this year
of 1935.
The major changes to be effected by the
Bill will be found in Clauses 1 and 2.
Clause 1 applies the Superannuation Act,
1909, to women. Heretofore the superannuation of female civil servants has
been calculated in accordance with a
scale laid down by the Superannuation
Act, 1859. In 1909 revised arrangements
were applied to male civil servants, which
accorded to these officers, in place of
pension as prescribed in the Act of 1859,
pension on a smaller scale, together with
a lump sum on retirement or death. The
Act of 1909, to which I have referred,
was confined in its operation to male civil
servants, and it is now proposed to make
the provisions of that Act applicable to
female civil servants, a change which will
have the advantage of securing a measure
of uniformity. I should add that existing female civil servants will be allowed
to retain their present benefit under the
Act of 1859 if they desire to take advantage of it. That is Clause 1.
The second Clause provides for the
surrender by a civil servant on his or her
retirement of a portion of the pension to
which he or she would be entitled, in
return for which the officer will be
assured of the payment of a pension to a
dependent in the event of that dependent
surviving the pensioner, that is to say,
the widow or other natural dependent of
the pensioner. As hon. Members are no
doubt aware, the Superannuation Acts
make no provision for the payment of
pensions to dependents, and the provision
made in this Clause will, therefore, give
an opportunity to retiring civil servants,
if they so desire, to make some provision
for their widows or other dependents who
may survive them. These two Clauses,
as I have mentioned before, really form
the gravamen of the Measure, but there
are subsidiary matters which, perhaps,
it is desirable that I should submit to the
House.
In the third Clause hon. Members will
find laid down a uniform rule for the
reckoning of unestablished service given
by officers who subsequently become established. Hitherto the amount of credit to
be given in respect of such service has
varied in accordance with the particular
circumstances of each case, though the
practice has more and more tended in
recent years towards allowing one half to
count for superannuation purposes. That
is to say, when a non-established officer
becomes established half of his previous
service is allowed. The proposed
statutory provision will, therefore, be a
confirmation of existing practice and does
not connote the introduction of any new
principle.
The fourth Clause relates to the basis
upon which superannuation benefits will,
in future, be calculated. Under existing legislation the benefits are calculated
in some cases on the actual rate of salary
payable to the officer at the date of
retirement, and in some cases on the
average amount of salary received by him
during the three years preceding his retirement. Under this Clause the superannuation benefits will, subject to the
preservation of existing rights, be
calculated in all cases on the average
amount received over the three years preceding retirement. As this will result
in some saving in pension charges, the
proposal is accompanied by a small
increase in the amount of additional
allowance payable on retirement. In
other words, the financial effect does not
vary because the one phase of it will
balance the other. It is calculated that
the benefits payable under the New Clause
will be actuarially equivalent, taking the
Civil Service as a whole, to the benefits
which would be payable under existing
legislation.
I come now to Clause 7, the two intervening Clauses not being of much
moment. Clause 7 concedes a slight improvement of superannuation benefits in
Superannuation Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
the case of civil servants transferring to
approved employment outside the Civil
Service.
The ninth Clause gives more generous
compensation to civil servants who may be
injured in the course of their occupation.
The present provisions in this respect are
based on the Act of 1887, and contain
limitations which give rise under present
day conditions to hardships in individual
cases.
The tenth Clause is designed to provide, in respect of certain officers who
had given unestablished service in public
departments prior to the establishment of
the Northern Ireland Civil Service, power
to reckon this prior service in calculating their superannuation allowances.
Clause 11 gives the necessary statutory
authority for applying to certain existing
pensions the arrangements recently
arrived at in respect of the consolidation
of basic pay and bonus. This was carried
into effect, the House will remember, a
short time ago.
The other Clauses are of a purely
formal character, and do not need any
exhaustive explanation on my part.
They are unimportant and easily understood by reading the Bill. I would like
to point out that this Measure is not by
any means revolutionary or formidable in
character. It is unnecessary that I
should enter into any explanation as to
why it should be carried into effect. In
case there should be any doubt in the
minds of hon. Members, I may say that
it is to create uniformity in all conditions.
of the service in place of the difficulties
attaching to references to antecedent Acts
of Parliament. Therefore, it is not
revolutionary in any respect, and I close
by formally moving that it be read a
Second time.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.”
Mr. BEATTIE: I certainly agree with
the Minister of Finance when he says that
this Bill is not by any means revolutionary. It would be all the better if it
were a little revolutionary. The great
mistake of the Government in the past
has been that they were prepared to
accept the old method of doing things
and to apply them to modern
ditions of life. Not only does that preconvail in the Civil Service of Northern
Ireland, but it prevails in the Imperial
Civil Service also. Why should systems
which were in existence in this country
seventy years ago be applied to modern
conditions in Northern Ireland?
This Bill is a helpful Bill in so far as it
gives certain benefits to the civil servants
of Northern Ireland. I would like to
ask the Minister of Finance whether he
has yet considered the introduction of a
Bill of this character applying to other
classes of Northern Ireland service. I
am aware that at the time this Bill was
passed through the British House the
National Union of Teachers asked that a
similar Bill should be applied to teachers.
I think if it is good for civil servants it
should also be good for teachers.

Housing (Grants) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This is a short but
important Bill. Its object is to extend
the period of the housing subsidy for six
months. Under the existing Acts the
subsidy cannot be paid on any houses
which are not completed on or before the
31st March, 1936, and under the Bill now
before the House it is proposed to enable
payment to be made in respect of houses
completed on or before
30th
the
September, 1936.
It cannot, I think, be doubted that it
is necessary to continue the housing
grants for some time longer. The readiness of builders to go on building, as
indicated by the number of plans submitted for approval, is itself an indication of this, and I also understand from
the Ministry's housing inspectors that the
builders have long lists of applicants
waiting for houses. Further evidence is
the fact that, according to a return prepared earlier in the year for the Belfast
Corporation, there were only 32 houses
under £8 valuation vacant in Belfast.
It would appear, however, that we are,
at all events, within sight of the housing
shortage being met, and I do not, therefore, think it is desirable that we should,
at the moment, cover a longer period
than the six months proposed. Indeed,
I am not without hope that with this
extension sufficient additional houses may
As to the past, I may say that the
Government's efforts to deal with the
housing shortage have met with a great
measure of success. It was estimated in
1923 that in Belfast there was a shortage
of from 8,000 to 10,000 houses. Under
the various Housing Acts nearly 13,600
houses have been erected in Belfast, and
in all Northern Ireland, including
Belfast, about 30,700 houses have been
built with Government assistance. It is
estimated that by the end of next
September a further 6,000 will have been
erected, or nearly 37,000 in all.
Speaking on the Second Reading of the
Bill in 1923, I remarked that private
enterprise had been responsible for the
advantageous position in which Belfast
was situated in regard to housing prior
to the War, and said that I believed that
it was only by private enterprise that the
post-War situation could be relieved.
am not disparaging the work of local
authorities many of these,
and particularly the Belfast Corporation, have
made valuable contributions to relieving
the housing shortage-when I say that
private enterprise has fully justified the
reliance placed on it. Up to the end of
last month nearly 28,500 houses had been
erected in Northern Ireland under the
1923 Act, of which no less than 26,554
had been built by private builders.
All this building has had its natural
effect on rents, and, whereas in 1923
rents of 14s. to 15s. a week or even
higher were being asked for newly built.
working-class houses, it is possible to get
the same type of house to-day for 8s. to
10s. a week.
It has cost the Government a large
sum to bring about this satisfactory
result. They have contributed by way
of subsidy over two and three-quarter
million pounds, but I am not complaining about the expense; I do not think
money could have been better spent than
in providing houses, but I should like to
feel that the generosity of the Government was appreciated. While claiming
this much on behalf of the Government
I should like at the same time to thank
the local authorities who have cooperated so whole-heartedly by supplementing the Government assistance by
Housing Bill-

lump sum grants or by giving exemption
from rates. I am sure that without the
great assistance given by the local

move.

not included in this Bill a Clause which
would give effect to the oft-repeated lip
service that has been given to the support of local industries. I think that if
he had introduced a Clause insisting that
the specification should be so drawn up
that, where necessary, British materials
only should be used where the subsidy is
given, he would have given us confidence
in the oft-repeated statement that he and
the other Ministers wish, as far as possible, to support local industry. It may
be said that there will be certain difficulties, but I cannot accept that as a
final answer. I think it is probably ten
years since I first formed one of a deputation to wait upon the Minister to ask him
to arrange that the rents of these houses
which receive the subsidies should be
controlled, that is, that the subsidy would
only be given under certain conditions.
At that time we were informed it was a
total impossibility to do any such thing
having regard to the fact that all they
wanted were houses. I have no doubt
the Minister will again to-day say all
we want are houses, but I feel confident
that where they have had to change their
opinion and to change their policy in
regard to controlling the rent charged
in order to obtain the subsidy, it would
be quite possible, without in any way
stopping the building of houses to insist
that such material as, say, cement would
be all British-and, of course, when I
say British I hope that would mean
Northern Ireland in practice. It would
really mean Northern Ireland manufacture, having regard to the fact that
there are 25,000 tons of foreign cement
being imported into this Province at the
present time, and every ounce of that
cement could be produced at Magheramorne. In fact I think I am right in
saying that that particular concern is
largely dependent upon the other side of
the Channel for the consumption of the
cement which is produced.
Reference has been made on the other
side of the House to local brick being also
specified. I do not support that, having

Mr. CHRISTIE: I rise to support
all that was said by the hon. Member for
Antrim and the hon. and gallant Member
for Clifton. I regret that the Minister
has not yet seen his way to increase the
size of these houses. I think that the
members of the General Council of
Municipal Authorities unanimously recommended some time ago an increase
and decided that the houses were too
small. The hon. Member for Pottinger
spoke with reference to the size of the
houses for a man, his wife and four or
five children. How they were going to
be properly accommodated in a house of
550 superficial feet passes my comprehension. You do not get proper houses
built. You get houses built more like
glorified hen-houses. I happen to have
some little experience of building houses,
not only privately but on behalf of the
Borough Council of Coleraine. One
reason why we did not give a subsidy
in addition to the Government £25 was
that we did not want such small houses
built. We can build houses very much
larger than that without the subsidy, and
let them at prices any labouring man
can pay.
I remember well the Council of
Municipal Authorities meeting at Ballymena. We were honoured by a visit from
the Prime Minister, who said, in reply,
that he would always listen to the voice
of the General Council of Municipal
Authorities. But in this case the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home
Affairs, did not listen to the united voice
of the Council. I hope it is not too late
to change his mind and say that the
houses should be built of at least 650
superficial feet. I suggest that he should
go further and increase the grant and
give one towards a house provided with
a bath. If there is one member of the
community that requires a bath just as
much as any other body, it is the man
who is busily engaged all day. I think
that would be a step in the right direction, and the cost would not be so much
extra. But it is absolutely impossible to
put it into a house of 550 superficial feet.
I endorse what the hon. and gallant
Member for Clifton said about the use of
British material. I can go further and
say that in a house built with a subsidy
from the Government of Northern
Ireland, where the material can be produced at the same price, it must be Ulster
manufacture.
I can endorse also what the hon. and
gallant Member for Clifton said about the
importation of foreign materials. To me
it is not a good commercial proposition
on behalf of the Government to pay out
money which is not subsidising Northern
Ireland manufactures, but in reality subsidising the foreigner. In the case of
bricks the Belfast brickworks are fully
occupied, but there is plenty of natural
stone in Northern Ireland for stone-built
houses. There is also plenty of bricks in
Scotland, and I, for one, certainly urge
upon the Government that no foreign
material should be allowed in any building to which a Government grant is given.
I would also, if I am in order, offer that
suggestion to the Minister of Labour.
Where his Department make a grant only
North of Ireland material should be used,
and if that is not available then British
goods should be used.
To come back to the size of the house,
if you take a house of 550 superficial feet
and take a kitchen off that and then a
room at the back of that and two small
rooms above, the individual who takes it
cannot get even one easy chair if there is
going to be room for a bed in any of the
bedrooms. We want to improve the condition of the labouring classes and to
improve their conditions to such an
extent that we shall provide for the future
at least a race of healthy Ulster men and
women. I take this opportunity of endorsing to the fullest extent the request
made by the hon. Member for Antrim
that the size of the houses be increased.

28 NOVEMBER 1935
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and committed

Road and Railway Transport (Redemption of Stock) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill
deals with a purely technical point and
does not affect any matter of principle
whatsoever. Its purpose is to set right a
technical defect in connection with the
issue of transport stock provided for in
the act which was passed last Session.
As hon. Members will see, it is a oneclause Bill, which seeks to amend subsection 8 of Section 19 of the principal
Act. This sub-section provides that all
or any part of the Northern Ireland
Transport A and B Stock may be redeemed at par at the option of the Board
at any time after the expiration of thirty
years from the date of issue, and the last
five words give rise to a technical difficulty in connection with the issue and
subsequent dealing in the stock.
No difficulty would arise if there was a
single issue of stock, but a single issue
is not possible with regard to the stock
which is to be transferred to the vendors
as compensation for their undertakings.
There is a large number of undertakings
to be acquired, and the acquisition will
be spread over a considerable period of
time. Stock, therefore, will have to be
issued from time to time as the acquisition
takes place. Accordingly, under the
existing wording of the sub-section, the
date on which the option of the Board
to redeem would come into being would
be different for each block of stock issued,
and hon. Members will at once appreciate
the inconvenience that would arise from
this state of affairs.
It would mean that each separate block
of stock issued would require to have a
separate quotation, and that the difficulty of dealing in the stock would be very
great. The stock would be very much
less marketable and less popular as an
investment than would otherwise be the
case. Such a state of affairs would not
be in the interests of the stockholders, of
the public, nor of the Board.
The effect of the Amendment proposed
is simply that the Board may fix a common date at which they may exercise their
option to redeem stock to cover all
blocks of stock issued within a period.
Perhaps, if I were to give a concrete
example, it would make the matter a
little plainer.
The Clause that we now propose would
enable the Board to issue stock between
the 1st November, 1935, and, say, the
31st December, 1937, which might be
redeemed by the Board on or after the
31st December, 1967, and must be redeemed by the Board in 1995. This
would give the stock a common quotation,
no matter at which date within these
limits it was issued, and it would increase
the marketability and the popularity of
the stock. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and committed
to a Committee of the Whole House for
Tuesday next.

DISTRESS IN DERRY CITY.
Mr. McCARROLL: I desire to raise
a matter of which notice has been given
to the Ministry of Home Affairs. I do
so on behalf of the local Labour Party
in the city of Derry, and my object is
to endeavour to get the Ministry of Home
Affairs to issue an Order putting into
operation in the city of Derry the special
Distress Relief Act of 1928. I raised
his matter with the Ministry before,
and I was then informed that it was
entirely a matter for the local authority
and that the Ministry in no case moved
to put that Act into operation unless
the local authority took the initiative.
I do not know whether that is quite so
in every case, but at any rate, with your
permission, Mr. Speaker, I just want to
put the case again in the hope that I
may be more successful on this occasion
than I was before.
My object is to induce the Ministry to
take cognisance of the serious distress
that exists in Derry City and to put that
Act into operation as they have already
put it into operation in the County
Borough of Belfast and in the urban
area of Newry. The local Labour Party
in initiating this question first communicated with the Ministry as far back as
September last. In reply the Ministry
said:
"With reference to your letter of
the 2nd instantthat is the 2nd September
"I am directed by the Minister of Home
Affairs to state that the Act to which
you refer is entitled the Poor Relief
(Exceptional Distress) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1928. This Act provides
that the Ministry of Home Affairs
may, if satisfied that exceptional distress exists in any Union, issue an
Order authorising the Board of
Guardians of the Union, subject to
certain conditions, to grant outdoor
relief. You will observe that an
Order of the Ministry of Home Affairs
is necessary before the Board of
Guardians
can make any outdoor
relief payments under the Act. Up to
the present only two Orders have been
made by the Ministry, viz., in respect
of Belfast County Borough and Newry
Urban District."
The other matter dealt with in that
letter is the question of the refund to
Boards of Guardians in respect of expenditure incurred by them owing to the
postponement of the Appointed Day-a
matter with which the Minister of
Labour has already dealt to-day-and is
to the effect that local authorities would
be recouped in respect of any moneys
they might pay in relief distress.
Next a deputation from the local
Labour Party approached the Board of
Guardians in respect of this matter, and,
as I submit, made out a strong case in
favour of having the Act extended to
Derry. They gave numerous instances
of great hardship amongst the people in
the city, and pointed out that if the
Appointed Day had become operative at
the time originally stipulated a number
of people who are now suffering hardships would be getting higher rates of
benefit. As I say, they made out an
exceedingly good case, and their demand.
was that rates of relief not less than
those which are being paid in the city of
Belfast should be paid in the city of
Derry.
A comparison of the lists of relief
shows extraordinary differences.
In
Belfast a man and his wife, I understand, get 20s per week. Where there
are one or two children the payment is
24s per week; where there are three
or four children, 28s per week; and where
there are five or more children the payment is 32s per week. I want to compare those figures with some of the

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McCarroll]
rates of relief at present being paid in
Derry, and to submit that there is no
justification in the world for lesser payments in Derry than in the city
of Belfast. I have half-a-dozen cases
taken at random. I do not propose to
weary the House by going into them in
any great detail. I just want to give
the bald facts. Here is a case of an
ex-soldier, a man who joined up at the
age of seventeen in the Inniskilling
Fusiliers. He is living with his father, who
has an old-age pension of 10s per week.
The outdoor relief given to that man is
5s. In Belfast that man would be entitled to 24s a week. In another case,
also of an ex-soldier, there are four
members in the family and the total
outdoor relief granted in Derry City is
12s a week.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame.
Mr. McCARROLL: Five shillings is
given in cash and 7s by way of food,
and there is no other income in that
house. I should point out that in that
case the rent that that family is paying
is 5s; that is, that out of the 12s they
get for that family, 5s is required to
meet the rent. I am not mentioning
the names of these persons, but if the
Minister likes I will give them to him.
Another case is of a man 35 years of
age with a wife and three children. The
total relief given in that case is also
12s, 7s on a food ticket and 5s in cash.
And the rent that that man has to pay
for the house in which he, his wife,
and three children live is 4s per week,
leaving 8s on which to maintain the
husband, wife, and three children. By
the way, the youngest child is 22 months
old.
I have another case of a family of
four. One of them has a pension of 10s
per week, and the outdoor relief granted
is 5s. That is, the total income of that
house is 15s per week, and the rent is
4s per week. Here is an even worse case
of a man of thirty-eight years of age.
with a wife and four children, the oldest
of them five years of age. The total
amount they get in outdoor relief is 14s,
to maintain six persons, and out of that
14s they have to pay 5s a week for rent.
I should mention that in all the cases
to which I have referred there is no
other income in those families. The
final case to which I am going to refer
is also the case of an ex-Serviceman who
gets 6s a week outdoor relief, has no
other income, and pays 3s of it as the
rent of the room in which he lives.
I submit that on those facts alone I
have completely established the case that
grievous hardship exists amongst those
people, sufficient, in my judgment, to require the Minister of Home Affairs to
investigate the conditions, and if there
is any failure-and I submit that there
is failure-on behalf of the local
authority then I submit that the Minister of Home Affairs should take the
matter definitely out of their hands, and,
in view of all those facts, compel the
local authority to put this Act into
operation.
I will immediately be met with the
argument that at the present time there.
is a sum of £450 per week being paid
out in outdoor relief in the City of Derry,
and that that involves a very heavy
liability upon the rates; but I submit
that when it is a question of relieving
dire distress, such as exists at present,
if it is a choice between a greater charge
upon the rates and the continuance of
this distress, then I would say by all
means let the rates be raised to such an
extent as would relieve that distress, and
if possible do something to alleviate the
poverty that prevails in the community.
As I have already said, if the
Appointed Day had been made operative as
originally proposed, many of these people,
at any rate, would be getting larger
benefit, and, of course, the local authority
would have been relieved in respect of the
grants that have already been given. But
why should these poor people-a family
of six asked to live on 14s a week-be
obliged to suffer great hardships by reason
of the fact that for some reason or other
the Appointed Day had to be postponed?
I think it is a fair proposition that, no
matter who is to suffer by the postponement of the Appointed Day, it should not
be the people who are in distress, and who
are obliged to pay more per week for
the rent of the wretched houses in which
they live than they have for food.
I should say that this matter was
brought to the notice of the Guardians,
and a special committee was appointed
to revise all the cases in which it was
thought that there was an inadequate
amount allowed. With all respect to the

Board of Guardians, I think that no
human being could expect any other
human being to exist on the rates paid
in Derry. The hon. Member for
Shankill, in the course of a speech

said that it would be a very salutary

But these people have not even 10s a

not putting it too high when I appeal

to say that there is at least as good cause
for the operation of the Act in Derry as
there is in Newry and Belfast.
I do not want to take up the time of
the House unduly, but there is one thing
that I want to stress in connection with
this matter. I think it is a despicable
thing to find the local authority taking
into consideration, in the fixing of these
miserable rates of relief, private charity
given to certain families. I think that
is wholly indefensible. I speak from
absolute knowledge, when I say that there
are cases in which families are getting
relief from private charitable organisations amounting to from 4s to 7s a week,
and it is almost incredible, but it is true,
that the local authority takes into consideration the grant of that private
charity in fixing the amount of outdoor
relief. That means that the charitable
organisations in the city are being used
to subsidise the rates. I do not think
that could be defended on any possible
ground. I want to state the case
frankly as I can, and in view of the facts
I have given I think that I have
established a case for investigation by the
Ministry. If they make the investigation I feel that they will come to the conclusion that the local authority is not
dealing adequately with the matter, and
that they will take steps, pending the
coming into operation of the larger part
of the Unemployment Assistance Scheme,
to do something in these cases.

The local authorities in that place have

Mr. BEATTIE: I may come back now
to the Shankill Road, to Derry city, and

Day has been mentioned by the last two
speakers, and they have rightly asked
Northern Ireland to go out of step with
Great Britain. That is justifiable. In
Great Britain it does not matter if the
Second Appointed Day never comes into
operation. In Northern Ireland it is
necessary and essential for the well-being
of 70,000 unemployed that it should come
into operation. In Great Britain they
have a scale of relief in the public health
committees that is equal to the scale of
relief given under unemployment assistance. That is, in the English, Scottish,
and Welsh districts they have the same
scale operating to-day as would be operating under the regulations for the Second
Appointed Day. In Northern Ireland
we have a scale of relief doled out that
was in operation 60 years ago.
You are
asking people to live under the conditions.
of 60 years ago.
Belfast has improved lately owing to
the 1933 demonstration, and through
that protest the Home Secretary was able
to improve the condition of the outdoor
relief man. He secured a small increase,
but that small increase was very far short
of the worst city in Great Britain, Scotland, or Wales. We have in Belfast the
figures quoted by the hon. Member for
Derry, 24s for a man and wife, which is
at least 25 per cent. less than the districts
in England. Then Derry comes along,
50 per cent. worse than Belfast, and with
Belfast's 25 per cent. worse than Great
Britain, they are only getting 25 per cent.
of the concessions given in Great Britain.
That is the reason for Members on this
side of the House asking the Government
to deviate away from step by step on this
Appointed Day and make a start on
their own, and say "we have 100,000
people in Northern Ireland on outdoor
relief under the charge of the Guardians
at the moment for whom we must provide, and the only way we can provide
for them is that we must make the
Second Appointed Day, say 25th December
or 1st January, independent of what the
National Government is doing." In
view of the grave disparity between the

Great Britain you would be justified in

it was the intention of the Minister of
Labour to include that pension in the
calculation of the family income, because
he has excluded dependants' benefit.
Mr. ANDREWS: To have the matter
perfectly clear, I would like to know if
this is a matter under unemployment
assistance or a matter under unemployment benefit.
Mr. BEATTIE: Assistance.
Mr. ANDREWS: Then it is a matter
really for the Board and not for the
Minister. The hon. Member began by
saying the Minister of Labour was doing
it. The Minister of Labour is not
doing it.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Ministry of
Labour has set up a Board to administer
Part II of the Unemployment Assistance
Act. That Board is in conformity with
that and you are responsible for the
regulations that were laid on the Table
of this House. You are the sole authority
so far as getting them through this House
is concerned.
Mr. ANDREWS: Partly.
Mr. BEATTIE: We never had an
opportunity of getting the regulations,
but on their passing through the House
I asked for what was to be taken into
consideration in the calculation of the
family income. I never thought for a
moment that a pension to a mother for
the loss of a son in the Great War was
to be included in view of the excluding
of dependants' benefit.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have a great deal
of sympathy with the case the hon. Member puts up, and I will have the matter
brought before the Board.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is all I want.
I shall be very pleased to hear the result.
I think the Board would be sympathetic.
I am not condemning the Board because
it was an omission from the regulations.
I want to say that I am satisfied that
we are not the only persons in the building who have sympathy for the unemployed. We are not the only persons in
Northern Ireland who have sympathy
with the unemployed. I want more than
sympathy. I want practical sympathy,
and I believe the Government are in a
position to give that practical sympathy,
and if they feel that there is any assistance required and they do make a real
effort to give practical sympathy I am
sure every Member on this side of the
House will go to their assistance. I now
leave my complaints and my support of
the two hon. Members to the consideration of the House.
Mr. HANNA: The hon. Member for
Foyle gave notice in my Ministry as he
indicated that he proposed to raise this
matter on the adjournment of the House
to-day, and my attention has been
drawn, both before the House met and
by the hon. Member, to the letter
addressed to Mr. Withers, the letter of
6th September. Although that letter is
strictly accurate, in so far as it states
facts and law, I quite appreciate that
it did create some little uncertainty as
to what exactly the law was in regard
to that matter. With a view to answering the hon. Member, I have had prepared by my advisers a note which for
greater accuracy I propose to read and I
will hand a copy to the hon. Gentleman
opposite.
Adjournment-
Distress in Derry City
3 DECEMBER 1935
The question of whether an Order
for Special Relief is necessary or
district is one which
proper in any
must be dealt with in the first instance
by the local authority. If a local
authority, possessed of all the facts and
figures relating to their area, and
having all local knowledge concerning
it, decide, after due deliberation, that
the existing provisions of the Poor Law
Code are adequate and suitable for
the local needs, the Ministry is not
prepared to go to the extreme length
of forcing upon them an Order which
they would be unwilling to administer.
Now the hon. Gentleman has stated
with considerable moderation, and the
strength of his case, I venture to assure
him, has not been reduced by the terms
in which he made his appeal to my
Ministry in this matter. It is asked
that there should be further investigation into the matter. I take this opportunity of saying that I will have a fresh
report obtained within the next few days,
and I will then go into the matter very
carefully. Having regard to the fact that
that is the attitude I propose to adopt
the hon. Member will understand and
appreciate that I will not debate some
of the matters he has raised.
There is one thing, however, that I
would like to point out. That is that
without any Order for the payment of
exceptional relief it is within the power
of the guardians to give such an amount
as they think proper in the cases cited
by the Member for Foyle. They are not
controlled either by any Order or the
want of any Order. If they want to be
a little more generous it is a matter that
is entirely within their own discretion,
and the relief need not necessarily be so
small. However, I propose to obtain the
very latest information I can get about
the position, and of course in those circumstances I will not indicate that I
have any mind in the matter at the
moment.
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn," put, and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at seventeen
minutes after Four o'clock until
Twelve noon on Tuesday, the 17th
December, provided always that
in the event of any Bill or Bills
being returned from the Senate
with amendment, Mr. Speaker
may give notice that the House
shall meet at such earlier date as
he may consider necessary, and
thereupon the House shall meet at
the time stated in such notice and
shall transact its business as if it
had been duly adjourned to that
date, and at its rising shall
adjourn until Twelve noon.
Tuesday, the 17th of December.

Oral Answers to Questions.
ALCOHOL AND ROAD ACCIDENTS.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that a committee of the British
Medical Association has, at the request
of the British Minister of Transport,
been investigating the relation of alcohol
to road accidents; whether this committee has recently issued its report;
whether he has seen a copy of this report,
and, if so, whether he will endeavour to
have the facts contained therein brought
to the notice of all motorists in Northern
Ireland; and whether, if he has not yet
seen the report, he will take steps to get
a copy, so that the information contained
in it may be used for the prevention of
accidents in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As I informed hon.
Members on a previous occasion, I propose issuing for the instruction and
guidance of motorists and other road
users a pamphlet which will be of a very
comprehensive character, and will indicate to drivers of vehicles of all classes
the conduct they should adopt in the
interests of public safety, and amongst
other matters the undesirability of indulging in intoxicants when driving or
about to drive. This pamphlet is at
present in course of preparation.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: Arising
out of that reply, and in view of the
unbiased character of this Committee,
might I ask the right hon. Gentleman if
he will endeavour to make it quite clear
in that pamphlet, about which I am
sure we are all glad to hear, that quite
small quantities of alcohol are capable
of affecting injuriously the efficiency of
motor drivers, even amounts of no more
than one glass-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
must only ask a supplementary question.
He may not debate the merits or demerits of the problem.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: I was only
anxious to make my question clear. Will
the Minister make it quite clear that quite
small quantities of alcohol, amounting to
no more than one glass, will affect very
injuriously the efficiency of motor drivers,
and that is a most important factor in
road accidents?
Mr. BEATTIE: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman will he make a return
to this House of the percentage of
accidents due to alcoholic drink, and is
it a fact that the hon. Member's question
is based on practical experience?
(Laughter.)
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman does alcohol contribute
in any appreciable degree to road accidents in this area?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid
hon. Members are coming to me as an
expert (Laughter)—and, while I appreciate the compliment, I really am not in
a position to give a definite answer to
such questions.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
17 DECEMBER 1935
R.I.C. BADGE ON R.U.C.
BARRACKS.
2. Mr. BLACK asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state why
the badge of the Royal Irish Constabulary
has been affixed above the door of the
recently erected police barracks on Woodstock Road, and why the badge of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary has not been
affixed in a prominent place on the front
of this barracks; whether the Government
will give directions for the immediate
removal of the Royal Irish Constabulary
badge from the said barracks and for the
substitution therefor of the badge of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary; whether the
badge of the Royal Irish Constabulary has
been affixed to any other police barracks
in Northern Ireland erected since the
disbandment of the Royal Irish Constabulary fourteen years ago, and, if so,
can he state the reason; whether the
Government will take steps to ensure that
a Royal Ulster Constabulary badge (and
no other police badge) shall be prominently displayed on the front of every
Royal Ulster Constabulary barracks in
Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In the interests
of economy it was decided as a temporary
arrangement to continue to make use of
the existing stock of Royal Irish Constabulary barrack badges, and as it is
obviously desirable that all barracks
should bear the same badge no differentiation in this respect has been made in
regard to new or old barracks.
The question of a general issue to all
barracks of a similar type of badge in
which the title "Royal Ulster Constabulary" will be substituted for "Royal
Irish Constabulary" is at present under
consideration, and I hope that it will
soon be possible to arrange for the removal
of the badges to which the hon. and
learned Member has taken exception.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Arising out of the
answer of the right hon. Gentleman, may
I ask if the Minister will take steps to
correct the geographical inexactitude of
the word "Ulster" in this context, seeing
that the Royal Ulster Constabulary police
only 5,300 square miles of the 8,400
square miles in Ulster?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I am not
prepared to alter the title "Royal Ulster,"
of which we are all very proud. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. CAMPBELL: Is it not a fact that
the Royal Ulster Constabulary, like all
Ulstermen, are Irish and proud of it,
except for a few of hybrid nationality?
Mr. BLACK: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman would he state in shillings and
pence the amount of economy that was
effected by placing this R.I.C. badge on
this particular barracks?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not know
whether my hon. and learned Friend
refers to the cost of substituting new
badges for the old ones.
Mr. BLACK: No. The economy that
was effected.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I could not
really tell the hon. and learned Member
that. All I can tell him is that the cost
of putting up the new badges will amount
to something like £1,000.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I ask the
hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr. Campbell) where he gets his definition of Ulster
and the number of counties in it. As I
understand, it originally consisted of two
counties, and then four. To which of
these does the hon. and learned Member
refer?
Mr. CAMPBELL: If I may answer the
question, I would say that I always understood that Ulster consisted of nine
counties, three of which you have now
disavowed.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think we had better
proceed with the notices of presentation.
